sections.title: The tool rail
sections.text:
The vertical strip of tools down the left edge of the editor, plus their keyboard shortcuts.
The tool rail holds every drawing, painting and selection tool. Click a tool to activate it, or press its shortcut key. Hovering or focusing a tool shows a small tip to its right with the tool's name and shortcut.
Tools are arranged in groups separated by thin dividers: selection and layout tools first, then the paint tools, then vector tools, then the view tools. The AI Generate button and any extension tool buttons sit below, and the foreground/background color widget is pinned to the very bottom.
Move: Selects and drags layers on the canvas. A single click picks the top layer under the pointer, with transparent pixels falling through to whatever you actually see beneath them. A fresh click auto-selects the whole group a layer belongs to; drag on empty canvas to rubber-band multiple layers.
Select: Works like Move but always targets the exact element you click, even when it sits inside a group (direct selection). Reach for it when Move keeps grabbing the whole group instead of the one piece you want.
Rectangular Marquee: Drag out a rectangular selection. Selections limit where painting, filling and effects take effect, so use it to protect the rest of the image.
Lasso Select: Draw a freehand selection outline by dragging. On release the loop closes into a selection. Good for organic, non-rectangular areas.
Magic Wand: Click to select an area of similar color. The Tolerance option sets how close colors must be to be included, and Contiguous limits the selection to the connected patch you clicked.
Smart Select [AI, Local AI]: Click an object and a built-in AI model traces its outline for you. Every extra click refines the same selection, and Alt-click removes an area you did not mean to include.
Crop: Trims the canvas down to a chosen area. Drag a crop box (or type an exact size), then click Apply or double-click inside the box to commit.
Brush: Paints soft, anti-aliased strokes in the foreground color. By default the finished stroke goes into the active layer, the way you would expect from any editor, and a switch puts each stroke on a layer of its own instead. Opacity caps the whole stroke while Flow controls how fast paint builds up, and a Style decides whether the paint is plain alpha or behaves like a real medium.
Pencil: Draws hard-edged strokes with no softness and no build-up. Use it for crisp, pixel-precise lines.
Eraser: Rubs out pixels on the active image or raster layer; the layer is converted to pixels on first edit. It takes the same tips as the Brush, so you can erase through a texture instead of only dragging a round hole. Shapes and text are not erased this way, they are changed through their own properties.
Paint Bucket: Fills an area with the foreground color. Clicking a shape recolors its fill, clicking text recolors the text, clicking a stroke recolors it, and clicking an image flood-fills by color. A click that hits nothing adds a full-canvas fill layer at the bottom.
Gradient: Drag to paint a color blend across the layer or selection. The direction and length of the drag define the gradient. Dragging on an existing gradient layer just re-aims it.
Clone Stamp: Copies pixels from one part of an image to another. Alt-click sets the source point, then paint elsewhere to stamp those pixels in. Works on the active image or raster layer.
Blur/Sharpen Brush: Paints a blur or a sharpening effect onto an image or raster layer. Switch between the two modes in the options bar.
Text: Adds editable type. Clicking the Text button in the rail immediately drops a ready-to-type, centered text box. With the T shortcut you can instead click once for point text or drag a box for text that wraps.
Shape: Drags out a vector shape. Pick which one from a grid of previews rather than a list of names: eighteen of them, from rectangle and ellipse to pill, arch, shield, tag, ribbon and blob. Every shape stays editable afterwards, and any of them can be turned into node-editable path points.
Pen Tool: Draws precise paths one anchor at a time. Click to place corner points, drag to pull out curved bezier handles, and click the first point again (or double-click) to finish. The result becomes either a filled shape or a stroked path.
Eyedropper: Samples a color from anywhere on the canvas into the foreground color. Fully transparent pixels are ignored.
Hand: Drags the canvas to pan the view around without moving any layers.
Zoom: Click to zoom in, Alt-click to zoom out, or drag a box to zoom straight to that area.
AI Generate [AI]: Opens the AI panel on the right so you can generate a new image or transform the current one from a text prompt. It is a shortcut to the panel, not a tool you draw with on the canvas.
Extension tools [Extension]: Installed extensions can add their own buttons to the bottom of the tool rail, after a divider. What each one does depends on the extension that added it.
Tool tip (hover label): Hovering, or keyboard-focusing, any tool pops a small label to the right showing the tool's name and its shortcut key, so you can learn the shortcuts as you work.

sections.title: Shape picker
sections.text:
Eighteen shapes, chosen by looking at them.
The button in the options bar shows the shape you are holding. Click it and the rest open as a grid of previews. Each preview is drawn from the same path data the canvas uses, so what you see is what you get.
The list is deliberately short. A shape is something to put a text in, to clip an image into, or to build on, and a hundred silhouettes would make the common ones harder to find rather than easier.
The nine classics: Rectangle, Ellipse, Line, Polygon, Star, Arrow, Heart, Speech Bubble and Badge. Polygon and Star take a side count, and rectangles, polygons and stars take corner rounding.
Nine more: Triangle, Diamond, Pill, Arch, Shield, Tag, Ribbon, Cross and Blob. The Pill stays a capsule at any width, the Arch is the window shape for holding a photo, and the Tag has a real hole punched in it.
Still a real shape: Whichever you pick, you get a vector layer with fill, stroke, corner settings and the option to convert it to editable path points. The preview is a picture of it, not a picture instead of it.

sections.title: Foreground & background colors
sections.text:
The two color swatches and their helpers pinned at the bottom of the tool rail.
The foreground color is the main paint color used by the Brush, Pencil, Paint Bucket, Gradient, Shapes and new Text. The background color is a secondary color used by a few tools and set by the Eyedropper's Alt-click.
Foreground color: The active paint color. Click the swatch to open the color picker and choose a new one.
Background color: The secondary color. The Eyedropper's Alt-click sets it, and some tools use it as a second color. Click to open the color picker.
Swap colors: Swaps the foreground and background colors with each other.
Reset to black/white: Resets the foreground to black and the background to white in one click. The small black-and-white icon sits at the lower-left of the widget.

sections.title: Color picker (popover)
sections.text:
The shared color picker that opens from any color swatch in the editor.
The same popover appears everywhere you set a color: the foreground and background swatches, tool fill and stroke fields, text color and shape color. It returns a hex value, switching to an 8-digit hex (with alpha) whenever the opacity is below 100 percent.
Under the picker it lists reusable swatch groups so you rarely have to type a code twice.
HSV picker: The large square plus the hue strip at the top. Drag inside the square to set saturation and brightness, and drag the strip to pick the hue.
Opacity: Sets the color's transparency. Below 100 percent the color is emitted as an 8-digit hex that carries the alpha, so it stays translucent on the canvas.
HEX / RGB / HSL: Three tabs that switch the numeric fields below between a hex code, red/green/blue channels, and hue/saturation/lightness.
Pick from screen: Samples any pixel anywhere on your screen using the browser's system eyedropper. Only shown in browsers that support it.
Hex color: Type an exact color as a 3, 6 or 8 digit hex code. The leading `#` is added for you if you leave it off.
R / G / B: Red, green and blue channel inputs for entering a color by its RGB values.
H° / S% / L%: Hue, saturation and lightness inputs for entering a color the HSL way.
Save to my swatches (star): The star next to the hex field toggles the current color in your personal saved swatches. A filled star means the color is saved.
Brand Kit / Palette swatches: Captioned rows of colors pulled from your Brand Kits and from palettes saved in the Color Schemer, for one-click reuse.
Document colors: The palette that Image, then Colors, then Extract Colors from Image pulled out of the active layer: up to twelve colors, kept for the current session. It does not appear on its own and it is not a list of every color used in the document.
From image: The dominant colors sampled automatically from the current artwork.
My swatches: The colors you starred. They are remembered across sessions.
Recent colors: Colors you applied recently, remembered across sessions.
Default swatches: A fixed set of preset swatches, greyscale first then colors ordered by hue.

sections.title: Brush, Pencil, Eraser & Clone Stamp options
sections.text:
The options bar shared by the pixel-painting tools; each control only appears for the tools that use it.
These four tools share one options bar at the top of the canvas. The Brush shows the most controls; the Pencil is the hard tip (no Flow or Hardness); the Clone Stamp drops Flow and has no color or tip picker.
Size: The brush diameter in pixels. Type a value or drag the label to scrub it. [Shown for: all four tools]
Color: The paint color, which is the shared foreground color, shown as a swatch you can click to change. [Shown for: Brush, Pencil]
Brush (tip): Chooses the tip shape and texture. Options run from Hard Round and Soft Round to textured tips like Chalk, Charcoal, Spray, Halftone, Stars and Confetti, each shown with a live stroke preview. The brush panel shows all of them at once, in groups. [Shown for: Brush]
Opacity: Caps how opaque the finished stroke can become, no matter how many times the tip passes over. [Shown for: all four tools]
Flow: How much paint each pass lays down; strokes over a spot build up. Lives in the brush panel (it left the options bar to keep the bar lean).
Hardness: The softness of the tip edge; lower values feather the edge more. Hidden for the Pencil and for stamp-style Brush tips that have their own texture. [Shown for: Brush, Eraser, Clone Stamp]
Symmetry: Paints mirrored or rotated twins of every stroke. Vertical and Horizontal mirror across the canvas center line, Fourfold does both at once, and Star 3 to Star 12 spin the stroke around the canvas center - the vocabulary matches the Particle Strokes extension. [Shown for: Brush, Pencil, Eraser]
Presets: Saved brush-setting chips (size, opacity, flow and hardness). Click one to apply it; Alt-click removes it. [Shown for: Brush, Eraser]
Save preset (+): Saves the current brush settings as a new named preset chip. [Shown for: Brush, Eraser]
Style: How the finished stroke meets the pixels underneath. Normal is plain alpha; the other five mix pigment, so blue over yellow becomes green rather than grey. [Shown for: Brush, Pencil]
Each stroke on its own layer: Puts every stroke on its own recolorable stroke layer instead of painting into the active layer's pixels. Only offered for the Normal style: the wet media always paint into the layer, because a living wash cannot be split into per-stroke layers. [Shown for: Brush, Pencil]
Tip shape sliders: Scatter, Spacing, Opacity jitter and Size jitter, plus Hue, Saturation and Brightness jitter for the color. Shown only for tips that stamp a mark rather than draw a line. Each starts at the tip's own value, and one button puts them all back. [Shown for: stamping tips only]
Paper: The document's sheet for all wet media: Auto (each medium on its traditional surface), Hot press, Cold press, Rough, Canvas or Laid paper. Changing it affects new strokes; a wash that is still wet dries on the paper it started on. [Shown for: Brush]
Pen pressure: With a stylus, pressure drives the wet media: more water from a watercolor brush, more paste from an oil brush, more dust from a charcoal stick, and the stroke width breathes with it. A mouse always paints at full pressure.
Pen tilt: Leaning the stylus answers per medium, with no dial to set: charcoal and pastel on their side lay a broad, light, soft-edged mark that lets the paper's tooth show - the classic shading grip. A flatter brush paints wider and wetter with its belly, a flat knife spreads its load thinner. A mouse always paints upright.
Smoothing: Stroke stabilization: the brush point trails the cursor on a short string and only moves once the string is taut, so hand jitter and hard corners round into calm curves before any paint is laid. 0 is raw input; higher values are a longer string. Works for every style, wet media included, and the stroke still ends exactly where the hand stopped.

sections.title: Paint styles
sections.text:
Ten ways a stroke can behave - most of them as living, wet paint.
Normal is plain alpha blending, the way most editors paint. Every other style runs as living paint: the stroke stays wet on the canvas, flows, mixes and dries in front of you, driven by a physical simulation on the graphics card. Wet paint mixes as pigment - blue into yellow becomes green - and reacts with what already lies on the layer: a wash glazes it, water redissolves it, oil smears it along the stroke.
Each style brings its own dials to the brush panel (drying speed, grain, open time, pickup and more), its own three tuned brushes, and responds to pen pressure in its own way: watercolor presses more water out of the brush, oil presses more paste onto the canvas, charcoal is almost all pressure.
While a stroke is wet it lives above the layer; it bakes into the layer as a single history step when it dries, when you press Dry now, or when you save, export or undo. On browsers without WebGL2 the styles fall back to a fast static version of the same look.
Normal: Plain alpha blending. The fastest of the ten, because it skips the paint simulation entirely.
Watercolor: A real wash: the water flows and blooms, pigment rides it, edges dry darker (the coffee ring), grain settles into the paper's valleys, and standing water redissolves dried paint on the layer. Dials: drying speed, grain, edge darkening, pickup.
Water: A brush with no pigment at all. Wet the paper for wet-in-wet painting, push standing color around, or scrub dried paint on the layer back into motion - it redissolves harder than any loaded brush. Dials: wetness, drying speed, pickup.
Ink: Dense and staining: it flows less than watercolor, fixes fast, and barely lifts once it has set. Dials: wetness, bleed, drying speed.
Gouache: Opaque body color on the paste engine: it covers, stays where the brush puts it, mixes while open and dries matt. Real gouache redissolves, and so does this one - the brush lifts dried layer paint back into the stroke. Dials: wetness, drying speed, grain, pickup.
Acrylic: Loaded and covering with a fast lock: once it sets, it stays set, and the brush barely lifts it again. Semi-gloss body with visible bristle work. Dials: wetness, drying speed, coverage, pickup.
Oil: Thick paste that stays open for a long time: while it is open, new strokes mix into it as pigment, the paint drags along the stroke direction, and repeated passes build real impasto thickness that catches the light with a glossy specular. It also picks dried layer paint up into the stroke. Dials: wetness, smearing, open time, pickup.
Charcoal: A dry stick on toothy paper: the dust catches the ridges of the grain first, so light pressure breaks over the paper and heavy pressure fills the valleys. Sets moments after the hand stops. Dials: pressure, tooth.
Pastel: Charcoal's colored, softer sibling: true color instead of the darkened stick, more dust per pass, less bite in the tooth - velvet instead of scratch. Dials: pressure, tooth.
Smudge: A blender with no paint of its own: it picks up whatever lies under it - wet paint and dried layer paint alike - and smears it along the stroke, mixing as pigment on the way. Dials: pickup, smearing, open time.
Paper: One sheet for the whole document, chosen in the options bar: Auto gives every medium its traditional surface (cold-pressed paper for the washes, canvas for the pastes, laid paper for the dry sticks); Hot press, Cold press, Rough, Canvas and Laid paper apply one surface to all of them. More tooth holds more pigment and breaks dry strokes harder.
Body and gloss: The paste media stand proud of the sheet: thickness is a real height field, lit from the upper left, with a specular that follows the medium - oil shines, acrylic half-shines, gouache stays matt. Wet paint glosses harder than dry.

sections.title: Brush panel
sections.text:
A floating window with every brush setting in reach while you paint.
It opens by itself when you pick the Brush, the Pencil or the Eraser, and it closes again when you switch to another tool. It is not a seventh tab in the right rail; it floats over the canvas the way the Navigator does, you can drag it anywhere by its header, and where you put it is remembered.
The left column holds the tips as rendered strokes, five to a row: the active style's three tuned brushes pinned on top, then Media brushes, Paint, Dry media, Calligraphy, Spray & texture, Dots & pattern and Shapes. The right column holds the Style grid, the style's own dials (drying speed, grain, open time, pickup and friends), the numbers you reach for constantly, the tip shape sliders, and the color wheel. Every slider row can also be scrubbed: drag the label or the number for point-exact values, Shift makes it ten times faster.
Show or hide it: View menu, the same place the Navigator is switched on and off. The close button in its header switches it off too. It only appears while a paint tool is active.
Style brushes: Each paint style ships three brushes tuned for it - wash heads for the watery media, bristle and knife heads for the pastes, stick heads for the dry media. They sit pinned at the top of the tip strip, and picking a style puts its first brush in your hand.
Style dials: The wet styles bring their own sliders: Drying speed, Grain, Edge darkening, Wetness, Bleed, Coverage, Smearing, Open time, Tooth, Pressure and Pickup - each style shows only the dials its physics actually has.
Tip previews: Every tip drawn as a real stroke with the engine that will paint it, so the preview cannot lie about what the tip does. Click one to switch.
Color wheel: A hue ring with a shade square inside it: drag the ring to turn the hue, drag inside to pick the shade. Your recent colors sit underneath. The Eraser has no color, so this part of the panel is not shown for it.
Color modes: Solid, Jitter and Gradient, in one row under the wheel. One at a time, because they are three answers to the same question rather than three switches to combine.
Reset: On the Tip shape heading. It puts the scatter and spacing back to what the tip itself says, and the color scatter back to the amounts the brush ships with.

sections.title: Painter's palette (right-click)
sections.text:
Right-click while painting opens a small palette at the cursor.
Everything you reach for mid-stroke, without traveling to a panel: the color wheel, the colors you used last, the exact size and opacity, and for wet media the Dry now button. It closes on Escape, Enter or a click outside.
Color wheel: The full wheel, sized to the palette. It sets the shared foreground color, same as the panel's wheel.
Color under the cursor: The heading carries an eyedropper with the color that sat under your right-click - wet paint included. One click makes it the paint color; it only appears when that color differs from the one you hold.
Recent colors: The last 18 colors you painted with, newest first. Click to reuse.
Size and Opacity: The two numbers you change most, with scrubbable labels and values.
Dry now: Bakes the living wash into the layer immediately instead of waiting for it to dry - one history step, same result.

sections.title: Draw a brush tip
sections.text:
Build your own brush tip out of shapes.
The button sits at the top of the tip strip in the brush panel. It opens a square you fill with shapes: discs, rings, stars, polygons, bars, leaves, arcs, free painting, and an icon or emoji dropped in. Press Surprise for a whole blueprint at once.
A tip is a SHAPE, so whatever you leave transparent stays empty, and the Cut out option punches a real hole. The color comes from the stroke, not from the shapes: what you build here decides where paint lands, not what color it is.
The tip is kept as a recipe rather than as pixels. It stays editable, it renders crisp at any brush size, and it travels inside the document, so a design you hand on paints the same on the other machine.
Elements: Disc, Ring, Star, Polygon, Bar, Leaf, Arc, Dots, free Paint, Icon, Emoji and Image. Drag one to move it; each has its own settings, such as Sides, Waist, Vein, Sweep and Line width.
Cut out: Turns an element into a hole instead of a shape. A tip with a hole in it paints a ring, which no amount of stacking would give you.
Surprise: Rolls a whole tip from one of sixteen blueprints, from Stardust and Blossom to Comet, Snowflake and Gear. A starting point to change rather than a finished answer.
Saved tips: Save keeps a tip for later, across documents. Saved tips are listed in the brush panel above the shipped ones; clicking one COPIES it into the open document, which is what lets the picture survive being opened somewhere else.
Edit one again: Click the tip you are already holding a second time. Editing changes every stroke already painted with it, because a stroke records the tip it used rather than a copy of it.

sections.title: Color modes
sections.text:
Three answers to one question: which color does each mark get.
One flat color repeated a thousand times is the thing that reads as a computer no matter how good the tip is. Real media never lay the same color down twice: a loaded brush carries pigment that is not perfectly mixed, and a handful of petals is never one green.
Three buttons under Color in the brush panel pick one answer at a time. Solid is the color you chose. Jitter scatters around it, mark by mark. Gradient runs a ramp along the stroke, from where you set down to where you lift off.
They work on every tip. A stroke is a row of marks whatever the tip looks like; the round ones simply lay theirs close enough together to read as a line. Picking a mode is also enough on its own, because both Jitter and Gradient arrive with settings that already do something.
Solid: The color from the wheel, on every mark. What a brush has always done, and where it starts.
Hue jitter: Under Jitter: how far around the color wheel a mark may land. A little goes a long way, and this is the one that carries the effect - a red stroke reaches into orange and pink long before the other two show at all.
Saturation jitter: Under Jitter: how much the strength of the color may vary from mark to mark.
Brightness jitter: Under Jitter: how much lighter or darker a mark may be. On its own it reads as depth rather than as a different color.
Gradient: A ramp along the stroke. The bar is the same multi-stop editor the Gradient tool uses: click it to add a stop, drag one to move it, double-click to recolor it, right-click to drop it. Transparency travels with the stops, so a ramp that ends on nothing fades the stroke out as you lift off.
Repeats: How often the ramp runs over one stroke. It turns around at each end instead of jumping back to the first color, so a repeat never leaves a seam in the middle of a line.
Only under the Normal style: The color modes are hidden under Watercolor, Gouache, Acrylic, Oil and Smudge. Those styles work the color out from the pigment and read only coverage from the stroke, so a second opinion about color would sit there doing nothing.
The same every time: A mark keeps its shade. Strokes are re-rendered from their path whenever the picture is drawn, so the shades are rolled from the mark position rather than freshly each time; a saved design opens looking exactly as you left it.

sections.title: Text options
sections.text:
The options bar shown for the Text tool and for a selected text layer.
These controls set the type style. While you are editing text with the caret inside the box, the character-level controls (font, size, weight, italic, underline, color) style just the selected characters; alignment and curve stay layer-wide.
Line height defaults to `1.05` and letter spacing to `0`; those two live in the Properties panel.
Font: Picks the type family from the built-in system and self-hosted font libraries.
Weight: Sets the font weight from thin to heavy.
Font size: The type size in pixels. Type a number, or drag the `px` label to scrub the value up and down.
Bold: Toggles bold by flipping the weight between 400 and 700.
Italic: Slants the text into an italic style.
Underline: Draws an underline beneath the text.
Uppercase: Non-destructive all-caps toggle (v1.300): layout, canvas and exports render the text in capitals while the stored text keeps its original case - switch it off and the original casing returns.
Align: Horizontal alignment of the text: left, center or right.
Vertical align: Aligns the text to the top, middle or bottom of its box.
Curve: Bends the baseline into an arc. Negative curves the text downward, positive curves it upward, and 0 keeps it straight.
Color: The text fill color, shown as a swatch that opens the color picker.
Layout: Lives in the floating context bar over the selected text, not in the options bar above the canvas. It opens a popover with rendered layout suggestions for the current text, so you can restyle a headline in one click. Shown only for eligible text layers.
Style (preset): Not in the options bar: the ready-made text effects sit behind the **Presets** button in the context bar's Annotate group, and only while a text layer is selected. See the text style presets section for the full list.
List (bullets / numbering): Non-destructive paragraph lists (v1.301): every non-empty line gets a bullet or its running number in canvas renders, exports and SVG, while the stored text keeps its raw form. Toggle between none, bullets and numbering.

sections.title: Shape options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Shape tool.
Shape: Chooses which shape the tool draws.
Fill (pattern): Fills the shape with either a solid color or a repeating pattern.
Fill (color): The shape's fill color, which is the shared foreground color.
Stroke: The outline color of the shape. Leave it transparent for no outline.
Stroke width: The thickness of the shape's outline in pixels.
Radius: Rounds the corners of a rectangle. Higher values give softer corners.
Sides: The number of sides on a polygon. Shown only when Polygon is selected.
Stroke style: Switches the outline between Solid, Dashed and Dotted. Dotted draws round dots via line caps; both work on line and arrow shapes too.
Dash / Gap: For dashed and dotted strokes: the dash length and the space between segments, in pixels. Defaults follow the stroke width. They appear on the Move tool's contextual options for a selected shape layer, not while the Shape tool is drawing.

sections.title: Blur/Sharpen Brush options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Blur/Sharpen Brush.
Mode: Switches the brush between softening (Blur) and adding edge contrast (Sharpen).
Size: The diameter of the effect brush in pixels.
Strength: How strong each pass of the brush is.
Hardness: The softness of the brush edge; lower values feather the effect.

sections.title: Magic Wand options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Magic Wand.
Tolerance: How similar a color must be to the clicked pixel to be included in the selection. Higher values grab a wider range of colors.
Contiguous: When on, only the connected patch you click is selected. When off, every matching color across the whole image is selected.

sections.title: Paint Bucket options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Paint Bucket.
Tolerance: How close a color must be to the pixel you click to be filled. Higher values fill a wider range.
Contiguous / Global: Contiguous fills only the connected region you click; Global fills every matching pixel in the layer at once.
Opacity: How opaque the fill is.
Fill: The fill color, which edits the shared foreground color so the toolbar and brushes stay in sync.

sections.title: Crop options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Crop tool.
Ratio: Constrains the crop box to a fixed aspect ratio, or leaves it free. Social presets also line up with each platform's safe zone.
W / H: The exact crop width and height in pixels, editable while a crop box is active.
Apply: Commits the pending crop, resizing the canvas to the box. Disabled until you have a crop box.
Cancel: Discards the pending crop box and leaves the canvas untouched.

sections.title: Gradient options
sections.text:
The options bar for the Gradient tool.
Preset: Picks a saved gradient preset to start from.
Type: The geometry of the blend: a straight Linear ramp, a Radial burst from the center, or an Angle sweep around a point.
Gradient bar (stops): Edits the color stops that make up the gradient. Add, move and recolor stops along the bar.
Reverse: Flips the order of the stops so the gradient runs the opposite way.

sections.title: Move tool contextual options
sections.text:
When the Move tool is active, the options bar shows the selected layer's most-used controls.
What appears depends on the selected layer's type. A selected text layer shows the full Text options instead.
Fill (shape): Recolors a selected shape's fill. [Shown for: shape layers]
Stroke (shape): Sets a selected shape's outline color. [Shown for: shape layers]
Width (shape): The selected shape's outline thickness in pixels. [Shown for: shape layers]
Pattern (shape): Fills the selected shape with a repeating pattern instead of a solid color. [Shown for: shape layers]
Opacity (image): The opacity of the selected image, raster or smart layer. Applies to every selected layer at once. [Shown for: image, raster, smart layers]
Blend (image): The blend mode, controlling how the layer mixes with the layers beneath it. [Shown for: image, raster, smart layers]

sections.title: Zoom options
sections.text:
The options bar shown while the Zoom tool is active.
Zoom hint: The Zoom options bar shows a reminder of the controls: click to zoom in, Alt+Click to zoom out, and drag for a marquee zoom to a specific area.

sections.title: Floating context bar (layer quick actions)
sections.text:
A small toolbar that floats above the selected layer while the Move tool is active, giving one-tap access to the most common layer actions.
When you pick a layer with the Move tool, a compact bar appears just above it. It follows the layer on screen and disappears when nothing is selected.
The buttons change with the layer type: a color swatch only shows for shapes and text, the `Insert variable` button only shows for text, and an `Edit` button only appears when the layer was made by a tool that can reopen it (chart, table, QR code, mockup, background, smart object, or an extension generator).
Duplicate (⌘J): Makes an exact copy of the selected layer (or whole group) and places it just above the original. Use it to repeat an element without redrawing it.
Vertical align (top/middle/bottom): A single button that cycles a text layer's vertical alignment inside its box: top, then middle, then bottom, then back to top. The icon shows the current setting. Only appears for text layers.
Text align (left/center/right/justify): A single button that cycles a text layer's horizontal alignment: left, center, right, and (for text boxes only) justify. The icon shows the current state. Only appears for text layers.
Layouts: Opens a popover with six ready-made layout suggestions rendered from this layer's own text, so you can restyle a headline in one tap. Only appears for text that can be laid out.
Edit (Chart / Table / QR Code / Mockup / Background / Smart Object): Reopens the tool that created the layer so you can change it. The label matches the source: `Edit Chart`, `Edit Table`, `Edit QR Code`, `Edit Mockup`, `Edit Background`, `Edit Smart Object`, or `Edit ` for an extension generator (3D text, maps, and so on).
Color: A color swatch that opens the color picker to recolor the layer in place. It sets the fill for a shape and the text color for a text layer. Only appears for shape and text layers.
Bring forward (⌘]): Moves the selected layer one step up the stacking order so it sits in front of the layer that was above it.
Send backward (⌘[): Moves the selected layer one step down the stacking order so more layers cover it.
Zoom to layer: Fits the canvas view to the selected layer with a little padding around it, so you can work on it up close without hunting for it.
Align & distribute: Opens a small grid of align and distribute buttons right above the layer. See the Align and distribute flyout for the individual options.
Insert variable: A `{{ }}` button that inserts a dynamic token into a text layer, such as a post title or site name, so the text updates from real data. Only appears for text layers.
Delete (⌫): Removes the selected layer (or group). It is always the last button in the bar.

sections.title: Align and distribute flyout
sections.text:
The pop-up grid opened by the context bar's Align and distribute button, matching the align grid in the properties panel.
A single selected layer aligns to the whole canvas. When several layers are selected, they align to the outer edges of the group instead.
The two distribute buttons space layers out evenly and need at least three layers selected to do anything (they are greyed out otherwise).
Align left: Lines up the selected layers by their left edges.
Align horizontal centers: Lines up the selected layers so their horizontal centers share the same vertical line.
Align right: Lines up the selected layers by their right edges.
Align top: Lines up the selected layers by their top edges.
Align vertical centers: Lines up the selected layers so their vertical centers share the same horizontal line.
Align bottom: Lines up the selected layers by their bottom edges.
Distribute horizontally: Spreads the selected layers so their left edges sit at equal distances. Layers of different widths therefore keep different gaps between them. Needs three or more layers selected.
Distribute vertically: Spreads the selected layers so their top edges sit at equal distances. Layers of different heights therefore keep different gaps between them. Needs three or more layers selected.

sections.title: Transform handles (resize and rotate)
sections.text:
The box with grab handles that surrounds a selected layer, used to resize and rotate it directly on the canvas.
Select a layer with the Move tool and a bounding box appears with square handles on the corners and edges plus a rotate handle. Drag a handle to change the size, or drag near a corner outside the box to spin the layer.
Hold modifier keys while dragging to constrain the transform. A layer can never be made smaller than 2 pixels wide or tall.
Corner and edge resize handles: Drag a corner handle to resize in two directions at once, or an edge handle to stretch one side. Corner handles on images and smart objects keep their aspect ratio automatically.
Rotate handle: Drag just outside a corner to rotate the layer around its center. The angle is normalized to a range of -180 to 180 degrees.
Shift while resizing (keep proportions): Hold Shift while dragging a corner handle to keep the layer's width-to-height ratio fixed, so it scales evenly instead of stretching.
Shift while rotating (snap to 15°): Hold Shift while rotating to lock the angle to a hard 15 degree grid, useful for straight or exactly diagonal alignment.
Alt while resizing (from center): Hold Alt (Option) while resizing to grow or shrink the layer around its center point instead of the opposite handle.
Rotation detents: During free rotation the angle gently snaps to the nearest 15 degree multiple when you come within 3 degrees of it, so level and diagonal are easy to hit.
Text box corner resize scales the font: Dragging a corner handle of a text layer scales the font size along with the box, so the type grows proportionally. Rich text runs keep their relative sizes.
Group resize and rotate as one unit: When a group is selected, a corner handle scales the whole group uniformly around the opposite corner, and the rotate handle spins every member around the group's center so the layout stays rigid.

sections.title: Move and Select tool gestures
sections.text:
The click, drag, and modifier-key behaviours of the Move tool (V) and the direct-select Select tool (O).
The Move tool auto-selects the whole group a layer belongs to, so a grouped design moves as one piece. The Select tool (or holding Cmd/Ctrl with Move) instead targets the exact element you clicked, even inside a group.
Empty space and modifier keys unlock extra selection tricks like rubber-band select, duplicate-on-drag, and add-to-selection.
Click to select (auto-select group): Clicking a layer selects it. With the Move tool this resolves to the outermost group the layer belongs to, so grouped artwork selects and moves together.
Drag empty canvas to rubber-band select: Press on an empty part of the canvas and drag a box to select every layer it touches. Each touched layer resolves to its group, so you select whole units.
Alt-drag to duplicate: Hold Alt (Option) and drag a layer to instantly create a copy and drag the copy away, leaving the original in place. The new layer is named with a `copy` suffix.
Shift-click to add or remove: Hold Shift and click layers to add them to the current selection, or click an already-selected layer to remove it, building a multi-selection.
Cmd/Ctrl-click to select inside a group: Hold Cmd (Ctrl) and click with the Move tool to pick the exact element under the cursor instead of its group. This is the same as using the Select tool.
Double-click to edit or drill in: Double-click a layer to act on it: text opens for editing, a smart object opens its contents, a cover/contain image lets you reposition the picture inside its frame, a pen shape opens anchor editing, and a grouped child is selected on its own.
Snap to guides while dragging: When snapping is on and you drag a single layer, it snaps to the edges and centers of other layers and shows smart guide lines to help you line things up.

sections.title: Selection tool modifiers (add, subtract, replace)
sections.text:
How Shift and Alt combine new selections with the current one for the Marquee (M) and Lasso (L) tools.
By default a new marquee or lasso replaces whatever was selected. The modifier keys let you grow or trim an existing selection instead of starting over.
Replace (plain drag): Dragging a new marquee or lasso with no modifier keys replaces the current selection with the new one.
Shift-drag to add to selection: Hold Shift while dragging to add the new area to the existing selection, growing it.
Alt-drag to subtract from selection: Hold Alt (Option) while dragging to cut the new area out of the existing selection.
Click to deselect: A plain marquee drag smaller than a few pixels (in effect a click on empty canvas) clears the current selection.

sections.title: Smart Select interactions
sections.text:
How the AI-powered Smart Select tool (K) builds and refines a cutout from clicks.
Smart Select finds the object under your click using a local segmentation model, so nothing leaves your server. Each extra click refines the same mask rather than starting over.
The model must be downloaded first. If it is missing, the tool points you to `Settings, then WunderPaint, then Local AI Models`.
Click to add a point: Click on an object to select it. The tool marks a positive point there and returns a soft-edged mask of the object.
Alt-click for a negative point: Hold Alt (Option) and click to add a negative point, telling the model to leave that area out of the selection.
Keep clicking to refine: Every additional click adds another point to the same mask, so you can select a laptop and then click its screen to include it, without losing what you already had.
Model required: If the Smart Select model is not installed, the tool shows a message with a link to download it under Settings before it will run.

sections.title: Pen tool interactions
sections.text:
How the Pen tool (P) places anchor points, draws curves, and finishes as a filled or outlined path.
Click to drop straight corner points, or click and drag to pull out smooth bezier curve handles. Build the path point by point, then close or finish it.
When you finish, the path becomes either a filled shape or a stroked outline.
Click to add a corner point: Each click drops a new anchor point and connects it to the previous one with a straight line.
Drag to pull curve handles: Click and drag when placing a point to pull out symmetric bezier handles, turning the join into a smooth curve.
Click the first point to close: Once you have at least three points, click back on the first anchor to close the path into a loop.
Double-click to finish: Double-click to end an open path without closing it, then choose how to turn it into a layer.
Fill Path: Finishes the pen path as a filled shape using the current foreground color. Best for solid custom shapes and icons.
Stroke Path: Finishes the pen path as an outline stroke in the foreground color, with no fill. Best for lines, arrows, and open curves.

sections.title: Shape, gradient, and crop gestures
sections.text:
Modifier keys and drag behaviours for the Shape (U), Gradient (D), and Crop (C) tools.
Shift to draw an even shape: Hold Shift while drawing a shape to constrain it to equal width and height (a perfect square, circle, and so on).
Alt to draw from the center: Hold Alt (Option) while drawing a shape so it grows outward from your starting point in all directions instead of from a corner.
Line direction: When the shape is a line, the drag direction is remembered so the line runs the way you dragged, even diagonally up or to the left.
Gradient: drag to set direction: With the Gradient tool, drag across the canvas to set where the gradient starts and ends and in which direction it runs. If a gradient layer is already active, the drag re-aims it.
Gradient: Shift to constrain to 45°: Hold Shift while dragging a gradient to lock its direction to the nearest 45 degree increment for clean horizontal, vertical, or diagonal fills.
Crop: double-click to apply: After dragging a crop box, double-click inside it to apply the crop, resizing the document to the box and shifting the layers to match.

sections.title: Zoom, Eyedropper, and Clone Stamp gestures
sections.text:
Click and modifier behaviours for the Zoom (Z), Eyedropper (I), and Clone Stamp (S) tools.
Zoom: click to zoom in: A plain click with the Zoom tool zooms in around the point you clicked.
Zoom: Alt-click to zoom out: Hold Alt (Option) and click with the Zoom tool to zoom out around the cursor.
Zoom: drag a box to zoom to area: Drag a rectangle with the Zoom tool to zoom the view so that exact area fills the canvas.
Eyedropper: Alt-click sets the background color: A plain click samples the pixel under the cursor into the foreground color; hold Alt (Option) to send it to the background color instead. Fully transparent pixels are ignored.
Clone Stamp: Alt-click sets the source: Alt-click first to set the point you want to clone from, then paint elsewhere to copy those pixels. The tool reminds you if you paint before setting a source.

sections.title: Paint, erase, and fill behaviours
sections.text:
Behaviours shared by the Brush, Pencil, Eraser, and Paint Bucket that go beyond their sliders.
The paint and fill tools change what they touch depending on the active layer and any live selection. A selection acts as a stencil so paint only lands inside it.
Pen pressure: With a pressure-sensitive pen or tablet, how hard you press scales the brush and eraser stroke, so light strokes are thinner and firmer strokes are fuller.
Paint on a layer mask: When a layer's mask chip is selected, the Brush and Eraser paint the mask instead of the layer. Painting with black hides parts of the layer and white reveals them.
Eraser needs a pixel layer: The Eraser works only on image or raster (pixel) layers. Select one first; shapes and text are changed through their own properties, not erased.
Paint Bucket fill behaviour: The bucket recolors the exact shape or text you click, floods a matching region of a pixel layer within the tolerance, or, if you click empty canvas, drops a full-canvas fill layer at the bottom. A selection limits the fill to inside it.

sections.title: Text tool placement
sections.text:
The different ways the Text tool (T) creates text depending on where and how you click.
The toolbar Text button drops a ready-to-type, centered text box with one click. The Text tool itself (via the T shortcut) gives you the classic click-or-drag placement plus text-on-path and text-in-shape.
Text tool button drops a centered box: Clicking the Text tool in the rail immediately places a centered, ready-to-type text box in the middle of the canvas, the one-click path most people expect.
Click to add point text: A single click with the Text tool starts a free-growing point text at that spot, sized from the current font settings.
Drag to make a text box (area text): Drag out a rectangle with the Text tool to create a fixed-width text box. Text wraps inside the box, and only area text can be justified.
Click near a path to put text on the path: Click close to a drawn pen path or stroke and the new text flows along that path. The path is copied onto the text and hidden, and the two stay grouped as one unit.
Click inside a shape to flow text in it: Click inside a filled shape and the text flows to fit inside that silhouette (area text in a shape). The text is centered and picks a color that reads on the shape's fill, and the pair stays grouped.

sections.title: Blend and Opacity (panel header)
sections.text:
The two controls at the top of the Layers panel set how the active layer mixes with the layers beneath it and how see-through it is.
These controls always act on the **active layer** (the one selected in the list). Both are disabled when no layer is selected.
**Blend** picks the mixing formula (see the full list of blend modes). **Opacity** sets overall transparency from 0 to 100 percent.
Blend: Opens a dropdown of the 16 blend modes and applies the chosen one to the active layer. As you hover each option the canvas **live-previews** the result; clicking commits it, while clicking away or pressing `Escape` reverts to the mode you started with.
Opacity: A slider that sets how transparent the whole active layer is, from 0 (invisible) to 100 percent (solid). The live number to the right shows the current value; releasing the slider records one undo step.

sections.title: Blend modes (all 16)
sections.text:
Every blend mode offered by the Blend dropdown, and what each one does to the layer below it.
A blend mode decides the math used to combine the active layer with everything painted beneath it. `Normal` just stacks; the others darken, lighten, add contrast, or transfer color.
The list is the same everywhere the editor shows a blend menu.
Normal: Shows the layer exactly as it is, with no interaction with the layers below (only its opacity affects the mix). This is the default for every new layer.
Multiply: Multiplies the layer colors with the ones below, so the result is always darker. Pure white disappears and black stays black, which makes it ideal for shadows, ink, or darkening a photo.
Screen: The opposite of Multiply: it always lightens. Pure black disappears while white stays white, so it is the go-to mode for glows, light leaks, and highlights.
Overlay: Multiplies the dark areas and screens the light areas, boosting overall contrast while keeping midtones. Good for punchy contrast passes and texture overlays.
Darken: Compares the layer and the layers below channel by channel and keeps whichever pixel is darker. Lighter areas of the top layer drop out.
Lighten: The opposite of Darken: it keeps whichever pixel is lighter, per channel. Darker areas of the top layer drop out, useful for combining highlights.
Color Dodge: Brightens the layers below based on the brightness of the top layer, producing intense, blown-out highlights. Great for glints and bright light effects.
Color Burn: Darkens the layers below based on the darkness of the top layer, producing deep, saturated shadows. The counterpart to Color Dodge.
Hard Light: Like Overlay but driven by the top layer instead of the base: dark areas multiply and light areas screen, giving a strong, harsh contrast.
Soft Light: A gentle version of Hard Light that softly dodges light areas and burns dark ones, like shining a diffuse light through the layer. Good for subtle contrast and tinting.
Difference: Subtracts the darker color from the lighter one per channel, so identical areas turn black and differences show as inverted color. Handy for comparing or aligning layers.
Exclusion: Similar to Difference but with lower contrast and softer, greyer midtones. A gentler inversion effect.
Hue: Takes only the hue of the top layer while keeping the saturation and brightness of the layers below. Shifts colors without changing their intensity or shading.
Saturation: Takes only the saturation of the top layer, keeping the hue and brightness below. Boosts or mutes color richness without changing the actual colors.
Color: Takes the hue and saturation of the top layer while keeping the brightness below. This is the standard way to tint or colorize a black-and-white photo.
Luminosity: Takes only the brightness of the top layer while keeping the hue and saturation below. The exact opposite of the Color mode.

sections.title: Filter layers box
sections.text:
A search box that narrows the layer list to layers whose name matches your text.
Filter layers…: Type here to show only the layers whose name contains your text (case-insensitive). It searches the rows that are currently on screen, so layers inside a collapsed group are not found until you expand it. Clear the box to show every layer again.

sections.title: Layer Comps
sections.text:
Named snapshots of which layers are shown, where they sit and how transparent they are, saved and reapplied with one click.
A layer comp remembers four things per layer under a name: whether it is visible, its x and y position, and its opacity. Size, rotation, blend mode, styles and the stacking order are not part of a comp. Switching between comps lets you compare arrangements or present variations without duplicating the file.
The section is collapsed by default and expands automatically once at least one comp exists. The count of saved comps is shown next to the heading.
Layer Comps (header): Click the heading to expand or collapse the list of saved comps. The triangle (`▸` or `▾`) shows the open state and a number in parentheses shows how many comps you have.
＋ (Save current state as layer comp): Saves the current layer arrangement as a new comp. You are prompted for a name (it suggests `Layer Comp 1`, `Layer Comp 2`, and so on).
Comp name (Apply): Clicking a saved comp's name restores your layers to that snapshot. It adds one undo step so you can go back.
↻ (Update layer comp): Overwrites the saved comp with the document's current state, keeping the same name. Use it after you tweak a layout you want the comp to remember.
× (Delete layer comp): Removes the saved comp. Your current layers are not changed, only the stored snapshot is deleted.

sections.title: Layer list and per-row controls
sections.text:
The scrolling stack of layers, and every icon-button and behaviour on a single layer row.
Layers are listed top-first: the layer at the top of the list sits in front of the ones below it. Groups can be expanded to show their indented children.
Each row carries a visibility toggle, an optional group caret, a thumbnail, the name, an optional mask chip, a lock toggle, and a delete button. Clicking a row selects it; right-clicking opens the context menu.
Select layer (click): Clicking a row makes that layer the active layer, so the header, tools, and properties all act on it. Press `Enter` on a focused row to do the same.
Add to selection (Shift / Cmd / Ctrl click): Hold `Shift`, `Cmd`, or `Ctrl` while clicking to add or remove a layer from a multi-selection. Selecting several layers lets Group, Convert to Smart Object, and other actions work on all of them at once.
Show / Hide layer (eye): The eye icon toggles the layer's visibility on the canvas. A hidden layer is dimmed in the list and is not exported. Each toggle is a separate undo step.
Expand / Collapse group (caret): Only groups show this triangle. Click it to open the group (revealing its indented children) or close it. Non-group rows show an empty gutter so thumbnails stay aligned.
Layer thumbnail: A small preview of the layer's content (groups show a folder icon instead). Double-click a thumbnail to zoom the canvas to that layer's area.
Smart Object badge [Free]: A small badge on the thumbnail marks a layer as a Smart Object, meaning its original content is preserved and can be edited non-destructively. Hovering shows the label `Smart Object`.
Data binding badge (link): A link badge on the thumbnail shows the layer is bound to dynamic content (such as `{{post.title}}`). Hovering reveals which field it is linked to.
Clipping indicator (arrow): A small down-arrow to the left of a clipped layer shows it is being masked by the layer directly beneath it. Set or remove it with Create/Release Clipping Mask.
Color label stripe: A colored bar on the left edge of a row shows the color label assigned to that layer, for visually sorting or grouping related layers. Set the color from the right-click menu's Label row.
Layer name: Shows the layer's name. Double-click the row to turn it into an edit box; type a new name and press `Enter` (or click away) to save, or `Escape` to cancel.
Mask chip: Appears only when the layer has a layer mask. Click it to enter mask-edit mode (the tool switches to a brush): paint white to reveal, black to hide, with a red overlay marking hidden areas. Alt-click the chip to disable or re-enable the mask; a disabled mask is shown dimmed.
Lock / Unlock layer: Toggles a lock that protects the layer from edits and moves on the canvas. It is not a write protection for everything: the Transform fields in the Properties panel and Delete still act on a locked layer. The icon shows a closed padlock when locked and an open one when unlocked.
Delete layer (row trash): Removes just this layer immediately. This is the per-row trash button; the toolbar and context menu also offer a Delete that respects the current multi-selection.
Drag to reorder: Drag a row up or down to restack it. A line above or below the target shows where it will land; dragging onto the middle of a group (a dashed outline appears) drops the layer inside that group. Remember the top of the list is the front of the image.

sections.title: Bottom toolbar
sections.text:
The row of buttons at the foot of the panel for creating, duplicating, restacking, masking, and deleting layers.
Every button except Add layer and New group is disabled until a layer is active.
These are quick equivalents of the most common right-click actions.
Add layer: Creates a new, empty raster layer the size of the document and places it just above the active layer. New layers are named `Layer 1`, `Layer 2`, and so on.
New group: Creates a new group folder. If layers are selected, they are moved into the new group so you can organize related layers together.
Add mask: Adds a layer mask to the active layer. With no selection it adds a white (reveal-all) mask; with an active selection the selected area becomes visible and the rest is hidden. Disabled when no layer is active.
Duplicate: Makes a copy of the active layer (or the whole selection, groups included) directly above the original. Disabled when no layer is active.
Move up: Brings the active layer one step forward in the stack (up the list, toward the front of the image). Disabled when no layer is active or it is already on top.
Move down: Sends the active layer one step backward in the stack (down the list, toward the back of the image). Disabled when no layer is active or it is already at the bottom.
Delete: Removes the active layer or the whole current selection. Disabled when no layer is active.

sections.title: Right-click context menu
sections.text:
Every item in the menu that appears when you right-click a layer, including color labels, editing generated layers, masks, grouping, and Smart Objects.
Right-click a layer to open this menu. If you right-click a member of a multi-selection the selection is kept, so actions like Group or Convert to Smart Object apply to all of them.
Some items only appear for certain layer types, for example Edit QR Code on a QR layer or Edit Smart Object on a Smart Object. Mask items switch between adding a mask and managing an existing one.
Label: A row of six color swatches plus a No-label option (`∅`) that tags the layer with a color stripe for visual sorting. Choose a color to set it or the empty swatch to clear it.
Edit QR Code: Appears only on a QR-code layer. Reopens the QR editor so you can change the encoded text, colors, or style. The layer re-renders when you finish.
Edit Background: Appears only on a generated background layer. Reopens the Background studio to change the pattern, gradient, or colors of that background.
Refresh (data-bound studios): On groups inserted by a data-bound studio (for example Dynamic Showcases), **Refresh <studio name>** re-runs the saved query and swaps the cards in place with one click, no dialog. Appears next to the Edit entry whenever the studio supports live refresh.
Edit Mockup: Appears only on a mockup layer. Reopens the Mockup editor so you can swap the artwork or change the device or scene.
Edit Smart Object [Free]: Appears only on a Smart Object layer. Opens the object's contents in a nested editing session; saving updates every place the object is used. This is the non-destructive way to change embedded content.
Edit Chart / Edit Table: Appears only on a chart or table layer. Reopens the chart or table editor to change the data, type, or styling. The label reads Edit Table for table types and Edit Chart otherwise.
Edit (extension generator) [Extension]: Appears on layers created by an installed extension (the label shows the generator's name, for example Edit Pattern). Reopens that extension so you can regenerate or tweak the layer.
Duplicate: Makes a copy of the layer or selection, placed directly above the original. Groups duplicate as a whole.
Merge Down: Flattens the active layer into the single layer directly below it, combining them into one raster layer. Use it to permanently commit a layer onto the one beneath.
Flatten: Merges every layer in the document into one flat image. This is destructive: separate layers can no longer be edited afterward.
Convert to Smart Object [Free]: Wraps the selected layer(s) or group into a single Smart Object, preserving the originals so you can re-edit them later without losing quality. Groups convert together with their whole contents.
Rasterize: Turns the active layer into plain pixels, baking in text, shapes, effects, or a Smart Object. Do this when you need to paint directly on the layer, but note it can no longer be edited as text or a shape afterward.
Properties: Opens the Properties tab in the right sidebar for the active layer, where its detailed settings live (including Smart Filters and effects).
Create / Release Clipping Mask: Clips the layer to the shape of the layer directly beneath it, so it only shows where that base layer has pixels. The label toggles to Release Clipping Mask when the layer is already clipped. Clipping a top-level pair wraps them in a group so they move together. It is offered on groups too, but does nothing there: a group cannot be clipped.
Add Layer Mask: Adds a layer mask to the active layer (shown only when it has none yet). With a selection active the selected area becomes visible and the rest hidden; otherwise it adds a white reveal-all mask.
Apply Layer Mask: Bakes the mask into the layer's pixels: hidden areas become truly transparent and the mask itself is removed. Shown only when the layer already has a mask.
Invert Layer Mask: Swaps the mask's hidden and visible areas. Shown only when the layer has a mask; handy when you masked the wrong side.
Enable / Disable Layer Mask: Temporarily turns the mask off (showing the whole layer) or back on, without deleting it. The label reflects the current state. Same as Alt-clicking the mask chip.
Delete Layer Mask: Removes the mask entirely and restores the layer to full visibility. Shown only when the layer has a mask.
Group / Ungroup: On a normal layer or multi-selection this creates a group folder around them; on a group it dissolves the folder and frees its children. The label switches based on what you right-clicked.
Delete: Removes the layer or the current selection. Shown in red as a destructive action.

sections.title: Copy Styles and Paste Styles
sections.text:
Transfer a layer's whole appearance (opacity, blend mode, filters, adjustments, and effects) onto other layers, even in another tab.
These two actions are reached by right-clicking a layer on the canvas or from the Edit menu, and they pair with the Layers panel to reuse a look across layers.
Copy Styles remembers the active layer's appearance. Paste Styles applies it to every selected layer: the universal fields (opacity, blend mode, filter, adjustments, and effects) always transfer, while type-specific paint (text character styling, shape fill and stroke, and their gradients or patterns) only transfers when the target is the same kind of layer. The layer's actual content, position, and size are never changed.
Copy Styles: Remembers the active layer's whole appearance: its opacity, blend mode, photo filter, adjustments, and layer effects, plus type-specific styling. The copied look is shared across tabs, so you can paste it onto a layer in another open document.
Paste Styles: Applies the last copied look to every selected layer. Universal fields (opacity, blend, filter, adjustments, effects) always land; text or shape paint (fonts, colors, strokes, gradients, patterns, text effects) transfers only when the target matches the source layer's type.

sections.title: Save Layer Comp dialog
sections.text:
The small dialog that names a new layer comp before it is saved.
When you click the ＋ in the `Layer Comps` header, this dialog opens so you can name the snapshot you are about to save. A layer comp records the current visibility, position, and layout of every layer, so you can save several arrangements of the same document and switch between them later.
This dialog is the only step between clicking ＋ and the comp appearing in the list.
Name: The text field for naming the layer comp you are about to save. It is pre-filled with a running name like `Layer Comp 1` that counts up with each new comp, and you can type over it with anything you like. Confirming with an empty name cancels the save.

sections.title: Layer color labels
sections.text:
The color chips in the right-click menu that tint a layer row for visual grouping.
The `Label` row at the top of a layer's right-click menu holds six preset colors plus a clear option. Picking one paints a thin colored stripe down the left edge of that layer's row.
Labels are purely visual. They help you flag or group layers by meaning (for example all text layers or all backgrounds) without renaming anything.
Label color swatches: Six preset colors you can assign to a layer as a visual tag. Click a swatch to stripe that layer's row in the chosen color. From left to right the colors are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.
No label (∅): The empty swatch marked with ∅ at the end of the `Label` row. Click it to remove any color label and return the row to its normal, unstriped look.

sections.title: Layer row extras and shortcuts
sections.text:
Double-click, right-click, and modifier-click gestures on a layer row that are not shown as buttons.
Beyond the visible eye, lock, mask, and trash buttons, each layer row responds to a few hidden gestures. These follow common Photoshop habits, so they are easy to miss unless someone points them out.
All of these act on the row you interact with, and the ones that change the document are recorded in history so you can undo them.
Rename layer: Double-click a layer's name to turn it into an editable field, then type a new name. Press `Enter` or click away to keep the change; press `Escape` to cancel. Renaming is saved in history so it can be undone.
Double-click: zoom to layer: Double-click a layer's thumbnail to zoom the canvas so that layer fills the view. The editor frames it with roughly 15% padding on each side. This is a quick way to jump to a small element without scrolling and zooming by hand.
Open layer menu: Right-click any layer row to open its context menu, which holds actions like Duplicate, Merge Down, masks, grouping, and Delete. If you right-click a layer that is part of a multi-selection, the whole selection is kept so the action applies to all selected layers; right-clicking a layer that is not selected picks just that one first.
Alt-click mask chip: Hold `Alt` and click a layer's mask chip to disable or re-enable its mask without deleting it. A disabled mask dims to about 40% and stops hiding pixels. A plain click instead enters mask paint mode and hands you the Brush, where white reveals and black hides, with hidden areas shown under a red overlay.
Drop into group: While dragging a layer, hover over the middle of a group row until it shows a dashed outline, then release to move the layer inside that group. Dropping near the top or bottom edge of a row instead places the layer above or below that row.
Select with keyboard: A layer row can take keyboard focus; press `Enter` while it is focused to make that layer the active layer. This lets you move through the list and pick a layer without using the mouse.
Group folder icon: Groups do not show a picture thumbnail. Instead they show a folder icon in the thumbnail slot, so you can tell groups apart from image and content layers at a glance.

sections.title: Adjustments (tonal sliders)
sections.text:
The Adjust panel's tonal controls: three one-click auto corrections and seven live sliders that color-grade the selected layer without altering its pixels.
The Adjustments block lives in the **Adjust** tab. Every slider here is non-destructive: the values are stored on the layer's `adjust` object and re-render live, so you can drag them back to zero at any time with no quality loss.
All controls need an active layer. With nothing selected the sliders and auto buttons are disabled. A slider's read-out shows a `+` in front of positive values (for example `+30`).
Auto Levels: One-click tonal fix that stretches each color channel (red, green, blue) to use the full black-to-white range. Use it to instantly brighten a flat, dull or slightly washed-out photo.
Auto Contrast: Stretches overall brightness to the full range using a single luminance curve, so color relationships stay intact. Choose this over Auto Levels when Auto Levels introduces an unwanted color cast.
Auto Color: Automatic white balance using a gray-world estimate, damped so it never overshoots. Use it to neutralise a color cast (for example an overly orange indoor shot or a blue snow scene).
Brightness: Lightens or darkens the whole layer evenly. Move right to brighten, left to darken.
Contrast: Increases or decreases the difference between light and dark tones. Higher values make shadows deeper and highlights brighter; lower values flatten the image.
Saturation: Controls how intense every color is, uniformly. Drag right for richer color, drag all the way left for grayscale.
Hue: Rotates every color around the color wheel by the chosen number of degrees. Use it to shift the whole palette (for example turn reds toward orange or blue toward teal).
Temperature: Warms or cools the image. Positive values push toward warm orange tones, negative values toward cool blue tones.
Exposure: Simulates giving the shot more or less light, biased toward the highlights. Use it to rescue an under- or over-exposed image.
Vibrance: A gentler saturation that boosts muted colors more than already-saturated ones, protecting skin tones from going neon. Reach for this before Saturation when you want a natural lift.
Create Adjustment Layer: Bakes the current slider settings into a new full-canvas Adjustment Layer placed above the active layer, then clears the layer's own adjustments. Use it to grade everything below it and keep the grade editable and re-orderable in the Layers panel.
Reset: Clears all seven sliders on the active layer back to zero in one step, removing the whole adjustment. Disabled when no layer is selected.

sections.title: Color (fill / foreground picker)
sections.text:
The Adjust panel's color block: a full embedded color picker plus a one-click gradient-fill gallery for shape and text layers.
The Color section carries a full embedded color picker. What it edits depends on selection: with a shape layer selected it sets that shape's **fill**; with a text layer selected it sets the **text color**; with anything else (or nothing) selected it sets the toolbar **foreground color**.
Picking a solid color on a layer that currently has a gradient or pattern fill switches that fill back to solid so the color actually shows.
Color picker: The embedded picker with an HSV field, hex / RGB / HSL inputs, an alpha (transparency) control and every swatch group. Drag in the field or type a value to choose a color; it applies immediately to the selected shape fill, text color, or the foreground color.
Gradient fill: A grid of ready-made gradient swatches that appears only when a shape or text layer is selected. Click one to fill the layer with that gradient in a single step; shapes receive a linear gradient by default.

sections.title: Filters (preset looks)
sections.text:
A grid of one-click preset filters that layer a live, non-destructive CSS look over the active layer, previewed on a thumbnail of that layer's own content.
Filters live on the **Effects** tab. Each chip shows a small preview of your actual layer with the look applied. Clicking a chip stores the choice on the layer (as its `filter`), so it is fully non-destructive and re-editable, and only one preset filter is active at a time (a new choice replaces the old).
Filters are CSS looks (they combine grayscale, sepia, saturate, contrast, brightness and hue-rotate). The same chips also appear in Easy Mode.
Original: The unfiltered layer. Click it to remove any preset filter and return to the untouched look.
B&W: Full black-and-white by removing all color. Use it for a clean monochrome look.
Sepia: A warm brown antique tone with slightly boosted contrast, for an aged photo feel.
Warm: Pushes colors warmer and richer with a small brightness lift. Good for cosy, sunlit scenes.
Cool: Shifts colors toward cooler blue-green and dims very slightly. Suits crisp, modern or wintry looks.
Vibrant: Strongly boosts saturation and contrast for a punchy, colorful result.
Faded: Lowers saturation and contrast and lifts brightness for a soft, washed-out matte look.
Vintage: A retro film treatment: mild sepia, reduced saturation, added contrast and a slight warm hue shift.
Noir: High-contrast black-and-white with a slightly darker exposure, for a dramatic cinematic mood.
Punch: Adds contrast and saturation with a tiny brightness lift for a crisp, energetic image.
Meadow: A fresh green-leaning look with a warm hue shift and gentle contrast and brightness lift. Suits nature and outdoor shots.
Dusk: A cooler, moodier evening grade: reduced saturation, warm-to-cool hue shift, higher contrast and lower brightness.
Sunbleach: A bright, over-exposed summer look: low saturation and contrast, strong brightness lift and a touch of sepia.
Arctic: A cold, airy blue grade with a hue shift, extra brightness and slight contrast. Good for snow and icy scenes.
Cocoa: A rich warm-brown tone with boosted saturation and contrast and a slightly darker exposure.
Neon: An extreme saturation and contrast boost with a warm hue shift for a bold, electric look.
Mist: A soft, hazy look: low saturation and contrast with lifted brightness, as if seen through fog.
Cinema: A movie-style teal-and-warm grade with added contrast, gentle saturation, slightly darker exposure and a hint of sepia.

sections.title: Effects (pixel effects)
sections.text:
A grid of pixel-level effects, each shown as a rendered thumbnail of your layer; effects with settings open a parameter popover, effects without settings apply on click.
Effects live on the **Effects** tab, below Filters. Each chip renders a preview of the active layer with the effect at its default settings. Effects with adjustable parameters open a settings popover when clicked; effects with no parameters (Invert, Auto Levels, Auto Contrast, Auto Color) apply immediately.
On a **Smart Object** these are applied as non-destructive **Smart Filters** that stay re-editable. On any other layer they are applied destructively, and vector layers (shape / text) rasterize first. Installed extensions can add their own effects to this grid.
Gaussian Blur: Smoothly blurs the layer using a high-quality Gaussian (three box-blur passes). Use it to soften detail, create depth, or build a backdrop.
Sharpen: Increases edge crispness with a Laplacian sharpen. Use a light amount to recover detail; high amounts add bite but can look harsh.
Unsharp Mask: Professional sharpening that boosts only edges above a threshold, using a blurred copy as the mask. Gives cleaner, more controllable sharpening than plain Sharpen.
Box Blur: A fast, uniform box blur. Cheaper than Gaussian and gives a slightly boxier softening; handy for quick backgrounds.
Noise / Grain: Adds random grain. Keep size at 1 for fine digital noise, or raise it for chunkier film grain. Turn on Monochrome so the grain has no color speckle.
Pixelate: Averages the image into square blocks for a blocky, low-resolution mosaic. Larger cells give bigger pixels; often used to censor a region.
Posterize: Reduces each channel to a small number of tone levels, flattening smooth gradients into bands for a poster or screen-print look.
Threshold: Converts the layer to pure black and white by cutting at a brightness level: pixels brighter than the level go white, the rest go black.
Invert: Inverts every color to its opposite, creating a photo-negative. Applies instantly with no settings.
Gamma: Brightens or darkens the midtones without moving pure black or white. Values above 1 lift midtones; below 1 deepen them.
Duotone: Maps the layer's brightness between two chosen colors: shadows take the shadow color, highlights the highlight color. Great for two-tone poster art.
Levels: The classic Levels control: remap the input black/white points and midtone gamma, and clamp the output range. Use it for precise contrast and tonal placement.
Curves: The Curves tool: bend a smooth tone curve through your own control points for fine, arbitrary tonal and contrast control. Starts as a straight identity line.
Vignette: Darkens (or lightens) the edges toward the corners to draw the eye to the centre. A positive amount darkens; a negative amount brightens the edges.
Tilt-Shift: Keeps a horizontal band in sharp focus and blurs above and below it, faking a shallow-depth miniature look. Position the band and set how wide and how strong the blur is.
Color Splash: Keeps only colors near a chosen hue and turns everything else grayscale. Pick the hue to preserve and how wide a range around it survives.
Halftone: Recreates a printed halftone: brightness becomes a grid of black dots that grow in dark areas. Set the dot spacing and the screen angle.
Glitch: A digital-corruption look: shifts the red and blue channels, slices rows sideways in random blocks, and can darken alternate lines. Change the seed for a different random variant.
Glow: Adds a soft luminous bloom by screening a blurred copy back over the image, making bright areas glow. Set the spread (radius) and how strong the glow is.
Emboss: Turns the image into a gray relief where edges look raised or carved, lit from a corner. Strength controls how pronounced the relief is.
Edge Detect: Finds and highlights outlines with a Sobel filter, drawing edges bright on black. Use it for line-art or sketch bases.
Shadows / Highlights: Independently lifts or deepens the darkest areas and recovers or boosts the brightest, weighted by how dark or light each pixel is. Ideal for opening up shadow detail while taming blown highlights.
Denoise: Removes speckle and noise with a median filter, smoothing flat areas while keeping edges. Raise strength for more passes on very noisy images.
Auto Levels: The same per-channel auto tone stretch as the Adjust panel's button, offered here as an effect chip. Applies instantly with no settings.
Auto Contrast: The same luminance contrast stretch as the Adjust panel's button, as an effect chip. Applies instantly with no settings.
Auto Color: The same gray-world white balance as the Adjust panel's button, as an effect chip. Applies instantly with no settings.
Color LUT: Applies a 3D color lookup table (a `.cube` LUT) for a one-shot cinematic grade. This effect is hidden from the grid and is added through the Load LUT (.cube) import rather than clicked here; its intensity mixes the graded result back with the original.

sections.title: Text Styles (one-click looks)
sections.text:
A gallery of ready-made text looks that appears only for text layers; each tile is previewed with your own text and applies a complete fill, outline and effect combination in one click.
Text Styles show at the top of the Effects panel when a **text** layer is selected. Every tile renders using your layer's own text and font, so the preview is the result. Clicking a tile replaces the layer's current effects with that style's fresh combination of fill, outline and text effects.
Everything stays non-destructive: after applying a style you can fine-tune it in Character, Text Effects and Warp.
Plain: Strips every text effect, outline, shadow and gradient back to a clean solid fill. Use it to start over.
Sticker: A red fill wrapped in a white-then-dark double outline, like a cut-out sticker.
Comic: Bold yellow letters with a dark outline, a double ring and a halftone dot shadow, for a comic-book caption.
Gold: A polished gold gradient fill with a dark-gold outline and a soft bevel for a metallic sheen.
Chrome: A cool silver chrome gradient with a dark outline and bevel, for a shiny metal finish.
Neon: White letters with a hot-pink neon glow, mimicking a glowing sign or tube light.
Fire: A yellow-to-red flame gradient with an orange glow, for a hot, burning headline.
Ice: A cool blue gradient with a white outline and a pale blue glow, for a frozen, icy look.
