Retro 3D: Cream letters extruded into a teal 3D block shadow and slightly skewed, for a retro poster feel.
Flat shadow: A blue fill with a long, flat 45-degree drop shadow, the classic flat-design long-shadow look.
Print offset: A dark fill with a cyan mis-registered offset and a small echo, imitating a risograph print.
Letterpress: Soft gray letters pressed inward with a debossed highlight and shadow, like ink stamped into paper.
Playful: Rainbow-cycling colors with bouncy per-letter jitter, for a fun, kid-friendly title.
Reflection: White letters with a mirrored reflection below and a soft shadow, for a glossy glass look.
Wave: Blue outlined letters warped into a wave with a small drop shadow, for a flowing banner.
Glitch: Pale letters with chromatic RGB fringing and sliced glitch distortion, for a broken-signal look.
VHS: Cyan-tinted letters with chromatic offset, scanlines and a soft glow, imitating an old VHS tape.
Rubber stamp: Red letters with a rough grunge texture and a slight skew, like an inked rubber stamp.
Standing: Warm gradient letters with a bevel, a diagonal shine and a slanted ground shadow, so the text appears to stand upright on a surface.
Neon sign: Hollow tube letters with a glowing pink neon-tube stroke and no solid fill, like a wired sign.
8-bit arcade: Pixelated yellow letters extruded into a short 3D block, for a retro arcade game title.
Slime: Green letters with dripping blobs and an inner glow, for a gooey slime effect.
Speed: Red outlined letters with a horizontal motion blur and forward skew, so the text looks like it is rushing past.
Highlight: Dark letters over a rough yellow marker highlight, as if swiped with a highlighter pen.
Paper cut: Dark letters sitting on a soft rounded paper card with a subtle drop shadow, for a layered paper-craft look.
Party: Rainbow letters with jitter and scattered confetti, for a celebratory, festive title.
Candy: Pink letters with diagonal candy stripes and a double ring outline, for a sweet, playful look.
Vegas marquee: Dark red letters studded with glowing golden bulbs, straight off a casino front.
Scoreboard: Red LED pixels on a dark chip, the stadium display look.
Blueprint: Pale hollow glyphs with a technical grid inside, like a construction drawing.
Varsity: Blue letters with a white inline and a red outer outline, the college-jersey classic.
Knockout: The text punched as holes out of a dark rounded panel.
Origami: Sky-blue paper facets with a teal block shadow, like folded paper.
Off air: TV static inside the letters with color-fringed ghosting and scanlines.
Comic shade: Bright comic lettering with a dark halftone shade, outline and block depth.
Checkerboard: A black-and-white checker fill with a clean outline.
Topography: Deep green letters ringed by contour lines, like a trail map.
Sparkle gold: Gold foil with white star glints on top.
Rose gold: A soft rose metal ramp with a gentle gloss streak.
Silver: A cool chrome ramp with subtle sparkles.
Vaporwave: A pink-to-cyan gradient with color fringing and scanlines, the retro-web aesthetic.
Cyberpunk: Acid yellow with glitch slices and a cyan offset ghost.
Graffiti: Spray-grain orange with a heavy outline, drips and a tag-style slant.
Western: Saddle-brown letters with a cream inline and block depth, the saloon-poster look.
Neon blue: A glowing blue neon tube on hollow glyphs.
Neon mint: A glowing mint-green neon tube on hollow glyphs.
Bubble pop: Glossy pink candy letters with inner glow and a dotted offset shadow.
Honey: An amber gradient with dripping edges and a syrupy shine.
Lava: A fire gradient with a hot glow and molten red drips.
Newsprint: A black-and-red misprint: the ink plate shifted off its outline plate.
Stamped: Weathered red ink with a stitched outline, like a rubber stamp.
Kawaii: Pastel pink with white-and-blue rings, sparkles and a soft inner glow.
Disco: A lilac chrome ramp with purple speed rays and sparkles.
Racing: A checkered-flag fill with a slant and a motion blur trail.
Midnight: A deep blue gradient under tiny white stars with a soft blue glow.
Frost: Icy pale blue with a white inner glow, cold outer glow and frost sparkles.
Sunset stack: A warm sunset gradient over stacked retro offset shadows.
Ocean: Wavy blue water bands inside the letters with a reflection below.
Mermaid: Teal-to-violet wave bands with sparkling glints.
Soda: An orange fizz gradient full of rising bubbles.
Champagne: Warm gold foil with fine rising bubbles.
Stone: A gray rock ramp with cracks and a chiselled bevel.
Iceberg: Pale ice with blue fracture lines and a cold glow.
Sale seal: White text on a red starburst badge, ready for price tags.
Price star: Dark text on a yellow starburst, the supermarket price flash.
Editorial: Plain dark text whose shadow is drawn as diagonal hatching.
Love note: Pink letters filled with tiny white hearts.
Starry: Navy letters filled with little golden stars.
Circuit: Green circuit traces on a dark board with a phosphor glow.
Terminal: Green LED pixels on black, the retro terminal screen.
Army: A camouflage fill with a weathered stencil edge.
Highland: A red-and-navy tartan weave fill.
Gingham: A light red-and-white picnic check.
Poolside: An aqua gradient warped by a gentle water ripple.
Mirage: A desert-heat gradient that shimmers and fades upward.
Gold ring: Dark letters wrapped in a golden gradient outline.
Neon ring: Dark letters wrapped in a cyan-to-magenta gradient ring with a violet glow.
Retro diner: Cream letters with a maroon inline and a teal offset shadow, 50s diner style.
Bumblebee: Bold yellow-and-black horizontal stripes.
Hazard: Diagonal yellow-and-black warning stripes with block depth.
Peppermint: Red-and-white candy stripes with a green dotted shadow.
Galaxy: A violet nebula gradient with star glints and a purple glow.
Denim: A fine indigo twill fill with orange stitch dashes.
Chalk: Rough white strokes with a dusty, hand-drawn edge.
Horror: Blood-red letters dripping over a dark aura.
Golden ticket: Dark text on a golden starburst with sparkles.
Boom: Comic-yellow letters on red speed rays with a tilted block shadow.

sections.title: Text Effects
sections.text:
A large gallery of individual, stackable text decorations for text layers; clicking a tile switches the effect on with sensible defaults and opens its settings card over the canvas.
Text Effects appear for **text** layers, below Text Styles. Each tile is previewed on a single large glyph so the effect is clearly visible. Clicking a tile turns that effect on and opens a floating settings card on the canvas with its sliders and color rows; an active tile re-opens its card. Effects are removed from inside their card, not by re-clicking the tile.
Effects are non-destructive and stack, and the text stays fully editable. The ranges below come from each effect's settings card.
Long shadow: Casts a long, solid drop shadow at an angle behind the text, the flat-design long-shadow look.
Block shadow: Extrudes the letters into a solid 3D block projected at an angle, for depth and weight.
Glow: Adds a soft colored glow (outer halo) around the letters.
Echo: Repeats fading copies of the text stepped in one direction, for a trailing echo effect.
Skew: Slants the whole text horizontally and/or vertically for an italic or leaning look.
Outline: Draws a single colored stroke around the letters.
Neon: A bright glowing neon halo in a chosen color, stronger than the plain Glow.
Splice: Offsets a colored copy of the letters and knocks it out where they overlap, for a sliced two-part look.
Halftone: Casts a shadow made of halftone dots offset behind the text, for a printed comic feel.
Reflection: Mirrors a fading copy of the text beneath it, like a reflection on glass.
Multi outline: Wraps the text in two to five concentric colored outlines (rings). The first three carry their own color; further rings continue the outermost one.
Bevel: Adds a beveled highlight-and-shadow edge so the letters look raised.
Letterpress: Presses the letters inward with a subtle top shadow and bottom highlight, like ink debossed into paper.
Image fill: Fills the letters with an image or texture of your choice instead of a flat color. Pick the image in the settings card.
Letter dance: Randomly rotates and offsets each letter for a lively hand-placed look. Change the variant for a different arrangement.
Color cycle: Colors the letters across a rainbow gradient. No settings; it just switches on.
Chromatic: Splits the red and blue channels apart for a chromatic-aberration RGB fringe.
Glitch: Slices the letters into shifted horizontal bands for a digital glitch. Change the variant for a new random cut.
Shine: Sweeps a bright diagonal shine band across the letters, like a glint on metal or glass.
Scanlines: Overlays evenly spaced horizontal lines across the text for a CRT screen or retro look.
Grunge: Eats away at the letters with a rough noise texture for a distressed, worn look.
Stitch outline: Draws a dashed outline around the letters, like a sewn stitch or cut line.
Inner glow: Adds a colored glow inside the edges of the letters rather than outside.
Neon tube: Turns the letters into hollow glowing tubes, like bent neon-sign glass.
Motion blur: Smears the letters in one direction to suggest speed or movement.
Marker: Draws a rough hand-drawn highlighter swipe behind the text. Change the variant for a different rough stroke.
Circle mark: Draws a rough hand-drawn circle or ellipse around the text, as if circled by pen.
Scribble line: Adds a rough hand-drawn scribbled underline beneath the text.
Paper cut: Places the text on a rounded card with a soft shadow, for a layered paper-cut look.
8-bit: Pixelates the letters into blocky low-resolution squares for a retro game look.
Sketch: Redraws the letter outlines as loose hand-sketched pen strokes with multiple passes.
Confetti: Scatters small colorful confetti pieces around the text for a festive feel.
Stripes: Fills the letters with repeating diagonal stripes in up to three colors.
Drip: Drops liquid drips down from the bottom of the letters, like paint or slime.
Ground shadow: Lays a squashed, slanted, blurred shadow on the ground under the text so it appears to stand up.
Gradient: Fills the letters with a two-color gradient at any angle.
Chrome: Gives the letters a shiny reflective chrome finish with adjustable shine, contrast and tint.
Comic dots: Fills the letters with halftone comic dots over a solid background color.
Spray: Sprays a grainy stippled texture over the letters, like airbrush or spray paint.
Highlight: Places a clean rounded highlight block behind the text, like a highlighted label.
Underline: Adds an underline beneath the text with a choice of styles, thickness and offset.
Sticker: Wraps the text in a thick colored sticker border with a drop shadow, like a cut-out sticker.
Speed lines: Radiates comic-style burst lines outward from the text for energy and impact.
Two tone: Splits the letter fill into two colors across an adjustable dividing line.
Gold foil: Adds a metallic gold-foil tint with small sparkle highlights. Change the variant for different sparkle placement.
Retro stack: Stacks up to three offset color copies behind the text for a layered retro poster shadow.
Misprint: Offsets a thin colored outline copy off-register, imitating a misaligned print run.
Fade: Fades the text to transparent across a chosen direction for a soft dissolve.
Soft blur: Applies a gentle blur to the whole text, for a soft or out-of-focus look.
3D: Renders the letters as a full 3D extrusion with separate top and bottom face colors, a depth (side) color and a shine border.
Sparkles: Scatters seeded four-point star glints across the letter faces, like catchlights on something shiny.
Inline: Draws a thin contour line inset inside the glyph edges, the classic varsity-jersey lettering look.
Contour lines: Rings the letters with up to four concentric hollow outlines marching outward, like elevation lines on a map.
Marquee lights: Places glowing light bulbs along the glyph edges, the fairground and casino marquee look.
Knockout: Punches the letters as holes out of a rounded panel, so whatever lies beneath shows through the text.
Checker fill: Fills the letters with a two-color checkerboard pattern.
Halftone shade: Shades the letters with a comic dot screen that grows denser toward one side.
TV static: Fills the letters with seeded monochrome noise, like an analog TV with no signal.
LED board: Rebuilds the fill as glowing round pixels on a dark chip, like a stadium scoreboard.
Origami fold: Lays alternating light and dark facets across the letters, like folded paper catching the light.
Blueprint: Replaces the fill with hollow outlined glyphs and a fine technical grid inside, the construction-drawing look.
Waves fill: Fills the letters with alternating wavy horizontal bands, a stylized water look.
Motif fill: Fills the letters with a repeating little shape of your choice: hearts, stars, plus signs or rings.
Camo fill: Fills the letters with seeded organic camouflage blobs in four earthy tones.
Circuit board: Fills the letters with repeating circuit traces and solder pads on a dark board.
Plaid fill: Fills the letters with a woven tartan of crossing translucent bands and thin accent lines.
Bubbles: Scatters fizzy little bubbles with highlights inside the letters, like a fresh soda.
Cracked: Runs seeded branching fracture lines across the letters, for stone, ice or shattered looks.
Ripple: Displaces the finished text in a sine wave, like its reflection in moving water or heat haze.
Star seal: Puts a starburst badge panel behind the text, the classic price-sticker and quality-seal shape.
Hatch shadow: Casts the drop shadow as diagonal line shading instead of a solid shape, an editorial-illustration touch.
Gradient outline: Wraps the letters in an outline filled with a two-color gradient ramp.

sections.title: Warp (text)
sections.text:
A gallery of preset shape warps for text layers that bend the whole word along a curve while keeping the text fully editable.
The Warp section shows for **text** layers. Each tile previews a warp shape on your text. Clicking a shape bends the text along it (a render-time mesh distortion, so the text stays editable) and opens a floating settings card with a **Bend** control. Choose None to remove the warp.
Bend sets how strongly the shape is applied (it defaults to 50, and tiles preview at a fixed bend).
None: Removes any warp and returns the text to a straight baseline.
Arc: Bends the whole line of text along a circular arc, curving it up or down as one piece.
Arch: Arches the text like a rainbow, raising the middle while the ends stay lower.
Arc Lower: Curves only the bottom edge of the text into an arc while the top stays flat.
Bulge: Swells the middle of the text outward so it looks fatter in the centre.
Squeeze: Pinches the middle of the text inward, narrowing it toward the centre.
Flag: Ripples the text in an S-shaped wave, like a flag waving in the wind.
Wave: Sends the text along a smooth up-and-down wave.
Rise: Tilts the text upward so it rises from left to right in a slanted ramp.
Fisheye: Bulges the text as if seen through a fisheye lens, enlarging the centre.
Twist: Rotates the text progressively along its length for a twisting ribbon effect.
Cone: Flares the text wider at one end and narrower at the other, like a cone or funnel.
Fish: Distorts the text into a fish or eye shape, pointed at the ends and full in the middle.
Bounce: Pushes the bottom of the text into a bouncing curve while the top stays put.
Ripple: Adds repeating small ripples across the text for a rippled-water look.
Melt: Stretches the bottom of the letters downward as though the text is melting.
Perspective: Tilts the text into a perspective plane so one end looks farther away.
Pinch: Pulls the text inward toward a central point for a pinched, sucked-in distortion.

sections.title: Adjust panel (color and slider behaviour)
sections.text:
How the Adjust panel's color block and tonal sliders bind to whatever layer you have selected.
The Adjust panel holds the tonal sliders and the color block. A few of its behaviours are easy to miss because they depend on which layer is selected.
Color picker target: The color block in the Adjust panel changes the **fill** of the selected shape, or the **color** of the selected text layer. With no shape or text layer selected, it sets the foreground color instead.
Solid color resets a gradient or pattern fill: If the selected layer currently uses a gradient or pattern fill, choosing a solid color switches its fill type back to solid so the color actually shows.
Gradient fill swatches: When a shape or text layer is selected, a grid of gradient preset swatches appears under the color block. Click one to fill the layer with that gradient. Shapes also receive a linear gradient direction.
Live per-layer adjustments: The Brightness, Contrast, Saturation, Hue, Temperature, Exposure and Vibrance sliders apply live to the selected layer and stay non-destructive. `Create Adjustment Layer` moves them onto a separate full-canvas layer, and `Reset` clears them.
Sliders and Auto buttons need a selected layer: The seven adjustment sliders and the `Auto Levels`, `Auto Contrast` and `Auto Color` buttons are disabled until you select a layer, because they act on the active layer.

sections.title: Effects panel (how looks apply)
sections.text:
The rules behind the Filters, Effects and text look tiles: previews, parameter dialogs, and destructive versus non-destructive application.
Every tile in the Effects panel previews the real result and clicking one applies it. Whether the result is baked into pixels or kept editable depends on the layer type.
Live preview thumbnails: Every filter, effect, text style and warp tile shows a small thumbnail rendered from your actual selected layer, so the tile previews the real result before you click.
Effect settings dialog: Clicking an effect that has adjustable parameters opens a settings dialog so you can tune it before applying. On a plain raster layer an effect without parameters applies immediately; on text, shape, group, generator and QR layers it first asks whether to convert the layer to a Smart Object, keeping it editable, or to bake it to pixels.
Applied as non-destructive Smart Filters: When the selected layer is a Smart Object, effects are added as Smart Filters that stay non-destructive. This note appears under the Effects grid so you know the effects can be re-edited or removed later.
Applied destructively (vector layers rasterize first): On a normal (non-smart) layer, effects are baked into the pixels. For a vector layer such as text or a shape you are asked first: convert it to a Smart Object and the effect stays editable along with the text, or choose Apply to pixels and the layer is rasterized, which fixes its content. This note appears under the Effects grid for non-smart layers.
Text Styles, Text Effects and Warp appear for text layers: The `Text Styles`, `Text Effects` and `Warp` sections only appear when a text layer is selected. The `Filters` and `Effects` sections are always shown for any renderable layer.
Select a layer to apply filters and effects: With nothing selected, the Effects panel shows this prompt instead of the tiles. Select a layer to enable the filters, effects and text looks.

sections.title: Warp settings (Bend)
sections.text:
The strength control for text warps, which lives in a floating card over the canvas rather than inline in the panel.
Picking a warp shape tile bends the text along that shape. The amount of bend is set in a small settings card that floats over the canvas.
Bend: Bend sets how strongly the chosen warp shape distorts the text. Higher values curve, arch or wave the text more. The text stays fully editable because the warp is a render-time mesh distortion.
Warp settings card: Choosing any warp shape opens a small settings card floating over the canvas that holds the Bend control. Re-picking the active shape re-opens the card, and choosing `None` removes the warp entirely.

sections.title: Transform
sections.text:
Move, resize, rotate, scale, flip and reset the selected layer or group.
The **Transform** section sits at the top of the Properties panel for every layer type. For a single layer the boxes show that layer's own position and size. For a group they show the combined bounding box of all its members, so editing X/Y moves everything together and flips mirror the whole unit about its shared centre.
Numeric fields accept typed values, and their labels (`X`, `Y`, `W`, `H`) are drag-to-scrub: press on the label and drag left or right to change the value smoothly.
X: Horizontal position of the layer's top-left corner, in canvas pixels. Type a number or drag the `X` label to scrub. For a group it shifts every member by the same amount so their spacing stays intact.
Y: Vertical position of the top-left corner, in canvas pixels. Type or scrub the `Y` label. Moving a group shifts all its members together.
W: Width of the layer in pixels. Type a value or scrub the `W` label. Disabled for groups, because a group has no real box of its own; resize a group with the Scale slider instead.
H: Height of the layer in pixels. Type or edit directly. Disabled for groups.
Rotation: Rotates the layer around its own centre. `0°` is upright, negative values turn it counter-clockwise. For a group the slider is a relative nudge that spins every member around the group's shared centre and snaps back to `0°` when you release it.
Scale: Grows or shrinks the layer about its centre as a live percentage, then snaps back to 100% on release so it reads as a relative nudge rather than a fixed size. Text scales its font size along with the box, and a group scales all members about their shared centre so the whole group grows uniformly.
Flip H: Mirrors the layer left to right. On a group it mirrors every member about the group's centre. Click again to flip back.
Flip V: Mirrors the layer top to bottom. On a group it mirrors all members about the group centre. Click again to undo.
Reset: Clears rotation and both flips in one click, returning the layer to upright and unmirrored. Its tooltip reads `Reset rotation and flips`.

sections.title: Fill & Stroke (shapes)
sections.text:
Set how a shape layer is filled and outlined, plus corner rounding and polygon or star point counts.
The **Appearance** section appears for shape layers (rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star and custom paths). It controls the fill (a flat color, a gradient, or a repeating pattern), the stroke color and thickness, and shape-specific geometry like corner radius and the number of sides or points.
The gradient and pattern sub-controls here are the same ones used by the text Fill toggle in the Character section.
Fill: Chooses how the shape is filled. `Solid` is one flat color, `Gradient` blends between color stops, and `Pattern` tiles a repeating motif. Switching to Gradient or Pattern the first time seeds sensible defaults (a two-stop gradient, or the dots pattern).
Color: The solid fill color, shown when Fill is set to Solid. Click the swatch to pick a color, or type a CSS color value (for example a hex code) in the text box next to it. [Shown when: Fill = Solid]
Type: The gradient style, shown when Fill is set to Gradient. `Linear` runs in a straight line, `Radial` spreads out from the centre, and `Angle` (conic) sweeps around like a color wheel. [Shown when: Fill = Gradient]
Gradient: The gradient bar with draggable color stops. Drag a stop to move it, click the bar to add a stop, and click a stop to recolor it. This defines the colors the fill blends between. [Shown when: Fill = Gradient]
Angle: Direction of a linear or angle gradient, in degrees. Hidden for radial gradients (which have no direction). Slide from 0° to 360° to rotate the color flow.
Pattern: Picks the repeating motif used to fill the shape, shown when Fill is set to Pattern. Choosing None falls back to the dots pattern. [Shown when: Fill = Pattern]
Pattern scale: Zooms the pattern tile in or out as a percentage of its natural size. Higher values make the motif larger and more spaced out.
Stroke: The outline color drawn around the shape. Click the swatch to pick a color or type a value; leave it empty (placeholder `none`) for no outline.
Stroke Size: Thickness of the outline in pixels. Scrub the label or type a number; 0 means no visible stroke. Values are clamped to whole pixels and never go below 0.
Radius: Rounds the corners of a rectangle shape. Only shown for rectangles. Larger values give softer, more pill-like corners. [Shown when: Shape = rectangle]
Points / Sides: How many points a star has, or how many sides a polygon has. The label reads `Points` for a star and `Sides` for a polygon. Only shown for those two shapes. [Shown when: Shape = polygon or star]
Stroke style: Solid, Dashed or Dotted outline for the shape, with Dash and Gap fields appearing for the dashed styles. Text outlines offer the same choice next to the outline width.
Line ends: For line shapes (v1.300): two dropdowns pick a decoration for the start and the end of the line - Arrow, Triangle, Dot or Bar. Heads render in canvas output and SVG exports alike; dashes stop at the shaft, the heads stay solid.
Line endpoint handles: A selected line shows two round grips on its ends instead of the eight resize handles (v1.299): drag either end to re-aim the line directly while the other end stays anchored; Shift snaps to 45° steps.

sections.title: Character (text properties)
sections.text:
Everything about how a text layer looks: font, size, weight, color, spacing, alignment, curve, outline, marker, shadow and background pill.
The **Character** section appears when a text layer is selected. It edits the whole layer by default. While you are inside a live rich-text edit on the canvas, the font, size, weight, color, tracking, bold, italic and underline controls instead apply to just the selected words, so you can style parts of a paragraph differently.
Some controls only appear in certain states: Justify shows only for a fixed-width text box, the Curve slider hides once text is attached to a path (replaced by path controls), and the PSD rasterized-look toggle appears only on text imported from a PSD.
Text: A two-row text box holding the layer's words. Edit here to change the copy without double-clicking on the canvas. You can also type dynamic tokens like `{{post.title}}` for templates.
Font: The typeface picker. Opens the font library so you can choose a font family for the text (or the selected words while editing).
Size: Font size in pixels. Type a number or scrub the `Size` label. While editing, it sizes only the selected characters.
Wt: Font weight (thickness), from Light to Black. Pick a numeric weight from the dropdown. `Wt` is short for weight.
Fill: How the letters are filled: `Solid` color, `Gradient`, or `Pattern`. Choosing Gradient or Pattern reveals the same Type, gradient bar, Angle, Pattern and Pattern scale controls used for shapes.
Color: The text color. Click the swatch to pick a color or type a CSS/hex value. While editing, it recolors only the selected words.
Tracking: Letter spacing: extra space added between characters. Negative values tighten the letters, positive values spread them apart.
Line height: Vertical spacing between lines, as a multiple of the font size. Lower values pack lines tighter, higher values open them up.
Curve: Bends the whole text into an arc. `0` is a straight line; positive values curve it one way, negative values the other. Hidden once text is attached to a path.
Path start: Where along a path the text begins, when the text is attached to a path. Slide to shift the text forward or backward along the curve. [Shown when: Text is on a path]
Reverse direction: Flips text-on-a-path to run along the other side of the curve (for example from inside to outside a circle). Only shown when text is attached to a path. [Shown when: Text is on a path]
Detach from path: Removes the text from its path so it becomes normal straight text again. Only shown when text is on a path. [Shown when: Text is on a path]
Outline: Draws a colored stroke around the letters. Pick an outline color with the swatch and set its thickness in the number box. Picking a color auto-sets a sensible width if none is set yet.
Marker: A hand-drawn highlighter behind the words. Pick a marker color with the swatch; the `Remove` button next to it clears the marker. It marks whole lines by default, or just the selected words while editing.
Shadow: Drop shadow behind the text. Tick the checkbox to switch it on, then pick a shadow color with the swatch. Choosing a color also turns the shadow on.
Background: A colored pill or box behind the text. Pick a background color with the swatch, set the corner radius in the number box, or press `None` to remove it.
Show original rasterized look (PSD import): For text imported from a PSD, this checkbox shows the original flattened pixel version instead of the live editable text. Only appears when a rasterized fallback exists. [Shown when: Text has a PSD raster fallback]
Bold: Toggles bold on the text. Turning it on sets the weight to 700; turning it off returns to 400.
Italic: Slants the text into an italic style. Click again to turn it off.
Underline: Draws a line under the text. Click again to remove it.
Uppercase: Non-destructive all-caps toggle (v1.300): layout, canvas and exports render the text in capitals while the stored text keeps its original case - switch it off and the original casing returns.
Align left: Aligns each line of text to the left edge of the text box. This is the horizontal alignment for the lines within the layer.
Align center: Centres each line of text horizontally within the text box, so line starts and ends are balanced around the middle.
Align right: Aligns each line of text to the right edge of the text box.
Justify: Stretches lines so they fill the full width of the box, adding space between words to make flush left and right edges. Only shown for fixed-width text boxes, since point text has no fixed width to stretch to. [Shown when: Fixed-width text box]
Align top: Vertical alignment: pins the text block to the top of its box. Use this when text should sit at the top and grow downward.
Align middle: Vertical alignment: centres the text block between the top and bottom of its box. This is the default for auto-height (point) text.
Align bottom: Vertical alignment: pins the text block to the bottom of its box, so it grows upward from the baseline area.
List (bullets / numbering): Non-destructive paragraph lists (v1.301): every non-empty line gets a bullet or its running number in canvas renders, exports and SVG, while the stored text keeps its raw form. Toggle between none, bullets and numbering.

sections.title: Align & Distribute
sections.text:
Line up and evenly space the selected layers or groups.
The **Align & Distribute** section shows a row of six icon buttons for alignment and two buttons for distribution. Alignment lines objects up to a shared edge or centre. Distribution spreads three or more objects out with equal gaps.
These are unit-aware: they keep grouped layers together and align the group as a single object rather than pulling its members apart.
Align left: Lines up the selected objects so their left edges match. With two or more selected the reference is the selection's own bounding box; with a single object it is the canvas, so the object moves to the canvas edge.
Align horizontal centers: Lines up the objects so their horizontal centres share the same vertical line. With two or more selected they centre on each other; with a single object it centres on the canvas.
Align right: Lines up the selected objects so their right edges match, snapping to the rightmost edge.
Align top: Lines up the objects so their top edges match, snapping to the highest edge in the selection.
Align vertical centers: Lines up the objects so their vertical centres share the same horizontal line. Objects shift up or down until centred on each other.
Align bottom: Lines up the selected objects so their bottom edges match, snapping to the lowest edge.
Distribute H: Spreads the selected objects out horizontally so the gaps between them are equal. Disabled until enough objects are selected to space apart.
Distribute V: Spreads the selected objects out vertically so the gaps between them are equal. Disabled until enough objects are selected.

sections.title: Fill and gradient type options
sections.text:
The individual choices inside the Fill toggle and the gradient Type/Kind selectors that shape and text fills use.
Shape and text layers share a Fill toggle with three choices: `Solid`, `Gradient`, and `Pattern`. When you pick Gradient, a Type toggle lets you choose the gradient shape. A standalone gradient layer offers the same choices under a Kind dropdown.
These are the option values inside those lists. Each one changes what extra controls appear below.
Solid: The first choice in the **Fill** toggle. Fills the shape or text with one flat color. Pick it when you want a single solid color instead of a gradient or a repeating pattern. Choosing it shows the `Color` swatch below.
Linear: A gradient whose colors blend along a straight line from one side to the other. Use it for simple top-to-bottom or side-to-side color blends. When Linear is selected an `Angle` slider appears so you can set the direction.
Radial: A gradient whose colors radiate outward in rings from the center. Use it for a spotlight or soft glow look. It has no single direction, so the `Angle` slider is hidden for this type.
Angle: The conic (angular) gradient type: colors sweep around the center like a color wheel. This is the **Angle** choice inside the gradient Type toggle, not the Angle direction slider. An `Angle` slider still appears to set where the sweep begins.
Kind: The gradient type dropdown shown for a dedicated gradient **layer** (as opposed to a gradient fill inside a shape or text). Switches the whole layer between Linear, Radial, and Angle.

sections.title: Transform: hidden affordances
sections.text:
Two behaviours in the Transform section that are not obvious from the visible controls.
Scrub labels (drag to change a value): Many number fields have a draggable label. Press on the label text and drag left or right to scrub the value down or up without typing, then release to save the change. This works for `X`, `Y`, `W`, `H`, font `Size`, `Stroke Size`, `Radius`, and the `Min size` / `Max size` fit fields.
Use the Scale slider to resize a group: Tooltip shown on the `W` and `H` boxes when a group is selected. A group has no box of its own, so its width and height fields are greyed out. Resize a whole group with the `Scale` slider instead, which grows every member together.

sections.title: Character: extra buttons and inputs
sections.text:
Smaller controls inside the Character section that sit alongside the main text-style rows.
Text path: Label for the row of buttons that appears once text has been attached to a path. It groups the `Reverse direction` and `Detach from path` buttons. Shown only while the text layer is following a path.
None (background pill): Clears the color of the text background pill so the text sits on no fill. It sits next to the `Background` swatch and is greyed out when there is no background color set.
Corner radius (background pill): Sets how rounded the corners of the text background pill are. Higher values give a more pill-shaped highlight behind the text; zero gives square corners. It is the small number box in the `Background` row.
Remove (marker): Removes the highlighter marker from the text. While editing, if you have words selected it clears the marker on just those words; otherwise it clears the marker for the whole layer. The button appears only when a marker is present.

sections.title: Dynamic content
sections.text:
Binds a text or image layer to a post or site source so a template fills it with real content per post.
This section turns a normal layer into a **dynamic** one. A text layer can pull a post title, excerpt, custom field, or any variable; an image layer can pull the generated background, the featured image, or a brand logo. When the template runs against a post, the value is dropped in for you.
Bound text gets an auto-fit range (Min size and Max size) so long text shrinks to fit its box. If every variable in a text layer resolves empty, that layer is hidden for that post.
Brand Kit: Chooses which Brand Kit supplies the custom variables listed in this panel and which kit the post preview resolves with. The choice is stored on the document, so it travels inside saved templates. A run of the template can still override it.
Variable: Binds the layer to a source such as a post title, excerpt, featured image, or the generated background. The list is grouped by source and only shows variables that match the layer type (text sources for text layers, image sources for image layers). Pick a variable to make the layer dynamic.
None: The first entry in the Variable list. Leaves the layer unbound so it keeps the exact text or image you placed. Selecting it also clears an existing binding.
Custom field…: A Variable entry, available for text layers only, that binds the layer to a WordPress custom field (post meta) by its key. Selecting it reveals the Meta key box below. Works on image layers too: a meta key holding an image attachment ID or URL swaps the image per post.
Meta key: The custom-field key to read, for example `my_field_key`. Each post shows that field's value where the layer sits. This box appears only after you choose `Custom field…`.
Min size: The smallest font size the auto-fit may shrink bound text down to when it is too long for its box. Text that still overflows at this size is shortened instead. Shown for bound text or text that contains variable tokens.
Max size: The largest font size the auto-fit will grow bound text to when it is short. Together with Min size it sets the range the text is allowed to move between. Shown for bound text or text that contains variable tokens.
In text: Opens a variable picker so you can drop a token (like `{{post.title}}`) into the middle of the layer's own text. Use it to mix fixed words with dynamic values, for example `Read more: {{post.title}}`. Available for text layers that are not fully bound to a single Variable.
Empty value hides the layer: When the template runs, if every variable in a text layer resolves to empty, the whole layer is hidden for that post. This keeps designs tidy when a field is missing. It is a behaviour, not a control, and applies to text made of `{{tokens}}`.
Auto crop for dynamic images: When you bind an image layer, it defaults to a centered Cover crop so an arbitrary source photo is not squashed into the box. You can change this afterwards in the Image Fit section. It is the default behaviour on first binding, not a button.
Generated background note [AI]: When a layer is bound to the generated background, the panel notes it will be replaced by that image at run time and suggests keeping a placeholder photo in it while you design. This is a helper message shown for the `ai.background` binding.

sections.title: Image Fit
sections.text:
Controls how a placed or dynamic source image maps into the layer's box.
Three modes decide how an image sits inside its frame: Stretch distorts to fill, Cover crops to fill, and Fit shows the whole picture with empty space. Cover and Fit keep a focal point (the anchor) that defaults to the center.
On a raster layer that already has baked pixels, these settings do not touch the current pixels; they only govern how the dynamic replacement image is placed when a template runs.
Stretch: Stretches the image to fill the box exactly, ignoring its aspect ratio. It is fast but can squash or distort the picture. This is the legacy default for image layers.
Cover: Scales the image to fill the whole box and crops whatever overflows, while keeping the aspect ratio. Use it for photo backgrounds where the frame must be completely filled with no gaps.
Fit: Scales the image so the entire picture is visible inside the box, keeping the aspect ratio and leaving empty (letterbox) space on the short side. Use it when nothing may be cropped, for example a full logo.
Anchor (reposition on canvas): With Cover or Fit, the image keeps a focal point that decides which part survives the crop, or where the letterboxed image sits. It defaults to the center. There is no grid here; double-click the layer on the canvas to drag the image and set that point freely.
Raster replacement note: On a raster layer that has baked pixels, a helper message reminds you the fit does not change the current pixels. It only controls how the layer's dynamic replacement image is placed when the template runs.

sections.title: Appearance (shape)
sections.text:
Fill, stroke, and geometry controls for a vector shape layer.
This section appears for shape layers. Choose a Solid, Gradient, or Pattern fill, add a stroke, and adjust the shape geometry (corner radius for rectangles, or the number of sides or points for polygons and stars).
Fill: Segmented toggle that chooses how the shape is filled: Solid color, Gradient, or Pattern. Switching to Gradient seeds two stops if none exist; switching to Pattern seeds the `dots` pattern.
Color: The solid fill color of the shape, shown when Fill is set to Solid. Pick from the swatch popover or type any CSS color into the text box next to it.
Type (gradient): When Fill is Gradient, chooses the gradient shape: Linear (straight band), Radial (from a center point outward), or Angle (a conic sweep). The Angle slider below is hidden for Radial.
Gradient (stops): The color-stop bar for the gradient fill. Drag the handles to move stops, and click a stop to change its color and position. Extra room is left below the bar for the draggable handles.
Angle (gradient): Rotates a Linear or Angle gradient around the shape. Shown only when Type is not Radial. Zero degrees runs left to right.
Pattern: When Fill is Pattern, picks the repeating pattern used to fill the shape (dots, stripes, and others). Choosing None falls back to the `dots` pattern.
Pattern scale: Resizes the pattern tile inside the shape. Lower values make a denser, smaller pattern; higher values make a larger, sparser one.
Stroke: The outline color drawn around the shape. Pick a color from the swatch, or type `none` (leave blank) to remove the outline.
Stroke Size: The thickness of the shape's outline in pixels. Set it to 0 for no outline. Drag the label to scrub or type a value.
Radius: Rounds the corners of a rectangle shape. Higher values give softer, more rounded corners; 0 keeps sharp corners. Shown only for rectangle shapes.
Sides / Points: Sets the number of sides for a polygon, or the number of points for a star. The label reads `Points` for stars and `Sides` for polygons. Shown only for polygon and star shapes.

sections.title: Gradient (gradient layer)
sections.text:
Properties for a standalone gradient fill layer.
This section appears when the selected layer is a dedicated gradient layer (a full gradient fill rather than a shape or text). Choose the gradient kind, set the direction or the reach and center, edit the color stops, and reverse them.
Which control shows depends on Kind: Linear gets an Angle slider, Radial gets Size, Center X and Center Y. A gradient layer stores its geometry as a from point and a to point; the sliders read those points back and write them, so what you see always matches the layer.
Kind: Chooses the gradient shape for the layer: Linear (straight band), Radial (center outward), or Angle (conic sweep). The Angle slider below appears only for Linear; Size, Center X and Center Y appear only for Radial.
Size: Sets how far a radial gradient reaches from its center out to its last stop. Drag it right to widen the fade, left to tighten it into a small spot. The readout at the right shows the reach as a percentage of the layer's diagonal, and the center stays where it is while you drag.
Center X: Moves the center of a radial gradient sideways inside the layer. 0 puts it on the left edge, 50 in the middle, 100 on the right edge. The reach you set with Size is kept.
Center Y: Moves the center of a radial gradient up and down inside the layer. 0 puts it on the top edge, 50 in the middle, 100 on the bottom edge. The reach you set with Size is kept.
Angle: Rotates a Linear gradient by moving its start and end points. Shown only when Kind is Linear. The value is read back from the stored from and to points.
Gradient bar (stops): The color-stop bar for the layer. Drag handles to move stops and click a stop to recolor it or change its position.
Reverse: Flips the order of the color stops so the gradient runs the opposite way. Each stop's position is mirrored (position becomes 1 minus position) and the stops are re-sorted.

sections.title: Smart Object and Smart Filters
sections.text:
Non-destructive filter stack and content controls for a Smart Object layer.
A Smart Object holds its original image (or PSD) untouched and applies a live stack of filters on top. Filters can be reordered, switched off, or removed without ever damaging the source pixels.
From here you can also open the Smart Object's contents for editing, replace the source with a new file, or flatten it back to a normal pixel layer.
Source info: A read-only line at the top showing the Smart Object's source size, its kind (PSD or Image), and whether the original file is embedded. It helps you confirm what the Smart Object contains.
Toggle filter: The checkbox beside each filter in the list turns that Smart Filter on or off without removing it. A disabled filter dims in the list and stops affecting the image. Use it to compare with and without an effect.
Move up: Moves the filter one place higher in the stack, changing the order effects are applied in. Disabled for the top filter. Order matters because each filter runs on the result of the one before it.
Remove: The X button deletes that Smart Filter from the stack. The source image is unaffected because filters are non-destructive.
Add [Extension]: A dropdown that appends a new Smart Filter to the stack. It lists all built-in effects plus any effects added by extensions (hidden ones are excluded). New filters start enabled with their default parameters.
Edit Contents: Opens the Smart Object's inner document so you can edit its layers or image, then return and see the filters re-applied. This is the re-entry point for editing what is inside the Smart Object.
Replace…: Swaps the Smart Object's source for a different image or file while keeping the layer's position, size, and filter stack. Use it to reuse a placement with new artwork.
Rasterize: Flattens the Smart Object and its live filters into a plain pixel (raster) layer. This bakes the current look permanently and removes the ability to edit contents or filters. Use it only when you no longer need the non-destructive stack.

sections.title: Blending Options (layer styles)
sections.text:
Photoshop-style, non-destructive layer effects; tick a box to add each one.
Blending Options add live effects around and over a layer's shape, such as a stroke, shadows, glows, and overlays. Tick a style to enable it and reveal its parameters below; untick to remove it. Effects stack and update live.
These styles apply to almost every layer type, including groups, where they wrap the group's combined silhouette. Adjustment layers do not get Blending Options.
Stroke: Draws a colored outline around the layer's edge. Choose its thickness, color, and whether it sits outside, centered on, or inside the edge. Good for making text or shapes pop against a busy background.
Drop Shadow: Casts a soft shadow behind the layer to lift it off the background. Control its color, opacity, angle, distance, blur, and spread. The most common depth effect.
Inner Shadow: Casts a shadow inside the layer's edges, making it look recessed or cut into the surface. Control color, opacity, angle, distance, and blur.
Outer Glow: Adds a soft glow radiating outward from the layer's edges. Set its color, opacity, blur, and spread. Use it for a halo or light-bloom look.
Color Overlay: Fills the layer with a flat color on top of its content at the chosen opacity. Handy for tinting or recoloring a shape or image without editing it.
Inner Glow: Adds a soft glow that spreads inward from the layer's edges toward the middle. Control its color, opacity, and blur. Good for a subtle inner light.
Bevel & Emboss: Adds highlight and shadow along the edges to fake a raised or carved 3D surface. Set the size, strength, and whether it looks raised (Up) or recessed (Down).
Satin: Overlays a soft, folded sheen inside the layer for a satin or cloth-like finish. Control color, opacity, angle, distance, and blur.
Pattern Overlay: Lays a repeating pattern over the layer at a chosen opacity and scale. Pick the pattern and how large the tile is. Useful for texture or halftone looks.
Gradient Overlay: Lays a gradient over the layer at a chosen angle and opacity. Edit the color stops on the bar and rotate with the angle. Good for tinted, directional color washes.

sections.title: Layer style parameters
sections.text:
The shared controls that appear beneath each enabled layer style.
When you enable a Blending Options style, its own set of parameters unfolds below it. The same controls are reused across styles, so only the ones a given effect supports appear. This section describes each of those shared controls.
Color: The color of the effect, chosen from a swatch popover. Appears for styles that use a single color, such as Stroke, Drop Shadow, Color Overlay, and glows.
Gradient stops: The color-stop bar for Gradient Overlay. Drag and edit stops to build the gradient that is laid over the layer.
Opacity: How strong or see-through the effect is. Lower values let more of the layer show through. Shown for most styles.
Size: The overall thickness or reach of the effect, for example the width of a Stroke or the depth of a Bevel. Larger values make the effect bigger.
Position: For the Stroke style, where the outline sits relative to the layer edge: Outside the shape, Centered on the edge, or Inside the shape. Inside keeps the outer silhouette crisp; Outside grows the visible size.
Angle: The direction the effect comes from, for shadows, satin, and gradient overlays. Rotate it to move a shadow around the layer or aim the gradient.
Distance: How far a shadow or satin is offset from the layer. Higher values push the shadow further away, making the layer feel more lifted.
Blur: How soft the effect's edge is. Zero is a hard edge; higher values give a softer, more feathered look. Shown for shadows, glows, and satin.
Spread: Grows the solid core of a shadow or glow before the blur is applied, making it thicker and more intense. Shown for Drop Shadow and Outer Glow.
Strength: How pronounced the Bevel & Emboss relief is. Higher values deepen the highlight and shadow for a stronger 3D feel.
Direction: For Bevel & Emboss, whether the surface looks raised or carved: Up (raised) pushes it toward you, Down (recessed) sinks it in.
Pattern: For Pattern Overlay, the repeating pattern laid over the layer. Choosing None falls back to the `dots` pattern. Extensions can add more patterns.
Scale: For Pattern Overlay, how large the pattern tile is. Higher values enlarge the tile so the motif repeats less often.

sections.title: Extension property sections
sections.text:
Extra property sections that installed extensions add for certain layers.
Installed extensions can register their own sections in the Properties panel. Each one renders below the built-in sections and can be shown only for layer types it cares about. This is how add-ons (for example generators and studios) provide their own editing controls right where you edit a layer.
Because the section is re-mounted per layer rather than per edit, sliders inside it stay smooth while you drag. The exact controls depend on the extension you installed.
Extension section: A property section provided by an installed extension, appearing under the built-in sections when its condition matches the selected layer. Its title and controls come from the extension itself, so what you see varies by add-on. Extensions read live layer values so their controls stay in sync as you work. [Shown when: The extension's own condition matches the layer]

sections.title: Shape fill modes
sections.text:
The three fill modes offered by the Fill toggle at the top of a shape layer's Appearance panel.
The `Fill` toggle switches a shape's body between a flat color, a color gradient, or a repeating pattern. Picking a mode reveals that mode's own controls just below it.
These are the individual options inside the Fill toggle; the toggle itself is documented separately.
Solid: Fills the shape body with a single flat color, taken from the `Color` swatch below. This is the starting fill mode unless the layer already carries a pattern.
Gradient: Fills the body with a multi-stop color blend. Choosing it reveals the gradient `Type`, gradient bar, and `Angle` controls, and if the layer has no stops yet it seeds a two-stop blend from the current fill color to orange.
Pattern: Fills the body with a repeating tile pattern. Choosing it reveals the `Pattern` picker and `Pattern scale` slider; if no pattern is set it starts on the `dots` pattern.

sections.title: Gradient direction types
sections.text:
The three gradient shapes shared by the shape/text gradient Type toggle and by the Gradient layer's Kind menu.
When a fill is set to Gradient (on shapes and on text) the `Type` toggle offers these three shapes. A dedicated Gradient layer offers the same set through its `Kind` menu.
Linear and Angle also show an `Angle` slider; Radial hides it because it spreads from the center outward.
Linear: Blends the colors along a straight line across the layer. Use it for simple top-to-bottom or side-to-side fades. The `Angle` slider sets the line's direction.
Radial: Blends the colors outward in rings from the center to the edges, good for spotlights and soft glows. The angle control is hidden for this type because a radial blend has no single direction.
Angle: Sweeps the colors around a center point like a clock hand (a conic gradient). Use it for cone or pie-slice color effects.

sections.title: Layer style option menus
sections.text:
The named dropdown choices inside the Stroke and Bevel & Emboss layer effects in Blending Options.
Most layer effects expose only sliders, but two of them add a menu of named choices: where a Stroke sits relative to the edge, and which way a Bevel & Emboss is lit.
These are the individual options; the Position and Direction menus themselves are documented with their parent effects.
Outside: Draws the stroke fully outside the shape's edge, so the fill stays untouched and the layer grows slightly. This is the default stroke position.
Center: Straddles the stroke on the edge so half of its width sits inside the shape and half outside.
Inside: Draws the stroke fully inside the edge, so the layer keeps its size and the stroke eats into the fill.
Up (raised): Lights the top of the bevel so the layer looks raised toward you. This is the default direction for Bevel & Emboss.
Down (recessed): Lights the bottom of the bevel so the layer looks pressed into the surface.

sections.title: Dynamic content help notes
sections.text:
The inline explanatory notes shown under a bound layer in the Dynamic content panel.
When a text or image layer is bound to a variable, a small help note appears explaining what happens when the template runs against a real post. The note text changes with the layer type and the chosen binding.
Text auto-fit note: Shown under a bound text layer. It explains that text which does not fit first shrinks toward the `Min size`, then gets shortened, and points you to `View, Preview with Post` to test against real content.
Dynamic image note: Shown under a bound image layer. It explains that the image source is swapped in per post when the template runs and is placed into the box using the `Image Fit` settings.

sections.title: Smart Object filter list
sections.text:
The heading and per-row labels of the Smart Filters stack on a Smart Object layer.
A Smart Object keeps its filters as a live, re-orderable stack that never touches the embedded original. The list sits under a small heading; each row shows the filter name with controls to toggle, reorder, or remove it.
Smart Filters: The heading over the stacked list of non-destructive filters applied to this Smart Object. Filters render from top to bottom and can be reordered at any time without changing the embedded source.
Filter name: Each row shows the applied filter's label between its on/off checkbox and the reorder and remove buttons. The label dims when the filter is switched off but stays in the stack.
Filter: The default placeholder text in the `Add` menu, shown before you pick an effect to append to the filter stack. Selecting any effect from the list adds it, enabled, to the bottom of the stack.

sections.title: Right panel tabs
sections.text:
The tab strip at the top of the right dock that switches the panel between Layers, Properties, Adjust, Effects, History and AI Studio.
The right side of the editor is a single panel that shows one tab at a time. Click a tab to switch what the panel shows. Installed extensions can add their own tabs after these six.
The panel width is adjustable and remembered between sessions, and it grows automatically if a tab's content is too wide to fit.
Layers: Switches the panel to the **Layers** list, where you stack, reorder, show or hide, group and blend the layers of your document. This is the default working view for building a design.
Properties: Opens the **Properties** panel, which shows the settings of the selected layer: position, size, text options, image fit and so on. Tool settings are not here, they live in the options bar above the canvas.
Adjust: Opens the **Adjust** panel for color and tone corrections on the active layer: brightness, contrast, saturation, hue, temperature, exposure and vibrance. Curves and Levels are not here, they live under the Filter menu.
Effects: Opens the **Effects** panel for filters and visual effects applied to the active layer.
History: Opens the **History** panel: the list of every step you have taken, named snapshots you have saved, and the saved file versions of an existing image. Use it to jump back and forth in time.
AI Studio [AI]: Opens the **AI** panel (labelled AI Studio on the tab), with the prompt box plus all local and cloud AI tools. Use it to generate images, edit layers and run one-click AI helpers.
Extension panel tabs [Extension]: Installed extensions can add extra tabs to the right of the six built-in ones. Each extension renders its own controls into the panel body. If you have no extensions installed, no extra tabs appear.
Drag to resize the panel: A thin handle on the left edge of the panel. Drag it left or right to make the whole right dock wider or narrower. The width you set is saved and reused next time.

sections.title: AI Studio panel (top controls)
sections.text:
The header, provider selector, prompt box and main generate/edit buttons at the top of the AI panel.
The AI panel is split into two parts. The top (documented here) holds the prompt box and the main buttons that create or transform a whole image. Below that sit the quick-action grids for **Local tools** and **AI cloud** tools.
Local tools run entirely in your browser and need no key. Cloud tools send your image to a configured AI provider and may cost money. If you have not configured any provider, the panel shows only the local tools and a note pointing you to Settings.
AI Assist: The heading at the top of the AI panel. It marks the start of the AI tools and has a small status dot next to it.
Provider pills: One pill per AI provider you have configured in Settings. Click a pill to choose which provider runs the cloud actions (Generate, Edit Layer, and the AI cloud grid). Only providers you have set up appear here.
No provider, local tools only [Local AI]: The message shown in place of the provider pills when you have not configured any AI provider. It tells you that only the key-free local tools will work until you add a provider in Settings.
Prompt box: The large text field where you describe what to generate or change, for example `add soft morning light` or `make the background minimal and cream colored`. The prompt feeds Generate, Edit Layer, From Sketch, From Post and the cloud actions that need instructions (Inpaint, Replace BG).
Prompt style button: A small style picker above the prompt box that appends a look or art direction to your prompt text (for example a photographic or illustration style). Use it to steer the visual style without typing it out.
Format: The small label above the aspect ratio row. It marks the set of buttons that choose the shape of the generated image.
Auto: The default aspect ratio choice. It matches the document's own aspect ratio, so the generated image comes out shaped like your current canvas.
Aspect ratio chips: Fixed shape choices for generation, next to **Auto**. Pick one to force the generated image into that ratio instead of matching the document. Providers work on fixed grids, so these cover the common ratios.
Generate [Cloud AI]: The primary button that creates a brand-new image from your prompt and adds it as a new layer. Needs a configured provider and some prompt text. Respects the chosen Format (aspect) and, if enabled, the brand details. [Requires: Provider + prompt]
Edit Layer [Cloud AI]: Sends the active layer to the AI and rewrites it according to your prompt, keeping it as the same layer. Use it to change an existing image (recolor, restyle, add or remove elements) rather than start from scratch. Needs a provider and prompt. [Requires: Provider + prompt]
From Sketch [Cloud AI]: Turns your whole canvas (a rough, multi-layer sketch) into a finished image, using the flattened canvas as a reference and your prompt for direction. Use it to render a quick layout mock-up into a polished picture. Needs a provider and prompt. [Requires: Provider + prompt]
From Post [Cloud AI]: Opens a post picker; the chosen post's title, excerpt and content ride along with your prompt so the AI can, for example, make a quick article infographic. If you leave the prompt empty it falls back to a generic illustrative prompt. Needs a provider. [Requires: Provider]
Include brand details [Cloud AI]: A checkbox (shown only when you have at least one Brand Kit) that appends the selected kit's colors and fonts to the prompt, and attaches its logo as a reference image, for Generate, Edit Layer, From Sketch and From Post. Turn it on to keep AI results on-brand.
Brand Kit selector: A dropdown next to **Include brand details** that appears only when you have more than one Brand Kit. Pick which kit's colors, fonts and logo the AI should follow. It is disabled until Include brand details is checked.

sections.title: AI Local tools
sections.text:
The key-free AI helpers that run entirely in your browser; your image never leaves your site.
These tools work with no AI provider and no API key. They run in the browser, so there is no per-use cost and nothing is uploaded. Each button acts on the active image layer (or the current selection where noted).
Extension AI tools, if you have any installed, also appear in this grid and run in the same progress and error handling.
Select Subject [Local AI]: Detects the main subject of the active image and turns it into a selection. Use it as a fast way to get a selection before cutting out, removing an object, or applying an edit to just the subject.
Remove Object [Local AI]: Erases the selected area and fills it from the surrounding pixels. First make a selection (Smart Select `K`, or **Select Subject**), then click this. For tricky fills the cloud version is stronger. [Requires: A selection]
Remove BG [Local AI]: Cuts out the subject of the active image layer and makes the background transparent. Use it to isolate a product or person for compositing.
Blur Background [Local AI]: Keeps the subject sharp and blurs everything behind it for a portrait look. It asks you for the blur strength in pixels before running.
Depth Blur [Local AI]: Opens a graduated background blur built from a depth map, with a focus and strength slider for a true depth-of-field effect. Use it when a single flat blur is not enough and you want the blur to increase with distance.
Blur Faces [Local AI]: Finds every human face on the active layer with the local Florence-2 model and pixelates it beyond recognition, in one step and without a key. Use it before publishing photos of people.
Vectorize [Local AI]: Traces the active image into editable vector shapes (SVG paths) and places them as new shape layers. Use it to turn a logo or flat graphic into clean, scalable vectors.
Upscale [Local AI]: Doubles the source resolution of the active image layer. The layer keeps its size on the canvas, but zooming in and exporting come out sharper.
Enhance [Local AI]: A one-click automatic boost of color, contrast and sharpness on the active image layer. Use it for a quick overall improvement with no settings.
Refine Edges [Local AI]: Smooths and slightly tightens the cutout edge of the active image layer. Use it to clean up fringes left behind by Remove BG.
Crop to Subject [Local AI]: Crops the canvas down to the detected subject, leaving a small margin. Use it to auto-trim empty space around the main object.
Sticker [Local AI]: Cuts out the subject and adds a white sticker outline with a soft shadow. Use it to make a die-cut sticker style graphic in one click.
Text Behind Subject: Builds the magazine look in one click: duplicates the active image layer, cuts out its subject locally and slides an editable headline between background and cutout. The headline is selected afterwards, ready to type.
Color Pop: Keeps the subject in color and turns everything else black and white. The same local subject mask as Remove BG drives it, with soft edges that blend instead of cutting, so hair and fur survive the border.
Product Shot: Cuts out the subject and centers it on clean white with a soft contact shadow, sized with comfortable margins. Every product photo looks like a catalog page; the original layer is replaced, undo brings it back.
Neon Rim: Dims the background and wraps the subject in a glowing colored rim. The glow borrows the first vivid color of your Brand Kit when one is set, and falls back to neon cyan.
Speed Blur: Zoom-blurs the background outward around the subject while the subject itself stays sharp - instant motion for cars, sports and action shots.
Depth Fog: Adds atmospheric haze staged by a real depth estimate: clear up front, misty in the distance. Runs the same local depth model as Depth Blur.
Extension AI tools [Extension, Local AI]: Any AI tools added by installed extensions appear alongside the built-in local tools and run in the same progress and error handling. What you see depends on which extensions you have installed.

sections.title: AI Cloud tools
sections.text:
The AI helpers that run on your configured provider and may cost money.
These tools send your image (and, where relevant, your prompt and selection) to the AI provider chosen in the provider pills. They need a configured provider key and may incur cost.
If no provider is configured this whole grid is inactive and a note links you to Settings to add one.
Enhance Layer [Cloud AI]: Sends the active layer to the AI and recreates it at much higher quality: sharper, cleaner and more detailed, while keeping the same subject, colors and composition. Use it when the local Enhance is not strong enough.
Enhance Design [Cloud AI]: Flattens the whole canvas as a reference and redesigns it to a professional standard, keeping the layout, text and composition but making it noticeably more polished. The result is added as a new layer on top.
Remove Object [Cloud AI]: Erases the selected area and lets the AI reconstruct what was behind it. First make a selection (Smart Select `K`, or **Select Subject**), then click this. Stronger than the local version for tricky fills. [Requires: A selection]
Inpaint [Cloud AI]: Repaints only the selected area from your prompt; everything outside the selection stays untouched. Steps: select an area, type what should go there in the prompt box, then click this. [Requires: Selection + prompt]
Outpaint [Cloud AI]: Extends the picture outward, inventing more scenery. It fills empty canvas around your image, or enlarges the canvas by 25% per side if it is already full. An optional prompt steers what appears.
Colorize [Cloud AI]: Adds natural, realistic color to a black-and-white photo on the active image layer. Use it to bring old monochrome photos to life.
Cartoon [Cloud AI]: Redraws the active image layer as a clean, vibrant cartoon illustration. Use it to stylize a photo into a drawn look.
Restore Photo [Cloud AI]: Repairs an old or damaged photo on the active layer, removing scratches, dust and noise and improving clarity. Use it on scanned or aged photographs.
Replace BG [Cloud AI]: Cuts out the subject locally, then generates a brand-new background from your prompt behind it. Type the background you want in the prompt box first, then click this. [Requires: Prompt]
Variations [Cloud AI]: Generates alternative takes on the active layer and shows them in a chooser so you can keep the one you like. This tool appears only when an OpenAI provider is configured. [Availability: OpenAI only]
Design Review: A vision model looks at the flattened document like an art director: one overall verdict plus three to six concrete findings (area, issue, suggested fix). The answer comes in the editor language from Settings, Help - independent of the WordPress locale.
Improve Text: Five stronger alternatives for the selected text layer, in the same language and about the same length as the original. Picking one replaces the layer text; undo restores the original.
Editable vector (paths): A checkbox under the Format row: the image model draws the prompt as flat artwork and the local tracer converts it into editable shape layers - real paths, not pixels. Distinct from the Asset Generator, whose text model writes simple SVG directly.

sections.title: AI progress and choices
sections.text:
The working status card, cancel control and the variation chooser that appear while and after AI runs.
While any AI action runs, a status card shows what is happening and lets you cancel. Some actions (like Variations) end by asking you to pick from several results.
Working status card: A small card that floats over the top right of the canvas while an AI action runs. It names the current step (for example `Generating image…` or `Editing layer…`) and reminds you it can take a few seconds.
Cancel [AI]: Stops waiting on the current AI action and hides the status card. If a result still arrives after you cancel, it is discarded rather than applied.
Choose a variation: The dialog that opens after **Variations** finishes. It shows the alternative results in a grid; click (or press Enter on) one to keep it as a new layer. The rest are discarded when you pick or close.

sections.title: History panel
sections.text:
The step-by-step undo stack with time travel, named snapshots, and the saved file versions of an existing image.
Every action you take is recorded as a step, and the last hundred are kept - on very large images fewer, because the stack is also capped by how much memory it holds. Click any step to jump the whole document to that point in time. Hovering a step shows a thumbnail preview of how the canvas looked then.
When you are editing an image that already exists in the Media Library, a **Saved versions** footer lists the file versions saved on the server, and lets you restore an earlier one.
History · N steps: The header of the History panel. It shows how many steps are currently recorded in the session's undo stack.
Snapshot: Saves a named marker of the current state so you can find and return to it easily later. It asks for a name (default `Snapshot`) and adds a pinned entry to the step list.
History step: One entry in the step list, labelled with the action it represents (for example a text, shape, brush or crop operation) and a matching icon. Click it, or press Enter, to time-travel the document to that exact point.
Current step: The step you are currently sitting on is highlighted as the current one. It marks where in history the document is right now.
Future steps: Steps that come after the current one (because you traveled back in time). They are dimmed. Clicking one moves forward to it; doing new work from an earlier point may replace them.
Step preview thumbnail: A small floating image that appears when you hover over a history step, showing how the canvas looked at that step. It helps you find the right point before clicking. Previews are cached so re-hovering is instant.
Saved versions: A footer that appears only when you are editing an image already in the Media Library. It lists the file versions saved on the server, newest first, so you can roll the file back to an earlier save.
Version item: One saved server version, showing its version number, the date and time it was saved, and its file size in kilobytes. Each has a Restore button.
Restore: Rolls the file back to that saved version. It asks you to confirm; the current file becomes a new version first (so nothing is lost) and then the editor reloads on the restored version.
CURRENT: A badge on the last row of the Saved versions list marking the version the file is currently on. It has no Restore button because it is already active.

sections.title: Actions panel
sections.text:
Record sequences of edits, replay them, save reusable looks, share them as JSON, and batch-apply them across many images.
The Actions panel lets you record the operations you perform (filters, effects, adjustments, resize, rotate, flip, flatten) into a reusable action, then replay it on any image with one click.
You can also save just the active layer's filter and adjustments as a **Look**, export and import actions as JSON files to share them, and run an action across many Media Library images at once with Batch Process.
Recorder: The top section of the panel, holding the record controls and the Save Look button. This is where you capture a new action.
Record: Starts recording your edits into a new action. While recording, apply the filters, effects, adjustments and image operations you want to capture; they are listed live below the button.
Stop & Save: Stops recording and asks for a name to save the action under (default `My action`). The button also shows the number of steps captured so far. If nothing was recorded it tells you and saves nothing.
Save Look: Saves the active layer's current filter and adjustments as a reusable look (a single-step action). It suggests the filter's name as the default. Disabled when no layer is active, or if the layer has no filter or adjustments to save. [Requires: An active layer with a filter or adjustments]
Recording step list: The live list shown while recording, with one bullet per captured step. Before you do anything it shows a hint reminding you to apply filters, effects, adjustments, resize, rotate, flip or flatten.
Saved Actions: The middle section listing every action and look you have saved yourself. When it is empty it points at the bundled set below, which works right away: fifty-six ready-made actions in six groups (Web & Sizes, Photo Fixes, Looks & Styles, Artistic, Privacy & AI, Social Formats). Each item you saved can be played, deleted, and is included in Export; the bundled ones can only be played.
Action item: One saved action in the list. It shows a marker (a palette for a look, a play arrow for a recorded action), the name, and the chain of steps it will run. Has its own Play and Delete buttons.
Play: Runs the action's steps on the current document, in order. A spinner shows while it runs, and a success message names the applied action when it finishes. Only one action can play at a time.
Delete (action): Removes one of your own saved actions or looks from the list. It deletes immediately with no confirmation, so use it deliberately. The bundled actions have no delete button; they are part of the plugin.
Export: Downloads the actions you saved yourself as a single JSON file (`wpie-actions.json`). Use it to back up your actions or share them with someone else. The bundled actions are not exported, since every installation already has them. Disabled when you have saved none of your own.
Import: Loads actions from a JSON file (such as one exported earlier) and adds them to your list. It opens a file picker and reports how many actions were imported.
Batch: The bottom section, explaining that you can apply an action to many library images at once.
Batch Process…: Opens the batch dialog, where you pick an action and run it across many Media Library images in one go. Use it to apply the same edit or look to a whole set of photos.

sections.title: AI tool groups (Local vs Cloud)
sections.text:
The AI Studio quick actions are split into two labelled groups by where the work runs.
Below the `Generate` and `Edit Layer` buttons, the quick actions are sorted into two grids under their own headings. The split tells you at a glance which tools are free and private and which ones call a paid provider.
Local tools: Heading over the first grid of quick actions. Everything under it runs entirely in your browser with no API key. The note under the heading reads `These run entirely in your browser, no key needed, and your image never leaves your site.` Use these for fast, private edits at no cost.
AI cloud: Heading over the second grid of quick actions. These call your configured AI provider and may cost money; the note reads `These run on your configured AI provider and may incur cost.` If no provider is set up yet, the note instead says the tools need a provider key and shows an `add one in Settings` link. [Requires: Configured AI provider]
Blur radius (px): A small dialog that opens when you click **Blur Background**. Type how strongly to blur the background behind the subject, in pixels. Higher numbers give a stronger, softer out-of-focus look.

sections.title: Variation picker dialog
sections.text:
The chooser that opens after Variations, where you keep one of four AI takes.
Running **Variations** opens a `Choose a variation` dialog with a grid of alternatives generated from the active layer. You keep exactly one.
Variation: Each image tile in the `Choose a variation` dialog is one AI alternative of the active layer. Click a tile to keep that one as a new layer; the other tiles are discarded.
Pick the variation to keep; the rest are discarded.: The subtitle under the dialog title. It reminds you that choosing one tile throws the other options away, so there is no way to keep several at once.
Close: The X button in the top corner of the `Choose a variation` dialog. It closes the dialog without keeping any variation. Clicking the dark area outside the dialog does the same thing.

sections.title: History panel dialogs and version details
sections.text:
The naming and confirmation dialogs behind the Snapshot and Restore buttons, plus the saved-version metadata.
Two buttons in the History panel open extra dialogs, and each saved version carries a small metadata line.
