Chrome knot: A polished chrome torus knot turning under band lighting, its highlights tinted by the palette.
Crystal shards: Floating crystal shards with thin-film dispersion that shifts color with the viewing angle.
Cube ocean: A field of cubes riding a wave, each instance offset in phase - a rolling geometric ocean.

sections.title: Motifs: Lens & film
sections.text:
Seven camera-optics and celluloid motifs: lens flare, light leaks, star glints, sunbeam dust, spotlight sweep, film burn and film dust.
The Lens & film family recreates what real cameras and film prints do to light. These motifs shine as overlays: they add the optics of a movie shot on top of a photo or design without touching the artwork itself.
Lens flare: A hot light source with a star burst, halo ring and anamorphic streak, plus a chain of iris ghosts (hexagons, rings, discs) mirrored through the frame center. The source orbits once per loop so the whole chain glides across the frame.
Light leaks: Big warm washes of light breathing at the frame edges, plus one leak sweeping through the frame once per loop - the classic analog film-scan look.
Star glints: Cross-shaped star-filter sparkles that flare up one after another over a soft heart glow - the jewellery-commercial twinkle.
Sunbeam dust: A volumetric light shaft from a top corner with dust motes drifting and twinkling inside it - the projector-room look. Size widens the beam, Amount adds dust.
Spotlight sweep: Stage spotlights sweeping from above, their cones crossing over a soft floor haze like a premiere night. Amount sets the number of beams.
Film burn: Celluloid catching heat: a smouldering frame edge with burn spots that bloom and fade in their own loop windows, plus a subtle projector gate flicker.
Film dust & scratches: Old-print damage: scratch lines that jump position with each projector frame, drifting hairs, dust specks and a gentle gate flicker. Pairs with the Grain slider for a complete vintage print.

sections.title: Insert & export
sections.text:
Insert the effect as an editable layer, or export a seamless WebM loop or a live HTML snippet.
The footer holds the output actions. Inserting adds a still frame as an editable generator layer you can reopen and tweak later. The exports produce a looping video file or a self-contained embed that plays the live effect on your site.
Insert background: The primary button in Background mode. Inserts the effect as a new full-document image layer, remembering all settings so you can reopen and edit it later.
Insert overlay: The primary button in Overlay mode. Inserts the effect as a new transparent overlay layer on top of your design, remembering all settings for later editing.
Update layer: The primary button when you reopened an existing effect layer to edit it. Rebakes the still and saves the new settings back into that same layer. [Shown when: Editing an existing effect layer]
WebM loop: Records the animation as a seamless WebM video file and downloads it as `3d-effects-loop.webm`. Use this for a looping video background.
HTML snippet: Copies a small HTML snippet to your clipboard that plays the live, interactive effect on your website. Paste it into an HTML block. Hidden if the extension's runtime file cannot be located.
Cancel: Closes the studio without inserting or changing anything.
Close: The x in the header closes the studio, the same as Cancel.

sections.title: Effect families (menu groups)
sections.text:
The optgroup headings that split the eighty-plus motifs into fifteen families inside the Effect dropdown.
When you open the **Effect** dropdown on an effect layer, the motifs are grouped under fifteen family headings. The headings themselves are not selectable, they just organize the list so you can find a motif faster.
Energy: Group heading for the high-voltage motifs: lightning, lasers, pulse waves, electric arcs, energy orb, fireworks and electron orbitals. Pick from here when you want charged, glowing bursts.
Particle forms: Group heading for shaped particle clouds: wave grid, particle sphere, warp tunnel, plexus net, starfield and DNA helix. Use these for structured, geometric point fields.
Light: Group heading for beam and glow motifs: god rays, anamorphic flares, aurora, light pillars and bokeh lights. Choose these for soft cinematic lighting.
Atmosphere: Group heading for ambience motifs: fog banks, nebula, sparks and embers, smoke and neon rain.
Cosmos: Group heading for space motifs: black hole, supernova, neon planet, debris field, meteor shower, galaxy spiral, solar surface, comet and pulsar beacon. The largest family.
Retro sci-fi: Group heading for retro-futuristic looks: synthwave grid, time tunnel, fractal morph, glyph rain, portal and tesseract.
Wonders: Group heading for the particle-formation pair (build and dissolve your text or layer) plus lava metaballs.
Fluid & material: Group heading for liquid and surface motifs: ferrofluid, liquid chrome, ink bloom and caustics.
Sci-fi & tech: Group heading for interface motifs: HUD hologram, glitch datamosh, circuit flow, radar sweep and hex pulse.
Light, color & music: Group heading for spectral motifs: prism split, holo foil, neon sign, music visualizer and chroma rings.
Motion & organic: Group heading for kinetic motifs: crystal shatter, mobius ribbon, fireflies, falling petals, flames, light trails and firefly swarm.
Waves & audio: Group heading for wave motifs: audio waveform, neon silk waves, wave field visualizer, dot wave, neon flow lines, spectrum bars and water ripples.
Volumetric: Group heading for the raymarched volume motifs: volumetric storm, gyroid structure and liquid metal blobs.
Sculpted objects: Group heading for sculpted 3D showpieces: chrome knot, crystal shards and cube ocean.
Lens & film: Group heading for camera-optics and celluloid motifs: lens flare, light leaks, star glints, sunbeam dust, spotlight sweep, film burn and film dust.

sections.title: Blend (per effect)
sections.text:
The four blend modes in the per-layer Blend dropdown that set how each effect combines with the layers beneath it.
Every effect layer in the stack has its own **Blend** dropdown. It controls how that layer's pixels mix with whatever is drawn below it in the stack.
Add: Adds the effect's light to the layers below, so colors build up and glow brighter. This is the default and suits most glowing motifs.
Screen: Lightens the layers underneath but never blows fully to white, a gentler version of Add. Reach for it when Add looks too hot.
Normal: Draws the effect straight over the layers below with no lightening, using only its own opacity. Use it when you want the effect to cover rather than glow.
Multiply: Darkens by multiplying with the layers below, so bright areas survive and dark areas deepen. Handy for smoke or shadowy overlays.

sections.title: Backdrop options
sections.text:
The choices in the Backdrop dropdown that set the dark background behind a Background-mode effect.
The **Backdrop** dropdown only appears in **Background** mode (it is hidden for overlays, which stay transparent). It picks the dark gradient the effect sits on.
Palette bg: Uses the dark background gradient that ships with the chosen palette, so the backdrop always matches your colors. This is the first option in the list.
Midnight: A deep blue-black gradient, good for cool or icy palettes.
Charcoal: A neutral near-black gradient that stays out of the way of any palette.
Black: A pure flat black backdrop. Best when you want the effect to float on nothing.
Custom: Lets you pick your own backdrop color with the editor's color picker. Selecting it reveals a color button next to the dropdown.

sections.title: Camera move options
sections.text:
The four motion paths in the Camera move dropdown that animate the viewpoint over the loop.
The **Camera move** dropdown makes the whole viewpoint drift over one loop, on top of whatever the effect is doing. It always returns to the start so the loop stays seamless.
Static: The camera holds still and only the effect animates. This is the default.
360° orbit: The camera circles the scene once per loop for a full turntable spin.
Pendulum: The camera swings gently left, then right and back, like a slow pendulum.
Dolly: The camera pushes in and pulls back along its view axis for a breathing depth move.

sections.title: Distortion (refraction) options
sections.text:
Six refraction fields that warp the finished image: off, heat haze, water ripple, glass, shockwave and gravity lens.
**Distortion** applies a refraction warp across the finished frame, as if the image were seen through a moving lens. It affects the whole scene, not one layer.
Off: No refraction; the scene renders crisp. This is the default.
Heat haze: Warps the image with a rising, shimmering heat-haze ripple.
Water ripple: Adds concentric water-like ripples that bend the picture outward.
Glass: Bends the scene as if seen through rippled or frosted glass.
Shockwave: Sends an expanding ring of distortion outward, like a blast wave passing through the frame.
Gravity lens: A gravitational lens: space swirls around an orbiting singularity whose dark horizon swallows the light behind a bright photon ring.

sections.title: Shape mask options
sections.text:
The choices in the Shape mask dropdown that clip the effect inside a shape or word.
**Shape mask** clips the whole effect so it only shows inside a chosen window. Everything outside the shape is hidden, which turns any motif into a lit sign or emblem.
Off: The effect fills the whole frame with no clipping. This is the default.
Circle: Clips the effect inside a soft circle, hiding everything outside it.
Heart: Clips the effect inside a heart outline.
Star: Clips the effect inside a five-point star.
Text: Clips the effect inside your own word or letters. Choosing it reveals the Mask text field where you type the word.

sections.title: Particle formation source
sections.text:
The two source-type buttons shown when a layer's motif is Particle formation.
When an effect layer is set to the **Particle formation** motif, a **Source** switch appears. It decides what shape the particles gather into.
Text: Builds the particle formation from a word you type into the text field below the switch. This is the default source.
Layer: Builds the particle formation from the outline of a captured editor layer instead of text. Press `Use active layer` to grab the layer selected in the editor, then the particles form its shape.

sections.title: Loop length options
sections.text:
The three loop durations in the Loop switch that set how long one seamless cycle lasts.
The **Loop** switch sets how many seconds one full seamless cycle takes before it repeats. Shorter loops feel more energetic, longer ones calmer.
3s: A short three-second cycle for snappier, more energetic repeats.
5s: The default five-second cycle, a balanced pace.
8s: The longest eight-second cycle for slower, calmer motion.

sections.title: Kaleidoscope segment options
sections.text:
The segment counts in the Kaleidoscope switch that mirror the frame into symmetric wedges.
**Kaleidoscope** mirrors the finished frame into equal wedges around the center, turning any motif into a symmetric, mandala-like pattern.
Off: No mirroring; the scene plays normally. This is the default.
2×: Mirrors the frame into two symmetric halves.
3×: Mirrors into three symmetric wedges.
4×: Mirrors into four wedges.
6×: Mirrors into six wedges.
8×: Mirrors into eight wedges for a dense, mandala-like symmetry.

sections.title: Color cycle options
sections.text:
The rotation counts in the Color cycle switch that shift every color around the hue wheel over the loop.
**Color cycle** rotates all of the effect's colors around the hue wheel across one loop, so the palette slowly shifts through a rainbow and returns to where it started.
Off: Colors stay as set by the palette. This is the default.
1×: Rotates every color once fully around the hue wheel over one loop.
2×: Two full hue rotations per loop, a faster rainbow shift.
3×: Three full hue rotations per loop, the fastest color churn.

sections.title: Beat pulse options
sections.text:
The pulse rates in the Beat pulse switch that throb the brightness in time like a beat.
**Beat pulse** pumps the overall brightness up and down a set number of times per loop, so the effect feels like it is reacting to a beat.
Off: Brightness stays steady. This is the default.
2: Two brightness pulses per loop, a slow throb.
4: Four pulses per loop.
8: Eight pulses per loop, a fast, strobe-like beat.

sections.title: Side panel groups
sections.text:
The five card headings that organize the controls down the right side of the studio.
The right-hand panel is split into labelled cards. Each heading groups a set of related controls.
Surprise: The card holding the `Surprise me!` button and its color lock. One click rolls a fresh curated look.
Favorites: The card that stores looks you keep with the star button. It stays empty, showing a short note, until you save your first favorite.
Presets: The card of ready-made recipes (Thunderfront, Hyperspace and so on) that you can load in one click.
Effects: The stack card where you add, tune and remove effect layers. Its heading shows the current layer count, for example `Effects · 2`.
Look: The card with the palette, backdrop, finish (bloom, vignette, grain) and every global toggle such as camera move, kaleidoscope and distortion.

sections.title: Other controls
sections.text:
Smaller controls and behaviours not covered elsewhere: the surprise color lock, the seed reroll dice and the inserted layer name.
Random colors: The default choice in the `Colors` lock under the Surprise button: each surprise also rolls a random palette. Switch it to a Brand Kit or a named palette instead so every surprise stays on your colors.
Reroll seed: The small dice button beside the Seed field. It rolls a new random seed and re-renders, giving the current effects a fresh random arrangement without touching any slider.
3D Effects: The name given to the layer that is added to your document when you insert an effect. Look for `3D Effects` in the Layers panel to find or re-edit it later.

sections.title: Studio overview and dialog
sections.text:
A fullscreen motion studio that composes animated reels, intros and overlays on a real timeline, fully local WebGL with no AI and no uploads.
A motion studio inside the editor: compose animated reels, intros and overlays on a real timeline, fully local WebGL with no uploads. Six clip types stack in front of each other: extruded 3D text in premium materials, particle text that gathers out of stardust and disperses again, images with Ken Burns moves and slide transitions, animated backdrops borrowed from the Cinematic Effects motifs, and gradient shapes.
Every clip gets an entrance, an idle behaviour and an exit with proper easing, positioned by dragging bars on the timeline. Pick a platform format such as Reel, Story, Square or widescreen, or simply use the document size, then scrub and play.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Export a WebM video, insert a still as an editable layer, or drop a transparent overlay onto your design.
Motion Graphics (title): The dialog header shows the studio name and a short subtitle. In edit mode the subtitle reads `Adjust the animation, the layer updates in place`, otherwise it describes reels, intros and overlays.
Close: The X button in the top right closes the studio without inserting anything. Clicking the dark backdrop or pressing Escape does the same.
Scrub or click the ruler · space = play/pause: A hint shown over the preview. It reminds you that you can drag or click the time ruler to scrub, and that the spacebar starts and stops playback.
Preview drag to move: Click a clip directly in the preview frame to select it, then drag to reposition it. Clicking an empty area of the preview deselects the current clip and brings back the Scene panel.
Undo (keyboard): Steps back one change across the whole scene. Every completed edit is snapshotted, so undo reliably returns the previous state.
Redo (keyboard): Re-applies a change you just undid.
The video records in real time - keep this tab focused.: A note in the footer. Because export captures the live preview frame by frame, switching away from the tab can drop frames or stall the recording.

sections.title: Format, duration and playback toolbar
sections.text:
The toolbar above the timeline sets the canvas format and length, controls playback, and holds undo, redo and timeline zoom.
This strip sits at the top of the timeline area. It defines the overall shape and duration of the reel and gives you transport controls.
Scenes run at a fixed 30 frames per second.
Format: A dropdown that sets the canvas aspect ratio and pixel size for the whole scene. Changing it resizes the preview and re-fits everything.
Reel 9:16: Tall vertical format for Reels, Stories and TikTok. Sets the canvas to 1080 by 1920 pixels.
Square 1:1: Square format for feed posts. Sets the canvas to 1080 by 1080 pixels.
Post 4:5: Portrait feed format. Sets the canvas to 1080 by 1350 pixels.
Wide 16:9: Landscape format for YouTube, headers and presentations. Sets the canvas to 1920 by 1080 pixels.
Document: Matches the exact width and height of the image you are editing, so the animation fits your current document.
Duration: A number field that sets how long the whole reel runs, in seconds. Clip bars that extend past the new end are clamped.
Play / Pause: Toggles preview playback. The icon switches between a play triangle and a pause bar. The spacebar does the same.
Time readout: Shows the current playhead position and the total duration, for example `2.4s / 8.0s`.
Undo: Steps back one change. Disabled when there is nothing earlier to return to.
Redo: Re-applies the last undone change. Disabled at the top of the history.
Timeline zoom out: Shrinks the timeline back towards the default width so you see the whole reel at once.
Timeline zoom in: Stretches the timeline wider so short clips and fine timing are easier to grab and adjust.

sections.title: Add clip bar
sections.text:
Six buttons that drop a new clip of a given type onto the timeline at the playhead.
The `Add clip` row holds one button per clip type. A new clip starts at the current playhead position and runs for about four seconds (clamped to the scene length), then becomes the selected clip so its properties open on the right.
A scene can hold up to twelve clips.
3D text: Adds an extruded 3D text clip, the kind used for big titles and logos. It starts with the word `HELLO`.
Caption: Adds a flat caption clip (a 2D text line or label) for subtitles, tags and small copy.
Particle text: Adds particle text that gathers out of a cloud of points into a word and can disperse again.
Image: Adds an image clip with optional mask and Ken Burns moves. You pick the picture after adding it.
Effect: Adds an animated effect backdrop drawn from the shared effect motif catalog (embers, aurora, galaxy and many more).
Shape: Adds a solid or gradient shape (rectangle or ellipse) for panels, bars and color blocks.

sections.title: Timeline (clip bars, ruler, rows)
sections.text:
The lower panel where clips appear as bars you drag to move, resize by the ends, and scrub with the ruler.
Each clip is one row. The top row is the front-most clip in the stack. Drag the middle of a bar to move it in time, or drag either end handle to change its start or end. The time ruler along the top scrubs the playhead.
Dragging snaps magnetically to the scene edges and to the start and end of every other clip, so cuts line up cleanly. Timing also snaps to a tenth-of-a-second grid.
Time ruler: The strip of second marks along the top of the timeline. Click or drag it to move the playhead to any moment. Scrubbing pauses playback.
Clip bar (move): The colored bar for a clip. Drag its body to slide the clip earlier or later without changing its length.
Left handle: The grip on the left edge of a bar. Drag it to change the clip start. The start cannot pass within 0.2 seconds of the end.
Right handle: The grip on the right edge of a bar. Drag it to change the clip end. The end cannot pass within 0.2 seconds of the start.
Magnetic snapping: While dragging, edges jump to nearby snap points: the scene start, the scene end, and the start and end of every other clip. This makes clips butt up or align without fiddling.
Row label and selection: Each row shows the clip type icon and a name (the clip text, effect motif, or a custom name). Click the label to select the clip and open its properties. Click the active row again to deselect and return to the Scene panel.
Move up: The up-arrow on a row moves the clip one step forward in the stack, so it draws in front of the next clip.
Move down: The down-arrow moves the clip one step back in the stack, behind the next clip.
Duplicate: Copies the clip with all its settings and drops the copy just after it, shifted about 0.3 seconds later. The copy becomes selected.
Remove clip: Deletes the clip from the scene. If it was selected, the panel returns to the Scene view.

sections.title: Scene panel (backdrop, look, loop, camera)
sections.text:
The panel shown when no clip is selected: it sets the background, the post look, seamless looping and the global camera move.
When nothing is selected, the right panel greets you with Scene settings, the Music track, and the Templates gallery. These apply to the whole reel, not a single clip.
Changing a look setting refreshes the preview after a short debounce.
Backdrop: The solid background color behind all clips. Opens the editor color picker.
Bloom: How much bright parts of the scene glow and bleed light. Higher values give a dreamier, more cinematic look.
Vignette: Darkens the corners of the frame to draw the eye to the center. Higher values mean a stronger, moodier edge.
Seamless loop (full-length clips): When on, clips that span the entire duration are quantized so the first and last frame match exactly, giving a jump-free repeating loop. Best for headers and backgrounds.
Camera: A global camera move applied to the whole scene over its length. Adds life without touching individual clips.
Static: No camera motion. The frame holds still.
Push in: The camera slowly moves closer over the reel, a classic slow zoom for titles and premieres.
Orbit: The camera circles the scene, revealing the 3D depth of text and particles. Pairs well with looping logos.
Drift: A gentle floating drift that keeps the frame subtly alive.

sections.title: Music (audio track)
sections.text:
Add a music or audio track that plays in the preview and is recorded into exported video, with volume, offset, fade and a per-clip beat pulse.
The Music card lives in the Scene panel. Load a track from the media library or your computer. It plays during preview and is captured when you export a video.
A short note above the buttons tells you whether a track is loaded (`Track loaded - plays in preview and export.`) or not (`No music yet - add a track below.`).
Media library (music): Opens the WordPress media library filtered to audio, so you can pick a track already on your site. Shown only when the media library is available.
Upload (music): Opens a file picker to load an audio file from your computer as the track. The file is read directly into the scene.
Remove (music): Clears the loaded track. Shown only once a track is present.
Volume: How loud the track plays in preview and export.
Track offset (s): How many seconds into the audio file playback should begin, so you can skip an intro and start on the part you want.
Fade out at the end: When on, the music fades down to silence as the reel reaches its end instead of cutting off abruptly.
Beat pulse (music): A per-clip checkbox in the clip Timing card. When on, that clip throbs its scale in time with the music, so titles and shapes pulse on the beat. Needs a loaded track to react.

sections.title: Templates (starter reels)
sections.text:
A gallery of ready-made scenes; one click loads a complete, self-contained reel you can then edit.
The Templates card in the Scene panel lists starter reels. Clicking one replaces the whole scene with that template and starts playing so you can see it immediately.
Templates with an image clip use an empty photo placeholder, so you drop your own picture in afterwards. Copy is often shown in German as an example and can be edited on any clip.
Neon Intro: A synthwave-grid backdrop with a zooming `NEON` 3D title and a `NIGHT DRIVE` caption. Good for music and nightlife intros.
Sale Reel: A fiery vertical promo with a bouncing gold `SALE` title and a red discount pill. Built for sale announcements.
Logo Sting: A short square sting where a `LOGO` gathers from particles over a violet galaxy and disperses. A quick brand bumper.
Quote Reel: A calm portrait quote card with a typewritten serif quote over drifting fireflies. Good for inspirational posts.
Product Intro: A vertical product opener with a chrome `NEU` title on an ellipse plate and a call-to-action pill. Drop in a product below.
Epic Trailer: A dark, heavily vignetted trailer with fog, embers and a slow gold `LEGACY` title. Cinematic and dramatic.
Countdown: A 3, 2, 1 neon countdown that bursts into fireworks and a gold `GO!`. For launches and go-live moments.
Photo Reveal: A wide layout with a circle-masked photo sliding in with a Ken Burns move next to a `REVEAL` title. Add your photo.
Split Promo: A split square layout with a rounded photo on one side and a candy `SALE` title plus caption on the other.
Movie Night: A moody cinema look with god rays, smoke and a copper `PREMIERE` title with a gold info pill.
Product Teaser: A square teaser with a rounded product image, a particle `BALD` word and a mono date caption. Add your product.
Tech Intro: A toxic-green circuit and hologram backdrop with a typewritten `SYNTAX` title and a terminal-style caption.
Story Opener: A vertical story cover with an aurora backdrop, a circle-masked photo and a `Es war einmal ...` line. Add your photo.
Game Day: A high-energy sports promo with steel `GAME DAY` text that pulses to the beat and a red kickoff pill.
Memories: A warm keepsake reel that crossfades two rounded photos over fireflies with a floating serif line. Add two photos.
Loop Header: A seamless looping website header with a silk backdrop, a shine-swept gold `STUDIO` title and a floating tagline. Loop and drift camera are on.
Neon Sign: A neon `OPEN` sign that flickers on over a city backdrop with a `24 / 7` caption. For shops and venues.
Glitch Promo: A glitchy tech promo where a steel `SYSTEM` title glitches in on the beat over an electric glitch effect.
Beat Drop: A vertical music reel with audio bars and a wavefield, a candy `DROP` title and captions that pulse to the beat.
Luxury Gold: An elegant wide reel with fireflies, a shine-swept gold `ELEGANCE` title and a small serif subline, with a slow push-in camera.
Chrome Reveal: A square reveal with a chrome `TITAN` title cascading in with a shine sweep and a supporting caption.
Orbit Logo: A seamless looping logo bumper: a particle `LOGO` shimmering over a galaxy while the camera orbits.
Speed Teaser: A fast wide teaser with neon flow and trails, a steel `FASTER` title glitching in, and a drift camera.
Aurora Loop: A seamless vertical loop with an aurora and fireflies and a floating `Nordlichter` serif line. Calm and ambient.
Night Premiere: A portrait premiere card with rays and smoke, a flickering copper `NACHT` title and a showtime pill, with a push-in camera.
Cinematic Title: A film-title look with fog and god rays and a slowly extruding steel `ODYSSEE` title over a credit line.

sections.title: 3D text clip
sections.text:
An extruded 3D text clip for big titles and logos, with the editor's fonts, twelve materials and depth.
Select a 3D text clip to open these controls at the top of the properties panel, above the shared Position, Motion and Timing cards.
3D text supports the richest set of entrance moves, including letter cascades, typewriter, extrude grow, neon flicker and glitch in.
Text: The words to render in 3D. Line breaks are kept.
Font: The typeface for the 3D letters. The list holds the studio's built-in display fonts (Anton, Bebas Neue, Cinzel, DM Serif, Fredoka, Bangers, Lobster, Pacifico and more) plus up to forty of your editor fonts.
Material: The surface look of the extruded letters. Twelve premium presets cover metals, glass, neon and more.
Face color: Overrides the color of the front face of the letters. Opens the editor color picker.
Depth: How far the letters extrude towards the camera. Higher values look chunkier and more three-dimensional.
Spacing: The gap between letters (tracking). Negative values tighten the word, positive values spread it out.
Stagger: How much the per-letter timing is offset during animated entrances like the letter cascade. Higher values make letters arrive more spread out in time.

sections.title: Caption clip (2D text)
sections.text:
A flat text line for subtitles, tags and small copy, with four font families, four styles and an optional pill background.
Select a caption clip (the text2d type) to edit these controls. Captions render as crisp flat text, ideal over photos and effects.
The caption text field is a two-row textarea, so you can add line breaks.
Text (caption): The caption copy. Supports multiple lines.
Font (caption): The font family for the caption.
Sans: A clean sans-serif (Helvetica Neue or Arial). The default, good for most captions.
Display: A heavy display face (Arial Black or Impact) for bold, punchy labels.
Serif: A classic serif (Georgia or Times New Roman) for editorial and elegant lines.
Mono: A monospace face (Courier New) for code, timers and terminal looks.
Style: How the caption is decorated. Choosing Pill reveals a pill color control.
Plain: Plain colored text with no outline, shadow or background.
Outline: Text with a stroked outline for contrast over busy footage.
Shadow: Text with a drop shadow so it stays legible over bright areas.
Pill: Text sits inside a rounded filled pill. Adds a Pill color control for the background.
Color: The text color of the caption.
Pill color: The fill color of the pill background. Shown only when the Pill style is selected.
Size: The caption font size in scene units. Larger values fill more of the frame.

sections.title: Particle text clip
sections.text:
Text that gathers out of a cloud of glowing points and can disperse back into stardust.
Select a particle text clip to edit these controls. It reads best as a short word or two.
Particle text uses the gather entrance and disperse exit, with a shimmer idle.
Text (particle): The short word the particles form. Kept brief for a clean gather effect.
Color (particle): The color of the particles.
Density: How many particles make up the text. Higher values give a denser, more solid word but cost more to render.
Particle size: The size of each point. Larger particles look bolder and blur together, smaller ones look finer and more starry.

sections.title: Image clip
sections.text:
A photo clip with an optional mask, Ken Burns and pan idle moves, and three ways to load the picture.
Select an image clip to edit these controls. Until you load a picture, a note reads `No image yet - import one below.` and the import buttons appear.
Image clips can slide, zoom and fade in, and their idle behaviours include Ken Burns push and pull and sideways or vertical pans.
Mask: Crops the image into a shape. Use it to make circular avatars, rounded cards or soft ellipses.
None (mask): No mask, the full rectangular image is shown.
Circle: Crops to a perfect circle, ideal for profile photos and logos.
Rounded: Crops to a rounded rectangle for a soft card look.
Ellipse: Crops to an oval that follows the image aspect.
Image preview: Once a picture is loaded, a thumbnail preview of it shows in the panel so you can confirm the right image is set.
Media library (image): Opens the WordPress media library filtered to images. Prefers the large size of the chosen picture. Shown only when the media frame is available.
Active layer: Captures the currently selected layer from the editor and uses it as the image, so you can animate a design element you already made. Warns if no layer is selected.
Upload (image): Opens a file picker to load an image from your computer.

sections.title: Effect clip (motif backdrop)
sections.text:
An animated effect backdrop that draws any of the sixty-plus Cinematic Effects motifs, colored by palette or a custom color.
Select an effect clip to edit these controls. Effect clips are usually the bottom of the stack, providing an animated background behind text and photos.
The motif list is the shared effect catalog: over sixty motifs across families such as Energy, Light, Atmosphere, Cosmos, Retro, Wonders, Fluid and Waves. Effects run a continuous native loop as their idle, so they never freeze.
Motif: Which effect to draw. The dropdown offers the full motif catalog (embers, aurora, galaxy, fog, synthwave grid, fireworks, audio bars and many more), excluding the standalone particle formation motif.
Palette: The color scheme the motif uses.
Intensity: How strong and dense the effect is (its amount of particles, brightness or coverage). Higher fills the frame more.
Size: The scale of the effect features, for example particle size or pattern scale.
Tempo: How fast the effect animates. Higher values move quicker.
Custom color: Tints the effect with a single color of your choice, overriding the palette. Opens the editor color picker.
Palette colors: A button that clears the custom color and returns the effect to its palette coloring.

sections.title: Shape clip
sections.text:
A solid or gradient rectangle or ellipse for panels, bars, plates and color blocks.
Select a shape clip to edit these controls. Shapes are handy as backing plates behind text, split-screen panels or lower-third bars.
Give the same color to both color fields for a flat fill, or two different colors for a gradient.
Shape: Whether the clip is a rectangle or an ellipse.
Color: The main fill color, and the start color of a gradient.
Gradient to: The second color for a gradient fill. Set it the same as Color for a flat fill.
Width: The shape width as a percentage of the frame.
Height: The shape height as a percentage of the frame.
Corner: The corner rounding for a rectangle. Higher values round the corners more. Has no visible effect on an ellipse.

sections.title: Position and transform (per clip)
sections.text:
The Position card shared by every clip: place it in the frame, scale it, rotate it flat or in full 3D, and set its opacity.
The Position card appears for every selected clip, below the type-specific controls. Values are percentages of the frame or degrees.
The two 3D rotation sliders turn the clip in space, which is especially striking on 3D text and shapes.
X: Horizontal position of the clip. Negative moves left, positive moves right. You can also drag the clip in the preview.
Y: Vertical position of the clip. Negative moves down, positive moves up.
Scale: The overall size of the clip as a percentage. 100 is normal, higher enlarges, lower shrinks.
Rotation: Flat in-plane rotation (roll), spinning the clip like a clock hand.
Turn (3D): Yaw: turns the clip left and right around its vertical axis, showing its 3D side. Great on extruded text.
Tilt (3D): Pitch: tips the clip forward or back around its horizontal axis.
Opacity: How see-through the clip is. 100 is fully opaque, 0 is invisible.

sections.title: Motion drift (per clip)
sections.text:
The Motion card animates a clip from its base transform to an end offset across its whole length, a lightweight keyframe move.
The Motion card appears for every selected clip, below the Position card. It adds a slow continuous drift on top of the entrance and exit, so a clip can gently move or grow while it is on screen.
Set any drift to zero to leave that axis unchanged.
Drift X: How far the clip slides horizontally from start to end of the clip. Positive drifts right, negative drifts left.
Drift Y: How far the clip slides vertically over its length. Positive drifts up, negative drifts down.
Drift scale: How much the clip grows or shrinks over its length. Positive values slowly enlarge it, negative values shrink it.
Easing (motion): The speed curve of the drift, controlling whether the move accelerates, decelerates or runs steadily.

sections.title: Timing (entrance, idle, exit)
sections.text:
The Timing card shared by every clip: it shows the clip's start and end and sets its entrance, idle and exit animations with duration, easing and speed.
The Timing card appears for every selected clip. The available entrance, idle and exit animations differ by clip type, so the dropdowns only list moves that make sense for that clip.
The idle clock starts only after the entrance finishes, so a looping idle does not fight the reveal.
Start / End: A read-only readout of when the clip begins and ends, for example `0.4s - 7.6s`. Change these by dragging the clip bar on the timeline.
Entrance: How the clip appears at its start. The options depend on the clip type (for example 3D text can rise, drop, zoom, cascade, typewriter, extrude grow, flicker or glitch in).
Anim duration (entrance): How long the entrance animation takes, in seconds. It is capped to at most 60 percent of the clip length.
Easing (entrance): The speed curve of the entrance, from a smooth glide to an overshoot or a bounce.
While: The idle behaviour that plays continuously while the clip is on screen, after the entrance. Options depend on type (for example float, wobble, spin, pulse, shine for 3D text, or Ken Burns and pans for images).
Speed: How fast the idle behaviour animates. Higher values move quicker.
Exit: How the clip leaves at its end. Options depend on type (for example fade, fall away, zoom or spin for 3D text, disperse for particle text).
Anim duration (exit): How long the exit animation takes, in seconds. It is capped to at most 60 percent of the clip length.
Beat pulse (music): When on, the clip throbs its scale in time with the loaded music track. Needs a track to react.

sections.title: Easing curves
sections.text:
The six speed curves offered by every easing dropdown (entrance, exit and motion drift).
Easing shapes how an animation accelerates and decelerates. The same six curves appear wherever an Easing control is shown.
Smooth out: Starts fast and eases to a gentle stop. The default for most entrances and exits.
Smooth in-out: Eases in and out, slow at both ends and quick in the middle. Feels balanced and natural.
Smooth in: Starts slow and accelerates into the move. Good for exits that speed away.
Overshoot: Overshoots the target slightly then settles back, giving a snappy, springy feel.
Bounce: Lands with a bouncing settle, like an object dropping and rebounding.
Linear: Constant speed with no acceleration. Best for typewriter and mechanical moves.

sections.title: Animation catalog (entrance, idle, exit moves)
sections.text:
Every named animation move that can appear in the Entrance, While (idle) and Exit dropdowns, with what each does and which clips offer it.
The Entrance, While and Exit dropdowns list moves that suit the clip type, so not every move appears on every clip. This catalog explains each one.
Entrance and exit moves have a duration and easing; idle moves have a speed.
None: No animation for that slot. The clip simply appears, holds, or cuts out with no move. Available on every clip and every slot.
Fade: Fades opacity in or out. The most universal entrance and exit, available on every clip type.
Rise up: 3D text rises up into place from below as it enters.
Drop in: 3D text drops in from above, often paired with a bounce easing.
Zoom: Scales the clip up on entry or away on exit. Available on 3D text, captions and images.
Spin: Rotates the clip. As an idle it spins continuously; as an exit it spins away. Used by 3D text.
Letter cascade: 3D text letters arrive one after another in a staggered cascade. The Stagger control tunes the spread.
Typewriter: Reveals the text character by character like typing. Available on 3D text and captions. Pairs best with Linear easing.
Extrude grow: 3D text grows its depth from flat to full extrusion as it enters, a slow cinematic build.
Neon flicker: 3D text flickers on like a neon sign warming up.
Glitch in: 3D text glitches and jitters into place with a digital distortion.
Particle gather: Particle text gathers out of a scattered cloud into the word.
Particle disperse: Particle text scatters back into drifting points as it leaves.
Slide left: The clip slides in from the right, moving left into place (or off to the left on exit). Available on captions, images and shapes.
Slide right: The clip slides in from the left, moving right into place (or off to the right on exit). Available on captions, images and shapes.
Slide up: The clip slides in from below (or out upward on exit). Available on captions and images.
Wipe: A shape wipes open to reveal itself, like a growing bar.
Fall away: 3D text falls away out of frame as it exits.
Float: A gentle continuous floating bob while the clip is on screen. Idle for 3D text and captions.
Wobble: A soft wobbling sway. Idle for 3D text.
Pulse: A steady scale pulse (breathing). Idle for 3D text, captions and shapes.
Shimmer: Particles twinkle and shimmer while the word holds. Idle for particle text.
Shine sweep: A bright highlight sweeps across the 3D letters, like light glinting off metal. Idle for 3D text.
Ken Burns in: Slowly pushes into the photo (zoom in) while it holds. Idle for images.
Ken Burns out: Slowly pulls back from the photo (zoom out) while it holds. Idle for images.
Pan sideways: Slowly pans the photo left and right. Idle for images.
Pan vertical: Slowly pans the photo up and down. Idle for images.
Native loop: The only idle for effect clips: the effect runs its own continuous animation loop so the backdrop is always moving.

sections.title: Export and insert (footer)
sections.text:
The footer actions: cancel, export a WebM video, save the video to the media library, copy an HTML embed, and insert the result as a still or transparent overlay.
The footer holds every way to get your reel out of the studio. Video is recorded from the live preview in real time, so keep the tab focused while it records.
Insert actions add a still frame to your design as a layer that stays editable, since the scene is stored with the layer and reopens in this studio.
Cancel: Closes the studio without inserting or exporting anything.
Export video: Records the reel (with music) and downloads it as a WebM video file. The button shows `Recording…` while it captures in real time.
Video to library: Records the reel and uploads it straight into your WordPress media library instead of downloading it, ready to attach to posts.
HTML snippet: Copies an HTML embed snippet to your clipboard. Paste it into an HTML block on your site to run the scene live and looping in the browser (audio is stripped from the embed). Hidden if the runtime script is unavailable.
Insert overlay: Inserts a still frame with a transparent background as a layer, so the animation motifs sit on top of your existing design.
Insert still / Update layer: The primary button. For a new scene it inserts the current frame as an editable image layer centered in the document. When editing an existing studio layer it reads `Update layer` and rewrites that layer in place.

sections.title: Add clip and timeline interactions
sections.text:
The controls that create new clips and the click and drag interactions in the preview and on the timeline that were not covered elsewhere.
The **Add clip** row sits in the timeline toolbar. Next to it, the preview frame and the timeline both respond to clicks: you can grab a clip right in the frame, click empty space to step back to the Scene panel, or click an empty part of a track to move the playhead.
Add clip: A toolbar row with six buttons, one per clip type (`3D text`, `Caption`, `Particle text`, `Image`, `Effect`, `Shape`). Clicking a button drops a new clip of that type onto the timeline and selects it so its properties open on the right.
Click a clip in the preview: Clicking directly on a clip in the preview frame selects it and opens its properties, the same as clicking its timeline row. This is the pick step that precedes dragging it to a new spot.
Click empty preview to deselect: Clicking an empty part of the preview (where no clip sits) clears the selection and brings the Scene, Music and Templates panel back on the right. Use it to get out of a clip's properties quickly.
Click empty track to scrub: Clicking an empty area of any clip's timeline row (not on the clip bar itself) moves the playhead to that time and pauses playback. It is the same scrub you get from the time ruler, available on every row.
Playhead: The vertical line across the timeline that marks the current time. It tracks playback and moves when you scrub the ruler or a track, and its position stays in step with the timeline zoom.
Escape: Pressing the Escape key closes the studio without inserting anything, the same as the Close or Cancel buttons. Any unsaved animation in the dialog is discarded.

sections.title: 3D text materials
sections.text:
The full option list of the Material dropdown on a 3D text clip, twelve surface presets that set how the extruded letters catch light.
The **Material** control on a `3D text` clip picks one of twelve surface presets. Each preset sets the base look (metal, glass, glow and so on). You can still override the front tint with the **Face color** control after choosing a material.
These are the same twelve presets as the 3D Text Studio extension.
Gold: Warm, reflective gold metal. This is the default material for a new 3D text clip and suits premium, luxury or celebratory titles.
Chrome: A polished, mirror-like silver metal that reflects the scene around it. Good for sleek, high-tech or automotive looks.
Copper: A warm reddish-brown metal, softer and more vintage than gold or chrome. Fits retro, artisan or premiere styling.
Steel: A cool grey brushed-metal look with muted reflections. Works for industrial, sports or utilitarian headlines.
Glass: A clear, transparent glass surface that lets the backdrop show through the letters. Use it for light, airy or elegant titles.
Frosted: A translucent, matte frosted-glass look, softer and cloudier than clear glass. Good for gentle, premium overlays.
Neon: A glowing, emissive neon-tube look that reads as its own light source. Best on dark backdrops for nightlife, gaming or club styling.
Gloss: A shiny, colored lacquer or plastic finish with a bright highlight. A versatile, punchy look that takes the Face color well.
Matte: A flat, non-reflective finish with no highlights. Use it when you want the text color to stay even and calm without glare.
Candy: A bright, glossy candy-coat look with a saturated, playful sheen. Suits fun, youthful or promotional titles.
Hologram: An iridescent, rainbow holographic surface that shifts color across the letters. Great for tech, futuristic or Y2K styling.
Gradient: A two-tone color gradient that blends across the letters instead of a single flat tint. Use it for modern, colorful headlines.

sections.title: Shape type
sections.text:
The two options inside the Shape dropdown on a shape clip.
A `Shape` clip draws a solid or gradient block behind or beside your text. The **Shape** dropdown chooses its outline.
Rectangle: Draws the shape clip as a rectangle. This is the default. Combine it with the Corner control to round its edges into a pill or card.
Ellipse: Draws the shape clip as an oval or ellipse instead of a rectangle. Use it for badges, spotlights or soft backing shapes. This is the shape outline, separate from the image Mask ellipse option.

sections.title: Notes and status messages
sections.text:
The inline hints, empty-state notes and feedback messages the studio shows, none of which are buttons but each of which tells you the current state.
These strings appear in panels, on export buttons and as toasts. They are not controls you click, but they explain what the studio is doing or what it needs from you.
Adjust the animation, the layer updates in place.: The subtitle shown under the title when you reopen the studio on an existing 3D Animation layer. It signals edit mode: your changes overwrite that layer instead of adding a new one, and the primary button reads `Update layer`.
Track loaded - plays in preview and export.: A note in the Music panel confirming a music track is attached. The track plays during preview and is recorded into the exported video.
No music yet - add a track below.: The empty-state note in the Music panel when no audio is attached. Use the Media library or Upload buttons below it to add a track.
No image yet - import one below.: The empty-state note inside an Image clip's properties when it has no picture. Pick one with Media library, Active layer or Upload.
Recording…: The temporary label shown on the Export video and Video to library buttons while the reel is being captured. Recording happens in real time, so the wait roughly matches the clip's duration.
Select a layer in the editor first.: An error toast shown when you press Active layer inside an Image clip but no layer is selected back in the editor. Select a layer, then try again to pull it in as the clip's picture.
Motion Graphics needs WebGL.: An error toast shown if the studio cannot start because the browser or device has no working WebGL. The dialog closes because the 3D preview and export both require it.

sections.title: 3D Mockup Studio (overview)
sections.text:
A real-time three.js studio that wraps your design onto a 3D product model, then bakes it into the document as a transparent PNG layer.
Real-time 3D product mockups rendered in your browser: over a hundred models from smartphones, laptops and smart TVs to mugs, cans, bottles, bags, books, boxes, apparel, gift cards and podium staging, plus composed e-commerce hero scenes such as an unboxing, a skincare podium or a drink line-up with per-can artwork.
Fit and position your artwork per surface, or feed it from dynamic templates so a whole catalog can wear its own designs in automation runs. Orbit freely to the exact angle, tune shadow blur, length and direction, and add a ground reflection.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert the scene as a transparent PNG layer, bake a full 360-degree turntable as a sprite-sheet layer, download a self-contained drag-to-rotate HTML viewer, or export single frames for 360 player plugins. Everything stays editable via **Edit Mockup**.
Insert 3D Mockup: Opens the studio to build a new mockup. Your currently active layer is loaded as the starting artwork, and the model defaults to the smartphone.
Edit 3D Mockup: Reopens the studio on an existing mockup layer with the exact model, artwork, camera, light and finish it was baked with. Adjust anything and the layer updates in place.
3D Models: The mode that shows the parametric 3D model catalogue. This is the only mode available now; it fills the whole side panel with the model picker and its cards.
Drag to orbit: Click and drag inside the viewport to rotate the model. Horizontal drag spins it (Rotate/yaw), vertical drag tilts it (Tilt/pitch).
Wheel to zoom: Scroll the mouse wheel over the viewport to zoom the camera in and out. Zoom is clamped so the model never disappears.
Drag to orbit · wheel to zoom: The hint line shown at the bottom of the viewport, reminding you how to move the camera.
Show document: Toggles a flattened render of your open document behind the transparent mockup, so you judge the mockup over the real design instead of the checkerboard. When editing, the mockup's own layer is left out of that preview.
Close (X): Closes the studio without changing your document. The X sits in the top-right of the dialog header.
Cancel: Closes the studio and discards the mockup you were building. Nothing is inserted or updated.
Escape / click outside: Pressing `Escape`, or clicking the dark backdrop outside the dialog, closes the studio the same way as Cancel.

sections.title: Model picker
sections.text:
Choose which 3D object your artwork is wrapped onto, browsing 106 models across five categories.
The Model card holds a Category dropdown above a grid of thumbnail tiles. Pick a category to filter the grid, then click a tile to switch the model. The active tile is highlighted, and switching models rebuilds the 3D scene instantly.
Category: Filters the model grid to one product family so the plain models never mix with the composed hero scenes. Changing it only hides and shows tiles; it does not change the current model until you pick a tile.
Model tile: Each tile is one model, shown with a thumbnail and its name. Click it to load that model into the viewport; the tile you picked is marked active.

sections.title: Devices models
sections.text:
Screens and gadgets that show your artwork as a self-lit display or wrapped surface.
The Devices category holds eight electronic products. Screen models (phone, tablet, laptop, monitor, TV, watch) render your artwork unlit, exactly as designed, behind a glass sheen. The eReader instead prints it on a matte e-ink page.
Smartphone: A modern smartphone with a metal rail, edge-to-edge screen carrying your artwork, punch-hole selfie camera and a triple-lens back in the chosen body color. This is the model the studio opens on.
Tablet: An aluminium tablet with a uniform bezel; your artwork fills the screen. Good for app and web mockups on a larger display.
eReader: A matte e-ink reader. Your artwork prints on the paper-gray page with no glass gloss, so it reads like electronic paper rather than a backlit screen.
Laptop: An open laptop (lid tilted about 110 degrees) with a painted keyboard and trackpad; your artwork sits on the screen. Ideal for website and dashboard shots.
Monitor: A desktop monitor on a slanted arm and flat foot, with a slim bezel and a power LED in the chin; artwork fills the panel.
Smart TV: A wide flat-panel television on two blade feet; your artwork fills the near bezel-less screen. Best for landscape designs.
Smartwatch: A smartwatch showing your artwork on its rounded watch face. Suited to app icons and compact UI.
Phone Case: A phone case with your artwork printed across the back. Use it for merchandise and accessory designs rather than screen content.

sections.title: Print & Paper models
sections.text:
Flat printed pieces and signage, from postcards and posters to billboards and calendars.
The Print & Paper category holds eighteen printed products. Most take a single artwork on their printed face; a few are parametric (Canvas Print, Acrylic Sign, Clipboard, Desk Calendar) and the Poster Frames trio and Desk Calendar expose separate artwork surfaces.
Report (A4): A single A4 sheet or cover page lying with your artwork printed on it. Good for documents, letters and one-pagers.
Flyer: A printed flyer sheet carrying your artwork. Use it for promo leaflets and handouts.
Postcard: A postcard with your artwork on the face. Smaller and thicker than a flyer.
Sticker: A die-cut sticker with your artwork and a thin border. Good for labels and merch stickers.
Business Cards: A small stack of business cards with your artwork on the top card. Suits branding and identity designs.
Polaroid: An instant photo with the classic thick white border; your artwork fills the photo window.
Poster Frame: A framed poster hanging on a wall; your artwork sits inside the frame. Use it for wall-art and print mockups.
Roll-up Banner: A pull-up exhibition banner standing on its base; your artwork runs the full height. For trade-show and event visuals.
Billboard: A large outdoor billboard panel carrying your artwork. Best for wide advertising layouts.
Envelope: A mailing envelope with your artwork on the front. Pairs well with the Report for stationery sets.
Wall Calendar: A hanging wall calendar; your artwork prints on the top page. For calendar and seasonal designs.
Poster Frames (Trio): Three framed posters side by side, each of which can carry its own artwork via the Left, Center and Right surfaces. Good for a gallery-wall arrangement.
Poster (Clips): A poster held at the edges by metal clips; your artwork fills the sheet.
Poster (Pins): A poster pinned to a board; your artwork fills the sheet. A more casual poster presentation.
Canvas Print: A gallery-wrap canvas with your artwork stretched over the front and edges. Width, Height and Depth are adjustable.
Clipboard: A clipboard holding a stack of sheets with your artwork on top; the Sheets slider sets how thick the paper stack looks.
Acrylic Sign: A standing acrylic sign block with your artwork; Width and Height are adjustable. For reception and desk signage.
Desk Calendar: A wire-O desk calendar tent standing on the desk; the Angle slider opens or closes the tent, and Front and Back are separate artwork surfaces.

sections.title: Books & Cases models
sections.text:
Bound and boxed products: books, media cases and binders, several with adjustable size and multiple surfaces.
The Books & Cases category holds twelve models. The hardcover Book, Software Box and the open books let you set dimensions and place different artwork on each surface (front, spine, back, page spreads). The disc cases and vinyl slide their disc out by a Slide out amount.
Book: A hardcover book you can size with Height, Width and Thickness. By default only the Front carries artwork; the Spine and Back start plain but can each take their own design.
Softcover Book: A softcover (paperback) book with your artwork on the cover. A thinner, more flexible-looking alternative to the hardcover.
Open Book (standing): An open hardcover standing upright with the spread facing you; your artwork is split across the two pages. The Opening slider sets the angle between the halves, and the Outside jacket and Inside spread are separate surfaces.
Open Book (lying): An open book lying flat with the pages facing up; artwork is split across the spread. Opening sets how flat it lies, and here the Inside spread is the main surface with the Outside jacket optional.
Software Box: A retail software or product box; Width, Height and Depth are adjustable. The Front shows your artwork by default, with Spine, Top and Back available as extra surfaces.
DVD Case: A closed DVD keep case with your artwork on the cover. Use the disc variant if you want the disc showing.
CD Jewel Case + Disc: A CD jewel case with the disc sliding out; the Slide out slider sets how far. The Cover and the Disc are separate artwork surfaces.
DVD Case + Disc: A DVD case with the disc sliding out by the Slide out amount; Cover and Disc take their own artwork.
CD Jewel Case: A closed CD jewel case with your artwork on the cover insert.
Spiral Notebook: A spiral-bound notebook with your artwork on the cover. For stationery and branding sets.
Ring Binder: A lever-arch ring binder; the Spine slider sets its width. Your artwork prints on both the Front and the Spine label.
Vinyl Record: An LP record sleeve with the disc sliding out by the Slide out amount; the sleeve Cover and the record Label are separate artwork surfaces.

sections.title: Product & Packaging models
sections.text:
Physical goods and packaging where your artwork becomes a wrapped label, printed panel or fabric print.
The Product & Packaging category holds sixteen models: drinkware, bottles and jars, bags, apparel and shipping packaging. Cylindrical products wrap the artwork as a label band; boxes, pouches and totes print it on a flat face. Several are parametric or expose front/side surfaces.
Mug: A ceramic mug with a cream interior and ear handle; your artwork wraps the front of the body as a printed band, kept clear of the handle.
Coffee Cup (to go): A takeaway paper coffee cup with a lid; your artwork wraps around the cup. For cafe and to-go branding.
Can: An aluminium beverage can with a pull tab; your label wraps almost all the way around the straight wall.
Bottle: A cosmetic or pump-style bottle with a metallic cap; your artwork sits on a label band around the body.
Cosmetic Jar: A squat cosmetic jar with a screw lid; your artwork wraps the body as a label band. For skincare and beauty products.
Cosmetic Tube: A squeezable cosmetic tube with your artwork printed on the body. Pairs with the jar and bottle for beauty ranges.
Shopping Bag: A paper shopping bag with rope handles and an open top; your artwork prints on the front panel.
Tote Bag: A fabric tote bag with your artwork printed on the front. For merch and eco-branding.
Pillow: A soft cushion with a puffed cushion silhouette; the Front carries your artwork by default and the Back is an optional second surface.
Wine Bottle: A wine bottle with a label band carrying your artwork. For beverage and gift branding.
Pouch (stand-up): A stand-up food pouch (doypack) with your artwork on the front. For snacks, coffee and pet food packaging.
Shipping Box: A corrugated shipping box; Width, Depth and Height are adjustable and the Flaps slider opens the lid. Front carries artwork with the Side optional.
T-Shirt: A t-shirt with your artwork printed on the chest; the Width slider adjusts the fit. For apparel and merch.
Candle: A candle in a glass container with a wrapped label; Height and Width are adjustable. For home and spa products.
Pen: A pen with your artwork on the barrel; Length and Width are adjustable. A small promotional item.
Beverage Carton: A gable-top milk or juice carton; Width and Height are adjustable. Front carries artwork with the Side optional.

sections.title: Hero scenes
sections.text:
Ready-made compositions that arrange several models into one shot, each object able to carry its own artwork.
Hero scenes combine multiple models into a single arranged scene (for example a laptop, tablet and phone together). Every object in the scene is exposed as its own artwork surface, so you can give each one a different design through the per-surface pickers. By default each object uses the main artwork.
Hero: Devices: A laptop, tablet and phone arranged together, each screen taking its own artwork. For a product or app across screen sizes.
Hero: Desk: A laptop with a phone and mug on the desk. A warm workspace shot.
Hero: Branding: A shopping bag, box, mug and business cards together for a brand identity spread.
Hero: Café: A takeaway coffee cup, mug and business cards for cafe branding.
Hero: Beauty: A bottle, jar and tube together for a skincare or cosmetics range.
Hero: Print: A framed poster, report and business cards for a print and stationery showcase.
Hero: Merch: A tote bag, mug and sticker for a merchandise set.
Hero: On the go: A phone, coffee cup and smartwatch for a mobile, out-and-about scene.
Hero: Reading: A closed book, eReader and open book together for a publishing or reading theme.
Hero: App: A phone, tablet and smartwatch for showing one app across devices.
Hero: Monitor Desk: A monitor with a phone and mug on the desk for a workstation shot.
Hero: Stationery: A report, envelope and business cards for a corporate stationery set.
Hero: Office: A clipboard, pen and mug for an office desk scene.
Hero: Desk Set: A ring binder, spiral notebook and pen for a study or back-to-school set.
Hero: Shipping: A shipping box, pouch and sticker for a fulfilment or e-commerce scene.
Hero: Pantry: A beverage carton, jar and can for a grocery or pantry-shelf shot.
Hero: Drinks: A wine bottle, bottle and can together for a beverage line.
Hero: Spa: A candle, jar and tube for a spa or wellness theme.
Hero: Fashion: A t-shirt, tote bag and sticker for an apparel and merch scene.
Hero: Music: A vinyl record, poster and mug for a music release or band-merch scene.
Hero: Wall Art: A canvas print, framed poster and polaroid for a wall-art arrangement.
Hero: Event: A roll-up banner, flyer and business cards for an event or trade-show set.
Hero: Calendars: A wall calendar, desk calendar and postcard for a calendar product line.
Hero: Launch: A laptop, phone and shipping box together for a product-launch or unboxing scene.

sections.title: Model-specific options
sections.text:
Extra sliders that appear only for models that can change size, angle or how far a part opens.
When a model declares its own parameters, matching sliders appear under the Model card. Each model keeps its own values, so a Width you set on the box does not carry over to the box's or another model's Width. Size sliders use the model's own units (plain numbers); Opening and Angle are degrees; Slide out and Flaps are percentages.
Height: Sets the hardcover Book's height. Larger values make a taller book.
Width: Sets the hardcover Book's width (how wide the cover is).
Thickness: Sets the hardcover Book's spine thickness (page count feel).
Opening: Sets the angle between the two halves of the standing open book. Higher opens it flatter; 178 is nearly flat.
Opening: Sets how flat the lying open book lies; 179 is almost fully flat on the surface.
Width: Sets the Software Box's width.
Height: Sets the Software Box's height.
Depth: Sets the Software Box's depth (how thick front-to-back it looks).
Slide out: Sets how far the CD slides out of the jewel case, from fully in to fully out.
Slide out: Sets how far the disc slides out of the DVD case.
Spine: Sets the width of the ring binder's spine (how fat the binder is).
Width: Sets the Shipping Box's width.
Depth: Sets the Shipping Box's depth (front-to-back).
Height: Sets the Shipping Box's height.
Flaps: Opens the box's top flaps, from closed to fully open. Use it to show an open or sealed carton.
Width: Adjusts the t-shirt's fit (how wide the body of the shirt sits).
Width: Sets the Canvas Print's width.
Height: Sets the Canvas Print's height.
Depth: Sets how deep the gallery-wrap canvas stands off the wall.
Slide out: Sets how far the record slides out of its sleeve.
Height: Sets the candle's height.
Width: Sets the candle's width (jar radius).
Sheets: Sets how many sheets are stacked on the clipboard, changing the paper thickness.
Length: Sets the pen's length.
Width: Sets the pen's barrel width (thickness).
Width: Sets the Acrylic Sign's width.
Height: Sets the Acrylic Sign's height.
Width: Sets the Beverage Carton's width.
Height: Sets the Beverage Carton's height.
Angle: Sets how far the desk calendar tent is opened; lower stands it more upright, higher spreads the legs.

sections.title: Artwork source
sections.text:
Choose which of your document's content becomes the design wrapped onto the model.
The Artwork dropdown at the top of the side panel picks where the main artwork comes from. It offers the active layer, the whole flattened document, any named layer, and any dynamic template. When you reopen an edited mockup it also offers the artwork it was baked with.
Artwork: The main source dropdown. Whatever you pick here is rendered to a canvas and used as the design on the model (and as the fallback for every surface that is left on Main artwork).
Active layer: Uses your currently selected layer as the artwork. Image layers load at full quality; other layer types are rendered and trimmed to their content.
Whole document: Uses a flattened render of the entire document (all layers combined) as the artwork. Good for wrapping a finished design onto a product.
Template: (name): Uses a dynamic template as the artwork, rendered with the current preview-post context. These sources re-render for each post during automation runs, so every post gets its own cover on the mockup.
(layer name): Every named layer in the document is listed so you can wrap one specific layer onto the model. Nested layers are indented, and groups show a small triangle marker.
Saved artwork: When you reopen an existing mockup, this option restores the exact pixels it was baked with, even if the original layer has since changed.
Saved override: A fallback label shown when a mockup was saved pointing at a source (a layer or template) that no longer exists, so the dropdown still has a valid selection.
Template sources re-render per post in automation runs.: An on-screen note that appears when templates are available, reminding you that template-based artwork is regenerated for each post during batch or automation runs.

sections.title: Artwork fit & position
sections.text:
Control how the artwork is scaled and cropped onto the model's surface.
The Artwork card sets how the design fills the model's face. Areas the artwork does not cover stay transparent, so the material below (screen glass, ceramic, paper) shows through on a contain fit.
Fit: Chooses how the artwork is sized to the surface: crop-to-fill, fit fully inside, or stretch to the exact shape.
Fill (crop): Scales the artwork to cover the whole surface, cropping whatever overflows. Keeps the design edge-to-edge with no gaps; use the Position slider to choose which part is kept.
Fit inside: Scales the artwork so all of it is visible inside the surface, which can leave the material showing around the edges. Use it when nothing may be cropped.
Stretch: Stretches the artwork to the surface's exact aspect ratio, which may distort it. Use it only when the design already matches the shape.
Position: With Fill (crop), slides the crop window across the artwork to choose which part stays visible. It is disabled for the Fit inside and Stretch modes.

sections.title: Per-surface artwork
sections.text:
Give each face of a multi-surface model its own design, fit and crop.
Models that expose more than one surface (book front/spine/back, open-book spreads, disc cases, the poster trio, shipping box, carton and every hero scene) show a labeled picker per surface under the Model card. Each surface can use the main artwork, a plain unprinted face, or its own separate source, and can override the global fit and crop.
Surfaces default sensibly: the main face uses your artwork, while inner faces like spines and backs start plain. Hero scenes expose one surface per object so each product can carry a different design.
Surface pickers: One dropdown per surface (labeled Front, Spine, Back, Cover, Disc, Left, Center, Right, and so on) that sets what design that face shows. Surfaces only appear for models that have more than one.
Main artwork: Uses the studio's main Artwork source on this surface. This is the default for a model's primary face.
None (plain): Leaves this surface blank so the bare material (cover board, paper, disc) shows with no print. Used by default for inner faces like spines and backs.
Per-surface sources: Besides Main artwork and None, each surface offers the same sources as the main picker (Active layer, Whole document, a named layer, or a template), so different faces can carry different designs.
Default (artwork): The per-surface Fit option that inherits the global Artwork fit and position. Leave it here unless this face needs a different crop.
Per-surface Fit: Overrides how the artwork sits on just this surface, using the same choices as the global fit: Fill (crop), Fit inside or Stretch.
Per-surface Position: A small crop slider next to each surface's Fit that positions the crop window for that face; it is active only when that surface uses Fill (crop).

sections.title: View (camera)
sections.text:
Set the exact camera angle with sliders, matching what you get by dragging in the viewport.
The View card holds two sliders that rotate and tilt the model. They mirror dragging in the viewport: horizontal drag changes Rotate, vertical drag changes Tilt. Zoom is set by the mouse wheel.
Rotate: Spins the model left or right around its vertical axis (yaw). Use it to show more of a side, a spine or a wrapped label.
Tilt: Tips the camera up or down (pitch), from nearly level to a high top-down look. Use it for a flat-lay feel or an eye-level product shot.

sections.title: Light & Shadow
sections.text:
Tune the studio lighting and the ground shadow's strength, softness, length and direction.
The Light & Shadow card controls the overall brightness and the contact shadow the model casts on the ground. The shadow follows the camera, and its footprint is kept fully inside the baked layer so it is never clipped.
Light: Sets the overall brightness of the studio (ambient plus key light plus environment). Higher makes a brighter, punchier scene.
Shadow: Sets how dark and visible the ground shadow is. At 0 the shadow and its ground plane are turned off entirely.
Blur: Sets the softness of the shadow edge (penumbra width). Low is a crisp hard shadow; high is a soft, diffuse one.
Length: Sets how long the shadow stretches by lowering the key light. Higher throws a longer shadow, as if late in the day.
Direction: Rotates the light around the model so the shadow falls to a different side, measured relative to the camera view.

sections.title: Finish (reflection & body color)
sections.text:
Add a ground reflection and set the color of the model's non-artwork body.
The Finish card controls a mirror reflection on the ground and the body color of the model (the phone frame and back, mug ceramic, box card, and so on). The artwork surfaces are unaffected by the body color.
Reflection: Fades a mirror of the model into the ground beneath it, dropping off with distance. Higher gives a glossier, showroom-floor look; 0 turns it off.
Body: Sets the color of the model's material body: the parts that are not the artwork, such as a phone's frame and back, a mug's glaze or a box's board. Opens the editor's color picker when available.
Color swatches: Eight one-click preset body colors below the picker for fast changes. Clicking one sets the Body color and marks it active.

sections.title: 360 Spin export
sections.text:
Bake a full turntable rotation as a sprite sheet layer, a drag-to-rotate HTML viewer, or single frames.
The 360 Spin card bakes a whole turn of the model into frames with identical framing on every frame (no wobble during the spin). You can insert those frames as one sprite-sheet layer in the document, or download them as a self-contained viewer or a ZIP for 360 player plugins.
Frames: Sets how many still frames make up one full 360-degree turn. More frames give a smoother spin but a larger sprite sheet.
Size: Sets the pixel size of each frame cell in the sprite sheet. Larger is sharper but heavier.
Bakes a full turn as one sprite sheet layer, identical framing on every frame.: An on-screen note explaining that the spin is baked as a single sprite-sheet image with every frame framed the same way.
Insert sprite sheet: Bakes the full turn and inserts it into your document as one image layer holding all the frames in a grid. The layer remembers its spin settings, so Edit Mockup re-bakes the whole sheet.
Viewer (HTML): Downloads a ready-to-embed, self-contained HTML file that plays the spin and rotates as the visitor drags. Everything (the sheet image included) is inlined, so it works offline.
Frames (ZIP): Downloads the individual spin frames as PNGs in a ZIP, ready to feed 360 product-viewer plugins (WooCommerce spin viewers and similar).
Viewer = ready-to-embed HTML file, spins on drag. Frames feed 360 player plugins.: An on-screen note describing the two download buttons: the HTML viewer spins on drag, and the frames ZIP feeds external 360 players.

sections.title: Sprite sheets: what to do with a 360 spin
sections.text:
A sprite sheet is one image holding every frame of a turn. This is what you do with it after a studio has baked one.
Three studios bake a turntable spin the same way: **3D Mockup Studio**, **3D Text Studio** and **3D Gallery Studio**. All three hand you the same three routes out, and which one you want depends on where the spin has to run.
A sprite sheet is a flip book in one file. The frames sit side by side in a grid, and a player shows one cell at a time and steps to the next as the visitor drags. Nothing inside the editor plays a sheet: the studio makes one, and a viewer, a plugin or a few lines of your own code play it. That is the part that surprises people, so it is worth saying plainly.
Every frame is rendered at the same camera distance. The studio measures the widest angle first and frames them all to that, so the object does not swell and shrink while it turns. Without that, a spin jitters.
Which of the three routes to take: Take **Insert sprite sheet** when you still want to work on the picture: it arrives as one layer, so you can crop it, put your brand on it and export a single PNG. Take **Viewer (HTML)** when the spin simply has to work on a page and you would rather not add a plugin. Take **Frames (ZIP)** when a 360 player is already in place and wants numbered images.
What the grid looks like: The frames are laid out in a roughly square grid, not in one long strip. 24 frames become 5 columns by 5 rows and the last cell stays empty. At the default frame size that is one image of 1920 by 1920 pixels. Raising either dropdown multiplies that, which is the whole trade the two settings offer.
Playing a sheet yourself: Give an element the size of one cell, set the sheet as its background and move the background position by one cell per frame. Because the frames sit in a grid rather than a single row, both axes have to move: frame `i` sits at `-(i % cols) * cell` across and `-floor(i / cols) * cell` down. A plain CSS `steps()` animation only walks one axis, so a grid needs a few lines of JavaScript, or a player that understands sheets.
What is inside Frames (ZIP): One PNG per frame, named `frame-01.png` upwards and zero padded to the number of frames, in turning order. A viewer that sorts by file name therefore gets the rotation right with no renaming. Each image is one cell of the sheet, at the frame size you picked.
What the HTML viewer actually is: One self-contained file. The sheet is embedded inside it, so there is nothing else to upload and no request leaves the page. It spins by itself until the first drag, then follows the pointer. On a phone it turns on a horizontal drag and lets a vertical swipe scroll the page, so it does not trap the reader.

sections.title: Insert & editable layers
sections.text:
Bake the mockup into your document as a transparent PNG layer that stays editable and can re-render per post.
The footer holds the primary action. The mockup is baked at high resolution, trimmed to hug the model and its shadow, and placed as a transparent PNG image layer. Because the layer stores the full scene, you can reopen it later with Edit Mockup, and template-based mockups re-render automatically in automation runs.
Insert Mockup: Bakes the current view into a new transparent PNG layer and adds it to the document, centered and sized to about 85% of the shorter document side. The scene is stored on the layer so it stays editable.
Update Mockup: Shown instead of Insert when you opened the studio via Edit Mockup. It re-bakes the mockup into the existing layer, refitting the new render into the layer's box around its center so nothing distorts.
Editable layer (Edit Mockup): Every inserted mockup stores its model, artwork, camera, light and finish on the layer. Reopening it with Edit Mockup restores the exact scene so you can change anything and re-bake.
Automation re-render: When a mockup's artwork (or any surface) comes from a dynamic template, the extension re-renders that template against each post and re-bakes the mockup during automation runs, so every post gets its own design on the product. Mockups with fixed artwork keep their baked pixels.
Inserts as an editable layer - reopen anytime via Edit Mockup.: The footer hint reminding you that the result is a normal, re-editable image layer.

sections.title: Model categories (picker filter)
sections.text:
The Category dropdown above the model tiles narrows the grid to one product family.
