The model picker groups the parametric models into five families. Picking a category hides every tile that does not belong to it, so the plain products never mix with the staged **Hero** compositions.
This is a view filter only. It never changes your artwork or the selected model, it only decides which tiles are visible.
Devices: Shows only the screen and gadget models: **Smartphone**, **Tablet**, **eReader**, **Laptop**, **Monitor**, **Smart TV**, **Smartwatch** and **Phone Case**. Pick this family when you are mocking up an app screen or a device photo.
Print & Paper: Filters to flat printed pieces: **Report (A4)**, **Flyer**, **Postcard**, **Sticker**, **Business Cards**, **Polaroid**, **Poster Frame**, **Poster Frames (Trio)**, **Poster (Clips)**, **Poster (Pins)**, **Roll-up Banner**, **Billboard**, **Envelope**, **Wall Calendar**, **Desk Calendar**, **Canvas Print**, **Clipboard** and **Acrylic Sign**.
Books & Cases: Filters to books and media cases: hardcover **Book**, **Softcover Book**, **Open Book (standing)** and **(lying)**, **Software Box**, **DVD Case** and **CD Jewel Case** (with or without disc), **Spiral Notebook**, **Ring Binder** and **Vinyl Record**.
Product & Packaging: Filters to physical products and packaging: **Mug**, **Coffee Cup (to go)**, **Can**, **Bottle**, **Wine Bottle**, **Cosmetic Jar**, **Cosmetic Tube**, **Shopping Bag**, **Tote Bag**, **Pillow**, **Pouch (stand-up)**, **Shipping Box**, **T-Shirt**, **Candle**, **Pen** and **Beverage Carton**.
Hero scenes: Filters to the multi-object hero compositions (every tile whose name starts with `Hero:`). Each of these arranges several products in one staged shot instead of a single object.

sections.title: Per-surface artwork faces
sections.text:
Models with more than one printable side show a named artwork picker for each face, so every face can carry its own design.
When the selected model declares surfaces, the **Model** card lists one row per face below the model tiles. Each row is a source picker (Main artwork, None (plain), a layer, the whole document or a template) plus its own **Fit** and **Position** controls.
Faces default either to the **Main artwork** (they show your design straight away) or to **None (plain)** (they stay blank until you choose a source). The labels below are the face names as they appear in the code.
Front: Artwork for the front face of a multi-surface model, such as the book cover, the box front, the pillow front or the calendar front. It starts filled with your **Main artwork**.
Spine: Artwork for the narrow spine edge of a book, software box or ring binder. On the **Book** and **Software Box** it starts blank, on the **Ring Binder** it starts with the main artwork. This is the surface picker, not the ring binder's spine-width slider of the same name.
Back: Artwork for the back face. It starts blank (**None (plain)**), so you only fill it when you actually have a back-cover design.
Top: Artwork for the top face of the **Software Box**. It starts blank so the box top stays a plain body color until you add a design.
Outside: Artwork for the outer cover of an open book. On **Open Book (standing)** it carries the main artwork, on **Open Book (lying)** it starts blank.
Inside: Artwork for the inner spread (the open pages) of an open book. On **Open Book (lying)** it carries the main artwork, on **Open Book (standing)** it starts blank.
Cover: Artwork for the sleeve or case cover of a disc product. It defaults to the main artwork.
Disc: Artwork printed on the disc itself, for the case-with-disc models. Defaults to the main artwork so the disc face matches the cover.
Label: Artwork for the round center label of the **Vinyl Record**. Defaults to the main artwork.
Side: Artwork for the side panel of the **Shipping Box** or **Beverage Carton**. Starts blank so the sides stay a plain body color until you add a design.
Left: Artwork for the left frame in the **Poster Frames (Trio)** model, so the three framed posters can each hold a different image.
Center: Artwork for the center frame in the **Poster Frames (Trio)** model.
Right: Artwork for the right frame in the **Poster Frames (Trio)** model.
Hero scene object surfaces: Every **Hero** composition exposes one artwork picker per object it stages (for example **Laptop**, **Tablet** and **Phone** on `Hero: Devices`, or **Bag**, **Box**, **Mug** and **Cards** on `Hero: Branding`). Each object defaults to the **Main artwork** and can be pointed at its own layer, the whole document or a template.

sections.title: Studio window
sections.text:
The full-screen modal that hosts the 3D preview and every mockup control.
Opening **Insert 3D Mockup** (or **Edit 3D Mockup** on an existing mockup layer) mounts this modal inside the editor. The 3D preview sits on the left, the settings cards on the right, and a Cancel plus primary action in the footer.
3D Mockup Studio: The modal's title bar, badged with the editor brand mark. The line beneath the title changes with the mode: it explains what an insert does when you open a fresh mockup, and that edits update in place when you reopen one.

sections.title: Studio overview and insert
sections.text:
The 3D Text Studio dialog, its two modes, the live preview, and the buttons that bake the result into your document.
Extruded 3D typography and logos: type any text, or switch to logo mode and extrude any SVG, uploaded or taken straight from a vector layer of your document, multi-color fills preserved. Use the bundled display faces or any font from your editor library, including your own uploads, decoded locally so nothing leaves your server.
Shape it with depth, bevel and curve controls, pick premium materials such as gold, chrome, glass, neon glow or holographic, then click any single letter in the preview to give it its own color, material, size, depth, shift and rotation. Studio shadows and a ground reflection light the result.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert as a transparent PNG layer, bake a 360-degree spin as a sprite-sheet layer or a self-contained HTML viewer, and bind the text to post data so it re-renders per post in automation runs. Reopen anytime via **Edit 3D Text**.
3D Text: Switches the studio to text mode, where it extrudes the text you type. This is the default mode when you open the studio.
3D Logo: Switches to logo mode, which extrudes an SVG or a vector layer from your document instead of typed text. Selecting this hides the Text card and Curve control and shows the Logo card.
Show document: Toggles a one-time flattened render of your current design behind the transparent 3D scene, so you can judge the text over the real artwork instead of the checkerboard. When editing an existing layer, that layer is left out of the preview. [Availability: Shown only when the editor can render the document]
Preview (orbit, zoom, pick letter): The interactive 3D stage. Drag to orbit the camera, use the mouse wheel to zoom, and in text mode click any single letter to select it for per-letter styling.
Close: Closes the dialog without inserting anything. The `Esc` key and clicking the dark backdrop do the same.
Cancel: Closes the studio and discards your work, the same as Close.
Insert 3D Text: Renders the current 3D text at high resolution and adds it to your document as a transparent PNG layer, centered and scaled to fit. The button reads **Insert 3D Logo** in logo mode, and **Update 3D Text** / **Update 3D Logo** when you are editing an existing layer (it re-fits the new artwork into the same box).
Edit 3D Text: Reopens the studio for a layer that was created here, with every setting restored, so you can change the text, material or lighting and re-bake. This action lives on the layer itself (right-click or the layer menu), because the inserted layer remembers it came from 3D Text Studio.

sections.title: Text and layout
sections.text:
Type the text to extrude and control its alignment, spacing, line height and wrapping.
These controls live in the Text card, which is only visible in 3D Text mode. The text you type is extruded live in the preview.
You can mix in dynamic variables so the layer re-renders per post during automation runs, for example a post title or a brand field.
Your text…: The multi-line text box for the words you want in 3D. Type here and the preview rebuilds as you go. Press Enter for a new line.
{…} (variable button): Inserts a dynamic `{{binding}}` token at the cursor, for example `{{post.title}}`. During automation runs the token is replaced with the real value for each post, so one design produces many labeled outputs.
Dynamic: A fallback dropdown (shown only on older cores without the {…} button) that binds the whole text to one source. Pick a field to re-render the layer per post; the typed text stays as the design-time preview.
Custom text: The default choice in the Dynamic dropdown. It means the layer uses exactly the text you typed and does not re-render per post.
Align: Sets how multiple lines line up horizontally against each other. Use it when your text has more than one line.
Left: Aligns all lines to a common left edge.
Center: Centers each line on the middle axis. This is the default alignment.
Right: Aligns all lines to a common right edge.
Spacing: Widens or tightens the gap between letters (tracking). Negative values pull letters closer, positive values push them apart.
Line height: Sets the vertical distance between lines of text, as a percentage of the normal line spacing. Lower values pack lines tighter, higher values spread them out.
Wrap: Breaks long text into lines after roughly this many characters, so a long bound title becomes a poster-friendly block instead of one endless strip. Set to 0 to turn wrapping off.

sections.title: Fonts
sections.text:
Choose from 12 bundled display fonts, or any font already loaded in your editor library.
The font tiles are 12 display faces that ship inside the extension, decoded locally so nothing leaves your server. Click a tile to apply it.
Below the tiles, the Library dropdown lets you pick any font family the editor page already loads (built-in families and your own uploads), with a Weight selector for that family.
Anton: A tall, heavy condensed sans, good for bold impact headlines. This is the default font.
Bebas Neue: A tall all-caps condensed sans with an even, poster-like rhythm.
Montserrat: A geometric sans in its heaviest (black) weight, clean and modern.
Space Grotesk: A contemporary techy sans with slightly quirky letterforms.
Cinzel: A classical Roman-inscription serif in caps, elegant and formal.
Playfair: A high-contrast display serif with a refined, editorial feel (Playfair Display).
DM Serif: A stylish high-contrast serif with a warm display character.
Fredoka: A rounded, friendly sans that reads soft and approachable.
Bangers: A bold comic-book style caps face, great for loud, playful text.
Lobster: A connected script with retro-signage flavor.
Pacifico: A relaxed brush-style handwriting script.
Dancing Script: A lively, casual handwriting script with bouncy letterforms.
Library: Picks a font from the editor's own font library instead of the tiles above. Fonts are grouped into your uploads and the editor's built-in fonts; woff2 files are decoded locally in the browser.
Weight: Chooses the weight (for example 400 or 700) of the family picked in the Library dropdown. It only appears once you select a Library family, and lists the weights that family actually provides.

sections.title: Materials
sections.text:
Twelve premium material presets, each setting the surface look plus its own face and side colors.
Materials are shown as tiles in the Material card. Clicking one applies its physical look (reflection, metalness, glass, glow and so on) and also loads its matching Face, Sides and Glow values, which you can then override.
Metals and glass pick up long streaky highlights from the studio environment, so they look best with some rotation.
Gold: A warm polished gold metal. This is the default material.
Chrome: A bright, mirror-like silver metal that reflects the studio lights sharply.
Copper: A warm reddish-brown metal with a soft metallic sheen.
Steel: A cooler brushed-metal grey, more muted than chrome.
Glass: A clear refractive glass that transmits and bends what is behind it. Pairs well with a Backdrop so the refraction has something to show.
Frosted: A translucent frosted (milk) glass with a soft, diffused surface.
Neon: A glowing neon-tube look that emits its own light. Selecting it turns on a real bloom glow automatically.
Gloss: A glossy painted plastic with a shiny clear-coat highlight, in a vivid red by default.
Matte: A flat, non-reflective surface with soft even shading, for a subtle, understated look.
Candy: A glossy, saturated pink candy-coat, bright and playful.
Hologram: An iridescent holographic finish whose color shifts across the surface, for a futuristic look.
Gradient: A smooth color gradient down the face of the letters. Choosing it reveals the Bottom color control so you can set the second gradient color.

sections.title: Material colors and glow
sections.text:
Override the face, side and (for gradient) bottom colors, and dial in the emissive glow.
These controls sit under the material tiles. Picking a material preset fills them in for you, but you can change any color afterward to make the material your own.
Face: The color of the front faces of the letters (the part pointing at the camera). Uses the editor's color picker.
Sides: The color of the extruded sides and bevels of the letters (the depth). Set it darker than the face for a natural shaded edge.
Bottom: The second (bottom) color of the face gradient. This control only appears when the Gradient material is selected; the Face color acts as the top color. [Shown when: Material = Gradient]
Glow: Adds an emissive bloom halo around the letters, as if they give off light. The Neon material turns this up automatically, but you can add a glow to any material.

sections.title: Per-letter styling
sections.text:
Click a single letter in the preview to give it its own color, material, size, depth, shift and rotation.
In text mode, click any letter in the preview to select it. A per-letter panel then appears where you can override just that letter; a small pop marks the selected glyph.
Every control here has a neutral value that means "follow the whole text", so you only override what you change. Spaces cannot be styled.
Letter „x“: The panel heading shows which letter is selected. Click a different letter in the preview to switch, or click empty space to deselect.
Color: Sets a face color for just the selected letter, independent of the whole-text Face color.
Auto: Clears the selected letter's custom color so it follows the main text color again.
Material (Like text): Gives the selected letter its own material preset, chosen from the 12 materials. Leave it on **Like text** to keep the letter on the same material as the rest of the text.
Size: Scales just the selected letter up or down relative to the others, as a percentage. Useful for drop-caps or emphasis.
Depth: Overrides the extrusion depth for the selected letter, as a percentage. Push one letter deeper (or flatter) than the rest.
Shift: Moves the selected letter up or down from the baseline, as a percentage of its height, for a bouncing or staggered look.
Rotation: Tilts the selected letter clockwise or counter-clockwise for a hand-set, playful arrangement.
Reset letter: Removes all custom styling from the currently selected letter, returning it to the main text style.
Reset all letters: Clears every per-letter override at once. This button only appears while at least one letter has custom styling.

sections.title: Shape (depth, bevel, curve)
sections.text:
Control how thick, how rounded, and how curved the extruded text is.
The Shape card sets the 3D form of the letters themselves. The Curve control is hidden in logo mode.
Depth: Sets how thick the extrusion is, that is how far the letters stick out toward and away from you. Higher values make chunkier 3D text.
Bevel: Rounds the front and back edges of the letters. A little bevel catches the light for a polished edge; more bevel makes the letters look softer and rounder.
Curve: Bends the whole line of text along an arc. Positive values curve one way, negative the other, and 0 keeps it straight. This control is only available in 3D Text mode.

sections.title: View (rotate, tilt, zoom)
sections.text:
Aim the camera around the text with rotate and tilt sliders, plus mouse-wheel zoom.
The View card mirrors the drag-orbit of the preview: the sliders and the drag stay in sync, so you can set an exact angle or eyeball it by dragging.
Rotate: Turns the text left or right around its vertical axis (yaw). This is the same value you set by dragging the preview horizontally.
Tilt: Raises or lowers the camera to look down at or up toward the text (pitch). Matches vertical dragging in the preview.
Zoom (mouse wheel): Scrolling the mouse wheel over the preview zooms the camera in and out. There is no slider; it is a preview-only control.

sections.title: Light and shadow
sections.text:
Set the studio brightness and shape the cast shadow on the ground.
The Light & Shadow card controls the overall exposure and the shadow the text drops on an invisible floor. Shadow, Blur, Length and Direction only matter when Shadow is above 0.
Light: Overall brightness of the studio lighting. Higher values make faces and highlights brighter, lower values give a moodier look.
Shadow: The strength (opacity) of the shadow cast on the ground beneath the text. Set to 0 to remove the shadow entirely.
Blur: How soft the shadow edge is. Low values give a crisp, hard shadow; high values give a soft, diffused one.
Length: How far the shadow stretches away from the text, by lowering or raising the light. Longer shadows read like a lower sun.
Direction: The angle the shadow (and key light) falls from, so you can point the shadow left, right or behind the text. It stays consistent as you orbit.

sections.title: Finish (reflection and backdrop)
sections.text:
Add a mirror-floor reflection and set the background color behind the text.
The Finish card adds a ground reflection and lets you choose the backdrop. Leaving the backdrop transparent lets you drop the text straight into any design; a solid backdrop is also what glass refracts.
Reflection: The strength of a mirror-like reflection of the text on the ground plane, fading out with distance. Set to 0 for no reflection.
Backdrop: The background color behind the text, chosen with the color picker. When a color is set, the inserted layer keeps that solid background; leave it transparent to insert just the text.
Transparent: The first backdrop swatch (a checkerboard). It clears the background so the text is inserted as a transparent PNG, trimmed to its content. This is the default.
Backdrop swatches: Quick-pick color chips next to the picker for common backgrounds: dark, white, cream, navy and blue. Click one to set the Backdrop instantly.

sections.title: 3D Logo mode
sections.text:
Extrude an SVG file or a vector layer from your document into 3D, keeping its original colors.
Switch to 3D Logo with the mode toggle to reveal this card. It extrudes vector artwork instead of text: an SVG you upload, or a shape layer, group or SVG image asset already in your document.
All the material, shape, view, light and finish controls still apply, so a logo can be gold, glass, beveled and lit exactly like text. The Curve control is not available for logos.
Source: Chooses which vector artwork to extrude. The dropdown lists eligible layers from your document (shapes with a visible fill, groups containing such shapes, and SVG image assets), indented to show nesting, plus an entry for an uploaded SVG.
Saved logo: When you reopen a logo layer with Edit 3D Text, the Source dropdown starts on **Saved logo**, meaning it reuses the SVG markup stored with the layer so you do not have to pick the source again.
Uploaded SVG: A Source option that becomes selectable after you load an SVG file. It represents the file you uploaded rather than a layer from the document.
Load SVG file…: Opens a file picker to load an SVG from your computer as the logo source. Only filled paths are extruded (outlines are ignored).
Original colors: When checked, the logo keeps the fill colors from the SVG or vector layers (so multi-color logos stay multi-color) while still using the chosen material's physics. Uncheck it to paint the whole logo in the Face and Sides colors instead.

sections.title: 360 spin and exports
sections.text:
Bake a full turntable rotation as a sprite sheet layer, a drag-to-rotate HTML viewer, or single frames in a ZIP.
The 360 Spin card renders a full turn of the text or logo. Pick the number of frames and the frame size, then either insert the whole turn as one sprite-sheet layer or download it for use outside the editor.
Every frame uses identical framing so the spin looks steady, and the design stays editable through Edit 3D Text.
Frames: How many still images make up one full 360-degree turn. More frames give a smoother spin but a larger file.
Size: The pixel size of each square frame in the spin. Larger frames are sharper but heavier.
Insert sprite sheet: Bakes the full turn as a single sprite-sheet layer added to your document, with identical framing on every frame. Use this when a plugin or your own code plays the sheet as an animation.
Viewer (HTML): Downloads a single self-contained HTML file that shows the spin and rotates as the visitor drags. Ready to embed on a page with no dependencies.
Frames (ZIP): Downloads the individual spin frames as separate images in a ZIP archive, which feeds 360-player plugins (for example WooCommerce product viewers).

sections.title: Dynamic text sources (fallback dropdown)
sections.text:
On editors without the inline `{…}` variable picker, the **Dynamic** dropdown lists these bound sources, and the chosen field re-renders the text for every post in automation runs.
This dropdown only appears on older editor cores that lack the inline variable button. On current cores the field uses `{{token}}` variables instead.
The server can replace this built-in list with a fuller set of site fields (author, WooCommerce, ACF). When the post has no value for the chosen field, the design-time text is kept.
The **Brand Kit** group is always added on top of whatever list is shown.
Post: Group heading in the **Dynamic** dropdown for the built-in post fields listed below.
Post title: Binds the text to the current post's title, so each run bakes the post's own headline in 3D.
Post excerpt: Binds the text to the post excerpt (the short summary). Best paired with **Wrap** so long text breaks into lines.
Author: Binds the text to the post author's name.
Category: Binds the text to the post's category (the first category when several apply).
Publish date: Binds the text to the post's publish date.
Site name: Binds the text to your WordPress site name.
Brand Kit: Group heading for the brand-kit fields that resolve from the run's active brand kit.
Company: Binds the text to the brand kit's company name.
Website: Binds the text to the brand kit's website address.
Email: Binds the text to the brand kit's email address.
City: Binds the text to the brand kit's city.

sections.title: Font Library options
sections.text:
Options inside the **Library** dropdown that let you extrude any font from your editor instead of the 12 featured tiles.
The **Library** dropdown appears when the editor page exposes readable font faces. It lists every family the editor itself ships plus your own uploads; woff2 files are decoded locally so nothing leaves your server.
Picking a family here reveals the **Weight** dropdown and clears the highlighted featured tile above.
Featured tiles above: The default **Library** choice. It keeps one of the 12 bundled font tiles active and hides the **Weight** dropdown. Pick this to go back to the tile grid after choosing a library font.
Your uploads: Option group listing the custom fonts you have uploaded to the editor. Only shown when you have at least one custom font.
Editor fonts: Option group listing the font families the editor ships built in.

sections.title: Logo source (extra options)
sections.text:
The placeholder and layer entries inside the Logo mode **Source** dropdown.
In Logo mode the **Source** dropdown is filled from your document: every visible vector shape, every group that contains a shape, and every SVG image layer becomes a pickable source.
Choose a source…: The default first option of the **Source** dropdown before you pick a logo. When you re-open an existing 3D logo layer it reads **Saved logo** instead, meaning the stored SVG is still in use.
Document layers (list): Between the placeholder and **Uploaded SVG**, the **Source** dropdown lists each eligible layer by name, indented by how deeply it is nested in groups. Picking one extrudes that layer's filled paths (built-in shapes like star, heart or badge are converted to exact geometry).

sections.title: Insert / Update button (mode variants)
sections.text:
The primary footer button changes its label to match the mode and whether you are editing an existing layer.
The primary button bakes the scene to a transparent PNG (or a sprite sheet) and either updates the layer you opened or inserts a new centered layer. Its wording follows Text vs Logo mode and new vs edit.
Insert 3D Logo: The primary button label in Logo mode when creating a new layer. Bakes the extruded logo and drops it in as a new image layer. [Shown when: Logo mode, not editing]
Update 3D Text: The primary button label when you opened an existing 3D text layer via **Edit 3D Text**. Re-bakes and replaces that layer in place, refitting the new shape into its box. [Shown when: Text mode, editing]
Update 3D Logo: The primary button label when re-editing an existing 3D logo layer. Re-bakes and replaces that logo layer in place. [Shown when: Logo mode, editing]

sections.title: Dialog behaviors & shortcuts
sections.text:
Ways to open, seed, close and interact with the studio window beyond the visible controls.
These affordances are not buttons but they change how the studio opens and closes.
Esc (close): Pressing Escape closes the studio without inserting or updating anything.
Click outside the dialog: Clicking the dimmed area around the window (the backdrop) closes the studio, the same as **Cancel**.
Auto-seed from selection: What you had selected in the editor when you opened the studio pre-fills it. A selected **text** layer copies its text into the field (up to 120 characters). A selected vector **shape**, **group** or **SVG image** opens the studio straight in Logo mode with that layer as the source.
Drag versus click in the preview: In the preview a drag orbits the model, while a plain click (movement under 5 pixels) in Text mode selects the letter under the pointer for per-letter styling. Orbiting also updates the **Rotate** and **Tilt** sliders live.

sections.title: Settings panel sections
sections.text:
The right-hand control panel is split into labelled cards, each grouping related controls.
Each card carries a small icon and a heading. Two of the cards swap in and out with the mode: **Text** shows in Text mode, **Logo** shows in Logo mode.
Text: Card holding the text field and its variable picker, the dynamic binding, the font tiles and **Library**, plus **Align**, **Spacing**, **Line height** and **Wrap**.
Logo: Card holding the Logo mode **Source** dropdown, **Load SVG file…**, and the **Original colors** toggle.
Material: Card with the 12 material tiles, the **Face**, **Sides** and **Bottom** colors, the **Glow** slider, and the per-letter styling panel.
Shape: Card with the **Depth**, **Bevel** and **Curve** sliders that control the extrusion. (**Curve** is hidden in Logo mode.)
View: Card with the **Rotate** and **Tilt** sliders that set the camera angle on the model.
Light & Shadow: Card with the **Light**, **Shadow**, **Blur**, **Length** and **Direction** sliders for studio lighting and the cast shadow.
Finish: Card with the **Reflection** slider and the **Backdrop** color plus its swatches (including **Transparent**).
360° Spin: Card with the turntable **Frames** and **Size** dropdowns, **Insert sprite sheet**, and the **Viewer (HTML)** and **Frames (ZIP)** exports.

sections.title: Map Posters (overview)
sections.text:
A poster-map tool that turns any place on OpenStreetMap into editable layers inside the editor.
Poster-style maps of any place on earth, powered by OpenStreetMap: search a location, pick a design theme, pan and zoom the live vector preview, and add geocoded pins with routes and distances.
The streets themselves are yours to style: foil roads in gold, copper, chrome or color gradients, where the main arteries take the hot gloss band and the alleys sink into the rim, plus a neon glow slider that turns the city into lights. A shape mask frames the whole poster.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert the map with a classic title and coordinates block, all as editable layers, and reopen it anytime via **Edit Map Posters**. Map data is fetched server-side through the editor's privacy-friendly geo proxy and cached on your site.
Map Posters: The extension registers a generator called `Map Posters`. Run it from the editor's generator or insert menu to open the studio, or use `Edit Map Posters` on an existing map layer to reopen it on the exact same spot. [Requires: WunderPaint 1.144+ (geo proxy)]
Map Posters (dialog title): The heading shown at the top of the studio modal. It always reads `Map Posters` next to the editor brand badge.
Dialog subtitle: A one-line hint under the title. When inserting a new map it reads `Poster-style maps of any place on earth, as editable layers.`; when editing an existing map it reads `Adjust the map, the layer updates in place.`
Close: The x button in the top corner closes the studio without inserting or changing anything. Pressing `Escape` or clicking the dimmed area outside the dialog does the same.

sections.title: Live map preview
sections.text:
The large canvas on the left shows the exact composition that will be inserted, and you interact with it directly.
The preview renders the map plus the title text block in document coordinates, so what you see is what lands. It updates in place as you change any control.
You navigate the map by dragging and scrolling on the canvas itself. Small pans and zooms reuse cached data, so most moves need no network at all.
Drag to move: Press and drag anywhere on the map to pan to a new area. The centre latitude and longitude follow your drag and the map re-fetches detail as needed.
Wheel to zoom: Scroll the mouse wheel over the map to zoom in and out. Scrolling up zooms in (smaller radius), scrolling down zooms out (larger radius).
Drag a pin: If a pin sits under your pointer, dragging moves that pin instead of panning the map. Release to drop it at the new location.
Empty prompt: Before a place is chosen, the canvas shows `Search for a city, address or landmark to start the map.` as a placeholder. [Shown when: No location selected]
Loading map data: A `Loading map data` indicator appears over the preview while the geo proxy fetches OpenStreetMap detail for the current view.
Status messages: Short notices float over the preview for busy, error and truncation states. Examples: `Very dense area: some detail was skipped.`, `The map service is busy, retrying`, `Very large area: showing fewer details.` and `Could not load map data.`
Attribution (on the map): The line `© OpenStreetMap contributors` is inserted as its own text layer named `Attribution`, placed over the map. It is not painted into the map image itself, so **keep that layer**: OpenStreetMap data is licensed under the ODbL and the credit has to stay visible on anything you publish.

sections.title: Location (place search)
sections.text:
Search for any city, address or landmark to point the map, using OpenStreetMap's Nominatim geocoder through the editor proxy.
The `Location` panel is the starting point. Type at least two characters to get matching places, then pick one to centre the map there.
On the very first place you pick, the studio also chooses a sensible starting zoom based on the place type (city, town, village, suburb).
Search a place, e.g. Hamburg: The text field where you type a place name, address or landmark. Results appear as you type; press `Enter` to accept the first result.
Search results: A dropdown list of matching places under the search box. Each row shows the place name in bold and its region or full display name below. Click a row to select it.
Coordinates readout: A small line under the search box showing the live centre coordinates of the current view, formatted like `53.5440° N / 9.9870° E`. It updates as you pan and zoom.

sections.title: Theme presets
sections.text:
Ten curated color themes that restyle the whole map with one click; picking one also clears any custom color overrides.
The `Theme` panel is a grid of ten swatches. Each theme is a complete palette for background, water, parks, roads (from strong motorways to faint paths), text and pin color.
Selecting a theme resets the individual `Colors` overrides so you get the clean preset look. You can then tweak single colors afterwards.
Minimal: A clean light theme on a pure white background with dark grey roads. Best for bright, editorial posters.
Midnight: A dark navy theme with light roads and a sky-blue pin. This is the default theme when you open a fresh map.
Blueprint: A deep blue, technical-drawing look with white roads and a warm yellow pin. Evokes an architect's blueprint.
Terracotta: A warm cream background with earthy brown roads and a clay-red pin. A soft, sunny Mediterranean feel.
Forest: A dark forest-green theme with pale green roads and a yellow pin. Good for parks and nature areas.
Neon: A near-black purple background with glowing cyan and magenta roads. A bold, synthwave night look.
Vintage: An aged-paper cream with muted brown roads and a deep red pin. A classic antique-map feel.
Golden: A black background with gold roads and a gold pin. A luxurious, high-contrast night poster.
Rose: A soft blush-pink background with wine-red roads and a rose pin. A gentle, romantic palette.
Ocean: A pale, airy theme with strong blue water and a coral pin. Suits coastal and harbour maps.

sections.title: Colors
sections.text:
Theme colors, custom overrides, and the v1.12 foil gradients and glow for the streets.
The `Colors` panel lets you fine-tune the current theme without leaving it. Each row shows a swatch (the editor's color picker) plus an `Auto` reset.
Changing a single road color is smart: Map Posters spreads it across all road classes by fading toward the background, so one swatch still gives a coherent light-to-dark road hierarchy.
Background: Sets the map's base fill color, behind water, parks and roads. Overrides the theme background until you press `Auto`.
Roads: Sets the color of the strongest road class (motorways). The other road classes (primary, secondary, minor, path) are automatically derived by fading this color toward the background.
Water: Sets the fill and line color for seas, lakes, rivers and streams. Overrides the theme water color until reset.
Parks: Sets the fill color for parks, woods and other green areas. Overrides the theme green until reset.
Auto: The small `Auto` button on each color row removes your override and returns that color to the theme's value. Its tooltip reads `Back to the theme color`.
Road foil: Paints the streets with a curated gradient instead of the theme road colors - ten presets including gold, copper and chrome foils. Gold streets on black is the classic. Auto returns to the theme colors.
Color flow: How the gradient maps onto the streets: By road class gives main arteries the hot gloss band while alleys sink into the rim (instant depth), Across the poster runs one gradient over the whole map.
Glow: A neon halo under the main roads - the city reads as lights at night. Strongest on the dark themes; the route line glows along.

sections.title: Map options
sections.text:
Controls for zoom level, line weight, the poster shape mask and which map layers are drawn.
The `Map` panel holds the geometry and layer controls. The zoom slider mirrors wheel zoom, the line weight scales all strokes, the shape grid crops the map to a frame, and the checkboxes toggle individual OpenStreetMap layers.
Buildings only load when you are zoomed in close, so that toggle disables itself at wider radii.
Zoom: A slider that sets how much area the map covers, from a tight neighbourhood to a whole region. The readout shows the current radius in metres or kilometres. It stays in sync with wheel zoom on the preview.
Line weight: A slider that scales the thickness of every road, rail and water line at once. Lower values give a fine, delicate map; higher values give a bold, graphic one.
Shape: A row of ten icon buttons that crop the map into a frame shape. Choose Square for no crop, or one of the masks: Rounded, Circle, Pentagon, Heart, Hexagon, Diamond, Triangle, Arch or Star. Shaped maps outline their shape in the road color or foil - the heart gets its heart line, matching Star Map Posters.
Square (shape): The default shape: no crop, the map fills its full square frame. Internally the `none` mask.
Rounded (shape): Crops the map to a rounded-corner square (a squircle). A softer frame that still fills most of the area.
Circle (shape): Crops the map into a full circle centred in the frame. A classic round map medallion.
Heart (shape): Crops the map into a heart outline. Good for sentimental places like a hometown or wedding location.
Hexagon (shape): Crops the map into a point-up hexagon. A modern, badge-like frame.
Water: Toggles the drawing of seas, lakes, rivers and streams. Turn it off for a land-only map.
Parks and woods: Toggles the fill of parks, woods and other green areas (and sand or beach fills). Turn it off for a more abstract, monochrome map.
Railways: Toggles rail lines, drawn with cross-tie dashes so they read instantly as railways.
Footpaths: Toggles the faintest road class (footpaths and tracks). Turn it off to reduce clutter and keep only real roads.
Buildings: Toggles building footprints. These load only when you are zoomed in close; when unavailable the checkbox is disabled and its label changes to `Buildings (zoom in closer)`.

sections.title: Pins
sections.text:
Add labelled marker pins to the map, connect them with an optional route line and show the total distance.
The `Pins` panel lets you mark places on the map. Each new pin lands in the middle of the map and you drag it into position on the preview.
Every pin can carry a text label. Two or more pins can be joined by a straight or curved route line, with an optional total-distance pill.
Add pin: Adds a new marker pin at the current map centre, named `Pin 1`, `Pin 2` and so on. Drag it on the preview to place it exactly. If no place is chosen yet, it warns `Search for a place first.`
Pins land in the middle of the map, drag them into place.: A helper line under the Add pin button reminding you that new pins appear in the centre and are positioned by dragging on the preview.
Label (pin): A text field on each pin row that sets the caption drawn next to that pin on the map. Leave it empty for a pin with no text. Placeholder text is `Label`.
Remove pin: The x button on a pin row deletes that pin and its label. Its tooltip reads `Remove pin`.
Route: A dropdown that draws a dashed connecting line between your pins in order. Choose None for no line, Straight line for direct segments, or Curved line for a gentle arc between points.
Show total distance: When a route is drawn, this checkbox adds a pill showing the total great-circle distance along the route, placed at the midpoint of the longest segment.

sections.title: Text block
sections.text:
The title, subtitle and coordinates that are inserted alongside the map as separate editable text layers.
The `Text block` panel appears only when inserting a new map (not when editing an existing one). It composes a classic map-poster caption that lands as real text layers you can edit, restyle or move afterwards.
The title and subtitle prefill from the place you searched, and support dynamic variables like `{{post.title}}` so the poster can adapt per post in dynamic templates.
Layout: Chooses where the caption sits. `Classic poster` places a centred title, divider and subtitle below the map; `On the map` overlays the title in the map's lower corner; `No text` inserts the map alone.
Title: The main heading text, drawn in uppercase Montserrat bold. It prefills with the selected place name and stops auto-updating once you edit it by hand.
Subtitle: A secondary line under the title (for example the region or country), drawn in uppercase Inter. It prefills with the place region and stops auto-updating once edited.
Variable button: A small picker next to the title and subtitle fields that inserts dynamic tokens such as `{{post.title}}`. Because the caption becomes normal text layers, these resolve per post when the poster runs in a dynamic template. [Requires: Editor variable picker (Free 1.162+)]
Variables hint: An explanatory line reading `Variables like {{post.title}} resolve per post when the poster runs in a dynamic template.` It appears under the text fields when the variable picker is available.
Text size: A slider that scales the whole caption (title, subtitle and coordinates) up or down together. Use it to balance the text against the map.
Coordinates line: A checkbox that adds a coordinates line to the caption, showing the map centre like `53.5440° N / 9.9870° E`. It appears as its own text layer named `Coordinates`.
Divider (inserted layer): In the Classic poster layout, a short horizontal rule is inserted between the title and subtitle as a shape layer named `Divider`. It is drawn in the theme text color.

sections.title: Footer and insert
sections.text:
The attribution note and the bottom bar with Cancel and the Insert or Update button.
The bottom of the studio holds the required data credit, a navigation hint, and the primary actions. Inserting bakes the map to a 2048 px image and adds it, together with the caption text, as a group of editable layers.
When you opened the studio to edit an existing map, the primary button updates that layer in place instead of adding a new group.
Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL): A credit line at the bottom of the side panel naming the data source and licence. OpenStreetMap requires this attribution when you use its data.
Drag to move · wheel to zoom: A hint on the left of the footer reminding you how to navigate the preview: drag to pan, scroll to zoom.
Cancel: Closes the studio without inserting or changing anything, the same as the x button or `Escape`.
Insert Map: Bakes the current map to an image and inserts it into your document as a group named after the place, containing the map layer plus separate title, subtitle, divider, coordinates and attribution layers. Stays disabled until map data has loaded.
Update Map: Shown instead of Insert Map when you opened the studio by editing an existing map layer. It re-bakes the map and updates that layer in place, keeping its position and any surrounding layers.

sections.title: Panel section headings
sections.text:
The six labelled headings that divide the Map Posters sidebar into control blocks.
Map Posters's controls sit in the right-hand sidebar under six section headings. Each heading names the block of controls beneath it. They are labels only, not clickable, but they tell you where each setting lives.
Location: Heading over the place search field and the live coordinates readout. Everything under it sets which spot on earth the map is centred on.
Theme: Heading over the grid of ten preset color themes (Minimal through Ocean). Pick a tile to recolor the whole map at once.
Colors: Heading over the four color override rows: `Background`, `Roads`, `Water` and `Parks`. Use these to tweak a theme's individual colors.
Map: Heading over the map-shaping controls: `Zoom`, `Line weight`, `Shape` and the feature toggles (Water, Parks and woods, Railways, Footpaths, Buildings).
Pins: Heading over `Add pin`, the list of added pins, the `Route` selector and the `Show total distance` toggle.
Text block: Heading over the poster text controls: `Title`, `Subtitle`, the variable button, `Text size`, `Layout` and the `Coordinates line` toggle.

sections.title: Route options
sections.text:
The three choices in the Route dropdown that draw a connecting line through your pins.
When you have two or more pins, the `Route` dropdown decides whether and how they are joined by a line. Pins are connected in the order you added them.
None: No line is drawn between pins. Each pin just marks its own spot.
Straight line: Joins the pins in order with straight segments, like a direct point-to-point path.
Curved line: Joins the pins in order with a gentle curved arc instead of straight segments, for a softer travel-route look.

sections.title: Text block layout options
sections.text:
The three choices in the Layout dropdown that decide how the title, subtitle and coordinates sit around the map.
The `Layout` dropdown in the Text block section controls where the poster text goes. It only appears when you are inserting a new map.
Classic poster: Puts the map in the upper part of the canvas with a centred title, a short divider line, the subtitle and the coordinates stacked underneath. This is the traditional map-poster look.
On the map: Places the title and coordinates directly over the map, with no separate text band below it, so the map fills more of the canvas. A 3x3 grid appears with this layout and puts the block wherever you want it; the default is the lower left.
No text: Inserts only the map image with no title, subtitle or coordinates text layers. Use it when you want to add your own captions.

sections.title: Keyboard and mouse shortcuts
sections.text:
The keyboard and pointer actions that are not printed on any button.
A few Map Posters actions have no visible control. They work through the keyboard or by clicking outside the dialog.
Escape: Closes the Map Posters dialog without inserting anything, the same as pressing `Cancel`.
Click outside the dialog: Clicking the dimmed area around the dialog closes Map Posters without inserting. Clicks inside the dialog are ignored.
Enter (in the search box): Pressing Enter while typing in the place search selects the first matching result, so you can search and pick without using the mouse.

sections.title: States, inserted layers and messages
sections.text:
State-dependent labels, the names Map Posters gives inserted layers, and the status messages it shows while working.
Some labels only appear in a particular state, and inserting a map creates layers with set names. Map Posters also shows short status messages over the preview while it loads or renders.
Buildings (zoom in closer): When you are zoomed too far out for building footprints, the `Buildings` toggle is greyed out and its label changes to this. Zoom in until it re-enables to draw buildings.
Back to the theme color: Tooltip on the `Auto` reset button beside each color row. Clicking `Auto` drops your custom color for that element and restores the current theme's own value.
Coordinates: Name of the inserted text layer that holds the latitude and longitude line. It appears in the Layers panel after `Insert Map` when the `Coordinates line` toggle is on.
Map: Inserted map layers are grouped under a group named `Map: `, and the baked map image inside it is named `Map `. Rename or reorganise them like any other layer.
Pin: Each new pin is pre-named `Pin 1`, `Pin 2` and so on. Type in the pin's label field to give it a real name.
Edit Map Posters: Because the inserted map layer stores its settings, selecting it later and choosing Edit Map Posters reopens the studio on the exact same place, theme, pins and zoom. The primary button then reads `Update Map` and re-bakes the image in place.
Very dense area: some detail was skipped.: Shown when a location has more map data than can be drawn cleanly. Some minor detail is dropped, but the map still renders.
Very large area: showing fewer details.: Shown when the zoomed-out area is too big for full detail. Map Posters automatically reloads that area at a lower detail level.
The map service is busy, retrying: The shared OpenStreetMap data service is rate-limited in waves. When it is busy, Map Posters waits and retries automatically up to two times before reporting a failure.
Map Posters needs WunderPaint 1.144 or newer (geo proxy).: Shown if the host editor is too old to provide the server-side geo proxy that Map Posters relies on. Update WunderPaint to use the extension.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
Endless seamless patterns from a seed: motif builders, a rapport and curated palettes, with your own layers stamped in.
Seamless patterns from a seed. A couple of dozen motif builders, from doodle scatter, polka dots and stripes to fish scales, gingham, terrazzo, truchet and honeycomb, fill a design cell; a rapport such as straight, half-drop, brick or mirror turns it into a repeat tile; and curated palettes keep every roll of the dice harmonic.
Stamp any editor layer into the pattern, which turns a logo into a brand pattern in one click. Mix two doodle sets, add a riso offset-print layer and dashed or dotted line styles, and drag elements right in the preview, where they wrap around the tile edge live.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert the pattern as an editable fill layer, register the tile in the editor's pattern library so shapes and text can wear it, save favorites, or download the tile as PNG or SVG.

sections.title: Presets and surprises
sections.text:
The starting gallery: twelve ready-made looks, four fresh random rolls, a full dice button, and your own saved favorites.
The **Presets** card sits at the top of the side panel. Each tile is a live thumbnail. Click any tile to load that whole recipe (motif, doodle set, palette, dials, rapport) at once, then keep tweaking.
Every time you open the studio the four **Surprise** tiles are rolled again, so the gallery of chance is never the same twice. Favorites you save are kept with your WordPress account and appear below the presets.
Bauhaus grid: Loads a **Grid** motif of geometric shapes in the Bauhaus palette on a light ground with a straight repeat. A clean, primary-color grid look.
Memphis party: Loads a busy **Scatter** of Memphis-style squiggles and shapes in the Bauhaus palette with a half-drop repeat. Playful 1980s design vibe.
Botanical garden: Loads a scattered field of leaves and flowers (Botanical set) in the Sage palette. A soft, natural repeat for organic backgrounds.
Starry sky: Loads stars, moons and clouds (Sky set) in the Royal palette on a dark background. A night-sky repeat.
Terrazzo: Loads the **Terrazzo** motif (scattered stone chips and dust) in the Terracotta palette on a light ground. The classic speckled floor look.
Polka: Loads the **Polka dots** motif in the Rosé palette with a straight repeat. Evenly spaced dots.
Diagonals: Loads the **Stripes** motif set to diagonal in the Royal palette on a dark ground. Angled bands of color.
Ocean waves: Loads the **Waves** motif in the Ocean palette on a light ground. Flowing horizontal wave lines.
Fish scales: Loads the **Scales** motif in the Northern Lights palette. Overlapping half-circle scales, like a roof or a fish.
Vichy: Loads the **Gingham** motif in the Terracotta palette. The woven check of translucent crossing bars.
Herringbone: Loads the **Chevron** motif with four teeth in the Citrus palette on a dark ground. A zig-zag herringbone weave.
Heart mirror: Loads scattered hearts (Hearts set) in the Rosé palette with a **Mirror** rapport, so the hearts flip symmetrically across the tile.
? 1 to ? 4 (Surprise): Four curated random tiles, re-rolled every time you open the studio. Each pulls a vetted motif, doodle set, palette and dial mix so even the wildest throw still looks designed. Click one to load it.
Randomize everything: The **Surprise me!** button with the dice icon at the end of the preset grid. It rolls a fresh, curated random pattern into the whole studio: new motif, set, seed, palette, colorway, background, rapport and effects.
Save as favorite: Stores the current pattern recipe as a favorite saved with your WordPress account so you can reload it later, on any device. It saves the settings, not the picture, so a captured stamp is not kept (a stamped set falls back to Geometric).
★ favorites: The row of saved favorites below the presets, each a live thumbnail labelled with a star. Click one to reload it; click the small × on a tile to delete it.

sections.title: Pattern (motif and seed)
sections.text:
Choose the base motif, the doodle set that fills it, and the random seed that arranges everything.
The **Pattern** card is where you pick what the tile is made of. The **Motif** decides the overall structure; for the scatter, grid and diamond motifs a **Doodle set** decides which little shapes get placed.
The **Seed** is the random number behind the arrangement. The same seed with the same dials always produces the exact same tile, so patterns are reproducible.
Motif: The base structure of the pattern. Pick from fourteen builders (Scatter, Grid, Diamond, Polka dots, Stripes, Waves, Chevron, Scales, Gingham, Terrazzo, Truchet, Honeycomb, Ogee, Crosshatch). Changing the motif clears any manual playground edits.
Doodle set: The little shapes placed by the Scatter, Grid and Diamond motifs. Choose from seven sets (Geometric, Memphis, Botanical, Sky, Blobs, Confetti, Hearts) or **Own layer (stamp)** to use one of your own editor layers. This control only appears for those three motifs.
Second set: Optionally mixes a second doodle set into the scatter or grid, so two families of shapes appear together. Set to **Off** for a single set. Hidden when the primary set is a stamp.
Use active layer: Captures the currently selected editor layer (or group) as a stamp image, so your logo or artwork becomes the repeating element. Select a layer in the editor first, then click. This row appears when the doodle set is **Own layer (stamp)**.
Seed: The random number that fixes how elements are placed and colored. Shown next to the dice. The same seed plus the same dials always redraws the identical tile.
New seed: The dice button beside the seed number. Rolls a new random seed, giving a fresh arrangement of the same motif and colors. It also clears any manual moves, adds or removes you made in the preview.

sections.title: Motifs (the twenty-two builders)
sections.text:
The twenty-two pattern structures, from scattered doodles to woven weaves, each with its own set of dials.
Every motif fills one square design cell and is engineered to tile seamlessly: any shape that crosses a cell edge re-enters on the opposite side. The dials listed for each motif are the ones that appear when it is selected. **Opacity** is always shown as well.
**Scatter** and **Terrazzo** are the two motifs whose individual elements you can drag, add and remove right in the preview.
Scatter: Sprinkles doodles from the chosen set across the cell on a jittered grid, so they look random without clumping. The go-to motif for playful, freeform repeats. Its elements can be dragged, added and removed in the preview.
Grid: Places doodles on an even rows-and-columns grid. Tidy and regular, good for structured backgrounds. The **Variety** dial mixes in more shapes from the set.
Diamond: Like the Grid but every other row is offset by half a column, forming a diamond (half-brick) lattice of doodles.
Polka dots: A clean grid of dots with every other row offset. Turn **Variety** up past halfway to alternate large and small dots.
Stripes: Parallel bands of color. The **Direction** control makes them horizontal, vertical or diagonal, and **Variety** switches the width rhythm so the stripes feel designed rather than uniform.
Waves: Rows of smooth sine waves. **Amplitude** sets the wave height, **Frequency** the number of humps, and **Phase** how much each row is shifted from the one above.
Chevron: Rows of sharp zig-zags. **Teeth** sets how many points per row and **Amplitude** how tall they are. Makes herringbone and arrow looks.
Scales: Overlapping half-circle scales, like fish scales or roof tiles, each row lapping over the one below.
Gingham: The woven check of translucent horizontal and vertical bars crossing to make a plaid. Turn **Variety** up to give the two directions different colors.
Terrazzo: Scattered stone chips (blobs and angular shards) plus fine speckled dust between them, for the classic terrazzo floor look. Its chips can be dragged, added and removed in the preview.
Truchet: A grid of tiles each carrying a random quarter-arc or crossing diagonal, so curved or angular paths wander across the pattern. **Variety** trades some arcs for diagonals.
Honeycomb: A tessellating grid of hexagons. **Variety** controls how many cells are filled solid versus drawn as outlines.
Ogee: The classic onion or lattice net built from mirrored curved rails, with alternate rows offset by half a period.
Crosshatch: Two diagonal stripe layers crossing each other, the second thinner and a shade further along the palette, for a sketched hatch texture.

sections.title: Motif dials
sections.text:
The sliders that shape the selected motif; which ones appear depends on the motif, and Opacity is always there.
These dials live in the Pattern card, under the seed. Only the dials that make sense for the current motif are shown, so the exact range can differ between motifs (the values below are the common ranges seen in the code).
Count: How many elements or rows the motif draws. More count means a denser pattern. The exact range depends on the motif.
Columns: The same count dial, but labelled Columns for the grid-style motifs (Grid, Diamond, Polka dots, Scales, Honeycomb), where it sets how many columns fit across the cell.
Size: How big each drawn element is, as a percentage of its slot. Larger values make chunkier shapes.
Jitter: How far elements wander from their exact grid spot. Zero is perfectly regular; higher values scatter them for a hand-placed, organic feel.
Rotation: How much each element is randomly turned. Zero keeps everything upright; higher values tumble the shapes. In grids, values of 50 or more snap to clean right-angle turns.
Weight: Line thickness for stroked motifs and outlined shapes. Higher is bolder.
Variety: How much variation the motif introduces: more shapes from the set (grids), alternating dot sizes (polka), different width rhythms (stripes), two colors (gingham), or more diagonals (truchet).
Direction: For the Stripes motif only: sets the stripe angle. Choose Horizontal, Vertical, Diagonal down or Diagonal up.
Frequency: For Waves and Ogee: how many wave cycles fit across the cell. Higher values pack in more humps.
Teeth: For the Chevron motif: how many zig-zag points sit in each row. More teeth make a tighter zig-zag.
Amplitude: For Waves, Chevron and Ogee: the height of the wave or zig-zag. Higher is more pronounced.
Phase: For the Waves motif: how much each row is shifted sideways from the one above, from all-aligned to a rolling offset.
Opacity: The overall see-through level of the drawn shapes. Lower it to let the background show through. This dial appears for every motif.

sections.title: Doodle sets
sections.text:
The seven families of little shapes the Scatter, Grid and Diamond motifs place, plus the option to use your own layer.
A doodle set is a small library of drawn shapes. When the motif is Scatter, Grid or Diamond, the chosen set decides which shapes appear. You can also mix in a **Second set**, or replace the shapes entirely with a stamp of one of your editor layers.
Geometric: Filled and outlined circles, triangles, squares, a plus/star and a half-disc. Clean primary forms for structured, modern patterns.
Memphis: Squiggles, zig-zags, arcs, crosses and pill shapes in the playful 1980s Memphis design style.
Botanical: Leaves, sprigs, berries, a petal cluster and a vine, for natural, garden-like repeats.
Sky: Five- and four-point stars, a crescent moon, a shooting star, a sun and a scatter of tiny dots. Perfect for night-sky patterns.
Blobs: Soft, organic blob shapes with gentle wobble, some filled and one outlined. Good for abstract, fluid backgrounds.
Confetti: Little bars, squiggles, triangles, dots, arcs and diamonds, like scattered party confetti.
Hearts: Filled and outlined hearts, a small star, a tiny heart and a dot. Sweet, romantic repeats.
Own layer (stamp): Replaces the doodle shapes with an image of your own editor layer, captured with **Use active layer**. Turns a logo or graphic into a repeating stamp in one click.
Off (Second set): The default choice for the Second set control: use only the primary doodle set, with no mixing.

sections.title: Rapport (repeat and tile)
sections.text:
How the design cell repeats into a full tile, plus the tile resolution and preview zoom.
The **Rapport** card turns your one design cell into a repeating tile. The repeat mode decides how neighbouring cells are offset or mirrored. Tile size sets the export resolution, and the zoom and frame controls only affect how you view the preview.
Repeat: How the design cell is laid out into the repeating tile. Choose Straight, Half-drop, Brick or Mirror.
Straight: The plainest repeat: cells line up in a simple grid with no offset. One cell per tile.
Half-drop: Every second column is dropped down by half a cell, so rows never line up straight across. A classic textile repeat that hides the grid.
Brick: Every second row is shifted sideways by half a cell, like a brick wall. The horizontal cousin of half-drop.
Mirror: The cell is flipped horizontally and vertically across a two-by-two block, so the pattern reflects like a kaleidoscope and edges always match.
Tile size: The pixel resolution of one exported cell edge. Higher values give sharper PNG and library tiles at the cost of size. This sets export quality only; it does not change the design.
Zoom: How large the pattern appears in the preview, for inspecting detail or seeing the repeat. The mouse wheel over the preview also zooms.
Show tile frame: Draws a dashed blue rectangle around one repeat unit in the preview, so you can see exactly where the tile starts and ends. Off by default.

sections.title: Colors
sections.text:
Pick a palette or brand color, shuffle colorways, reverse the order, and choose the background.
The **Colors** card controls the palette and the ground. Twelve curated palettes keep every roll harmonic; you can also feed in a single brand color or, on Pro, a saved brand kit. The little swatch strip below shows the colors currently in play.
Palette: The color set used for the pattern. Choose one of twelve curated palettes, **Custom (brand color)** to build a palette from a single hex, or one of your saved brand kits (starred).
Base color: A color picker that builds a five-step palette (dark to light) around your chosen brand color. Only visible when the palette is set to **Custom (brand color)**.
New colorway: Rotates which palette color lands on which element, giving a different color arrangement without changing the palette itself. Cycles through five colorways.
Reverse order: Flips the palette from light-to-dark to dark-to-light (and back), swapping which colors read as foreground and accent.
Background: The ground behind the pattern. Transparent leaves it see-through, Light and Dark pull the lightest or darkest palette color, and Custom color opens a picker.
Transparent: A background option: no fill behind the pattern, so whatever is under the pattern layer shows through.
Light (palette): A background option: uses the lightest color of the current palette as the ground. Elements that would vanish into it are automatically skipped.
Dark (palette): A background option: uses the darkest color of the current palette as the ground, for pattern on a rich, dark field.
Custom color: A color picker for the background, shown when Background is set to Custom color. Sets any hex you like behind the pattern.

sections.title: Palette catalog
sections.text:
The twelve built-in five-color palettes, plus the custom brand color and Pro brand kits.
Each palette is five harmonic colors, ordered dark to light. Selecting one is instant; the swatch strip in the Colors card shows the exact colors. These are the choices in the **Palette** dropdown.
Northern Lights: Cool blues and teal fading to a warm cream. The default palette.
Sunset: Deep purple through magenta and coral to golden yellow, like a sky at dusk.
Bauhaus: Primary red, amber, teal and navy on off-white. Bold, graphic and design-school classic.
Ocean: Deep navy stepping up through mid-blues to a pale aqua. Cool and marine.
Terracotta: Earthy browns and clay oranges to warm sand. Natural and grounded.
Pastel: Soft blue, pink, butter, mint and lilac. Gentle and airy.
Neon Noir: Near-black violet with electric magenta, coral and green. High-contrast and nocturnal.
Sage: Muted greens from forest to pale sage on soft cream. Calm and botanical.
Ink: A pure greyscale ramp from near-black to light grey. Monochrome and versatile.
Royal: Deep indigo and purple rising to hot pink and warm gold. Rich and regal.
Citrus: Forest green through lime and chartreuse to pale yellow. Fresh and zesty.
Rosé: Deep wine through raspberry and rose to blush pink. Warm and romantic.
Custom (brand color): Builds a five-step palette (dark to light) around a single hex you choose in the Base color picker, so the pattern matches your brand color.
★ Brand Kit [Pro]: Your saved brand kits appear at the end of the palette list, starred. Selecting one copies its colors into the pattern, so the tile keeps those colors even if the kit changes later. Needs at least two valid colors.

sections.title: Effects
sections.text:
Add a riso offset-print look and switch the line style of stroked motifs.
The **Effects** card layers a couple of print-inspired finishes over the pattern. They apply on top of whatever motif and colors you have chosen.
Offset print: Adds a second, slightly shifted and translucent ink layer under the shapes, imitating the misregistered look of riso and offset printing. Zero is off; higher values push the ghost layer further. Applies to vector shapes only, not image stamps.
Line style: How stroked lines are drawn: Solid, Dashed or Dotted. Only affects outlined and line-based shapes, not filled ones. Carried through to the SVG export too.
Solid: The default line style: unbroken strokes.
Dashed: Breaks strokes into evenly spaced dashes.
Dotted: Breaks strokes into a row of round dots.

sections.title: Pattern library and export
sections.text:
Name the tile, save it as a reusable fill pattern, or download it as PNG or SVG.
The **Pattern library** card is where a finished tile leaves the studio. You can register it in the editor's pattern library so shapes and text can be filled with it, or download the raw tile as a raster PNG or a vector SVG that repeats seamlessly in any tool.
Name: A short label for the tile, used when you save it to the pattern library and as the layer name when you insert it. Defaults to `Pattern `.
Save as fill pattern: Registers the current tile in the editor's pattern library, so it becomes available as a repeating fill for shapes and text everywhere in the editor. Saved at the chosen Tile size.
Download PNG tile: Downloads one repeat tile as a raster PNG image at the chosen Tile size. The file name includes the motif and seed.
Download SVG tile: Downloads the tile as a standalone vector SVG that repeats seamlessly in any layout tool. If you used a layer stamp, its image is embedded in the SVG.

sections.title: Insert and dialog actions
sections.text:
The footer buttons that place the pattern into your document or close the studio.
The footer sits at the bottom of the dialog. Inserting adds the pattern as an editable fill layer at document size; the layer stays linked to the generator, so you can reopen it later and adjust every dial.
Cancel: Closes the studio without changing your document. The Escape key and clicking outside the dialog do the same.
Insert pattern: Adds the pattern to your document as an editable fill layer that covers the whole canvas. The layer keeps a link to the generator, so you can reopen and re-edit it any time. [Shown when: Creating a new pattern]
Update pattern: When you opened the studio by editing an existing pattern layer, this replaces the footer button and applies your changes back to that same layer in place. [Shown when: Editing an existing pattern layer]

sections.title: Playground (live preview)
sections.text:
The preview is interactive: drag, zoom, double-click and right-click to shape the pattern directly.
The big preview on the left is the pattern itself, tiled edge to edge. You can rearrange it by hand and every change wraps seamlessly around the tile boundary. A hint under the cursor reminds you of the gestures.
On the Scatter and Terrazzo motifs you drag individual elements; on every other motif dragging shifts the whole pattern. Right-clicking opens a small in-canvas menu (never a browser menu).
Drag to move elements: On Scatter and Terrazzo, click and drag the nearest element to reposition it. If it crosses the tile edge it re-enters on the opposite side, so the repeat stays seamless.
Drag to shift pattern: On all other motifs, dragging slides the whole pattern under the tile window, wrapping around the edges. Handy for lining the design up the way you want.
Wheel: zoom: Scroll the mouse wheel over the preview to zoom in and out, between 35% and 320%. This mirrors the Zoom slider.
Double-click: new colorway: Double-click anywhere in the preview to rotate to the next colorway, the same as the New colorway button.
Right-click menu: Right-click the preview to open a small menu with pattern actions. Which items appear depends on the motif.
Add element: A right-click menu item (Scatter and Terrazzo only) that drops a new random element at the point you clicked.
Remove element: A right-click menu item (Scatter and Terrazzo only) that deletes the element nearest the click point.
New colorway: A right-click menu item that rotates to the next colorway, the same as double-clicking.
Reset edits: A right-click menu item that clears all your manual playground changes (moves, adds, removes and pattern shift) and returns to the generated arrangement.
Show tile frame / Hide tile frame: A right-click menu item that toggles the dashed frame marking one repeat unit, the same as the Show tile frame checkbox.

sections.title: Stripe direction options
sections.text:
The four choices in the Direction dropdown, which only appears when the Motif is set to Stripes.
The `Direction` dropdown is a per-motif dial that shows up only for the **Stripes** motif. It decides which way the stripe lines run. The default is Diagonal down.
Horizontal: Draws the Stripes motif as level lines running left to right. Pick this for classic横 banded stripes.
Vertical: Draws the Stripes motif as upright lines running top to bottom. Use it for pinstripe or column looks.
Diagonal down: Tilts the stripes so they slope down to the right. This is the default direction.
Diagonal up: Tilts the stripes so they slope up to the right, the mirror of Diagonal down.

sections.title: Tile size options
sections.text:
The four fixed resolutions offered by the Tile size dropdown, which set how sharp the exported and saved tile is.
`Tile size` sets the pixel size of one design cell for everything that leaves the studio: the fill pattern you save to the library, the PNG and SVG downloads, and the fill layer you insert. It does not change the live preview, which always renders at its own size.
A larger tile size looks crisper but produces a heavier file. For multi-cell repeats (Half-drop, Brick, Mirror) the actual saved image is several cells wide or tall, so the final pixel size is a multiple of this value.
128 px: Renders each cell at 128 by 128 pixels. The lightest option, good for small repeats or quick tests.
256 px: Renders each cell at 256 by 256 pixels. This is the default and a good all-round balance of sharpness and file size.
384 px: Renders each cell at 384 by 384 pixels for a sharper tile at a larger file size.
512 px: Renders each cell at 512 by 512 pixels, the highest quality option. Best for large fills or print.

sections.title: Window controls and shortcuts
sections.text:
Ways to close the Seamless Patterns dialog and manage saved favorites, beyond the main action buttons.
Closing the dialog by any of these routes leaves the document untouched. Nothing is added or changed until you press **Insert pattern** or **Update pattern**.
Close: The small **X** button in the top right corner of the dialog. It shuts the studio without inserting or updating anything, so any preview tweaks are discarded.
Escape key: Pressing **Esc** closes the dialog, the same as the X or Cancel. A quick way to back out with the keyboard.
Click outside to close: Clicking the dimmed area around the dialog (the backdrop) closes the studio. Clicks inside the dialog are ignored so you will not close it by accident.
×: The small **×** badge on each saved favorite tile removes that favorite from your list. It does not affect the current pattern in the preview.

sections.title: Swatches, thumbnails and status notes
sections.text:
Read-only previews and the small status lines that report what the studio just did.
These are not controls you set, but panels and messages that show the current state: the live color swatches, the captured stamp thumbnail, and the feedback notes under the stamp and library buttons.
Palette color chips: A row of small swatches under Base color that shows the active palette's colors in the order they are used. It updates when you change palette, brand color, or Reverse order, so you can see the exact colors before applying.
Stamp preview thumbnail: A small square that shows the editor layer you captured as a stamp. It appears next to the Use active layer button when the Doodle set is set to **Own layer (stamp)**. [Shown when: Doodle set is Own layer (stamp)]
Layer captured as stamp.: The status line under the stamp button reports the result of a capture. It reads **Layer captured as stamp.** on success, or **Select a layer in the editor first.** if no eligible layer was active.
The tile repeats seamlessly in every direction.: The note under the library buttons. It starts as **The tile repeats seamlessly in every direction.**, changes to a confirmation after a successful save, and shows an error if the save fails.
Inserts the pattern as an editable fill layer in document size.: The hint text in the footer, next to Cancel and Insert. It explains that Insert pattern adds a rectangle the size of the whole document, filled with the tiling pattern, and that the layer stays editable so you can re-open the studio to adjust it later.

sections.title: Calendars (overview)
sections.text:
Calendars builds fifteen poster-style calendars as real, editable layers, with all date and astronomy math computed locally.
Poster-style calendars as editable layers: month grids, multi-month and year overviews, a circular year wheel, a moon phase calendar, a life calendar counting your weeks, a landscape wall planner, a year-in-pixels mood tracker, countdown and advent posters, perpetual birthday calendars, week planners, school timetables, habit trackers and opening-hours cards.
All astronomy is computed locally. Public holidays are off until you pick a country: Germany, Austria or Switzerland, and their names are given in German. Mark days by clicking straight into the preview: eight marker shapes, per-entry colors, date ranges as soft pills and an automatic legend. Month and weekday names follow your site language, week numbering follows ISO, and the week starts on Monday or Sunday, whichever you pick.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Everything lands with a transparent background as editable layers and reopens anytime via **Edit Calendars**.
Editable layers: Every calendar is inserted as a grid image layer plus separate title, subtitle and legend text layers, wrapped in a group. You can move, restyle or delete each piece like any other layer.
Insert Calendar: The primary button when creating a new calendar. It renders the grid, adds the text layers, and drops the finished group into your document.
Update Calendar: Replaces the Insert button when you reopened an existing calendar. It re-renders the same layer in place with your new settings instead of adding a second calendar.
Edit Calendars: Reopens the studio on an existing calendar layer with all its saved settings. Because the layer stores its generator setup, you can change the year, type, markers or theme at any time.
Cancel: Closes the studio without inserting or changing anything.
Close: The X button in the top corner. Closes the dialog and discards any unsaved changes, the same as Cancel.
Computed locally, localized to your site language: A footer note reminding you that all calendar math (week numbers, moon phases, weekday names) runs in your browser and follows your WordPress site language. No calendar data is sent anywhere.

sections.title: Calendar types
sections.text:
Fifteen calendar layouts, chosen from a grid of icon tiles at the top of the settings column; the tile you pick changes which options appear.
The Type grid holds fifteen tiles. Click one to switch layout. The selected tile is highlighted, the preview updates instantly, and the settings below rearrange to show only the controls that apply to that type.
Choosing a type also pre-fills a sensible title (for example the month name and year) until you type your own.
Month: A single-month grid, the classic calendar page. Supports week numbers, weekend tint, today marker, neighbor mini-months, moon phases and clickable day highlights.
Several months: A multi-month view that tiles two, three, four or six consecutive months, rolling over the year end. Good for a quarter or half-year on one poster.
Year: A full twelve-month year overview, all months as small grids on one page. Day highlights and labeled legend entries carry across every month.
Year wheel: A circular year calendar with the twelve months arranged around a ring and the year in the center. Can add a moon-phase band and equinox/solstice season rays.
Moon calendar: A year of principal moon phases (new, first quarter, full, last quarter), computed locally from astronomy. A wide landscape band per month.
Life calendar: Your whole life as a grid of small cells, one per week or per year, with lived time filled in. A reflective poster driven by your birth date and a life expectancy.
Wall planner: A landscape year wall planner: all twelve months as horizontal day strips, the format you pin above a desk. Supports weekend tint, holidays and highlights.
Year in pixels: A mood-tracker grid with one small square per day of the year. You color days in the preview, and each distinct labeled color becomes a legend entry.
Countdown: A countdown poster showing the number of days left until a target date, with an optional progress bar from January 1 of the target year. Great for a launch or a big day.
Advent calendar: A festive advent layout with 24 numbered doors. A fixed December design that needs no date input.
Birthday calendar: A perpetual birthday calendar grouped by month, ignoring the year. Add each person as a highlight with a name, and they appear under their month.
