Download ZIP: Renders every selected format and downloads them together in one ZIP file named ` -formats.zip`. This is the primary action.
Export status: A line in the Export card that shows progress while rendering or saving (for example `Saving to the media library… (3/6)`), and the final result.
Select at least one format.: An error shown if you try to export with no format selected. Pick a format first.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
Turn a code snippet into a framed, syntax-highlighted image and drop it into your design - highlighted locally, fully editable, and dynamic.
Code Shot turns a code snippet into a clean, framed image and drops it into your design. Paste your code or import a file and it is highlighted locally in your browser - auto-detected across 29 languages, from JavaScript and PHP to Python, Go, Rust and SQL.
Style it like a screenshot from a good editor: nine themes (Dracula, One Dark, GitHub, Nord, Tokyo Night and more), a macOS-style window with a title, line numbers, a gradient or solid background and a soft shadow. Emphasise the lines that matter with a focus mode, or tint added and removed lines with diff mode.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. The image lands as a re-editable layer; reopen it anytime via **Edit Code Shot** to change the code, the theme or the frame. Frame it to a social-ready ratio, or copy it straight to your clipboard.
It supports dynamic content: put {{fields}} into the code or the title and the image re-renders per post, so it works as a dynamic featured image. Nothing is uploaded - the highlighting runs entirely in your browser.

sections.title: Code and language
sections.text:
Where the code comes from and how it is read.
Code: The code editor on the left. Paste or type your snippet; the preview updates as you go.
Language: Auto-detect, or pick from 29 languages. Auto-detect guesses the language from the code.
Import file: Load a file from your computer; the language is guessed from its extension and the file name fills the window title.
Dynamic tokens: The {…} button inserts {{binding}} tokens, so the code can come from a post field and resolve per post.

sections.title: Appearance
sections.text:
The look of the code itself.
Theme: Nine editor themes, light and dark: Dracula, One Dark, GitHub Dark, GitHub Light, Solarized Dark, Night Owl, Monokai, Nord and Tokyo Night.
Window: macOS traffic-light dots, a plain bar, or no frame. Add a title in the Window title field.
Line numbers: Show or hide the line number gutter.
Font size: The code font size, rendered with the bundled JetBrains Mono.
Tab size: How many spaces a tab expands to.

sections.title: Emphasis
sections.text:
Direct the eye to the code that matters.
Highlight lines: Type line numbers or ranges (for example 2-4, 7) to place a subtle band behind those lines.
Focus (dim the rest): With lines highlighted, dims every other line so the highlighted ones stand out.
Diff mode: Tints lines that start with + green (added) and - red (removed), with a colored accent bar, like a code diff.

sections.title: Background and frame
sections.text:
The backdrop behind the window and the shape of the export.
Type: Gradient, solid color, or transparent.
Colors: The background color, plus a second color for the gradient.
Padding: The space between the window and the edge of the image.
Window shadow: A soft drop shadow under the code window.
Aspect ratio: Frame the image to a fixed ratio with the window centred.

sections.title: Insert, copy and dynamic
sections.text:
Get the image out: as a layer, to the clipboard, or as a dynamic featured image.
Copy image: Copies the rendered PNG to your clipboard, ready to paste into a chat or a document.
Insert code shot: Drops the image in as a re-editable layer, scaled to fit your canvas.
Edit Code Shot: Reopens the studio for the selected layer so you can change the code, theme, emphasis or frame, then Update.
Dynamic content: Because the code and title accept {{fields}}, a code shot re-renders per post - use it as a dynamic featured image.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
A day as a circular, color-coded schedule - time blocks as arcs around a 24-hour clock.
Day Ring turns a day into a circular schedule. Add time blocks - a label, a start, an end, a color - and each becomes a proportional arc around a 24-hour clock, with midnight at the top.
Overlapping blocks stack automatically onto concentric rings, so a stand-up inside your deep-work block both show. Blocks that run past midnight wrap around the top correctly.
Start from a template (work day, weekend, wedding, travel, kids, study), give each block an emoji, label them on the ring or in a legend, show durations, and pick a palette or a color per block.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. It drops in as a re-editable, canvas-filling layer; reopen via **Edit Day Ring** anytime. Bind the title to a post field with {{...}} tokens for a dynamic featured image. Nothing is uploaded.

sections.title: Time blocks
sections.text:
The left column: the blocks that make up the day, and one-click templates.
Label: The block's name, shown on its arc and in the legend.
Start / End: The block's time window. A block whose end is earlier than its start wraps past midnight (for example 23:00-06:30).
Block color: Chosen with the shared color picker. Blocks left without a color are filled from the palette.
Emoji: An optional emoji shown before the name, on the arc and in the legend.
Add block / Remove: Add a new block after the last one, or delete a block with the x.
Load a day: Fill the day from a template and set a matching title.

sections.title: Dial & title
sections.text:
The clock face and the text in its centre.
Title / Subtitle: Text in the centre of the ring. Use the {…} button to insert {{fields}} so the title is dynamic per post.
Hour ticks: The 24 hour marks around the dial (every sixth is longer).
Hour numbers: Hour labels around the dial (0, 3, 6, 9 …), midnight at the top.

sections.title: Style
sections.text:
How the arcs and labels look.
Palette: One of seven color sets used for blocks without their own color.
Ring thickness: How thick the arcs are drawn.
Gap: The spacing between concentric rings.
Rounded ends: Round or flat caps on each arc.
Labels on ring: Draw each block's name and emoji on its arc (small arcs fall back to the legend).
Legend: A list beside or below the ring: color, name and time.
Show durations: Add each block's length (for example 1h30) to the legend.
Arc depth: A soft radial gradient across each arc for a rounded, tube-like look.
Dark theme: Light or dark dial text, ticks and numbers.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
The backdrop behind the ring.
Type: Solid color, gradient, or transparent.
Colors: The background color, plus a second color for the gradient.

sections.title: Insert & dynamic
sections.text:
Drop the ring into your design, or drive it from your posts.
Insert day ring: Drops the ring in as a re-editable layer that fills the canvas.
Edit Day Ring: Reopens the studio for the selected layer so you can change the blocks, dial or style, then Update.
Dynamic content: A {{field}} in the title re-renders the ring per post, so it works as a dynamic featured image.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
Any GPX file becomes a poster: the route, the elevation, the stats and the typography of one run.
Turn any GPX file into a poster: your run, ride or hike as a clean route line, or as a data line colored by pace, heart rate or elevation read straight from the file, optionally on a real OpenStreetMap street map rendered through the editor's privacy-friendly geo proxy.
An elevation profile, kilometer markers, big race stats for distance, climb, time, pace and date, and poster typography all land as real editable text layers. Themes, line weight, colors and markers are adjustable, and a demo route is built in so you can try it without a file.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Everything is computed locally from your file, and any poster reopens via **Edit Route**.

sections.title: Route (load a track)
sections.text:
Load a GPX file (or use the built-in demo) to turn a run, ride, or hike into a poster.
Route Visualizer opens as a dialog with a live poster preview on the left and setting cards on the right. The first card, **Route**, is where you bring in the track the whole poster is built from.
On first open the studio already shows a built-in demo route so you can see a finished poster right away. Loading your own GPX file replaces it.
Load GPX file…: Opens your computer's file picker so you can choose a `.gpx` track exported from a watch, phone, or fitness app. The track's points, distance, elevation, and timestamps drive the whole poster.
Demo route: A sample track that is loaded automatically the first time you open the studio, so the preview is never empty. Load your own GPX file to replace it.
Route summary line: A small line under the load button that confirms the loaded track. It shows the track name, the total distance, and how many points remain after simplification.

sections.title: Design (theme, layout, text size)
sections.text:
Pick the poster's color theme, where the text sits, and how big the type is.
The **Design** card sets the overall look: the color theme that tints the map and text, the layout that decides where the title block lives, and a text size multiplier.
Theme: Chooses a named color preset that sets the background, route line, and text colors together. Switch themes to restyle the whole poster in one step.
Layout: Decides where the title, stats, and date sit relative to the map square. `Classic` puts a centred text block below the map; the corner options tuck the text into a top corner of the map; `No text` shows the route square only.
Text size: Scales every text element on the poster (title, subtitle, stats, date) up or down together. Use it when the title feels too small or too shouty for the layout.

sections.title: Route line (color, width, markers)
sections.text:
Style the route line itself: width, color, data-driven coloring, distance markers, and the elevation profile.
The **Route line** card controls the drawn track: how thick it is, what color it uses, whether the color follows your pace, heart rate, or elevation, and the extras drawn along and under it (kilometre markers, start and finish dots, and an elevation profile strip).
Line width: Sets how thick the route line is drawn, as a percentage of the default weight. Increase it for a bold poster line, decrease it for a fine trace on dense courses.
Route color: Sets the color of the route line using the editor's color picker. By default it uses the theme's line color until you choose a custom one.
Auto: Clears any custom route color and returns the line to the theme's default color. Sits next to the Route color picker.
Color mode: Colors the route line by data instead of a single color. `Solid` uses one color; `Pace`, `Heart rate`, and `Elevation` shade the line along its length by that value, with a min/max legend on the map.
Km markers: Places small labelled dots along the route at a fixed distance interval. `Auto` picks the smallest step that keeps the map to about 12 markers.
Start / finish markers: Draws a marker at the start point and the finish point of the route. Turn it off for a cleaner line with no end dots.
Elevation profile: Adds a small elevation profile strip along the bottom of the map square, showing the ups and downs of the course. It is disabled when the file has no elevation data.

sections.title: Map (street map background)
sections.text:
Optionally place the route on a real OpenStreetMap street map, fetched through your own server.
The **Map** card only appears when the editor's geo proxy is available. It lets you draw the route on top of real streets from OpenStreetMap, rendered locally after the map data is fetched and cached on your own server.
Street map background: Draws the route on top of a real street map instead of a plain themed background. Street data comes from OpenStreetMap, fetched through your own server and cached there.
Map status line: A small status line under the toggle that reports what is happening while map data loads. It shows progress, retries, and honest warnings when an area is too large, too dense, or returns nothing.

sections.title: Text (title, subtitle, stats line)
sections.text:
Type the poster's title and subtitle and choose which stats appear in the stats line.
The **Text** card fills the poster's text block. Enter a title and subtitle, then tick the values you want in the stats line under them. When the track has a name it is used as the title until you type your own.
Title: The large headline on the poster, usually the route or event name. It is auto-filled from the GPX track name and can be overwritten.
Subtitle: A smaller line under the title, for a place, date phrase, or short caption. Leave it empty to hide it.
Stats line: A header that labels the group of checkboxes below it. The ticked values are joined into a single stats line under the title.
Distance: Includes the total distance of the route in the stats line. Read from the track.
Elevation gain: Includes the total metres climbed in the stats line. It only appears when the route actually has a positive elevation gain.
Time: Includes the moving or elapsed time of the activity in the stats line, when the track has timestamps.
Pace: Includes the average pace (time per kilometre) in the stats line, calculated from distance and time.
Date: Adds a separate date line under the stats, showing the day the activity was recorded. It is formatted for your site language.

sections.title: Insert and close
sections.text:
Insert the finished route poster into the document, or cancel out.
The dialog footer explains what will be added and holds the two action buttons. Inserting adds the route as a baked image plus real, editable text and shape layers, grouped together.
Cancel: Closes the studio without changing your document. The same as pressing Escape, clicking the X, or clicking the dark area outside the dialog.
Insert Route: Adds the poster to your document: the route square as an image, plus the title, subtitle, stats, date, divider, and attribution as real text and shape layers, all in one group. Disabled until a route is loaded.
Update Route: Replaces the button label when you reopen an existing route poster. It re-bakes the image and settings in place instead of inserting a new group. [Shown when: Editing an existing route layer]

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
The waveform of a song, a heartbeat or an episode, styled into a poster or a player card.
The waveform of any audio file as a poster: pick a track from the media library, the wedding song, a heartbeat, a podcast episode, and style it as bars, a line, filled, dots, pulse, LED, a circle, ridgeline mountain lines, a spiral that winds the whole song into one image, sunburst rings, or a heartbeat running around a heart contour.
Color it solid, with curated gradients including gold, copper and chrome foils, or let the sound pick the colors, dark where the bass sits, bright where the treble lives. Add neon glow, a mirror reflection, or split the left and right channel into two colors.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert as a classic poster with title, subtitle and duration, or as a music player card with progress bar and timestamps, all as editable layers. The audio is analyzed locally in your browser, and every wave reopens via **Edit Soundwave Art**.

sections.title: Audio (pick a track and trim)
sections.text:
Choose an audio file from the media library and trim the range that becomes the wave.
Soundwave Art turns any audio file into a waveform poster. The **Audio** card is where you pick the track. It is decoded locally in your browser with the Web Audio API, so nothing leaves the page, and you can trim which part of the track the wave covers.
Choose audio: Opens the WordPress media library filtered to audio files, so you can pick the wedding song, a heartbeat, a podcast clip, or any track. The confirm button in that picker reads "Use audio".
Audio info line: A small line under the button showing the chosen track's title and its length once decoded.
Start: Trims where the wave begins, as a position along the track. Drag it in to skip a quiet intro. The readout shows the timecode.
End: Trims where the wave ends, as a position along the track. Drag it in to drop a long outro or fade.

sections.title: Style (wave shape and dynamics)
sections.text:
Twelve wave styles plus density, amplitude, height and cap controls.
The **Style** card sets how the waveform is drawn. Pick one of twelve visual styles, then shape it with density, amplitude, and height sliders and two toggles.
Bars: Draws the wave as separate vertical bars, one per sample bucket. The classic audiogram look.
Line: Draws the wave as a single continuous outline that traces the peaks. A clean, minimal look.
Filled: Draws the wave as a solid filled shape under the peak outline, for a bolder, poster-like block.
Dots: Draws the wave as columns of dots that rise and fall with the peaks, for a softer, dotted texture.
Pulse: Draws the wave as a single heartbeat-style pulse line with sharp spikes. Good for a heartbeat recording.
LED: Draws the wave as stacked LED segments, like a hardware level meter with discrete blocks.
Circle: Wraps the waveform around a ring so it radiates from the centre. Always rendered in a square tile.
Ridgeline: The song as stacked mountain lines, one row per slice of the track, each ridge occluding the ones behind it - the classic record-sleeve poster look. Reads a much finer peak profile than the bar styles.
Spiral: The whole song wound into a spiral from the center outward - the full track in one image. Bars taper toward the center so the inner windings stay crisp.
Sunburst: Two or three concentric rings of radial bars, each ring carrying a slice of the song, with room for a title in the middle - the vinyl-label look.
Heartbeat: The bars follow a heart outline, radiating outward from the contour - the wedding-song classic: the heartbeat runs around the heart.
Hexagon (contour): Like Heartbeat, but the bars run along a hexagon outline - a clean technical badge shape.
Density: Sets how many bars or samples make up the wave. Lower values give chunky, sparse bars; higher values give a fine, detailed wave.
Amplitude: Scales the height of the peaks. Raise it to exaggerate quiet passages, lower it to tame a loud, clipped track.
Wave height: Sets how tall the wave band is, as a share of the poster width. It applies to the flat (non-circle, non-shape) styles.
Rounded caps: Rounds the ends of the bars and lines instead of leaving them squared off. A softer look.
Transparent background: Drops the wave tile's background so only the wave itself is drawn, letting whatever is behind it show through.

sections.title: Theme
sections.text:
Choose a color theme for the wave and its background.
The **Theme** card is a dropdown of named presets. Each one sets the background and wave colors together. Picking a theme clears any custom colors you set under Colors.
Theme tiles: A dropdown of color presets. Pick one to recolor the background and wave in one step.

sections.title: Colors
sections.text:
Solid, gradient or sound-driven coloring plus glow, reflection and stereo split.
The **Colors** card lets you fine-tune the two colors the theme provides. Each row has a color swatch and an Auto button that returns it to the theme's color.
Background: Sets a custom color for the wave tile's background, overriding the theme. Opens the editor's color picker.
Wave: Sets a custom color for the waveform itself, overriding the theme. Opens the editor's color picker.
Auto: Clears the custom color on its row and returns it to the current theme's color. There is one Auto button per color.
Solid: One wave color from the theme or your override - the classic flat poster look.
Gradient: A curated color gradient across the wave. Ten presets including gold foil, copper and chrome metallics that read as printed foil.
Sound color: The sound itself picks the colors: bassy, soft passages take the first gradient color, trebly, bright passages the last. Every song gets its own unique color fingerprint.
Color flow: For gradients: run the colors along the wave from left to right, or map them to loudness so quiet parts and peaks get different colors.
Glow: Neon glow around the wave, drawn as layered halo passes. Strongest on dark themes - 0 turns it off.
Mirror reflection: Adds a fading mirrored copy below the wave, like a music player card. Available for the linear styles (bars, line, filled, dots, pulse, LED).
Stereo split (L/R): Draws the left channel above the midline and the right channel below, each in its own color. Only enabled for stereo tracks.
Right channel: The color of the lower, right-channel half when the stereo split is on.

sections.title: Shape (mask)
sections.text:
Optionally clip the wave into a square, rounded square, circle, heart, or hexagon.
The **Shape** card masks the wave tile into a decorative outline. Choosing anything other than Square draws the wave inside a centred square tile clipped to that shape.
Square: No mask: the wave fills its rectangle normally. The default.
Rounded: Clips the wave tile to a rounded square (squircle) for softer corners.
Circle: Clips the wave tile to a circle.
Heart: Clips the wave tile to a heart outline. A romantic frame for a wedding song or first dance.
Hexagon: Clips the wave tile to a hexagon.

sections.title: Text block
sections.text:
Add the poster title, subtitle, duration, and choose the text layout.
The **Text block** card adds the classic poster text under the wave. It only appears when inserting a new soundwave, not when editing an existing one. The title is filled from the track name until you type your own.
Layout: Classic poster (centered title, divider, subtitle and duration line), Player card (left-aligned title with a progress bar, dot and elapsed/total timestamps - a paused song as a poster), or no text at all.
Title: The large headline on the poster, usually the song or track name. Auto-filled from the audio title until you edit it.
Subtitle: A smaller line under the title, for the artist, a date, or a short phrase. Leave it empty to hide it.
Text size: Scales the whole text block (title, subtitle, duration) up or down together.
Duration line: Adds a small line showing the length of the trimmed clip (for example 3:42) under the subtitle.
Player card: Lays the poster out like a music player: progress track with a dot at the paused position, elapsed and total time, then title and subtitle left-aligned. Every part is a real editable layer.

sections.title: Video (audiogram export)
sections.text:
Preview and export an animated audiogram video with the audio, saved to the media library.
The **Video** card turns the still wave into a moving audiogram: the wave animates to the music and the audio is muxed in. You can preview it in the dialog and export it to the media library. Everything is recorded locally in your browser.
Format: Sets the video's aspect ratio and resolution. Square for feeds, landscape for players, portrait for stories and reels.
Animation: Chooses how the wave moves. `Equalizer` makes the bars dance to the live spectrum; `Progress` sweeps a playhead across the full wave; `Scrolling` moves the wave past a fixed centre line.
Include title text: Shows the title and subtitle text on the exported video frame. Turn it off for a clean wave-only clip.
Video background: Sets the stage color behind the wave tile in the video, overriding the automatic choice. Opens the color picker.
Auto (video background): Clears the custom video background and returns to the automatic stage color, which contrasts with the wave tile.
Play preview: Plays the audio and animates the wave in the dialog at half resolution, so you can check the motion before exporting. The button then reads "Stop preview".
Export video: Records the animated audiogram with sound and uploads it to the media library. Uses MP4 where supported, otherwise WebM.
Cancel export: Stops an export that is in progress and discards it. Only visible while recording.

sections.title: Insert and close
sections.text:
Insert the soundwave poster into the document, or cancel out.
The footer holds the two main actions. Inserting adds the wave as a baked image plus real title, subtitle, duration, and divider layers, grouped together.
Cancel: Closes the studio without changing your document. The same as pressing Escape, clicking the X, or clicking outside the dialog.
Insert Soundwave: Adds the poster to your document: the wave as an image, plus the title, subtitle, duration, and divider as real layers, all in one group. Disabled until an audio file is analysed.
Update Soundwave: Replaces the button label when you reopen an existing soundwave. It re-bakes the wave and settings in place instead of inserting a new group. [Shown when: Editing an existing wave layer]

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
The night sky over any place at any date, dressed up as a poster.
The night sky over any place at any date, as a poster: search a location, pick the moment, choose a theme and shape, and toggle constellation lines, the grid and the cardinal directions.
Then dress the chart up: foil constellation lines in gold, copper, chrome or color gradients, a neon glow slider, diffraction spikes on the brightest stars, real astronomical star colors, the actual Milky Way band computed for your place and moment, and a constellation highlight that lets one constellation, the birth sign, the favorite, shine bold while the rest of the sky steps back.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert the chart with a classic title, subtitle and date and coordinates block, all as editable layers. Everything is computed locally from the bundled star catalog, and any chart reopens via **Edit Star Map Posters**.

sections.title: Location, date and time
sections.text:
Search for a place and pick the exact date and time of the sky you want to chart.
Star Map Posters charts the real night sky over any place at any moment. The **Location** card is where you set the where and when: search a place, then pick the date and time.
The sky is computed locally from a bundled star catalogue, so it appears instantly. The only network step is the one-time place search. On a fresh open the studio seeds the last place you charted, or Oldenburg, Germany as a fallback.
Search a place: Type a place name to look it up through the editor's geo proxy. Matches appear as a dropdown of results; pick one to set the sky's location.
Search results: The dropdown list of matching places under the search box. Each row shows the place name and its region; click one to select it.
Coordinates line: A small line showing the latitude and longitude of the selected place, so you can confirm you picked the right spot.
Date: The calendar date whose sky is charted. Defaults to today. Pick a birthday, anniversary, or any meaningful day.
Time: The clock time on that date whose sky is charted. The stars rotate through the night, so the time matters.

sections.title: Theme
sections.text:
Choose a color theme for the sky, stars, and lines.
The **Theme** card is a dropdown of named presets, each setting the sky background, star and line colors together. Picking a theme clears any custom colors set under Colors.
Theme tiles: A dropdown of color presets. Pick one to recolor the whole chart (background, stars and lines) in one step.

sections.title: Colors
sections.text:
Theme colors, custom overrides, and the v1.7 foil gradients for the constellation lines.
The **Colors** card fine-tunes the three colors the theme provides. Each row has a color swatch and an Auto button that returns it to the theme's color.
Background: Sets a custom color for the sky background, overriding the theme. Opens the editor's color picker.
Stars: Sets a custom color for the stars, overriding the theme. Opens the editor's color picker.
Lines: Sets a custom color for the constellation lines and grid, overriding the theme. Opens the editor's color picker.
Auto: Clears the custom color on its row and returns it to the current theme's color. There is one Auto button per color.
Line foil: Paints the constellation lines and the horizon ring with a curated gradient instead of one color - ten presets including gold, copper and chrome foils that read as pressed foil on dark themes. Auto returns to the theme line color.
Glow: A neon halo around the constellation lines, the horizon ring and the bright stars. It also widens the star halos: more stars get a soft aura the higher the glow.

sections.title: Sky (stars, lines, grid, shape)
sections.text:
Set star size and toggle constellation lines, grid, cardinal directions, star colors, and the chart shape.
The **Sky** card controls what is drawn on the chart itself: how big the stars are, which reference overlays appear, whether stars carry their real colors, and the outline the whole sky is clipped into.
Star size: Scales every star's dot up or down. Larger stars read better at a distance; smaller stars give a finer, more accurate sky.
Constellation lines: Draws the lines that connect stars into constellations, from the bundled d3-celestial data. Turn off for a plain star field.
Coordinate grid: Overlays a faint coordinate grid on the sky, for a more technical, chart-like look.
Cardinal directions: Labels the horizon with the compass directions (N, E, S, W) so you can read which way you were facing.
Star colors: Tints each star by its real color (blue-white to red) instead of a single color, for a more lifelike sky.
Shape: Clips the chart into an outline: a circle (the natural sky dome), a full square, a rounded square, a heart, or a hexagon. Since v1.8.1 every shape draws its own edge line in the line color or foil - the heart gets its heart outline, just like the circle has its horizon ring.
Star spikes: Diffraction spikes (the star-filter cross) on the brightest stars of the night - a subtle four-point cross plus a fainter diagonal pair on the very brightest.
Milky way: A soft haze band along the real galactic plane, computed for your place and moment - if the Milky Way stood over that spot that night, this is where it was.
Highlight: Spotlights one of the 88 constellations: pick it from the list (Latin names) and its lines are drawn bold with a halo while the rest of the sky steps back - the birth-sign poster in one click. Only constellations above the horizon at the chosen moment are visible on the chart.

sections.title: Text block
sections.text:
Add the poster title, subtitle, and a date and coordinates line, and choose the text layout.
The **Text block** card adds the classic poster text around the chart. It only appears when inserting a new star map, not when editing one. The title and subtitle are filled from the searched place until you type your own.
Layout: Chooses where the text sits. `Classic poster` puts a centred block below the chart; `On the chart` tucks the title and date inside the sky circle; `No text` shows the chart only.
Title: The large headline, usually the place name. Auto-filled from the searched place until you edit it.
Subtitle: A smaller line under the title, for the region or a phrase about the moment. Auto-filled from the place's region until you edit it.
Text size: Scales the whole text block (title, subtitle, date line) up or down together.
Date and coordinates line: Adds a line with the chosen date and the place's latitude and longitude, so the poster records exactly which sky it shows.

sections.title: Insert and close
sections.text:
Insert the star map poster into the document, or cancel out.
The footer holds the two actions and a note that the sky is computed locally. Inserting adds the chart as a baked image plus real title, subtitle, date, and divider layers, grouped together. A small credit line reads "Yale Bright Star Catalogue · d3-celestial (BSD)".
Cancel: Closes the studio without changing your document. The same as pressing Escape, clicking the X, or clicking outside the dialog.
Insert Star Map: Adds the poster to your document: the sky chart as an image, plus the title, subtitle, date, and divider as real layers, all in one group. Disabled until a place is set.
Update Star Map: Replaces the button label when you reopen an existing star map. It re-bakes the chart and settings in place instead of inserting a new group. [Shown when: Editing an existing chart layer]

sections.title: Holiday Templates (starter pack)
sections.text:
An example pack that adds six seasonal starter templates to the editor, shipped to show the `registerTemplatePack` API.
**Holiday Templates** is a small demo extension. It registers one template pack (`registerTemplatePack`, needs editor API 2.1 or newer) whose six ready-made designs join the built-in Starter Templates. They show up in the template tray, in the Asset Library dialog (grouped under the pack label `Holiday Templates`), and in global search.
The designs themselves live in a `templates.json` file inside the package and are fetched only when needed, so a big pack never bloats the extension script. Pick one to start a new document, then swap the text and images for your own.
The template labels are in German because this pack ships as a real-world sample; the sizes and purpose are noted on each entry below.
Holiday Templates: The pack itself. Its six templates appear alongside the built-in starters in the template tray, the Asset Library dialog, and search, all grouped under this label.
Weihnachtsgruß — Elegant: An elegant square Christmas greeting card with a frame, a star, a headline, a rule line, a wish line, and a **From** field. Use it for a festive social post or e-card.
Geschenkgutschein: A square gift-voucher design with a card panel, ribbon and bow, a title, a value field, **For** and **From** lines, a footer, and a logo slot. Use it to hand out or sell a gift certificate.
Winter-Sale — Story: A tall vertical winter-sale layout sized for a phone story, with a night snow scene, a headline, a discount figure, a **What** line, a call to action, and a validity time. Use it for an Instagram or Facebook story promotion.
Weihnachtsmarkt — Einladung: A square Christmas-market invitation with a sky, a garland of lights, a title, a **Where** line, a small map, and times. Use it to invite people to an event.
Neujahrsgruß — Modern: A modern square New Year greeting built around a large year number with an overlay, plus a greeting, a thank-you line, a rule line, and a logo. Use it as a year-turn post or client thank-you.
Feiertags-Öffnungszeiten: A square holiday opening-hours notice decorated with fir branches, for posting which days and times your business is open over the holidays.

sections.title: Layer Namer (AI)
sections.text:
An example AI tool that auto-names your image layers by reading their content with a small local vision model, shown to demonstrate `registerAiTool` and the ML bridge.
**Layer Namer (AI)** registers an AI tool (`registerAiTool`, needs editor API 2.12 or newer). Its button sits under **AI Studio**, in **Local tools**. Run it and every image layer is captioned by the editor's own local caption model through `window.WPIE.bridge.ml.captionImage()`. The whole run stays in the browser; nothing leaves your site.
The caption model must be installed once, under `Settings, then Local AI Models` ("Alt text / captions"). If it is missing, the tool shows an error and stops. The generated caption is cleaned up (leading "a", "an", "the" removed, title-cased, trimmed to 48 characters) and written as the layer name.
Name Layers: The AI tool button. It reads each image layer and writes a short descriptive name based on what the picture shows, so a stack of raw "Image", "Image 2" layers becomes readable. Fully local, no API key needed.
Name Layers (AI): The settings dialog that opens when you run the tool. It tells you how many image layers will be captioned locally and offers one option before you start. Click outside the card or press **Cancel** to close it without doing anything.
Also rename layers that already have a custom name: A checkbox in the dialog. Off by default, so only layers with a default name (like `Image`, `Image 2`, `Layer 3`, or `Raster`) get renamed and your own names are kept. Turn it on to re-caption every image layer, including ones you named yourself.
Name layers: The primary button in the dialog. It closes the dialog and starts captioning: the model loads on first use (a toast says so), then each matching layer is renamed and a summary toast reports how many were named.
Cancel: Closes the dialog and does nothing. Clicking the dark backdrop outside the card does the same.

sections.title: Paper Doodles (asset pack)
sections.text:
An example asset pack that adds a shelf of simple doodle shapes to the Asset Library, shown to demonstrate `registerLibrarySection`.
**Paper Doodles** registers one Asset Library section (`registerLibrarySection`, needs editor API 2.0 or newer). It adds a **Doodles** chip to the Asset Library tray holding twelve hand-drawn vector shapes. Click a shape to drop it on the canvas, or drag and drop it, no extra code needed.
Each item is a `user-element` (an editable vector shape) built from a path inside a 100 x 100 box, so it scales and recolors cleanly like any other shape layer. The pack has no PHP, no build step, and no framework: previews are inline SVG data URLs generated on the fly.
Doodles: The Asset Library section this pack adds. Open the Asset Library and pick the **Doodles** chip to see the twelve shapes; click or drag any of them onto the canvas.
Heart: A rounded heart shape. Insert it as an editable vector layer that you can resize and recolor.
Star: A classic five-point star. Insert it as an editable vector layer.
Sparkle: A four-point sparkle or twinkle. Insert it as an editable vector layer, handy as an accent.
Speech Bubble: A rounded speech balloon with a tail. Insert it and add your own text on top.
Cloud: A puffy cloud outline. Insert it as an editable vector layer.
Lightning: A lightning bolt. Insert it as an editable vector layer for an energetic accent.
Arrow: A right-pointing block arrow. Insert it to point at something on your design.
Crown: A simple crown. Insert it as an editable vector layer, useful as a premium or winner accent.
Flower: A four-petal flower shape. Insert it as an editable vector layer.
Check: A checkmark or tick. Insert it to mark something as done or correct.
Sun: A sun with a ring of rays. Insert it as an editable vector layer.
Swoosh: A curved brush-stroke swoosh. Insert it as an underline or motion accent.

sections.title: Example Extension (reference)
sections.text:
A minimal reference extension that registers one effect, one Filter-menu item, and one panel, meant to be copied as a starting point for your own add-on.
**Example Extension** is the bare-bones sample to copy when building your own extension. It is plain vanilla JavaScript with no build step. In one file it shows the three most common editor-side registrations: a pixel effect, a Filter-menu item, and a right-dock panel.
The accompanying PHP file also shows the optional server-side hooks (adding data to `window.WPIE`, registering a custom stock provider, and reacting to saves), left as commented examples. Use this pack to learn the Extension API, not as a finished tool.
Scanlines (Example): A demo pixel effect that darkens every few rows to fake CRT scanlines. It appears in the **Filter** menu, in the **Adjust** panel, and as a Smart Filter, and because it is a registered effect the on-canvas preview matches the exported result exactly.
gap: The Scanlines parameter that sets how many pixel rows sit between each dark line. A smaller gap means denser lines; a larger gap spreads them out.
strength: The Scanlines parameter that sets how dark each line is. At 0 the effect is invisible; higher values darken the affected rows more (up to 80 percent darker at 100).
Example: Hello: A demo item added to the **Filter** menu. Choosing it pops a success toast that greets you and reports how many layers the document has, showing how a menu item reads editor state.
Example: A demo right-dock panel built with plain DOM (no framework). It displays the current document width and height and the layer count, showing how a panel renders from editor state.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
Photo sets arranged as designable cards and real 3D walls, from tight grids to scattered polaroids.
Photo galleries as designable cards and real 3D scenes: arrange any set of images as a grid, justified rows, masonry, mosaic, honeycomb, circles, hearts, stars, coverflow, a curved wall, a carousel ring, a card deck or scattered polaroids. Style gaps, corners, frames from hairline to polaroid and glass, captions and backgrounds, then tilt and orbit the whole wall in 3D.
Sources are static picks from the media library or dynamic: a post's featured image and all its images, a WooCommerce product with its gallery, or the newest posts, products or uploads. Dynamic galleries dropped into a dynamic template re-collect and re-layout their images per post or product in automation runs.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Export as a baked layer, a seamless video loop, an interactive drag-to-rotate HTML embed or a 360-degree spin, and reopen anytime via **Edit 3D Gallery**.
Requires a browser with WebGL2 and real graphics hardware. On software rendering the 3D scenes stays blank; Help, then System Status shows what your device reports.

sections.title: Source: static or dynamic images
sections.text:
Choose the photos that fill the gallery: a fixed set you pick by hand, or a dynamic set that re-collects itself per post or product.
3D Gallery Studio arranges any set of images as a designable wall. The **Source** card at the top of the panel decides where those images come from. There are two modes: a **static** set you pick from the media library, and a **dynamic** set tied to a post or product.
Dynamic galleries are the point of the extension in automation: drop one into a dynamic template and each generated post or product re-collects and re-lays-out its own images, so one design produces a fitting gallery for every item. This needs Free 1.237.0 or newer (extension API 2.7.0), which exposes the resolved images to the generator.
Media library (static): The default mode. Pick a fixed set of images from the WordPress media library; that exact set is laid out and stays the same wherever the gallery is used.
Pick images / Add images: Opens the media picker to choose images for a static gallery. Add more at any time; the chosen thumbnails appear as a strip you can reorder or remove from.
Post / Product (dynamic): Switches the source to a dynamic collection resolved from a post or WooCommerce product. Instead of fixed images, you choose what to collect (see the content-type rows below).
Content type: For a dynamic gallery, what to gather from the item.
Search posts: Type to find the specific post or product to preview a dynamic gallery against while you design. In automation the gallery follows the current item instead.
Max images: Caps how many images a dynamic gallery collects, so a long post or a big "latest" feed still makes a tidy wall.
Follow the current post in automation runs: When on, a dynamic gallery ignores the previewed item and re-collects images from whatever post or product the automation run is generating for. This is what makes one template produce a per-item gallery.
Shuffle order: Reshuffles the image order with a seeded random, so the wall looks arranged rather than sequential. The seed is stable, so re-renders stay identical.
Order: How the collected images are ordered before layout: as picked, or the shuffled arrangement.

sections.title: Layout families
sections.text:
Ten ways to arrange the images, from tidy grids to honeycombs, coverflow and scattered polaroids. Each adapts to the image count.
The **Layout** card picks the family that arranges the tiles. Every family is pure geometry computed from the image count, so a wall always looks complete whether it holds three photos or twelve. "Flat" families (grid, justified, masonry, mosaic, cells) form a wall you can then jitter and bend; the others place tiles in real depth.
Grid: Even rows and columns of same-size tiles, the classic Instagram-style block. Set the column count and aspect.
Justified rows: Rows where each image keeps its own aspect ratio and the row is stretched to a flush edge, like a photo-gallery contact sheet.
Masonry: Pinterest-style columns where tiles keep their aspect and stack with no row gaps, giving a portfolio wall.
Mosaic: An editorial mosaic that mixes large and small tiles into a woven block. Set columns to 0 to let it size itself.
Cells (honeycomb): A tessellating wall of shaped cells: hexagons, circles or diamonds packed into a honeycomb. Choose the cell shape and density.
Coverflow: A center image in focus with the rest angled away into depth on both sides, the iTunes-style flow. Set the angle and which tile is in focus.
Curved wall (arc): A wall bent into an arc that wraps toward the camera, set by the curve span in degrees.
Carousel ring: Tiles placed evenly around a ring you look into, ideal for a rotating product carousel.
Card deck (stack): Images stacked like a deck of cards with a slight fan, the top card fully visible.
Polaroid scatter: Photos tossed onto a surface at random angles and offsets, like a pile of polaroids. Seeded, so the scatter is repeatable.
Tile shape: For the cells family, the mask geometry of each tile. Beyond the packing shapes, tiles can also be cut to decorative masks.
Density / Columns: How many tiles across (or how tightly cells pack). More columns means smaller tiles and a denser wall.

sections.title: Tiles, frames and captions
sections.text:
Style the tiles: spacing, rounded corners, a frame around each photo, drop shadows, and optional title captions on pills.
The **Style** and **Captions** cards control how each tile looks. Gaps and corner radius shape the tiles; a frame style wraps each photo; captions add a title pill you can color and place.
Gap: The spacing between tiles, as a fraction of tile size. Zero butts photos edge to edge; larger values open the wall up.
Corner radius: Rounds the corners of every tile, from square photos to pill-soft cards.
Frame: The border treatment drawn around each photo.
Frame color: The color of the frame, with a row of quick swatches (whites, creams, wood tones, charcoal, grey and gold) plus a full color picker.
Shadows: A soft drop shadow under each tile that lifts the wall off the background. Set its strength.
Reflection: A faint mirror of the wall on the ground plane, for a showroom feel. Strength runs roughly 0.08 to 0.6.
Size variance: For scattered and stacked layouts, how much individual tiles differ in size, so the pile looks natural.
Jitter: Randomly nudges tiles of a flat wall off their exact grid position for a hand-placed look. Seeded and repeatable.
Captions: Turns on a title pill on (or below) each tile. When on, the caption cards below appear.
Caption text / Title: The caption shown on each tile. For dynamic galleries this can bind to the image title or the item name.
Caption font: The typeface for captions: pick from system fonts or the editor font library, in styles such as sans, serif, mono, condensed and handwriting.
Caption size: Scales the caption text relative to the tile.
Caption placement: Where the caption pill sits relative to the photo.
Pill background / color / opacity: The caption sits on a rounded pill. Set the pill background color, the text color and how opaque the pill is.

sections.title: 3D, camera and background
sections.text:
Tilt and orbit the whole wall in real 3D, set the camera, bend flat walls into depth, and choose what sits behind the gallery.
One three.js engine drives everything; "flat" is simply the head-on orthographic view. The **3D / Camera** card tilts and turns the wall and sets the lens, while **Background** decides what fills the scene behind it.
Rotate (turn): Turns the whole wall left or right around the vertical axis, showing its edge and depth.
Tilt: Tips the wall forward or back around the horizontal axis, for a looking-up or looking-down angle.
Field of view: The camera lens angle. A narrow field flattens perspective (telephoto); a wide field exaggerates depth.
Zoom / Distance: Moves the camera closer or further, framing the wall tight or with breathing room.
Bend: Curves a flat wall toward the camera at the edges, from perfectly flat to a gentle wrap.
Depth: Pushes tiles apart along the view axis so the wall gains front-to-back layering instead of sitting on one plane.
Focus tile / Focus size: For coverflow, which image is centered and in focus, and how much larger the focused tile is than its neighbours.
Orbit gesture: In the preview you can drag to orbit the wall and use the wheel to zoom, to find an angle by hand. The hint reads "Drag to orbit, wheel to zoom".
Background: What fills the scene behind the gallery.
Show document: Renders your current editor design behind the gallery so you can compose the wall against the real layout before baking.

sections.title: Presets
sections.text:
Twenty-four one-click starting points, from Insta Grid to Showcase Orbit, each setting a layout, styling and motion together.
The **Presets** row gives you a finished look in one click; every preset sets the layout family, tile styling, camera and animation together, and you can tune anything afterward. Use the category chips to filter, and "Show all" to expand the full set.
Preset cloud: The collapsible row of preset chips. It starts compact; "Show all 24 presets" expands it and "Show fewer" collapses it again.
Categories: The presets are grouped by kind in this reference (walls, cells, depth, scatter) to keep the list readable. The studio itself shows them in one row behind an expand button; there are no category chips to filter by.
Wall & grid presets: Flat-wall looks: Insta Grid, Gallery Wall, Masonry Portfolio, Editorial Mosaic, Justified Rows, Captioned Wall, Dot Wall, Floating Wall, Pulse Wall.
Shaped & honeycomb presets: Cell layouts: Honeycomb, Diamond Facets, and the circle-cell Team Circles.
Depth & motion presets: Presets that use real depth: Coverflow, Product Carousel, Product Arc, Curved Wall, Showcase Orbit, Cinema Pan, Hero Spotlight, Film Strip.
Scatter & deck presets: Casual piles: Polaroid Pile, Card Deck, Memory Board, Team Polaroids.
Preview on your current design: Presets and every change render live against your document, so you judge the gallery in place before inserting.

sections.title: Loop animation
sections.text:
Give the wall a gentle, seamless motion for the video and embed exports: orbit, spin, sway, float, pulse, drift or a cinema pan.
The **Animation** card adds motion that loops seamlessly, meaning the last frame matches the first, so a video or embed can repeat forever with no jump. Set the seconds per loop and the motion strength.
Animation (motion): The kind of looping movement applied to the whole wall.
Seconds: The length of one loop. Shorter is livelier; longer is calmer. The exports use this as the loop duration.
Swing / Strength: How far the motion travels, for example the swing angle of a sway. Swing runs about 4 to 30 degrees.
Seamless loop: All motions are built to loop cleanly ("Loops seamlessly in video and embed exports"), so the video-loop and HTML-embed outputs never stutter at the wrap.

sections.title: Export and insert
sections.text:
Turn the gallery into a baked layer, a seamless video loop, an interactive HTML embed or a 360-degree spin, and re-edit it any time.
The footer of the panel is where the gallery leaves the studio. Everything stays editable: an inserted gallery carries its settings, so "Edit 3D Gallery" reopens the studio on that exact wall.
Insert 3D Gallery: Bakes the current wall into your design as an image layer. The layer remembers its generator settings, so you can reopen and change it later.
To media library: Saves the baked gallery straight into the WordPress media library as a new image, without inserting it into the open document.
Video loop: Records the animated wall as a seamless video loop for social or hero use. Exports MP4 with a WebM fallback; set the length with Seconds. A still scene is not a problem: the recording switches the animation to Sway for the take and puts it back afterwards.
HTML embed: Exports an interactive, drag-to-rotate gallery as a self-contained HTML snippet driven by the bundled runtime.js (a [data-wpie-3dgallery] block). Visitors can orbit and zoom it live.
360 spin: sprite sheet: Bakes a turntable spin as a single sprite sheet image plus a tiny viewer, so the gallery can be spun by the visitor with no 3D at runtime.
360 spin: viewer: Inserts a standalone 360 viewer of the spinning wall.
360 spin: frames (ZIP): Downloads the individual spin frames as a ZIP, for use in your own slider or viewer.
Update 3D Gallery: When you opened the studio from an existing gallery layer (Edit 3D Gallery), this replaces that layer in place with your changes instead of adding a new one.
Show document (preview): A preview toggle that composites your current design behind the gallery, so you export it framed exactly as it will sit in the layout.

sections.title: Pro starter template packs
sections.text:
Pro adds 1404 extra starter templates in 29 packs, 17 of which bring their own gallery category, lifting the category chips from 12 to 29.
The free editor ships 255 starter templates in 12 built-in categories. Pro registers 29 additional packs on top through the editor's extension API, for **1404 extra templates**. Seventeen of them are category packs that add a brand new chip to the gallery, and the remaining twelve are top-up packs of 45 templates each that fill out the categories the free editor already has. A category pack holds 42 or 64 templates depending on its subject; the Dynamic Posts pack is the small one, with 16 designs built around post bindings.
Pro templates behave exactly like the built-in starters: they are fully editable documents, not flattened images. Clicking one opens it as a new document, in its own tab where tabs are available. Everything you find them with in the free editor keeps working, including the category chips and the color search.
The pack JSONs live in the Pro package and are fetched lazily, so nothing downloads until the gallery lists packs for the first time. The packs need Free 1.257 or newer, since that version introduced pack-declared categories. On an older free editor the packs are skipped rather than breaking the editor, so the extra templates simply do not appear.
Seasonal & Holidays: Category pack for seasonal and holiday posts. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Travel & Places: Category pack for travel, destinations and places. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Beauty & Wellness: Category pack for beauty, spa and wellness topics. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Community & Engagement: Category pack for community posts and audience engagement. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Life Moments & Cards: Category pack for life moments, greetings and cards. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Gaming & Streaming: Category pack for gaming and streaming channels. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Clubs & Non-Profit: Category pack for clubs, associations and non-profit work. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Trades & Services: Category pack for trades and local service businesses. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Real Estate & Home: Category pack with 44 templates for real estate listings and home topics. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Cars & Mobility: Category pack with 44 templates for cars, dealerships and mobility. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Kids & Family: Category pack with 44 templates for kids and family topics. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Tech & SaaS: Category pack with 44 templates for tech products and SaaS. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Finance & Insurance: Category pack with 44 templates for finance and insurance topics. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Podcast & Video: Category pack with 44 templates for podcast episodes and video channels. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Pets & Vets: Category pack with 44 templates for pets and veterinary practices. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
Fashion & Style: Category pack with 44 templates for fashion and style topics. Adds its own chip to the gallery filter bar.
More Starter Templates: The extras pack: 180 templates that do not add a category of their own. They carry the free editor's built-in category ids, 15 per category, so they top up all 12 built-in chips (Sales & Specials, Products & Launches, Events & Invites, Music & Nightlife, Food & Drink, Sports & Fitness, Business & Jobs, Tips & Courses, Quotes & Reviews, Editorial & Media, Data & Planning, Art & Posters) instead of appearing under a new one.
Starter Templates (tray): In the Asset Library tray under the canvas, the Starter Templates section lists the Pro templates alongside the built-in ones. Click a tile to open that template as a new document.
Starter Templates (full dialog): The Starter Templates tab of the full Asset Library dialog shows the same Pro templates with larger previews, the category chips and the color search.
Templates tab (New Image): On the Templates tab of the Create New Image dialog (File, then New, and the welcome start screen), the Pro packs appear below the built-in starters and above your own saved dynamic templates.
Pack subheading: Each pack's templates are grouped under a subheading carrying the pack's label, the same way extension template packs are grouped, so you can see which pack a template came from.
Category chips: The filter bar above the template grid. All is the default; the 12 built-in chips come first and the 16 Pro category chips are appended after them, for 28 categories. Clicking the active chip again clears the filter back to All.
Lazy loading: Pack contents are fetched from the Pro package only when the gallery first lists packs, so the extra templates cost nothing until you open a template surface.

sections.title: Template gallery: categories, color dots and search
sections.text:
The shared filter bar above every starter-template gallery: an All chip, one chip per category, and a row of color dots.
The same filter bar sits above the starter templates in the Asset Library dialog and in the Templates tab of the Create New Image dialog. Whatever you pick there filters the bundled templates and the templates of installed extension packs in one go, so a pack heading disappears when none of its templates match.
Categories are occasion-first: a template is filed under what it is FOR (a sale, a menu, a gig), not by how it looks. The preview already shows the look.
The search box next to the bar needs no AI model. Every template carries its own words and colors as plain data, so the gallery indexes the template name, the copy on each of its text layers, its category and the names of its dominant colors. Each whitespace-separated word you type must match, so typing more words narrows the result instead of widening it. That means "red menu" and "neon sale" both work, and typing a color name alone ("blue") filters just like clicking the blue dot.
Chips, dots and search combine: category AND color AND every search word must match for a template to stay in the grid. Clicking an active chip or an active dot again clears that filter.
All: The first chip, active by default. Clears the category filter so every category is shown at once. Clicking an active category chip returns you here as well.
Sales & Specials: Templates for discounts, offers and special deals. Click the chip to show only these; click it again to go back to All.
Products & Launches: Templates built around a product shot or a launch announcement.
Events & Invites: Templates for events and invitations: date, venue and headline layouts.
Music & Nightlife: Templates for gigs, club nights, DJ sets and releases.
Food & Drink: Templates for menus, dishes, drinks and hospitality posts.
Sports & Fitness: Templates for match days, training, gyms and fitness offers.
Business & Jobs: Templates for company posts, services, hiring and job ads.
Tips & Courses: Templates for how-tos, tips, lessons and course promotion.
Quotes & Reviews: Templates for quotes, testimonials and customer reviews.
Editorial & Media: Templates with an editorial or magazine feel: articles, covers, media posts.
Data & Planning: Templates for numbers, schedules, plans and comparisons.
Art & Posters: Templates for posters and decorative artwork where the design is the message.
Extension pack categories: An installed template pack can declare its own categories; they appear as extra chips after the twelve built-in ones. The first declaration of a category id wins and built-ins always win, so a pack can reuse a built-in id (its templates then join that chip) but cannot relabel it.
Filter by color (dot row): The twelve round swatches at the right of the filter bar. Each one keeps only the templates whose dominant palette contains that color; clicking the active dot clears the color filter. The buckets are the same ones the Media Library Manager uses, so "red" means the same thing in both searches.
How a template's colors are decided: Nothing is rendered or sampled. The gallery reads the template description: the document background, every visible shape fill and stroke, every text color and text background, and every gradient stop. Each color counts by the area it covers, near-transparent colors (under 35% alpha) are ignored, and colorful buckets are weighted higher than black, gray, white and brown, so a bright accent on a big dark background still counts. Up to four buckets that each hold at least a tenth of the weight are kept, strongest first.
red: Shows templates whose palette is dominated by red tones. The dot's tooltip is the bucket name itself.
orange: Shows templates with orange as a dominant color.
yellow: Shows templates with yellow as a dominant color.
green: Shows templates with green as a dominant color.
teal: Shows templates with teal as a dominant color.
blue: Shows templates with blue as a dominant color.
purple: Shows templates with purple as a dominant color.
pink: Shows templates with pink as a dominant color.
brown: Shows templates with brown as a dominant color. Brown counts as a neutral, so it is not weighted up the way the colorful buckets are.
black: Shows templates dominated by black and very dark tones. A neutral bucket, not weighted up.
gray: Shows templates dominated by gray tones. A neutral bucket, not weighted up.
white: Shows templates dominated by white and very light tones. A neutral bucket, not weighted up.
Growth Pack categories: Since v1.300 the free plugin bundles the Growth Pack: 500 marketing starter templates in five extra gallery categories - Email & Newsletter, Popups & Optins, Online Courses, Social & Pinterest and WooCommerce Store. They load lazily (pre-compressed) the first time the gallery opens and behave exactly like the built-in categories.

sections.title: Vignette & Film studio
sections.text:
One dialog that paints a vignette plus light leaks, film grain, dust, scratches, a frame and a retro date stamp onto a single re-editable overlay layer.
Opened from `Tools, then Vignette & Film`. The left half shows a live preview of your document with the overlay on top, the right half holds a preset row, a Blend row and one collapsible card per effect: Vignette, Light leaks, Film grain, Dust, Scratches, Frame and Date stamp. Every card has a checkbox in its header: unchecked, the effect is off and its sliders stay hidden. The overlay always renders at the full document size and is scaled into the preview, so grain and dust look exactly like the final pixels.
What you insert is a **generator layer**, not a flat pasted image. The layer keeps its settings under the id `wpie-core/vignette`, so `Edit` in the layer's context menu reopens this studio with every slider where you left it. Because all values are stored as relative percentages, the layer also re-renders itself at the target size whenever the document changes shape: dynamic templates, Magic Resize and format automation call the generator's resolve hook and repaint the overlay to the new box instead of stretching it.
If a plain radial gradient layer is selected when you open the studio (the way the starter templates ship their vignettes), the studio reads that gradient's look into its sliders and the primary button changes to **Replace layer**, converting the gradient into a studio layer at the same stack position.
Presets: A row of pills at the top of the control column. Clicking one replaces all settings at once with a curated look (and its suggested blend mode). Six pills show by default.
Show all 12 presets: Expands the preset row from the first six pills to all twelve, and reads **Show fewer presets** once open.
Subtle: Preset: a soft oval vignette only, low strength with a wide, heavily feathered falloff. The lightest of the looks.
Classic: Preset: the standard oval vignette, medium strength and a tighter size than Subtle. No film effects.
Film Noir: Preset: a strong, tight oval vignette plus film grain, and it switches the layer blend mode to Multiply.
Cinema: Preset: a Top edge vignette (shading from the top down) with light grain, for a graded movie-still feel.
Retro Film: Preset: oval vignette, heavier grain, light scratches and one warm light leak. The full analog look.
Golden Leak: Preset: a gentle wide vignette with two strong golden light leaks.
Old Photo: Preset: a dark brown vignette instead of black, strong grain and dark dust, like a print that aged in a box.
Instant Photo: Preset: light vignette and grain inside an off-white instant photo frame with the heavy bottom chin.
Filmstrip: Preset: vignette, grain and scratches inside a near-black filmstrip frame with punched perforation holes.
90s Snapshot: Preset: light vignette, grain, one warm leak and the orange date stamp in the bottom right corner. The stamp is filled with today's date if you have not typed your own text.
Rounded Matte: Preset: a very soft vignette behind a dark matte with rounded corners.
Dusty Print: Preset: an Edges vignette with dense light dust and a few scratches, like a dusty scan.
Blend: Picks the blend mode the finished overlay layer uses against the artwork below. Normal simply lays the overlay on top; Multiply deepens a dark vignette into the image. The preview honours your choice live.
Opacity (Blend row): The slider next to the Blend dropdown. Sets the layer's opacity, so you can dial a whole look back without touching its sliders.
Compare: Hold this button under the preview to hide the overlay and see the untouched document. Releasing brings the effect back.
Vignette: The header checkbox of the Vignette card. On by default, it paints the darkening (or lightening) falloff. Off, the whole card and its sliders disappear.
Shape: The dropdown that decides where the vignette falls off. Ten shapes are available, from a classic oval to single edges, letterbox bars and pillars.
Oval: Shape: a radial falloff around an adjustable center. Its radius comes from the image diagonal, so the look survives any format. Unlocks Feather, Center X and Center Y, and lets you drag the center in the preview.
Circle: Shape: like Oval, but the radius keys to the short side instead of the diagonal, giving a true round spotlight whatever the format. Also unlocks Feather and the Center sliders.
Edges: Shape: four straight ramps from the top, bottom, left and right edges inwards. The corners overlap and darken naturally, so the frame stays rectangular instead of round.
Corners: Shape: only the four corners fall off, the way an old lens loses light, while the edges stay clear.
Top: Shape: a single ramp shading down from the top edge. Good for headline text that needs contrast.
Bottom: Shape: a single ramp shading up from the bottom edge, the classic bed for a caption.
Left: Shape: a single ramp shading in from the left edge.
Right: Shape: a single ramp shading in from the right edge.
Letterbox: Shape: two ramps, one from the top and one from the bottom, for a cinematic band top and bottom. Their reach is a little shorter than a single edge ramp at the same Size.
Pillars: Shape: the same idea turned sideways, one ramp from the left and one from the right edge.
Color (Vignette): The swatch next to the Shape dropdown. The vignette does not have to be black: a dark brown ages a photo, a bright color can lift the edges instead of sinking them.
Strength (Vignette): How opaque the vignette gets at its darkest point. 0 makes it invisible, 100 paints the color at full opacity at the edges.
Size (Vignette): How far the falloff reaches. On the oval and circle shapes a larger value pushes the dark ring outwards and leaves more of the image clear; on the edge, letterbox and pillar shapes it sets how deep the ramp travels from the edge.
Feather: How soft the transition is between the clear center and the shaded edge. Low values give a hard ring, high values a long gentle fade. Shown for the Oval and Circle shapes only. [Shown for: Oval, Circle]
Center X: Moves the bright center of the vignette horizontally, in percent of the image width. 50 is the middle. Shown for the Oval and Circle shapes only.
Center Y: Moves the bright center vertically, in percent of the image height. Use it to put the clear spot on a face that sits off-center. Shown for the Oval and Circle shapes only.
Drag in the preview: With the Oval or Circle shape active, the pointer turns into a crosshair over the preview and dragging sets Center X and Center Y directly. A hint under the preview says so.
Light leaks: Card checkbox. Paints one to three soft colored glows anchored on an edge, biased to the top half like leaks in a real camera back. Overlapping leaks add up like light does.
Color (Light leaks): The base color of the leaks. Each blob drifts a little around this hue, so several leaks never look identical.
Strength (Light leaks): How bright the leaks burn into the image.
Size (Light leaks): How far a leak reaches into the frame, from a small edge flare to a glow across half the image.
Count (Light leaks): How many leaks are painted.
Variant (Light leaks): Reshuffles the leaks: their edge, angle, stretch and hue drift all follow this number. Same number, same leaks, every time the layer re-renders.
Film grain: Card checkbox. Sprinkles bright and dark speckles across the frame. It is sparse by design, only the outliers become visible grains rather than a full mosaic.
Amount: How strongly the grain shows. Higher values make the speckles more opaque, not more numerous.
Grain size: The pixel size of one grain. 1 gives a fine digital noise, 6 a coarse pushed-film texture. The grain is drawn without smoothing, so the cells stay crisp.
Variant (Film grain): Redraws the whole grain pattern with a different random seed. Nothing else changes.
Dust: Card checkbox. Scatters specks and the occasional curled fiber over the image, the way dust sits on a scanner or a negative.

sections.title: Dynamic Showcases dialog
sections.text:
Live WordPress data composed into one designed graphic: products, posts, reviews, your team or pasted spreadsheet rows become an editable card layout.
Turn live WordPress data into one designed graphic. Pick a source: WooCommerce products, blog posts, any public post type, real customer reviews, your team, an external RSS, Atom or JSON feed, or rows pasted straight from a spreadsheet. Filter it, click a layout in the live preview rail, and the real records compose into a single editable design.
Layout families cover products, posts, testimonials and people, from new-arrivals grids and spotlight heroes to review walls and team pages. A Custom Card mode repeats a card you design in the editor, a normal template with variables, as the tile, with per-record values filled in and empty elements hidden. Every element the source actually has, prices, sale badges, rating stars, chips, dates, gets its own row to toggle, resize and recolor, and long copy never clips: text auto-shrinks and shortens with an ellipsis.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Saved queries refresh in place, so the bestseller sheet you designed in spring re-composes itself with today's bestsellers.
Layout rail: The left column lists one card per layout with a mini preview rendered from neutral **example content** - the rail is a layout catalog, deliberately independent of your live data (the big preview shows the real records). Click a card to switch; the active layout is outlined.
Preview stage: The large center preview, rendered by the same engine that inserts the layers, over a checkerboard so transparent backgrounds are visible.
Show document: Overlays the current document behind the preview (with the showcase background hidden), so you can judge the composition against what is already on the canvas.
Status line: Bottom-left of the dialog: how many records were loaded and from where ("6 products, live from your site", "6 items, from pasted data"), plus loading and error states.
Insert / Update showcase: Inserts the composition as a named group of editable layers, or replaces the group in place (keeping its stacking position) when you came in through Edit.

sections.title: Source: products, posts, any post type, reviews, team, pasted data
sections.text:
Six data sources feed the same layout engine.
The Show dropdown decides where records come from. Query sources (products, posts, custom post types) re-run their filter against the live site every time the panel opens or refreshes; the pasted-data source parses rows you copied from a spreadsheet.
Products (WooCommerce): Live products with name, image, price, sale price and discount, rating from real reviews, category, short description, SKU and stock status.
Blog posts: Published posts with title, featured image, excerpt, date and category.
Any public post type: Every public post type of the site (pages, portfolios, events, listings...) appears in the dropdown and is treated like posts: title, featured image, excerpt, date, category.
Customer reviews: Approved WooCommerce product reviews and/or post comments as testimonial records: author, star rating, quote text, date and the reviewed product. E-mail addresses never leave the server.
Team (site users): Site users as team records: display name, role, bio, avatar and published-post count. Logins and e-mail addresses are never exposed.
External feed / API (RSS, Podcast, YouTube, JSON): Paste any RSS or Atom URL and the studio analyses its structure server-side: podcast feeds deliver episode covers and durations (shown as chips), YouTube channel feeds their video thumbnails, blog feeds their images. Individual JSON APIs work too - a web-radio now-playing endpoint, a headless CMS, any custom API: the server finds the record set (or treats a single object as one record), flattens nested values to dot paths, and mapping rows appear under the URL so you assign Title, Image, Price, Description, Category and Date to your fields - auto-detected in English and German, correctable by hand. A price mapping makes the rows product-shaped. The URL and mapping are saved with the graphic, so Refresh and dynamic templates re-pull the source; feeds are cached briefly (JSON two minutes, feeds fifteen) and fetched through WordPress with unsafe-URL rejection.
Pasted data (CSV / Excel): Rows pasted straight from Excel, Google Sheets or a CSV file; see the Pasted data section below.

sections.title: Pasted data: spreadsheet rows as records
sections.text:
Copy rows from Excel or Sheets, paste, done: delimiter detection, quoted fields and automatic column mapping.
The paste box accepts tab-separated rows (what Excel and Sheets put on the clipboard) as well as comma- or semicolon-separated CSV. Column names in the first row are auto-mapped to the record fields, in English and German (Produkt, Preis, Beschreibung, Kategorie all map correctly), and every mapping can be corrected by hand.
Rows WITH a mapped price column behave like products and feed the catalog layouts; rows without one behave like posts and feed the roundup layouts. The chosen layout re-validates automatically when the shape flips.
Paste box: The text area for raw rows. Delimiter (tab, comma or semicolon) is detected from the first line; quoted fields survive embedded commas.
First row contains column names: On by default. Off treats every row as data and names the columns Column 1, Column 2...
Column mapping (Title, Image URL, Price, Description, Category): Five dropdowns bind record fields to your columns. Auto-detected from the header names; adjust any of them and the preview re-renders.

sections.title: The twenty layouts
sections.text:
Four layout families plus your own: catalog, roundup, testimonials, team, and the Custom Card that repeats a user template. Twenty built-in layouts in total.
Each layout is a recipe that adapts to the document format, and every card keeps its designed PROPORTIONS: fewer items or fewer columns make larger cards up to a sensible size, never stretched stripes with billboard text - remaining space stays calm whitespace and the grid centers itself.
New Arrivals Grid: Product cards in a grid: image, name, rating stars, price with struck regular price, and a sale badge on discounted items.
Spotlight: One hero product left at full height, compact rows with thumb, name and price stacked right.
Price List: Menu-style rows: thumbnail, name and description left, price right, hairline separators.
Sale Sheet: Discount-first cards: the percentage is the hero element, price below.
Bestseller List: Ranked rows with a big accent number, thumb, name, description and price, ideal with the Best selling sort.
Compare Two: Two tall cards side by side with category chip, rating and price, for A-versus-B graphics.
Latest Posts: Post cards in a grid: featured image, category chip, title and date.
Hero + Stories: One big story card left (image, chip, title, excerpt, date), compact story rows right.
Top List: Numbered ranking rows with thumb, title and meta line, the "most read this month" classic.
Contents: Magazine table-of-contents rows: ghost index number, title, excerpt.
Review Wall: Testimonial cards: star rating, quote, author line with an initials disc (or their avatar), and the reviewed product.
Big Quotes: Full-width quote rows: stars and quote left, author block right.
Team Grid: Portrait cards: avatar (with a colored initials disc as fallback), name, role chip and bio.
Team List: Compact people rows: avatar disc, name and role left, bio right.
Custom Card: Repeat YOUR OWN design as the tile: build a card in the normal editor with variables like `{{wc.name}}`, `{{wc.price}}` or `{{post.title}}`, save it via File, then Save as Dynamic Template, and pick it in the Card section. The studio clones the card per record, scales it into the grid (the cell aspect follows your card), fills in each record’s values and hides elements whose value is empty - a discount label only appears on discounted products. A "Create starter card" button inserts a pre-wired example card to style. Editing the card template later updates every showcase that uses it on the next refresh.
