Available for EVERY source: products, posts, feeds and APIs use the standard variables, and reviews/team additionally offer semantic variables under the "Showcase records" picker group (review author, review text, rating, team role, bio and more) - the review author or team name also arrives as {{post.title}}, the avatar as {{post.featured}}. Coming from a page builder? This is the same idea as a loop template (Elementor) or a repeater (ACF): one card design that repeats per record, just rendered as a graphic.

sections.title: Content filters
sections.text:
Count, category, order, keyword and per-source filters decide which records make it in.
The Content section adapts to the source: query sources get category, order and search; products add stock filters and shop-specific sorting; reviews get their own filter row set.
Items: How many records to pull. The slider maximum always equals the ACTIVE layout’s capacity, so nothing is ever silently dropped - switching layouts adjusts the range.
Entries: Latest by filter / Hand-picked: Two ways to choose content. **Latest by filter** describes a query (category, order, search, stock filters) that re-runs on every refresh. **Hand-picked** lets you search and click exactly the entries you want - they appear in pick order, numbered chips remove them again, and the selection is saved with the graphic.
Category: The category-like taxonomy of the chosen post type: product categories for products, blog categories for posts, the first hierarchical taxonomy for other types.
Order: Newest first, Oldest first, A to Z, Recently updated; products add **Best rated**, **Best selling (all time)**, **Best selling (7 days)** (real sales from the last week via the WooCommerce analytics data) and price sorting in both directions.
Search: A keyword filter over the records.
Only on sale: Products only: restricts the query to items currently on sale.
Only in stock: Products only: restricts the query to items in stock.
Include (reviews): Reviews only: product reviews, post comments, or both.
Minimum rating: Reviews only: all ratings, 3 stars and up, 4 stars and up, or only 5 stars. Comments carry no rating and drop out once a minimum is set.
Sort (reviews): Reviews only: newest first or best rated first.

sections.title: Elements: per-piece toggles and columns
sections.text:
Switch individual card elements off without touching the layout.
Every optional card element has its own checkbox; layouts simply skip what is off. The column override reflows grid layouts.
Prices: Show or hide all price blocks, including struck regular prices.
Sale badges: Show or hide the discount badges on product cards.
Rating stars: Show or hide star rows on product and review cards.
Category chips: Show or hide category chips and role chips.
Descriptions: Show or hide short descriptions, excerpts and bios.
Dates: Show or hide date lines on post and review cards.
Columns: Auto, 1, 2, 3 or 4 columns for the grid layouts; Auto picks by item count.

sections.title: Header and copy
sections.text:
Headline, subhead and footer around the card grid, with an AI assist.
All three lines are optional; leaving them empty gives the cards the full canvas.
Header / Subhead / Footer: Three text lines composed around the grid; each becomes its own editable text layer.
Suggest header with AI: Writes a short header and subhead from the records currently on screen, using the editor’s own AI proxy. Optional; nothing depends on it.

sections.title: Style: presets, brand, colors, geometry, fonts
sections.text:
Six presets plus full overrides, resolved through your brand kits.
The preset sets the world (background, card color, ink, accent, fonts); everything after it is an override. With Use my brand kit colors on, the accent comes from the document’s active brand kit, exactly like every other studio.
Preset: Fourteen complete palette-and-font worlds: Clean, Editorial, Midnight, Bloom, Forest, Mono, Noir, Festive, Lux, Ocean, Sunset, Lavender, Slate and Terra.
Use my brand kit colors: Resolves the accent from the active brand kit (document kit first, then the site kit).
Brand kit: Pick which kit supplies the colors when the site has several; Site default follows the document.
Accent: A custom accent color; the Auto button returns to the brand or preset accent.
Background: A custom background color; Auto returns to the preset background.
Transparent background: Drops the background layer entirely so the showcase sits on whatever is behind it.
Corners: Corner-radius factor from 0 percent (square) to 200 percent of the preset rounding.
Spacing: Gutter density from 60 to 160 percent: tighter or airier grids without changing the layout.
Heading font / Body font: Full font pickers (brand, custom, system, editor and Google families) overriding the preset’s pairing.

sections.title: Refresh and dynamic behavior
sections.text:
A showcase saves its QUERY, not a snapshot: it can re-pull records any time.
The inserted group carries the full panel state. Edit Dynamic Showcases restores the panel against live data; **Refresh Dynamic Showcases** in the right-click menu re-runs the query and swaps the cards in place with one click, keeping the group’s position and stacking order.
Inside dynamic templates and automations the showcase re-renders itself with fresh site data on every run, so a "newest products" graphic in a dynamic image or an automation stays current without reopening the editor. An empty result keeps the previous cards: stale beats blank in a batch run.
Refresh Dynamic Showcases (right-click): One click in the canvas or layers-panel context menu: the saved query runs again and the cards are replaced in place. New products, posts or reviews appear; the position you dragged the group to is kept.
Dynamic templates and automations: During dynamic-content resolution (Preview with Post, automations, dynamic images) the showcase rebuilds from live data automatically, at the size it was designed at.
Stale beats blank: If a refresh returns no records (source offline, filter too narrow), the existing cards stay; a batch run is never broken by an empty query.

sections.title: 3D Objects Studio
sections.text:
Ready-made 3D objects for your designs: pick from a curated library, import GLB models or generate them with AI, orbit them live and bake the result into the document as an editable layer.
Ready-made 3D objects for your designs: a curated library across shapes, symbols, party, commerce, food, tech, seasonal, nature and abstract, each object with its own colors or repainted live with premium material presets from gold and chrome to glass, neon glow and toon.
Import your own textured GLB models and keep them in a server-side library shared across the site, or let AI build one: with a Meshy key, any media-library image or text prompt becomes a textured 3D model, saved straight to your library. Orbit with the mouse, pick light moods and camera angles, tune soft studio shadows and a ground reflection, and preview over your actual document.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. The object bakes onto the canvas as a transparent PNG layer and stays editable via **Edit 3D Object**.
Requires a browser with WebGL2 and real graphics hardware. On software rendering the viewport stays blank; Help, then System Status shows what your device reports.
Library: Over 150 ready-made 3D objects in nine categories (Shapes, Symbols, Party, Commerce, Food, Tech, Seasonal, Nature, Abstract), each rendered as a live thumbnail tile. Click a tile to load it into the viewport.
Show document: Renders your current design behind the transparent viewport, so you judge the object over the real artwork instead of a checkerboard.
Insert 3D Object: Bakes the current view as a transparent PNG layer, centered in the document. The layer stays editable: reopening the studio restores object, material, camera and light.
Drag to orbit / wheel to zoom: Drag anywhere in the viewport to spin the object, use the mouse wheel to zoom. The Rotate and Tilt sliders follow along.

sections.title: My models
sections.text:
Your site-wide 3D model library: every imported or AI-generated GLB, stored on the server with a preview thumbnail.
The card appears once the library holds at least one model. Models are shared with every editor user on the site; deleting or renaming is limited to the owner and administrators. Models and their thumbnails are included in plugin backups.
Model row: Shows the preview thumbnail, name and file size. Click the name to load the model into the viewport; the active model is highlighted.
Rename (pencil): Turns the name into an input field. Enter or clicking elsewhere saves, Escape cancels.
Delete (x): Removes the model and its thumbnail from the server. Only the owner or an administrator can delete a model; layers already baked from it keep working.
Preview thumbnails: AI-generated models keep the generator's own preview image; imported models get a small studio snapshot automatically. Older models receive a thumbnail the first time you load them.

sections.title: AI 3D (Meshy)
sections.text:
Generate a textured 3D model from a media-library image or a text description, powered by Meshy.
Requires a Meshy API key under Settings, then Integrations. Generation runs through your server (the key never reaches the browser), takes a few minutes and uses Meshy credits; a progress percentage and Meshy's preview image keep you posted. Finished models are saved straight into My models and loaded into the viewport.
Image to 3D: Choose image opens the media picker in an overlay; the selected photo (JPEG, PNG or WebP) is turned into a textured 3D model.
Text to 3D: Describe the object in the prompt field and generate. Works best with a short, concrete description of a single object.
Refine (better textures, slower): Runs a second Meshy pass after the text preview that adds high-quality PBR textures. Takes longer and uses more credits.
Model name (optional): Names the entry in My models. Left empty, the image title or the start of your prompt is used.
Retry import: If saving a finished generation fails, the button switches to Retry import: the next click only repeats the import and never re-charges a generation.

sections.title: Import GLB
sections.text:
Load your own textured 3D models: binary glTF 2.0 (.glb) with embedded textures, parsed locally in the browser.
Models are centered and scaled to the studio's standard size automatically. Files up to 50 MB are supported.
Choose file: Opens the file picker for a .glb file. Nothing is uploaded during parsing - the model is read locally.
Save to library: Stores the imported model in My models on the server (on by default), so it survives reloads and stays editable on baked layers. Unchecked, the model lives only for this session.

sections.title: Material
sections.text:
Repaint any object - library or imported - with one of 14 material presets, or keep its original colors.
Original shows each object's own colors. Every other preset repaints all parts with one surface: Gold, Chrome, Copper, Steel and Rose gold are fixed metals; Glass, Frosted, Gloss, Matte, Neon, Gradient, Pearl, Toon and Wireframe take your own color (Gradient takes two).
Color / Color 2: The tint for colorable presets; Gradient blends Color into Color 2 from top to bottom. Switching presets seeds a sensible starting color.
Glow: For the Neon preset: adds a bloom halo around the emissive surface (0 to 100).
Pearl: A clearcoated surface with real iridescence that shifts hue as the object turns.
Wireframe: Renders only the triangle edges of the mesh, the technical hologram look. Try it on the Globe.

sections.title: View
sections.text:
Camera controls: one-click angles plus precise sliders.
Front / Hero / Isometric / Top-down: One-click camera angles: straight-on, the classic three-quarter product angle, a 45-degree isometric view and a steep look from above.
Rotate: Spins the object around its vertical axis (-180 to 180 degrees). Dragging in the viewport moves this slider too.
Tilt: Raises or lowers the camera (-10 to 60 degrees).
Roll: Leans the object itself sideways (-180 to 180 degrees), for tumbling or floating compositions.
Zoom: Camera distance from 50 to 240 percent; the mouse wheel adjusts it too.

sections.title: Light & Shadow
sections.text:
Studio lighting with one-click moods, a soft ground shadow and an optional floor reflection.
Studio / Sunset / Dramatic / Soft: Lighting moods: neutral studio light, warm low sun with violet fill, hard single-source contrast, or bright and nearly shadowless.
Light: Overall brightness of the rig (0 to 100).
Shadow: Opacity of the soft ground shadow; 0 switches the floor off entirely.
Blur / Length / Direction: Shape the ground shadow: softness of its edge, how far it stretches, and the angle it falls at.
Reflection: A fading mirror image below the object, as if it stood on glossy studio flooring (0 to 100).

sections.title: Settings: 3D Model Generation (Meshy)
sections.text:
Connect a Meshy account so the 3D studios can generate textured 3D models from images and text.
Lives on the Integrations tab below Stock Images. Requests are proxied through your server with the stored key; finished models are saved to the 3D model library.
Meshy API key: Stored obfuscated like every provider key; the eye toggles visibility, Remove clears it. Sign up at meshy.ai - trial credits are free, then pay-as-you-go.
Test connection: Verifies the stored key against Meshy and shows your remaining credit balance.
AI model: Which Meshy generation model to use: Latest (recommended) always tracks the newest, or pin Meshy 7 / Meshy 6 / Meshy 5. Meshy 7 exists for image-to-3D only, so text-to-3D quietly falls back to the newest model that endpoint offers.
Detail quality: One friendly quality level for every generation: Standard (recommended), High (4K textures on Meshy 6 and newer, larger files), Ultra (High plus the extra refinement pass Meshy 7 runs on images - sharper geometry, slower, 5 credits more) or Low (a compact 10,000-polygon remesh, fast and small). From Meshy 6 on the mesh is left as generated except at Low, because remeshing grinds down the very geometry the newer models are better at. PBR material maps are always included.

sections.title: Assets menu
sections.text:
Everything that brings content into the document: the asset library, stock photos, AI asset generation, the media library manager, dynamic templates and brand kits.
Asset Library: Opens the full asset library dialog (also Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+L or the tray at the bottom).
Stock Images: Opens the stock photo search across your configured providers (Pexels, Pixabay, Unsplash).
Asset Generator: Opens the AI asset generator for gradients, text marks, shapes and illustrations.
Manage Media Library: Opens the media library manager without leaving the editor.
Dynamic Templates: Opens the dynamic template picker.
Brand Kits: Opens brand kit management (visible to users who may manage kits).

sections.title: Elementor widgets
sections.text:
Dynamic Image, Live Badge and Personalized Image as native Elementor widgets - thin wrappers around the same shortcodes the Gutenberg blocks use.
Search for "WPIE" in the Elementor panel. Because the widgets render through the existing shortcodes, an Elementor update cannot break the output - worst case the widgets simply do not register. A toggle under the Widgets & Blocks tab in Settings switches the bridge on and off (default on).
WPIE Dynamic Image: Picks a Dynamic Template and renders its auto-baked, data-bound graphic for the current post - including the optional campaign template with a from/until window. Saving the page in Elementor marks the instance stale, so the image re-bakes with the post's fresh values - the same applies to the shortcode inside Bricks layouts and Divi content.
WPIE Live Badge: Renders a baked live badge by its UID (from the editor's Dynamic Template Shortcodes dialog); bound values are filled in as the page is served. It is an SVG laid out by the browser, so it looks close to but not pixel-identical with the editor design - use the Dynamic Image widget when the embed must match exactly.
WPIE Personalized Image: Renders a personalized image from a dynamic template. Mapping happens in repeater rows - layer, URL parameter, fallback - with layer-name suggestions read from the selected template; a legacy text field (layer:parameter:fallback entries separated by |) still works when no rows are set.
Settings toggle: the Widgets & Blocks tab in Settings enables or disables the widget registration. Existing pages keep working either way - the underlying shortcodes stay available.
Layer suggestions: With a template selected, the Personalized Image panel lists the template's text layers and offers them as autocomplete suggestions in every mapping row.

sections.title: Stitch Patterns (studio)
sections.text:
Eight craft sheets: cross-stitch, diamond painting, fuse beads, knitting, C2C crochet, latch hook, real string art and string mandalas - with counting grids, legends and per-color usage estimates, all computed locally.
Craft sheets computed entirely in your browser: cross-stitch charts, diamond painting, fuse beads with pegboard split lines, a gauge-aware knitting chart that keeps your photo's proportions, C2C crochet, a latch-hook rug chart with per-color pack estimates, real string art threaded around physical nails with a numbered winding guide you can actually build from, and a string mandala of classic times-table chord patterns.
The source is the whole document, any layer picked by name, or the media library. Yarn colors come from the image, with an accent rescue so blue eyes survive quantization, from preset palettes, your brand kit or custom colors, and the chart is quantized to exactly those yarns. A counting grid, edge numbers and a legend with per-color usage in skeins, drills, beads or knots are included.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Every sheet takes a multi-line title in the editor font catalog, inserts as an editable layer and reopens via **Edit Stitch Patterns**.
Choose image: Opens the media library to pick the source photo. The large size is used when available.
Use active layer: Renders the currently selected layer and uses it as the chart source - a logo becomes a bead pattern in one click.
Grid width: Chart width in cells (24-120). The height follows the image aspect; for knitting it also respects the stitch gauge.
Colors: Palette size (6-24). Fewer colors mean an easier project, more colors a finer likeness.
Chart symbols: Toggles the counting symbols drawn into the cells and the legend.
Stitch gauge: Knitting only: cell height as a percentage of the width. Knitted stitches are wider than tall - the chart compensates so the finished piece keeps the photo proportions.
Pegboard size: Fuse beads only: the pegboard module (29 x 29 or 50 x 50). Bold lines mark the board boundaries so large motifs split cleanly across boards.
Insert chart: Bakes the chart with its legend and inserts it as an image layer, scaled to fit the document. Right-click the layer for Edit Stitch Patterns to reopen it.
Latch hook: A latch-hook rug chart: coarse tufted cells that read like knotted yarn, no symbols needed, and the legend estimates precut yarn packs (~320 pieces) per color.
Source: The chart pulls its image from the whole document (default), any single layer picked by name, or the media library - no empty state, the preview renders immediately.
Yarn colors: Auto mode quantizes the image with median cut and accent rescue (small vivid regions survive). Or pin the yarns: ten preset palettes, your brand kit or up to four custom colors - the chart is quantized to exactly those yarn colors and the legend counts them.
Title and font: Every chart takes an optional title of up to two lines, set in the editor font catalog with a 60-160% text size factor, colored by the first pinned yarn color.
String art: A real thread portrait: greedy error-accumulation threading around 144-360 nails with up to 3500 threads and three thread weights (fine, normal, bold) - every thread covers exactly the darkness it adds, thread-thickness aware so parallel bands cannot form, with contrast stretch and an edge boost that keeps faces readable. The preview weaves the FULL thread count. The thread takes your first pinned color, and an optional numbered WINDING GUIDE sheet lists the full nail order as a second layer - print it and actually build the piece.
String mandala: The classic times-table chord patterns: nail i connects to nail i x factor. Factor 2 draws a cardioid, 3 a nephroid, higher factors bloom into rosettes - no image needed, the thread takes your first pinned color.

sections.title: Photo Mosaic (studio)
sections.text:
Your image, rebuilt from many photos - the classic photomosaic, computed locally: sub-block matching, per-tile color adjustment, repeat lock.
Your image, rebuilt from many photos: the classic photomosaic, computed entirely in your browser. Pick the main image, the whole document, any layer or a media pick, then load tile photos from the media library, wedding guests, team shots, a whole folder.
Every grid cell is matched against the tiles' internal structure so the contours emerge from the photos themselves, a distance lock prevents repeats sitting next to each other, and the color match slider shifts each placed photo's own pixels toward the target tone, never an overlay, so every photo stays fully recognizable. The column count scales from a chunky look to poster detail.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert as an editable layer and reopen via **Edit Photo Mosaic**. Made for wedding posters from guest photos, team mosaics and yearbook covers.
Main image: What the mosaic depicts: the whole document (default), any single layer picked by name, or an image from the media library.
Tiles: The photos the mosaic is built FROM: pick any number from the media library (multi-select, merged and de-duplicated). Eight is the minimum, hundreds are welcome - wedding guests, team shots, a whole folder. A strip previews the loaded set.
How the picture emerges: The textbook pipeline: every grid cell is compared against each tile's INTERNAL 4x4 structure, so contours emerge from the photos themselves - a tile with a dark left half lands exactly where an edge runs. A distance lock keeps the same photo from repeating next to itself.
Color match: Shifts each placed photo's own pixels toward the target tone - a per-channel offset that keeps every photo fully recognizable (never an overlay). 0% shows pure tile matching; higher values pull the mosaic closer to the original's colors. With few tiles, raise it; with hundreds, lower it.
Columns: Grid resolution from 24 to 72 columns. More columns read better from a distance - poster prints want the high end.
Insert mosaic: Bakes the mosaic at full resolution and inserts it as an editable image layer. Right-click for Edit Photo Mosaic to reopen with the same tiles and settings.

sections.title: Text Art (studio)
sections.text:
Your image built entirely from characters: ASCII, emoji, packed words, readable text flows and silhouette text - glyph color, size and density carry the picture, never an overlay. All computed locally.
Your image, rebuilt from characters, bricks and tiles, computed in your browser: ASCII art with classic, block, braille, binary, Matrix rain, typewriter or your own charsets, emoji art with coverage-weighted color matching, and object mosaics from toy bricks, dice, puzzle-cube stickers, sticky notes, LED dot matrices, ceramic mosaic and keycaps whose legends cycle your own text.
Beyond photos there is a word portrait that grows and rotates your words with the image, readable lyrics and post-art flows straight from a WordPress post, silhouette text, and photo-free typography such as periodic-table element tiles, hidden-word letter grids and crossing letter tiles. Shape masks, a heart, a star, a giant letter or any emoji, replace the photo anywhere.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Everything inserts as an editable layer and reopens with all settings.
ASCII Art: A density ramp of characters, colored per cell. Five charsets: classic, blocks, braille, binary (the Matrix look) or your own characters, plus cell size, bold and contrast.
Emoji Art: Every cell becomes the emoji whose color matches best - coverage-weighted, so sparse emoji read correctly against the ground. Sets: mixed, hearts, nature, food, or type your own emoji.
Brick Art: The image rebuilt from studded toy bricks: every cell becomes a beveled brick with the round stud, colors snap to the classic brick palette (redmean matching keeps hues honest) or stay original via the Original colors toggle. Brick size sets the resolution.
Dice Art: The image laid out in game dice: brightness becomes the pip count, the mixed set combines white and black dice for twelve gray levels (or pick a single color set with six).
Cube Art: A magic-cube mosaic: every cell is one sticker in the six classic face colors, with the bold black grid separating the 3x3 cube faces.
Sticky Notes: The office-window mural: square sticky notes in neon pastels, each slightly rotated with a soft shadow. The ground select switches the wall between light and dark.
Dot Matrix: Retro display dots in three styles: LED wall (glowing image-colored dots), flip-dot (the two-tone station display, dithered) and pegboard (translucent bright pegs on a dark board).
Ceramic Mosaic: Roman-style tiles: irregularly cut ceramic pieces with grout in between, each tile's color slightly varied for the handmade look. Tile size sets the resolution.
Keycap Art: Keyboard keycaps as cells in the image colors - the legends cycle through your own text (or random letters). The text-meets-image fusion type.
Word Portrait: Your own words (one per line) packed line by line - size, weight and opacity follow the image between an adjustable min and max size, optionally with slight or wild per-word rotation.
Lyrics Art and Post Art: A continuous, READABLE text - a song text, poem or one of your WordPress posts (built-in post search) - where every glyph is tinted and optionally sized by the picture. Four layouts: rows, diagonal, waves, spiral.
Silhouette Text: The text fills only the subject shape. Cut-out layers use their transparency as a perfect mask; otherwise a luminance threshold with invert does the job.
Color modes: Image colors (boosted per glyph), a single color, or a GRADIENT across the artwork from your palette, brand kit or custom colors - on a dark or light ground, with a contrast control.
Insert artwork: Bakes the artwork and inserts it as an editable image layer. Right-click for Edit Text Art to reopen with all settings restored.
Element Art: Spells words with periodic-table tiles (BaCoN = Barium, Cobalt, Nitrogen). The matcher minimizes leftover letters; letters without an element become plain dimmed tiles. Styles: Classic, Neon glow and Chalkboard, with atomic numbers and optional element names.
Hidden Words: A full letter grid with your words hidden inside and highlighted in palette colors while the filler letters stay dimmed - the word-clock look. Grid density, optional diagonal placement and a dimming slider shape the poster.
Letter Tiles: Names and words as crossing letter tiles that share letters like a board game rack. Tile styles Wood, Ivory and Dark, with optional letter values in the corner. Needs no photo.
Shape (no image): A source option that replaces the photo with a built-in mask - heart, star, circle, diamond, a giant letter (monogram!) or any emoji. Word Portrait and Silhouette Text (and every other image-driven type) then work without any image.
Matrix / Typewriter charsets: Two extra ASCII ramps: Matrix (katakana rain, best on the dark ground with a green single color) and Typewriter (the classic typewriter portrait ramp, best on the light ground).

sections.title: Craft modes
sections.text:
Eight crafts share one grid engine: cross-stitch, diamond painting, fuse beads, knitting and C2C crochet.
Cross-stitch: Tinted cells with counting symbols, a bold ten-grid with edge numbers, and a legend with an approximate skein count per color (about 1700 full stitches per 6-strand skein at 14 ct).
Diamond painting: Faceted round drills on tinted cells, symbols for counting, and drill counts per color including a small reserve. The Drill shape select switches between square drills (full coverage, the common kit style, default) and the classic round drills.
Fuse beads: Beads with visible holes, pegboard split lines and per-color bead counts - iron-bead motifs straight from a photo or logo.
Knitting chart: Solid color cells in gauge-corrected proportions with row and stitch numbers on the edges.
C2C crochet: A corner-to-corner graphgan chart: color cells with symbols and stitch counts per color.
Latch hook: A rug chart: chunky cells sized for latch-hook canvas, with symbols for counting and a yarn count per color.
String art: Turns the image into a nail-and-thread plan rather than a grid chart: the pin ring and the thread order.
Mandala: Lays the motif out in rings around a centre instead of on a square grid, for round craft pieces.

sections.title: Drawing Templates (studio)
sections.text:
Six printable drawing templates from one image: paint by numbers, coloring page, tracing sheet, connect the dots, symmetry drawing and the grid drawing aid - all computed locally, inserted as editable layers.
Printable drawing templates from one image, computed entirely in your browser: paint by numbers with flattened color regions and a numbered legend, a coloring page with closed, smooth outlines, a dashed tracing sheet for pen practice, connect the dots where every part of the motif becomes its own numbered contour, a symmetry sheet with one half drawn and one half empty grid, and the classic grid drawing aid with labeled cells.
The source is the whole document, any layer picked by name, or the media library. Paint colors can be pinned to preset palettes, your brand kit or custom colors, and every sheet takes a multi-line title in the editor font catalog.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert as an editable layer and reopen via **Edit Drawing Templates**.
Choose image: Opens the media library to pick the source photo.
Use active layer: Renders the selected layer and uses it as the template source.
Paint by numbers: Flattens the photo into paintable color regions with thin contours, puts a number into every region and adds a numbered color legend. Colors sets the palette size, Smoothing melts small specks into larger patches.
Coloring page: Closed, smooth region outlines from the same pipeline family as paint by numbers - real colorable patches instead of noisy edge pixels. The detail slider sets how many regions the picture keeps.
Connect the dots: EVERY distinct part of the motif becomes its own numbered contour: running numbers across contours, a red ring marks each start, labels dodge collisions. Optional faint hint lines help younger kids.
Grid drawing aid: The classic drawing method: the photo in grayscale under a labeled red grid, next to an empty grid with the same labels for practicing proportions. Grid cells sets the resolution.
Insert template: Bakes the sheet and inserts it as an image layer scaled to the document. Right-click for Edit Drawing Templates to reopen it.
Tracing sheet: The same closed region outlines, but dashed in a light gray - the classic follow-the-dashed-line practice sheet, clearly distinct from the coloring page.
Symmetry drawing: One half shows the motif, the other half is an empty transfer grid across a dashed mirror line - complete the picture. Choose which half stays empty and how fine the grid is; the mirror line takes the accent color.
Source: Templates pull their image from the whole document (default), any single layer picked by name, or the media library - the preview renders immediately.
Paint colors: Paint-by-numbers colors come from the image by default. Or pin them: ten preset palettes, your brand kit or up to four custom colors - the sheet and its numbered legend use exactly those paints. The accent also colors the drawing-aid grid and the mirror line.
Title and font: Every sheet takes an optional title of up to two lines, set in the editor font catalog with a 60-160% text size factor.

sections.title: Party Printables (studio)
sections.text:
Twelve printable party templates from one dialog: banners, dielines, tags, toppers, wrappers, place cards, straw flags, photo props, bottle labels and sticker sheets - all computed locally and inserted as editable layers.
Printable party templates computed entirely in your browser: bunting and letter banners, a gift box dieline with optional printed ribbon and glue flaps, gift tags with punch holes, cupcake toppers and scalloped wrappers, folded place cards from a name list, mirrored so both sides read correctly, straw flags, a cone party hat dieline, photo-booth props, bottle labels and a print-and-cut sticker sheet with registration marks.
Sources are the whole document, any layer picked by name, or the media library. Colors come from palettes, your brand kit or your own picks, every text template offers the editor font catalog, and text fields accept line breaks for stacked lines on tags, flags and labels.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert as an editable layer and reopen via **Edit Party Printables**.
Bunting: Spells your text with one letter per pennant hanging on a drawn cord - triangle, swallowtail, flag or scallop pennants, adjustable pennants per row, and long phrases wrap onto extra rows automatically.
Letter banner: One big pennant card per letter, laid out as a grid - print one card per page for a large wall banner.
Gift box: A cube gift-box dieline: solid lines are cut, dashed lines are folds, glue flaps included. Your artwork covers each face individually or stretches across the whole net like wrapping paper, and an optional printed ribbon band with a bow wraps the folded box.
Gift tags: Eight tags per sheet with a punch hole and a centered text of up to three lines - on photo tags the text gets a soft shadow so it stays readable.
Cupcake toppers: Twelve circles per sheet with your motif or a monogram on a scalloped ring, ready to cut and glue onto sticks.
Cupcake wrappers: Arc-band dielines that wrap around a standard cupcake, with an optional scalloped top edge and a glue tab - striped from your colors or covered by your artwork.
Place cards: Folded tent cards from a name list (one name per line). The top half is printed upside down on purpose so both sides read correctly after folding.
Straw flags: Small double swallowtail flags that fold around a straw - the left wing is printed rotated so the text reads correctly on both sides.
Party hat: A cone party-hat dieline with glue tab. Without an image you choose the decor: radial stripes with an adjustable stripe count, confetti dots or a solid color with a contrast brim.
Photo props: Photo-booth props ready for wooden sticks: mustache, lips, glasses, bow tie, crown and a speech bubble that carries your text. Each prop shows a dashed marker where the stick is glued.
Bottle labels: Four wrap-around bottle labels per sheet with your artwork or a palette color and a centered text of up to two lines - with a soft shadow on photos.
Sticker sheet: Repeats your motif in a grid on an A4-style sheet with red cut contours and corner registration marks for print-and-cut plotters. Eight cut shapes (circle, rounded, square, heart, star, oval, hexagon, flower) - and without an image the stickers become color labels with an optional text.
Source: Image templates pull their artwork from the whole document (default), any single layer picked by name, or the media library - or switch to Colors to work with palette colors only.
Colors: Ten palettes, your brand kit colors, or up to four custom colors picked with the editor color picker - a single custom color is honored too. The template preview cards repaint live in the chosen colors.
Font, text size and line breaks: Every template that carries text offers the editor font catalog and a 60-160% text size factor. Text fields are multi-line: line breaks stack lines on gift tags, straw flags, bottle labels, stickers and the speech bubble - and on the bunting every line starts its own cord row.
Insert sheet: Bakes the sheet and inserts it as an editable image layer. Right-click for Edit Party Printables to reopen the dialog with all settings restored.

sections.title: Puzzle Sheets (studio)
sections.text:
Six printable puzzle types with optional solution sheets: word search, shaped mazes (including image silhouettes), sudoku, criss-cross word grids, secret-code cryptograms and addition pyramids - all computed locally, inserted as editable layers.
Printable puzzle types computed entirely in your browser: a word search from your own words with a hard mode, a real maze generated inside shapes from circle and heart to a big letter or the silhouette of an image, sudoku in three sizes with a guaranteed unique solution, a criss-cross grid where your words interlock, a secret-code number cryptogram from your own phrase, and an addition pyramid that stays solvable by pure logic.
Every sheet takes a title in the editor font catalog, colors come from palettes, your brand kit or your own picks, and each puzzle ships an optional solution sheet as a second layer.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Made for teachers, birthday parties, wedding favors and company flyers. Insert as editable layers and reopen via **Edit Puzzle Sheets**.
Word search: A letter grid built from your own words with adjustable size, an all-directions hard mode, an accent-framed grid and a bulleted word list. Words that do not fit are reported, umlauts are transliterated. Tiny per-language theme suggestions (animals, party, summer, christmas) fill the list to start - you type your own words.
Maze: A real maze generated inside a shape: circle, heart, star, hexagon, diamond, flower, a big letter - or the SILHOUETTE OF AN IMAGE taken from the whole document, any layer or the media library (the darker side of the picture becomes the maze area, specks are cleaned away). Difficulty sets the cell count; start is green, goal is red, the solution path lands on sheet two.
Sudoku: 4x4, 6x6 or 9x9 with three difficulty levels. Every puzzle is generated with a guaranteed unique solution; the solution sheet fills the missing digits in green.
Criss-cross: Your words interlock in a crossword-style grid: the longest word is prefilled in the accent color, the rest are filled in from the bulleted word bank. Words that cannot cross anything are reported.
Secret code: A number cryptogram from your own phrase (multi-line, up to four lines): every letter becomes a number, a few letters are given depending on the difficulty, and a legend at the bottom collects the used letters. The solution sheet decodes everything.
Number pyramid: Every brick is the sum of the two below. Four to eight rows, three difficulties - the givens are chosen so the pyramid stays solvable by pure logic, no guessing needed.
Title, font and colors: Every sheet takes an optional title of up to two lines, set in the editor font catalog with a 60-160% text size factor. Colors come from ten palettes, your brand kit or up to four custom colors - the accent colors the title, frames and word-list bullets while the puzzle content stays print-friendly dark.
Solution sheet: Each puzzle can insert a second layer with the solved sheet: highlighted words, the maze path, the filled sudoku, completed grids, the decoded phrase or the finished pyramid.

sections.title: Step Guides overview
sections.text:
Annotate a picture and keep every mark editable.
Turn any picture into an instruction and keep every mark editable. Every annotation is pinned to a place in the picture, so a leader still finds its target after the callout has been dragged across the frame, and a route still runs through its stations after a station has been moved.
The marks cover the whole job: numbered pins that renumber themselves when you insert a step, arrows that curve or turn at right angles with the head always on target, labels with smart leaders, sticky notes, frames and highlighter strokes, a spotlight that darkens everything but one area, blur, pixelate and a solid redaction bar, a magnifier that lifts a detail out and connects it back, measurements with turning labels, icon stamps from the editor's icon library, and routes through as many stations as you like, which also turns the same tool into a directions sketch over a map or a walkthrough of a floor plan.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. The background is your document, a single layer of it, a media-library image or an upload, and everything lands as editable layers.
Insert: Builds the marks as real shape and text layers, grouped, and closes the dialog. Reopen the group later with Edit Step Guides.
Update: Replaces the layers of a guide you reopened, instead of adding a second copy.
%d mark(s): The counter in the footer. Insert stays disabled while it reads zero.
Click into the picture to place it: Shown after you pick a mark type. Click once for point marks, drag for the ones defined by a rectangle or a line.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
What the marks are drawn on top of.
The background is only the reference for the marks. It is not baked into the result, so the layers you get can sit on top of the document you were already working on.
The document: Uses the whole document you have open as the picture to annotate. The default. When you edit an existing guide, the backdrop is the document without that guide, so the magnifier and blur always work on the clean design underneath.
A layer: Uses one single layer instead of the whole document. Pick a layer appears next to it.
Pick a layer: The layer chooser that appears once the background is set to A layer.
From the media library: Annotates any image from the library rather than the open document.
Upload a picture: Takes a file straight from your computer. It is read in the browser.

sections.title: Place: the thirteen marks
sections.text:
One button per kind of mark. Pick one, then click into the picture.
Numbered pins, notes and labels carry a step number and renumber themselves when you insert one in the middle. Frames, highlighter, spotlight, blur, pixelate, redaction and the magnifier are defined by a rectangle you drag; the rest are placed by their points.
Numbered pin: A numbered dot. Insert a pin in the middle of a sequence and everything after it renumbers itself.
Arrow: Points at something. The head stays on the target; the shaft can curve, run straight or turn at a right angle.
Label: A text box with a leader. The leader leaves the box on the side that faces what it points at.
Note: A sticky note in yellow with a slight tilt, for a remark rather than a label.
Frame: A plain rectangle around a region worth looking at.
Highlighter: A translucent marker stroke, as if drawn with a highlighter pen.
Spotlight: Darkens the whole picture except one ellipse or rectangle.
Blur: Blurs a region so it cannot be read. Strength sets how far.
Pixelate: Not a marker of its own: it is an option of the Blur marker that coarsens the region into blocks instead of softening it. See the marker options for the strength dial.
Redact: A solid bar over a region, for what should not be there at all rather than merely unreadable.
Magnifier: Lifts a detail out, enlarges it beside the picture and draws the lines back to where it came from.
Measurement: A dimension line with end ticks and a label that turns with the line.
Icon stamp: Places an icon from the editor Tabler set as a mark.
Route: A path through as many stations as you like, with station dots and an arrow at the finish. Turns the tool into a directions sketch or a walkthrough.

sections.title: Options of the selected mark
sections.text:
The controls that appear once a mark is selected, per kind.
Only the options that apply to the selected mark are shown, so the panel changes as you move through the list.
Text: The wording of a label, a note or a measurement.
Shape: Ellipse or Rectangle, for the spotlight and the region marks.
Strength: How far the blur goes, or how coarse the pixelation is.
Magnification: How much larger the magnifier draws the detail it lifted out.
Routing: Smooth, Straight or Elbow: whether an arrow or a route curves, runs direct or turns at right angles.
Line style: Solid, Dashed or Dotted, for arrows and routes.
Stations: The points a route runs through. Add, move or remove them and the path follows.
Size: The size of an icon stamp or a pin, relative to the picture.
Symbol: Which icon an icon stamp shows.
Up, Down, Delete: Reorder a mark in the list or remove it. Reordering a numbered mark renumbers the sequence.

sections.title: Style
sections.text:
One choice sets the whole look of every mark.
The color presets come in pairs of accent and ink so marks stay legible on both light and dark pictures. The spotlight and the redaction bar are always near-black regardless of the preset.
Colors: Ten paired presets: Signal red, Electric blue, Highlighter, Amber, Ink on paper, Mint, Violet, Coral, Night and Blueprint.
Accent color: Overrides the accent of the chosen preset with your own color.
Font: The typeface for labels, notes, numbers and measurements, from the editor font catalogue.
Pin shape: Circle, Rounded or Square, for the numbered pins.
Weight: Scales the thickness of every stroke at once, so marks stay visible on a large picture.

sections.title: Steps
sections.text:
An optional numbered list beside the picture.
The list is built from the marks that carry a number, in their current order, so it stays in step with the picture.
Add a step list beside the picture: Widens the result and writes the numbered marks out as a list next to the picture, with their text.

sections.title: Handwriting Fonts overview
sections.text:
Draw an alphabet, get a font this site can use everywhere.
Your own handwriting, turned into a real font the whole editor can use. Draw the letters on a proper type grid with baseline, x-height and ascender guides and the neighbouring letters faint beside you, or print the ruled sheet, fill it in with your favourite pen, photograph it, and let the registration marks straighten the page and read every cell in order.
Accented characters are composed for you: draw the plain letters and the accents once, and the umlauts and accents for German, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Italian land at the right height. One alphabet yields a whole family, Light, Regular and Bold as genuine weights plus an italic by slant. Cursive mode joins the letters visibly, and spacing comes from the real ink of each glyph, with a tracking slider and per-letter nudge on top.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. One click installs the finished font into the site's font library, where it appears in the font picker, brand kits, templates, curved text and every layer style. The font file doubles as the project file: reopen it later and every stroke is still editable.
Draw: Draw the letters here on a type grid.
Sheet: Print a ruled sheet, fill it in by hand, photograph it and let it be read.
Spacing: The workbench for side bearings, tracking and per-letter nudges.
%1$d of %2$d drawn: How much of the required character set exists so far.
Draw the letters marked as required before building.: Shown when characters the font needs are still missing.

sections.title: Drawing a character
sections.text:
A proper type grid, with the neighbours faint beside the letter.
Baseline, x-height, cap height, ascender and descender are drawn while you work, and the letters either side are shown faintly, so the shapes line up from the start rather than being corrected afterwards. Pressure is picked up where the device offers it.
Pen: A round pen whose width follows pressure where the device reports it.
Chisel: A calligraphy nib: the stroke thickens and thins with direction rather than with pressure.
Nib angle: The angle the chisel nib is held at.
Nib width: How broad the nib is.
Smoothing: Evens out a shaky hand without flattening the character of the stroke.
Erase: Removes single strokes rather than the whole character.
Clear character: Empties the character you are on and leaves the rest alone.
Undo: Takes back the last stroke.
Trace over: Shows a faint reference letter under your hand while you draw.
Heights: Baseline, x-height, Cap height, Ascender and Descender: the guides drawn across the grid.
Next: Moves to the next character in the set.

sections.title: The printed sheet
sections.text:
Write on paper, photograph it, let the registration marks do the rest.
The corner marks straighten the photographed page and the cells are read in order, so no letter has to be matched up by hand. One character per box.
Download as image: Saves the ruled sheet so you can print it.
%1$d characters on %2$d sheet(s).: How many sheets the chosen character set needs.
Choose a photo: Takes the photograph of the filled-in sheet.
Corners found, check them and read the sheet: The four registration marks were located. Correct them by hand if one sits wrong, then read the sheet.
Those four corners do not form a sheet: The marks do not describe a rectangle. Usually a corner was missed or the photo is cropped.
Reading the boxes: The cells are being read in order.
Found %d characters: How many boxes held writing.
No writing found in the boxes: The sheet was read but the cells were blank, or the contrast was too low.
Take these over: Moves what was read into the alphabet, where it can still be edited stroke by stroke.

sections.title: Spacing workbench
sections.text:
Side bearings come from the real ink, then you adjust.
Each glyph is measured from its own ink rather than from its box, so the spacing starts out even. Drag a gap or a letter edge in the preview line to adjust one pair.
Drag a gap or a letter edge: Adjusts the space between two letters, or one side bearing.
Tracking: Opens or tightens the whole alphabet at once.
Kern automatically: Works out the awkward pairs and adjusts them for you.
%1$d pair(s), %2$d letter(s) adjusted: What the spacing currently carries.
Reset this: Puts one pair or one bearing back.
Reset all spacing: Puts every adjustment back to the measured value.

sections.title: Weights, italic and joined writing
sections.text:
One alphabet, a whole family.
Because the strokes are kept, the same letters can be re-drawn thinner or thicker rather than smeared, which is what makes Light and Bold genuine weights instead of a fake outline.
Weights: Light, Regular and Bold, drawn from the same strokes with a narrower or broader pen.
Add an italic: Adds a slanted cut of the family.
Join the letters up: Cursive mode: entry and exit marks at a fixed height and the gaps closed, so the letters visibly connect.
Join here: Where a letter is entered and left, so neighbouring letters meet at the same height.
Overlap: How far joined letters run into each other.
Include: Which character set to build: every character, or only the ones still missing.

sections.title: Building and installing
sections.text:
One click puts the font in the site font library.
An installed font turns up in the font picker, brand kits, templates, curved text, text on a path, WordArt and every layer style, with no reload. The font file doubles as the project file.
Family name: What the font will be called in the picker. Defaults to My Handwriting.
Build and install: Builds the family and installs it into this site's font library, which is a site-wide setting and needs an account that can manage options. Without that right the family can still be built and downloaded as a font file.
Build and download: Builds the family and hands you the files instead of installing them.
Installed %s. It is in the font picker now.: Confirmation that the family is available site-wide.
Insert a specimen: Drops a sample of the finished font onto the canvas.
Add a text layer: Adds a text layer already set in the new font.
Copy CSS: Copies the font-face rule for use outside the editor.
Open an installed font: Reopens a font from the library for further editing.
Open a font file: Reopens a font file from disk. Every stroke is still editable.
This font has no project inside it.: The file is a normal font, not one built here, so there are no strokes to edit.
Saved drafts: Work in progress kept in this browser. Delete draft removes one.

sections.title: A second pair of eyes
sections.text:
The checks that run over a finished alphabet.
They point at the things that make handwriting look wrong at text size and are hard to see while drawing one letter at a time.
What was found: The list of things worth looking at before building.
%d character(s) sit oddly next to the others.: Their size or position differs from the rest of the alphabet.
%d character(s) moved onto the baseline: Letters that floated above or sank below the line were put back on it.
Stand them on the baseline: Applies that correction to the whole alphabet.
%d character(s) still needed: Characters the chosen set requires that have not been drawn.

sections.title: 3D Flip Studio overview
sections.text:
Everything made of paper that turns, curls and peels, as a real 3D object.
Everything made of paper that turns, curls and peels, as a real 3D object: a hardcover book you can actually leaf through, a limp glossy magazine, folded maps, menu cards, jigsaw puzzles, envelopes and a strewn pile of wavy sheets. Take hold of a page by its corner and drag: it lifts, curls the way paper curls, throws its shadow across the page underneath, and falls over once you let go past the middle.
Pages come straight from the media library, or from a PDF that is read page by page in your browser and never uploaded anywhere. The look is yours to shape: page shape, boards and backing, wave and corner-curl sliders, peel and pile controls for the loose models, plus light, shadow, camera and background.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Freeze any state and place it on the canvas as a picture with a transparent background, so a curled sheet or a half-peeled sticker can sit inside any design. Or copy one block of HTML that carries its own viewer and runs on any website, with no library, no CDN and no request to anyone else's server.
Drag to turn the scene, wheel to zoom.: Dragging away from a page corner turns the whole object; the wheel moves the camera closer.
Drag a corner to turn a page: Grabbing a corner turns that page rather than the object.
Spread %s of %s: Which opening you are on, with arrows either side.
%d image(s): How many pictures the model is currently made of.

sections.title: Model
sections.text:
Twenty-four kinds of paper thing.
The model decides what the object is made of and which controls apply: bound models get binding and covers, loose ones get waves, pile and peel.
Bound models: Book, Photo album, Magazine, Catalogue, Report and Spiral pad: things with pages that turn.
Loose sheets: Paper, Poster, Scroll, Sticky note, Photo print, Postcard, Laminated sheet, Ticket and Receipt.
Adhesive: Sticker, Label and Stamp: the ones that peel off a backing.
Folded and cut: Jigsaw puzzle, Folded map, Folding card, Folding flyer, Menu card and Envelope.

sections.title: Source
sections.text:
Where the pages come from.
Pictures come straight from the media library, or from a PDF that is read page by page in your browser and never uploaded anywhere. A dynamic source renders per post.
Add images: Opens the media library and adds the pictures you pick as pages.
Add a template: Uses a saved design as a page rather than a picture.
Reading page %s of %s: A PDF is being read page by page in the browser.
That PDF could not be read: The file is not a readable PDF, or it is protected.
Drag to reorder.: The page list can be rearranged by dragging.
Use front and back: Treats the pictures as alternating front and back sides rather than as one side each.
Post: A dynamic source: the pages come from a post, so the object renders per post on the front end.
Load preview: Fills a dynamic source with one post so you can see it while you design.
Clear all: Empties the page list.
Pick at least one page.: Shown when the model has nothing to show yet.

sections.title: Paper, binding and shape
sections.text:
What the object is made of.
Shape can follow the pictures you supplied or a fixed format. Fitting decides whether the artwork fills the page or fits inside it.
Shape: The page proportions: from the pictures, or a fixed format.
Fitting: Whether the artwork fills the page or sits inside it.
Paper: The stock: how matt or glossy the sheet is and how it takes the light.
Binding: Hardcover, softcover and the rest, for the bound models.
Cover color: The color of the boards when the cover is not a picture.
Cover on its own: Treats the first picture as the cover rather than as page one.
Paper per leaf: How thick a single leaf is, which is what makes a thick book look thick.
Thickness: The overall depth of the object.
Show the backing: Draws the sheet a sticker or label peels off.

sections.title: Turning, curl and peel
sections.text:
The movement, and where it is frozen.
Turned by is the control that matters for a still: it decides how far through the movement the object is caught, so you can freeze a page mid-turn or a sticker half off.
Curl: How strongly paper curls as it lifts.
Speed: How long a turn takes, in milliseconds.
Turned by: How far through the turn the object is frozen. This is what you set before taking a still.
Opening: How far a bound model is opened.
Open across, Open down: Which way a folding model opens.
Flap: The lifted flap of an envelope or a folding card.
Peel: How far a sticker or label is lifted off its backing.
Take it off: Peels the adhesive model right off the backing.

sections.title: Loose sheets and the pile
sections.text:
Waves, stacking and how the sheets are cut.
These apply to the models that are not bound: a pile of paper, a scattered set of prints, a jigsaw.
Waves: How wavy the sheets are, as paper that has been handled.
Wave direction: Which way the waves run across the sheet.
How many: How many sheets are in the pile.
Shuffle the pile: Rearranges the sheets into a different scatter.
Arrange differently: Another layout of the same sheets.
Cut differently: Another cut for the die-cut and jigsaw models.
Refold differently: Another fold pattern for the folding models.
Flatten: Lays the object flat, which is what you want for a plain product shot.

sections.title: Light, camera and background
sections.text:
The scene the object sits in.
The background is only for the preview when you insert a picture: the still is written out with transparency, so the object can sit in any design.
Light and scene: Where the light comes from and how hard the shadow is.
Camera: The angle and distance the object is seen from.
Choose a background: What sits behind the object in the preview and in the HTML embed.

sections.title: Two ways out
sections.text:
A still with transparency, or a self-contained embed.
The picture goes onto the canvas like any other layer. The HTML is one block that carries its own viewer inside it and runs on any website, with no library, no CDN and no request to anybody else server.
Insert as picture: Freezes the current state and puts it on the canvas with a transparent background.
Inserted with a transparent background.: Confirmation that the still is on the canvas.
Update the picture: Replaces the layer of a flip you reopened instead of adding a second one.
Copy the HTML: Copies one self-contained block that runs the flip on any website.
%d page(s) live only in this browser and would not show on a website. Put them in the media library first.: The embed points at real URLs, so pages that exist only as local files cannot travel with it.

sections.title: Help Assistant
sections.text:
Ask the editor a question and get an answer out of its own handbook.
The assistant answers from a knowledge base that ships inside the plugin (includes/data/help-kb.json), built from the same glossary source as this site. That is deliberate: it cannot answer with something the editor does not do. The wording of the answer, though, is written by the AI provider you configured: your question and the matching handbook sections are sent there from your server, so the assistant needs a text provider and its key.
When a question matches one of the guided tours that ship with the editor, it offers that tour instead of describing the controls.
Ask a question…: The input. Ask in your own words; the assistant looks up the matching sections and answers from them.
Send: Sends the question.
Show me (tour): Turns the answer into a guided tour: the editor spotlights each control in turn instead of naming it.
New conversation: Starts over with an empty thread. The previous exchange is not kept.
Suggested questions: The starting prompts on an empty thread, covering the things people ask first: adding and styling text, removing a background, dynamic templates, shape layers, actions and batch processing.

sections.title: Workspaces
sections.text:
Hide what you do not use, and keep it that way.
A workspace is the set of panels, sections and tools that stay visible, plus the size of the toolbar icons. Three presets are built in and you can save your own arrangement under a name.
The customise mode is the quick way in: turn it on and click anything in the editor to hide it, rather than hunting for it in a list.
Full: Everything, nothing hidden. The default.
Essentials: Fewer tools, bigger icons: the everyday set at a comfortable size.
Minimal: Just the basics, for a screen with little room or a job with few steps.
Customize by clicking: Turns on the picker overlay. Click any panel, section or tool in the editor to hide it; click Done when finished.
Hide:: The label the overlay shows on whatever is under the pointer, so you can see what a click would remove.
New workspace name: Saves the current arrangement under a name of your own.
Overwrite with the current layout: Updates a saved workspace to match what is on screen right now.
Apply this workspace: Switches to a saved arrangement.
Delete this workspace: Removes a saved arrangement. The built-in presets cannot be deleted.
Toolbar icon size: Large, Medium or Small, independent of which tools are visible.

sections.title: Smart Select: refining the result
sections.text:
The card that appears once a subject has been found.
Smart Select proposes an area; this is where you correct it before it becomes a selection or a cut. Clicking into the picture adds to the area, Alt-clicking takes away, so a missed arm or an included shadow is one click each.
Subject selected: Shown when the model has proposed an area. The highlighted region is what the buttons below will act on.
Click adds areas, Alt-click removes.: How to correct the proposal: click a missing part to include it, Alt-click an unwanted part to drop it.
Soft edge: Feathers the boundary, so a cutout does not sit on the background with a hard cut.
Grow / shrink: Moves the boundary outwards or inwards by a few pixels, which fixes a halo or a bitten-off edge without re-clicking.
Keep this: Keeps only the highlighted area on the layer and clears the rest.
Remove this: Deletes the highlighted area from the layer and keeps the rest.
Keep as selection: Turns the area into an ordinary selection instead of changing the layer, so any other tool can work with it.
New selection: Discards the proposal and starts the detection again.

sections.title: Origami overview
sections.text:
Design the paper, watch it fold itself, then print the sheet and the instructions.
Design your own origami paper and watch it fold itself. Pick a figure, put your picture, color or pattern on both sides of the sheet, and the preview folds your very paper into the finished crane, fox or box, step by step.
Every step of the written instructions is a station in 3D: click it and the paper stands mid-fold in front of you, ready to be turned and studied from any side, which is exactly the moment printed diagrams leave you alone. A region map shows which part of the sheet becomes the head, the wings or the lid, so a face lands where a face belongs.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. One click lays print-ready pages into the document: the folding sheet with cutting marks, the mirrored back for duplex printing, and classic instruction pages drawn from the same steps you just watched. Everything is computed in your browser.
Insert as picture: Places the folded figure as it stands in the preview into your document, as a picture layer.
Insert sheet + instructions: Lays the print ready pages into the document: the folding sheet, its mirrored back, and the instruction pages.
Rendering the pages: The status shown while the sheet and the instruction pages are being drawn. Larger figures take a moment.
Cancel: Closes the dialog and inserts nothing.

sections.title: Figure
sections.text:
Which model the sheet is folded into.
Each card is a complete folding sequence. Switching the figure keeps the paper you designed and refolds it.
Crane: The classic tsuru: bird base, reverse folds for neck and head, wings fanned at the end.
Fox: A short sequence with two ear points and a folded snout.
Heart: A flat heart, the usual card and garland shape.
Sailboat: Two sails and a hull from a single square.
Butterfly: Wings spread from a waterbomb base.
Fortune teller: The school yard cootie catcher, with four pockets for the fingers.
Jumping frog: A frog with pleated legs that actually hops when you flick it.
Masu box: The traditional open box, with the same corner fold repeated on all four sides.
Show where things land: Colors the flat sheet by region and names what each part becomes, so you can see which piece of your picture ends up as the head, the wings or the lid before you print.

sections.title: The paper
sections.text:
What the sheet looks like, front and back.
The sheet has two sides and the fold shows both of them. Each side takes a color, a pattern or a picture of your own.
Front side: The side that faces you on the unfolded sheet, and the one most of the finished figure shows.
Back side: The reverse. It appears wherever the folding turns the paper over, which is what gives a crane its two toned wings.
Color: The base color of that side, from the usual color popover including your brand kit swatches.
Pattern: A printed pattern over the base color: Plain, Dots, Stripes, Zigzag, Stars or Checks.
Pattern color: The ink the pattern is drawn in, separate from the base color underneath.
Pick a picture: Uses an image from the media library as that side of the paper. The fold carries it, so you can watch where a face or a logo ends up.
Remove picture: Drops the picture again and falls back to the color and pattern of that side.

sections.title: The folding preview
sections.text:
Watching the fold, and stopping it wherever you like.
The preview is a real three dimensional scene, not a video. You can stop at any step and turn the half folded paper around.
Play: Runs the whole folding sequence from the flat sheet to the finished figure.
Step slider: Scrubs through the sequence by hand. The read-out shows which step of how many you are on, and says Finished at the end.
Instructions: The written steps beside the preview. Each one is a station: click it and the paper jumps to that moment of the fold and stays there.
Turning the scene: Drag to turn the scene, wheel to zoom. This is the part a printed diagram cannot do, and it is why a half folded step is worth looking at from behind.
Angled: Camera preset: the default three quarter view from slightly above.
Front: Camera preset: straight on, useful for judging symmetry.
Three-quarter: Camera preset: turned further to the side, so layers separate visibly.
From above: Camera preset: looking straight down, which matches how printed diagrams draw the sheet.

sections.title: Scene
sections.text:
Light, ground and background of the preview, which is also what an inserted picture looks like.
These settings change the rendered scene, so they matter for Insert as picture. They do not affect the printed pages.
Lighting: Soft for even, diffuse light, Warm for a golden key light, Dramatic for hard shadows and strong contrast, Studio for a clean product look.
Ground: What the figure stands on: Shadow only for a cast shadow with no surface, Table for a visible plane, Mirror for a reflective floor, or None.
Background: The color behind the scene. Leave it transparent to drop the folded figure onto a design of your own.

sections.title: The printed pages
sections.text:
What Insert sheet and instructions actually puts into your document.
The pages are built from the same folding sequence you just watched, so the diagrams and the preview can never disagree. Everything arrives as editable layers.
Folding sheet: The flat paper at print size with cutting marks, carrying the front side you designed.
Folding sheet, back: The same sheet mirrored, so that printing it on the reverse lines the back side up with the front.
Print fold lines on the sheet: Adds the crease pattern to the printed paper: mountain and valley folds marked where they belong.
Folding instructions: Classic diagram pages, one drawing per step, with fold lines and arrows generated from the sequence.

sections.title: 3D Particle Studio overview
sections.text:
A live particle engine: any layer becomes a cloud of particles you can shape, move and light.
Point the engine at any layer and it rebuilds that layer out of particles, keeping its colors. The cloud can be poured into a shape, pushed by a motion field, fed by emitters and lit so its depth reads, all of it running on your graphics card and playing back in front of you.
Start from a preset and change any dial from there, or build a look from scratch: the number and size of the particles, the shape they take, how they move, and whether they leave trails, join into a plexus web or morph between forms. Drop magnets and vortices into the scene to pull the cloud around by hand.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Freeze the frame you like and place it on the canvas as a picture, or copy one block of HTML that carries its own viewer and keeps the engine running on any website, with no library and no request to anyone else’s server.
Drag to orbit, wheel to zoom.: Dragging turns the camera around the cloud; the wheel moves it closer.
Show document: Puts your original layer back on screen behind the particles, so you can line the cloud up with it.
%s particles · %d fps · %s: The status line: how many particles are on screen, the current frame rate, and the preset in play.
Timeline: A play head runs the animation on a loop; scrub it to land on an exact frame before you insert.

sections.title: Particles
sections.text:
How many particles, how big, and how they blend.
The top panel sets the raw material: the size of the swarm and how each particle draws.
Count: How many particles make up the cloud, from a sparse scatter to hundreds of thousands.
Size: How large each particle is drawn.
Variation: How much the sizes differ from one particle to the next, for a less uniform cloud.
Trails: How long a fading tail each particle leaves behind as it moves.
Opacity: How solid the particles are; lower values let the cloud build up where particles overlap.
Blend: Additive makes overlapping particles glow and add up to light; Normal keeps them opaque like paint.
Seed: The random starting point. The dice rolls a new one; the same seed always rebuilds the same cloud.
Sprite: The particle’s own shape: glow dot, star sparkle, spark cross, ring, snowflake, hex bokeh, confetti plate, smoke puff - or any shape, SVG or text layer of your document, baked into a tiny mask.
Tumble: Lets a share of the sprites spin and flutter like falling paper. Rotations complete in whole turns per loop, so the video still loops seamlessly.
Motion stretch: Elongates each particle along its on-screen motion, like a short exposure. Fast sparks become streaks, slow drifts stay round.
Depth blur: Depth of field: particles away from the focus plane swell into faint, soft bokeh discs while the sharp zone stays crisp. Computed per particle, so it costs nothing.
Focus: Slides the sharp plane of Depth blur through the swarm, from the nearest particles to the farthest.
Breed variations: Shows eight seed-children of the current look as small previews. Click one and it becomes the new parent, with its own children waiting - a quick way to explore the chaotic cards generation by generation.

sections.title: Shape
sections.text:
The form the cloud is poured into.
The shape sets where the particles sit before any motion moves them. Your layer turns the swarm into a portrait of the picture itself.
Grid, Sheet, Sphere, Ring: Simple forms: a flat grid, a filled sheet, a hollow sphere or a flat ring.
Galaxy, Helix, Cube: A spiral galaxy, a twisting helix and a filled cube.
Your layer: Builds the cloud from a layer in your document, so the particles form the shape of the picture and can keep its colors.
Torus knot, Ribbon, Möbius, Heart, Tornado: Five sculptural homes: a trefoil knot, a woven Lissajous ribbon, a one-sided Möbius band, the classic filled heart curve and a twisting funnel. Every field, trail and morph works on them like on any other shape.
Text: Type a few words and the swarm becomes them. The words are rasterised locally and sampled into particles, so they morph, disperse and travel like any other shape - and they survive into embeds, where the runtime rasterises them again.
Spread: How far the particles fill out the chosen shape.
Layer: Which layer the swarm is built from when the shape is Your layer.
Relief: How far the brighter parts of your layer push forward, giving the flat picture depth.
Use layer colors: Colors each particle from your layer, so a face stays a face while the cloud forms and dissolves.

sections.title: Flames & attractors
sections.text:
Pure chaos, rendered as light.
These shapes are not drawn, they are settled into: every particle repeats a chaotic formula a dozen times and lands exactly where the mathematics concentrates, so hundreds of thousands of particles become a glowing density picture of the attractor itself.
The seed picks a curated parameter set and varies it slightly, so the dice always land on something worth keeping.
Fractal flame: The classic iterated-function flame in its silky recipe: soft sine folds that build glowing ember structures. The palette follows the structure, not the position.
Night bloom: A flame recipe with a swirling map inside, blooming into petal-like violet folds.
Cosmic lace: A flame recipe folded through the disc, weaving ring-shaped golden lace.
Clifford veil: The Clifford attractor: folded veils with bright caustic edges, given layered depth so the camera can look around it.
Dream mist: The De Jong attractor: looping ribbons of mist. With a little motion stretch the drift shows as flowing streaks.
King's dream: Pickover's three-dimensional attractor, a genuinely deep cloud that rewards orbiting.
Lorenz butterfly: THE strange attractor: the Lorenz system, integrated live so the two wings of the butterfly emerge from hundreds of thousands of flowing particles. Drift lets the system breathe over the loop; trails turn it into streaming weather.
Aizawa orbit: The Aizawa system: a glowing plasma sphere with a bright polar jet, drawn by particles orbiting a chaotic flow. Slow pendulum orbits show its depth best.
Hopalong web: Barry Martin’s hopping map, settling into golden fractal webs. Every seed picks a curated parameter set and jitters it gently; the Breed button walks its children.
Mira bloom: The Gumowski-Mira map, blooming into coral swirls and star-shaped ornaments. Small parameter steps change the species completely - breeding seeds is the way to explore it.
Flame style: Chooses the flame recipe: Silky, Floral or Cosmic. Each one is a different family of variations, not just different colors.
Drift: Lets the chaotic parameters breathe over the loop, so the structure slowly morphs and returns to its start without a seam. Zero freezes the picture.

sections.title: Motion
sections.text:
The field that pushes the particles around.
A motion field moves the whole cloud at once. None holds it still.
Curl: A swirling, smoke-like flow that keeps the cloud turning in on itself.
Noise: A soft, organic drift that nudges every particle along a wandering path.
Waves: A rolling wave that passes through the cloud.
Twist: A rotation that winds the cloud around an axis.
None: Switches motion off and holds the cloud in its shape.
Amount: How strongly the field pushes.
Scale: How large the field’s pattern is, from fine detail to broad sweeps.
Cycles: How many times the motion repeats over one loop of the timeline.
Chladni: The vibrating-plate field: particles gather on the nodal lines where real sand would settle, and the figure changes frequency over the loop.
Flow (image): Streams the particles along the contours of a picture. Pick a layer and the studio bakes a flow map from it; every particle then drifts along the strokes for one cycle, fades and is reborn - the painterly, van-Gogh-like current behind the Flowing paint preset. Amount sets the stream length, Cycles how many times the current runs per loop.

sections.title: Trails, plexus and morph
sections.text:
Ways the particles relate to one another.
Beyond the individual particles, the cloud can draw connections and change between forms.
Plexus: Draws lines between particles that are close together, turning the cloud into a shifting web.
Morph: Moves the particles from one shape into another, so the cloud transforms between forms.

sections.title: Pins: magnets and vortices
sections.text:
Handles you place in the scene to pull the cloud around by hand.
Pins are markers you drop into the scene. Each one bends the motion of the particles near it, and you can move them to shape the flow.
Magnet: Pulls nearby particles towards it, or pushes them away.
Vortex: Spins nearby particles around it, so the cloud twists where the pin sits.

sections.title: Emitters
sections.text:
Sources that throw new particles into the scene.
An emitter is a spout that keeps feeding fresh particles, on top of the cloud you shaped.
Fountain: Sprays particles upward and lets them fall back down.
Rising embers: Sends soft, glowing specks drifting upward like sparks off a fire.
Ring burst: Throws a ring of particles outward from a point.
Light burst: A bright flash of particles scattering out in every direction.
Comets: Streaks that shoot across the scene trailing tails.
Fireworks, Confetti, Snowfall, Rain, Sparks, Smoke wisps: The weather-and-celebration set: rockets that rise and burst in three staggered shells, fluttering paper, drifting flakes, streaking rain, crackling sparks and slow smoke - all seamless loops.
Camp fire, Candle flame: Real fire: each particle is born white-hot and cools through yellow and orange into sooty red as it ages, because the color ramp follows the particle’s life. Motion stretch shapes the tongues; the candle is the same idea, small and calm.

sections.title: Presets
sections.text:
Ready looks to start from.
Each preset sets the shape, motion and particles together. Load one, then change any dial from there. The presets under Your layer build from the picture you point them at.
Metamorphosis, Nebula sphere, Galaxy, Helix tunnel, Flowing terrain, Supernova: Standalone looks that need no picture, from a slow morph to an exploding supernova.
Particle portrait, Wind dissolve, Assemble: Looks built from your own layer: a portrait made of particles, a picture blown apart by the wind, or one that assembles itself into place.
