Sand patterns, Torus knot, Light ribbon, Heart of sparks, Tornado, Starling swarm, Bokeh drift, Glitter: The v4 form cards: Chladni sand figures, sculptural light shapes, a murmuration that never repeats, floating bokeh with real depth of field, and a sheet of glinting glitter.
Flowing paint: Turns a layer of your document into flowing paint: the particles carry the picture’s own colors and stream along its contours in a seamless loop. Needs a picked layer, like Particle portrait.

sections.title: A still or a living loop
sections.text:
Two ways to leave the studio.
Stop the timeline where it looks best, then choose how the result comes back.
Insert: Places the current frame on the canvas as a picture layer.
Embed: Copies one block of HTML that keeps the engine running on any website, with no library and no outside request.
Cancel: Closes the studio without changing your document.

sections.title: Marble Bath overview
sections.text:
Paper marbling on a virtual water bath.
The centuries-old art of Ebru and Suminagashi, with its exact mathematics instead of a simulation: every drop and every pull of a comb is one move in the bath's history, and the picture is computed from that history - razor sharp at any export size, with every move undoable.
You marble by hand on the canvas in the middle: click to drop ink, hold to let the drop grow, drag a tool through the water. The classic patterns sit on the left as seeded starting points.
Insert: Renders the bath at export size and lands it as a re-editable generator layer: reopen it any time and the full history is still there.
Undo last move: Forgets exactly the newest move - one gesture, however many drops it laid: a whole flower or a whole splatter flick lifts out with one press.
Empty the bath: Starts over. The button asks by arming once (it turns red); a second press within a moment empties the bath.
Sprinkle drops: Scatters a seeded handful of small drops in your inks across the bath.

sections.title: The tools
sections.text:
Five ways to touch the water.
Each tool is one gesture on the bath. The pull length of a stroke is its force.
Ink drop: Click to drop ink; every earlier drop yields and is pushed into rings. Hold to let the drop grow, drag to scatter a trail of drops. Repeated drops on the same spot make the classic bullseye.
Rings: Drops several alternating-ink drops in one click - the traditional concentric start for flowers and curls.
Needle: A single stylus line: ink shears along your stroke, decaying with distance. Softness sets how wide the pull reaches.
Comb: A whole rake of parallel tines at once - the tool behind nonpareil and every feathered pattern. Tooth spacing sets the rhythm.
Wave: Sways the whole bath sideways along your drag direction - chevrons and bouquets are made of this.
Curl: Plants a vortex: drag right to wind clockwise, left for the other way. The colors wind around the centre and fade out at the curl radius.
Flower: Plants a whole Ebru flower - tulip, carnation or daisy - with one click: rings pulled into petals by needle strokes, a leafy stem of chained drops beneath. Drag before releasing to turn the flower and set its size. One move in the history, one undo.
Arc: A curved needle: ink shears along a circle around the point you pressed, fading away from the arc line. Drag out to the radius; dragging right pulls clockwise.
Ring comb: A whole comb bent into concentric circles - nonpareil in the round, for medallions. Tooth spacing sets the ring rhythm.
Splatter: The flick of the brush: a fast drag sprays a fan of tiny droplets along the stroke - the speckled finish of classic sheets. Works with the gall too.

sections.title: Patterns
sections.text:
The classic repertoire as seeded starting points.
Every pattern is built over YOUR current inks and stays fully combable afterwards. The dice re-marble the chosen pattern with a new seed.
Stone: The uncombed bath: layers of drops pressing each other into organic stones.
Gel-git: Stones pulled back and forth with a coarse comb - the dramatic flame zigzag every other pattern builds on.
Nonpareil: Gel-git pulled through a fine comb: the tight, even bows of classic endpaper.
Chevron: Nonpareil with a crosswise sway of exactly two tooth spacings - neighbouring rows shift against each other into herringbone arrows.
Bouquet: A wide comb pulled in an S - flowing flame bands that read as petals.
French curls: A grid of alternating vortices winds the combed bath into curls.
Peacock: Comb, sway and a gentle counter-comb: the feathered fans of the showpiece pattern.

sections.title: Inks and water
sections.text:
Five wells and the bath itself.
Ink colors are stored as WELL references: recolor a well (or load brand colors) and the finished marbling recolors with it.
Inks: Five wells; the active one is what the drop tool drops. Click a well to make it active, edit its color with the editor's own picker.
Use brand colors: Loads your brand kit into the wells - unique marbled art in your own colors instead of stock backgrounds.
Water color: The bath showing between the inks.
Clear water (transparent): The bath becomes transparent: only the marbled veins remain, ready to lie over your design as an overlay.
Gall (clear drop): The sixth well drops ox gall instead of ink: it displaces every color exactly like a drop, but what it leaves behind is water - open cells in the pattern, or windows onto your design when the water is clear.
Pigment: Makes the ink behave like real pigment: a darker rim gathers at every drop's edge and faint clouds drift inside it. Both live in the drop's own pre-image, so they stretch with the combing exactly - which is what real pigment does.
Paper grain: A faint paper tooth over the finished sheet.

sections.title: Film
sections.text:
The bath in motion, as WebM.
Two motions: the making itself, or the finished picture on gently moving water.
The making, replayed: Plays the history: drops patter in and bloom, strokes sweep through - the film of how your marbling came to be.
Living water loop: The finished bath sways on two gentle crossed waves, returning to its start - one seamless loop.
Preview: Plays the chosen motion once in the studio, without recording.

sections.title: 3D Earth Studio overview
sections.text:
The real Earth as a live globe: NASA maps, atmosphere, day and night, markers, routes and orbits - all computed in your browser.
The globe: A hyperrealistic Earth built on NASA public-domain maps - Blue Marble by day, Black Marble city lights by night, real cloud cover - all matched to one projection. Drag to orbit, wheel to zoom.
Looks: Eight one-click moods: classic Blue Marble, a night side full of city lights, the dawn terminator, a clean tech globe with borders, a dramatic low sun, a storm-cloud front, deep space with comets, and a pure white studio.
Show document: Renders your current design behind the transparent globe, so you see the overlay exactly where it will land.

sections.title: Sun, sky and surface
sections.text:
Where the light stands and what the surface shows.
Sun around / Season / Show the sun: Places the sun: around the equator and up or down with the seasons; the day-night terminator follows, soft the way the real one is. Switch the sun itself on and it appears as a blinding core with a huge diffuse corona - size and color are yours, and the color tints the light on the whole world.
City lights: NASA Black Marble city lights that glow only where it is dark - slide the sun away and watch the cities come on.
Atmosphere: The blue halo of air around the limb, day-blue in the light and deep indigo in the dark, with a soft rim on the surface itself. A separate Glow dial adds a wide blue shine around the whole planet, from a whisper to a full aura.
Clouds: Real NASA cloud cover on its own shell, lit by the same sun. Thin it out, switch it off, or leave the weather as the satellite saw it.
Relief & Ocean glint: Mountain ranges catch the light through a relief map derived from the day picture, and the sun leaves a glossy glint on water only.
Stars, shooting stars & comets: A living starfield of individually drawn points - each with its own size, tint and twinkle - never a stretched bitmap. Add shooting stars that burn across the view and a comet that rides through the picture once per loop; all of it repeats exactly, so the video loop closes.

sections.title: Countries
sections.text:
Natural Earth borders and highlights, matched to the same projection as every map on the globe.
Borders: Crisp country borders from Natural Earth, in any color and strength, drawn onto the globe on demand.
Highlight: Pick countries from the list and they fill with your highlight color - visible by day and by night.

sections.title: Markers & routes
sections.text:
Click the globe to plant a marker; the marker even knows which country it landed in.
Markers: A click on the globe plants a marker at that exact place, prefilled with the name of the country under it and editable into anything. On insert, named markers become REAL text layers beside the globe - restyle or move them like any text.
Routes (Chain / Hub): Great-circle arcs between your markers: a chain from city to city, or a hub with every spoke from the FIRST marker. With two markers both shapes are the same single arc - the difference begins at three. Arc height and line width are dials.
Satellite orbits: Up to four inclined orbit rings with satellites riding them - and in the video loop each satellite completes exactly two orbits, so the loop stays seamless.

sections.title: Export
sections.text:
A transparent still, one full turn as video, or the globe live on your website.
Insert: Freezes the globe as a transparent picture on your canvas - a re-editable generator layer that reopens with every setting as you left it.
Video loop: One full rotation of the globe as a WebM clip, download or Media Library. Seamless by construction: frame zero equals the last frame.
Embed (HTML): A tiny snippet that runs the globe live on your website - the maps load from your own site, visitors can spin the globe by hand, reduced motion gets a still, offscreen globes sleep.

sections.title: 3D Textile Studio overview
sections.text:
Your design on cloth that hangs, blows and drapes for real.
Drop a layer onto the fabric and it becomes cloth that behaves like the material you pick: silk falls soft, felt holds its shape, flag fabric snaps in the wind. Hang it from eyelets, blow it with a gust, drape it over a rail or pin it by one corner, and the folds form the way they would on the real thing, carrying your artwork through every crease.
A studio light and a movable camera set the shot, with control over the shadow so it sits where you want it. Everything is computed in your browser.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. When it looks right, lay the finished drape back into your document as a picture.
Drag to turn the scene, wheel to zoom.: Dragging turns the camera around the cloth; the wheel moves it closer.
Layer: Which layer is printed onto the cloth. Its thumbnail shows above.
Remove: Clears the artwork from the cloth, leaving the plain fabric.
Pluck: Take hold of the cloth with the pointer, tug it, let go and it swings back. With the toggle on, the drag moves the fabric instead of the camera - arrange the folds by hand before freezing the still.
Back side: The reverse of the cloth shows the design reading correctly (never mirrored), or carries its own second picture - a flag with two different faces.

sections.title: What it is
sections.text:
What the cloth becomes: a flag, a banner, a tablecloth, and more.
The scene decides how the cloth is shaped and held, and which controls apply. Hung scenes get eyelets, draped ones settle over a form.
Flag, Banner, Pennant: Cloth held on one side and left to move in the wind.
Curtain, Hanging cloth, Wall hanging, Canopy, Sail: Cloth hung from above or stretched, falling into vertical folds.
Over a rail, Pinned by one corner, Draped over an object, Hammock: Cloth that settles over a form or hangs from a single point.
Tablecloth, Round tablecloth, Beach towel, Picnic blanket, Rumpled backdrop, Cushion: Cloth laid over a surface or bunched up as a backdrop.
Clothesline: The sheet hangs from two clothespins set in from the corners and drawn slightly together: the slack between them sags, the free corners droop, and the wind plays with the whole lower edge. Laundry, not a banner.
Stage curtain: Two velvet panels cut from one sheet - the weave is severed down the middle, so each half is its own piece of cloth, gathered towards its own side. The parting in the middle is the point: half open, the stage shows through, and the design runs across both panels.
Bedspread: A cover over a mattress that is longer than it is wide: the cloth breaks over the long sides the way a tablecloth breaks over a rim, and the overhang falls down the flanks.

sections.title: Fabric
sections.text:
The material, and how much detail it holds.
Each fabric falls, folds and catches light differently, so the same design reads as silk, felt or a stiff flag.
Silk, Cotton, Linen, Flag fabric, Velvet, Felt: The six materials, from soft-falling silk to stiff felt and a snapping flag fabric.
Color: The color of the plain cloth behind and around your artwork.
Detail: How finely the cloth is simulated: higher detail gives smaller, truer folds at a little more cost.
Weave: How visible the fabric structure is up close: a plain over-under for the woven materials, pile streaks for velvet, a felted surface for felt. Zero hides it entirely.
Edge (Plain, Hem, Fringe): The finish of the cloth border. A hem adds a folded edge with a stitch line just inside it; a fringe cuts real teeth into the free edges, and because the print rides the simulated mesh, the fringe swings with the cloth.

sections.title: Wind
sections.text:
The air moving the cloth.
Wind sets the cloth in motion. With strength at zero it hangs still.
Strength: How hard the wind blows.
Direction: Which way the wind comes from, in degrees.
Gustiness: How much the wind pulses and varies rather than blowing steadily.

sections.title: Hanging
sections.text:
How the cloth is held up.
On hung scenes, the fixing points decide where the folds start.
Eyelets: How many points the cloth hangs from along the top, which sets how it gathers between them.

sections.title: Light and scene
sections.text:
The studio light and the shadow it casts.
A scene preset sets the surroundings, and the light controls shape how the cloth is lit and how it shadows.
Looks: Five one-click moods - clean studio, soft daylight, dramatic, warm evening, bright catalog - each driving light, shadow and environment together. The dials below stay available for the fine hand.
Studio: The lighting environment the cloth sits in.
Brightness: How strong the light is.
Shadow: How dark the shadow the cloth casts is.
Shadow softness: How blurred the shadow edge is, from a sharp edge to a soft falloff.
Shadow length: How far the shadow reaches, which reads as the height of the light.
Shadow direction: Which way the shadow falls, in degrees.

sections.title: Camera
sections.text:
Where you view the cloth from.
The camera frames the shot without changing the cloth itself.
Rotate: Turns the view around the cloth, in degrees.
Height: How high or low the camera looks from.
Zoom: How close the camera sits.

sections.title: Export
sections.text:
Beyond the still: one loop of wind as video, or the living cloth on your website.
Video loop: One full wind cycle as a WebM clip, downloaded or saved to the Media Library. The cloth first settles into its periodic motion, then exactly one cycle is taped, so the clip loops.
Loop: Seconds per wind cycle - the pace of the gusts in the preview and the exact length of the recorded video.
Embed (HTML): A snippet that runs the cloth live on your website, pictures baked in. Visitors can push the fabric with the pointer; reduced motion gets a settled still, offscreen embeds sleep, and the page keeps its scroll.

sections.title: Back into your document
sections.text:
Leaving the studio.
Turn the cloth to the angle you want, then bring the result back.
Insert as picture: Places the finished drape on the canvas as a picture layer with a transparent background.
Close: Closes the studio without changing your document.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
A real 3D molecule you can spin, style and drop into your design - from a library, the periodic table, or a typed SMILES string.
3D Molecule Studio builds genuine three-dimensional molecules and drops them into your design. Reach for it three ways: pick from a curated library that runs from water, caffeine and glucose to a buckyball, a DNA double helix, graphene, diamond and a carbon nanotube; tap the periodic table for a single labelled atom, an element card or the whole table as a poster; or type a SMILES string or a plain formula and let a local generator fold it into 3D.
However it starts, it renders like a studio shot: ball-and-stick, space-filling or wireframe, with true CPK element colors you can override, matte-to-neon materials, studio lighting and a transparent, solid or gradient background. Recolor any atom, switch on element labels, and measure a bond length or angle by clicking atoms. You can also import exact geometry from a MOL, SDF or PDB file when you need real coordinates.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. The molecule lands as a re-editable image layer with its own editable text caption; recolor, resize or restyle it and reopen anytime via **Edit 3D Molecule Studio**. Export a smooth 360-degree spin as a video.
Everything - the library, the SMILES 3D generator and file import - runs locally in your browser. Requires a browser with WebGL2 and real graphics, which every current desktop browser has.

sections.title: Three ways in: library, elements, build
sections.text:
Pick a molecule from the curated library, build one from a periodic-table element, type a SMILES string or formula, or import an exact file.
Library: The first tab: a curated set of ready-made molecules with real coordinates, each shown as a card with its name and formula. Click a card to load it.
Search molecules: A search box above the library grid. Type part of a name or formula and the list filters live across every category.
Category chips: Filter the library by group: **All**, **Everyday**, **Organic**, **Biology**, **Mind** (neurotransmitters and psychoactives) and **Nano & crystals** (buckyball, DNA, graphene, diamond, nanotube, salt lattice).
Surprise me: Loads a random molecule from the library - a quick way to explore what is in there.
Elements: The second tab: the full periodic table. Click an element to drop it in as a single labelled atom.
Insert periodic table poster: Instead of a single atom, inserts the whole periodic table as a colored poster image - a ready-made layer for teaching or decor.
Build: The third tab: type a **SMILES** string (for example CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O) or a common **formula** (H2O, CO2, CH4) and the studio folds it into a 3D structure with a local distance-geometry generator.
Build molecule: Turns the typed SMILES or formula into a molecule. Example chips below the field fill in common structures with one click.
Import MOL / SDF / PDB file: Loads exact geometry from a chemistry file: MOL and SDF (V2000) or PDB. Bonds come straight from the file, or are inferred from atomic distances when it lists none, so large molecules keep their real coordinates instead of being relaxed.

sections.title: Model, style and bonds
sections.text:
How the molecule is drawn: representation, surface material, bond coloring and the size of atoms and bonds.
Model: The representation. **Ball & stick** shows atoms as spheres joined by rods; **Space-filling** shows atoms at full van der Waals size with no bonds; **Wireframe** shows thin atoms and thin bonds.
Style: The surface material, lit by a studio environment. **Matte**, **Glossy**, **Metal**, **Glass** (translucent) and **Neon** (glowing).
Bonds: How bonds are colored. **Element color** splits each bond into its two atoms’ colors; **Neutral** draws every bond in a single grey.
Atom size: A slider that scales every atom sphere, from 0.6x to 1.6x, without changing bond geometry.
Bond thickness: A slider that scales the bond rods, from 0.5x to 2x.
Atom labels: Shows the element symbol on each atom as a crisp billboard label that always faces the camera.
Auto-spin: Slowly rotates the molecule in the preview so you can see it in the round. Turn it off to hold a fixed angle.

sections.title: Caption and info
sections.text:
An editable text caption under the molecule, and the About box that reads out its name, formula and mass.
Caption: What the caption shows: **None**, the molecular **Formula** (with proper subscripts, e.g. C₈H₁₀N₄O₂) or the molecule’s **Name**.
Caption font: The typeface for the caption, chosen with the editor’s full font picker. It stays editable on the caption layer after inserting.
Caption align: Aligns the caption text: **Left**, **Centre** or **Right**.
Caption color: The caption text color, from the internal color picker. It defaults to a dark tone so it reads on a light design, and is fully editable afterwards.
About: A panel that reads out the current molecule: its name, formula, molar mass in g/mol, atom count and a one-line description for library molecules.

sections.title: Atom colors and background
sections.text:
Override the color of any element, and set the studio backdrop behind the molecule.
Atom colors: One color swatch per element present in the molecule. Each starts at its true CPK color (oxygen red, nitrogen blue, and so on) and can be overridden to any color.
Background: Type: The backdrop behind the molecule: **Transparent** (drops onto your design as-is), **Solid color**, or **Gradient**.
Background: Colors: The background color pickers: a single **Base** for a solid fill, or **Base** plus **Gradient top** for a vertical gradient. Hidden when the background is transparent.

sections.title: Measure, preview and export
sections.text:
Read bond lengths and angles, preview against your design, and export the molecule as a layer or a spinning video.
Measure (click atoms): Turns on measuring: click two atoms to read the **bond length** in angstroms, or three to read the **angle** at the middle atom. Selected atoms get a bright highlight; dragging still orbits the view.
Show document: Renders your current design behind the transparent molecule, so you can frame it against the artwork before inserting.
Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom: The preview is a live 3D view: drag to orbit around the molecule and scroll to zoom.
Export spin: Records one full turn of the molecule and downloads it as a WebM video (dark backdrop, about four seconds). Runs entirely in the browser.
Insert molecule / Update molecule: Drops the molecule into your design as a re-editable image layer (grouped with its caption). When you reopen it from an existing molecule layer, the button reads **Update molecule** and edits that layer in place.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
A date-accurate 3D solar system you can spin, set to any date and drop into your design - photoreal, to scale, and fully editable.
3D Solar System Studio builds a real, three-dimensional solar system and drops it into your design. Pick a date and every planet moves to where it actually is, computed locally from real Keplerian orbital elements: the Sun, all eight planets with Saturn's rings, the Moon, the Galilean moons and Titan, the dwarf planets Pluto, Ceres and Eris, Halley's and Encke's comets, an asteroid belt and a Milky Way sky, each one toggleable.
One slider morphs the whole layout from an artistic, compact view all the way to true astronomical scale. It renders like a space documentary: photographic planet maps, a glowing Sun with a cinematic lens flare, a soft bloom glow, and fresnel atmospheres on the planets that have one. Add orbit lines and labels in your own font, color and size, and switch between a perspective and a top-down view.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. The scene lands as a re-editable image layer that fills your canvas; reopen it anytime via **Edit 3D Solar System Studio** to change the date, the bodies, the effects or the labels. Export a smooth spinning time-lapse as a video.
Everything - the positions, the textures and the rendering - runs locally in your browser. Requires a browser with WebGL2 and real graphics, which every current desktop browser has.

sections.title: Bodies, scene and presets
sections.text:
The left column: switch any body on or off, toggle the scene extras, and jump to a ready-made selection.
Body row: Each body is a row with its own color dot and an eye that lights up when it is shown. Click a row to show or hide that body; hidden rows dim.
Planets: The eight planets, from Mercury to Neptune, each at its date-accurate position.
Dwarf planets: Pluto, Ceres and Eris. Pluto is placed by date; Ceres and Eris ride a fixed orbit shape.
Moons: Earth's Moon plus Jupiter's Galilean moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto) and Saturn's Titan, each orbiting its parent.
Comets: Halley's Comet and Comet Encke, shown on their elongated orbits.
Asteroid belt: A ring of points between Mars and Jupiter.
Starfield: A field of background stars behind the scene.
Orbit lines: The elliptical path of each body. Toggle here under Scene, recolor under View.
Presets: Grand tour shows everything; Planets only hides moons, dwarfs and comets; Inner system keeps the Sun and the four rocky planets.

sections.title: Date and time
sections.text:
Set the moment the scene shows. Every date-accurate body jumps to its true position.
Date: A date picker. Every planet and Pluto moves to where it truly is on that date.
Time scrub (days): A slider that offsets the date by up to five years back or forward, so you can watch the planets move along their orbits.
Today: Resets the date to today and the time scrub to zero.

sections.title: View and scale
sections.text:
How the scene is framed and how compressed the distances are.
Scale (artistic to true): One slider morphs distances and sizes from a compact, artistic layout to true astronomical scale, where the planets become the tiny points they really are.
Angle: Perspective for a three-quarter view, or Top-down to look straight onto the orbital plane.
Orbit color: The color of the orbit lines, chosen with the shared color picker.

sections.title: Labels
sections.text:
Name the bodies on screen, in your own type.
Labels: Off, Names, or Names + data - the latter adds each body's distance in AU and its radius in km.
Font: The label typeface, chosen with the shared font picker - any font in your library, loaded before it is drawn.
Color: The label text color.
Label size: Scales the labels up or down.

sections.title: Effects and background
sections.text:
The cinematic layer: glow, sun flare, atmospheres and the sky behind it all.
Glow: A soft bloom that makes the Sun and the bright stars glow. Turn it off for a flat, diagram-like look.
Glow strength: How strong the bloom is, from none to double.
Sun flare: A cinematic lens flare anchored on the Sun, hidden automatically when the Sun is behind another body.
Atmospheres: A soft glowing rim on the planets that have an atmosphere: Venus, Earth, Mars, the gas giants and Titan.
Background: Deep space (a subtle gradient), Milky Way (a real panorama sky), Transparent, or a solid color.

sections.title: Preview, insert and export
sections.text:
See it on your design, drop it in as a layer, or save a spinning video.
Show document: Previews the solar system over your current design, so you can place it before inserting.
Insert solar system: Drops the scene in as a re-editable image layer that fills the canvas.
Edit 3D Solar System Studio: Reopens the studio for the selected layer so you can change the date, bodies, effects or labels, then Update.
Export spin: Records a smooth time-lapse of the planets moving along their orbits as a WebM video.

sections.title: Mystic Studio overview
sections.text:
Birth data becomes computed keepsake posters.
Mystic Studio turns a name, a date, a time and a place into wall art: a real natal chart with houses and aspects, the moon of that night, zodiac and Chinese zodiac posters, numerology cards and posters for two, including a true synastry wheel. Everything is computed, not decorated: planets from real orbital elements, the moon from a lunar series, the Chinese New Year from the actual new moon.
Pick a card on the left, fill in the person on the right and watch the poster in the middle. Birth times resolve through a bundled time zone atlas with historical daylight saving; the one-time place search is the only thing that uses a service, the charts never leave the browser.
Open it from the **Extensions** menu. Insert lands the art as a re-editable generator layer plus editable text layers for caption, keywords and meanings; reopen any chart via Edit Mystic Studio.
Cards: The rail on the left switches between the ten posters: Birth Chart, Moon Phase, Zodiac Poster, Chinese Zodiac, Life Path, Name Chart, Angel Number, Couple Chart, Synastry Chart and Couple Numbers.
Show document: Renders your current design behind the transparent preview so you can judge the poster in place.
Insert / Update: Inserts the poster as a group: the chart as a re-editable image layer, captions as text layers. When a chart layer is being edited, Update redraws it in place.

sections.title: Person, place and time
sections.text:
Who the chart is for, and when and where they were born.
The Person section feeds every card: the name becomes the poster title, the date drives all computation. Cards that depend on the sky at an exact moment, the Birth Chart, Moon Phase and Synastry Chart, also take a birth time and a place.
Name: Used as the poster title and, on the Name Chart, as the letters the numbers are computed from. Accepts {{fields}} for dynamic posters.
Date: The birth date. Everything else follows from it: positions, phase, sign, animal, numbers.
Time: The wall-clock birth time. The ascendant moves about one degree every four minutes, so houses need it; tick Time unknown and the wheel drops houses instead of guessing.
Time unknown: Draws the chart without houses and ascendant and says so in the status line, rather than pretending.
Search for a city: The editor’s own place search. The chosen spot pins latitude and longitude for the horizon math and names the poster’s place line.
UTC offset (advanced): Normally the bundled time zone atlas resolves the offset for that place and date, including historical daylight saving. Switch to Manual offset for edge cases; the status line always shows what was used.
Partner: Couple cards and the Synastry Chart add a second person: name and date, and for synastry an own birth time.

sections.title: Birth Chart
sections.text:
The classic natal wheel, honestly computed.
The zodiac ring with the twelve glyphs and degree ticks, the planets at their true geocentric positions, house cusps with numbers, the ascendant and MC marked, and the aspect web in the hub. Below it, the caption layers: name and date line, the big three keywords and a data block listing every position.
Show houses: Draws the twelve Placidus house cusps and numbers, with the AC and MC axes accented. Above polar latitudes the wheel falls back to Whole Sign houses and says so.
Show aspects: The web in the hub: sextiles and trines in the calm color, squares and oppositions in the tense one, closer aspects drawn stronger.
Strict orbs: Halves the allowed orb so only tight aspects survive; the web gets quieter.
Show degrees: Writes each planet’s degree and minute inside its sign next to the glyph.
Retrograde R: Planets moving backwards against the zodiac carry the small R astrologers expect.
Data block: An editable text layer listing every body with degree, minute, sign and retrograde flag.

sections.title: Moon Phase
sections.text:
The moon exactly as it stood over a date.
A NASA photograph of the moon, shaded to the computed phase of the date: a silver disc with a soft terminator, phase name, illumination percent and the moon’s zodiac sign in the caption.
Southern sky: Mirrors the lit side for viewers in the southern hemisphere, where the moon waxes on the other limb.
Phase caption: Phase name, illumination percent and Moon in sign, as an editable keywords line.

sections.title: Zodiac Poster
sections.text:
One sign staged large, from the real constellation.
The actual constellation figure, stars and lines from the bundled catalog, with the sign’s glyph, element, modality, ruling planet, date span and three curated keywords as editable layers.
Sign: Pick any of the twelve, or leave it on From the birthday and the sun position decides.
Layout: Constellation leads with the figure, Glyph sets the symbol large over a faint figure, Split stacks figure and glyph.

sections.title: Chinese Zodiac
sections.text:
Animal, element and polarity, with an honestly computed New Year.
The birth animal’s character staged large in an ornament ring, surrounded by all twelve animals with the own one highlighted, plus the element character and a drawn yin-yang. The year boundary is not a table: the Chinese New Year is computed from the actual new moon, so January birthdays land on the right animal.
Animal and element: Twelve animals cycle with the years, five elements every two years, yang and yin alternate; all three appear in the caption with the Chinese year.
Meaning: A short curated sentence per animal, as an editable text layer in all seven languages.

sections.title: Numerology cards
sections.text:
Life path, name chart and angel numbers.
Three cards compute numbers the Pythagorean way and stage them as art: the Life Path with its reduction cascade descending into one big numeral, the Name Chart with the letter grid and three medallions, and Angel Numbers with a short meaning.
Life Path: Month, day and year reduce separately and then together, master numbers 11, 22 and 33 stay unreduced; the whole calculation is drawn above the ring.
Name Chart: Every letter carries its value in the grid, vowels in the accent color. Destiny sums all letters, Soul Urge the vowels, Personality the consonants.
Angel Number: Any number, staged in a ray burst; the classic ones from 111 to 1212 bring a curated meaning line.

sections.title: Couple cards and synastry
sections.text:
Two people on one poster.
Three cards join two birth dates: the Couple Chart with both constellations, glyphs and the moons of both birth nights, Couple Numbers where both life paths meet in one shared numeral, and the Synastry Chart, a true bi-wheel.
Couple Chart: Both signs as constellation figures with their glyphs, the moon of each birth night, and the element pairing line.
Couple Numbers: Both life paths in small rings, swinging down golden paths into the shared number, with the reduction preserved.
Synastry Chart: One zodiac band, person A’s planets on the outer ring, person B’s inside in the accent color, and in the hub only the aspects BETWEEN the two charts. Houses and axes come from person A.

sections.title: Look and caption
sections.text:
Eight themes and the editable text layers.
One look system carries every card, and everything written lands as text layers in your fonts, never baked into the art.
Theme: Eight looks: Celestial, Vintage, Gold Foil, Line Art, Rose Gold, Silver Night, Emerald and Amethyst. The foil themes draw their lines in metallic gradients.
Title font: The poster title and the numeral cards use this family, picked from the editor’s font picker.
Include caption / keywords / meaning: Toggles which text layers come along: the title and date line, the keywords line, the data block on the Birth Chart, and the meaning sentence on the number cards.

sections.title: Papercut Art (overview & stage)
sections.text:
Layered paper pictures with real depth: a stack of paper layers, and everything on them stays an object you can pick, drag and change.
A picture is a stack of paper layers. Everything you place on one - a deer, a forest, a moon, a cloud, a horizon, your own words - stays an OBJECT: click it in the picture to pick it, drag it anywhere, turn it, resize it by its corner handles, roll a new variation, send it to the layer behind or in front, or delete it. The arrow keys nudge the selection, Delete removes it, and Ctrl+Z leads back.
Nothing is baked into the paper and nothing is tied to a horizon. An object may sit anywhere, several may share a layer, and any of them can be punched OUT of its layer as a hole instead of added to it.
Presets: Sixteen ready scenes (Misty Alps, Deer Woods, Night Wolf, Open Water, Whale Song, City Sunset, Heart Meadow, Eagle Heights, Bear Woods, Cat & Rooftops, Wordscape, Desert Oasis, Quiet Lake, Fox in the Field, Owl Hour, Horses at Dusk). A scene replaces the sheet stack, look and frame - your photo source and cut settings stay.
Looks: Eight color moods from the all-white Lightbox over Sunset, Forest and Night Glow to Noir & Gold. A look is a starting point on the three paper dials below; turning one simply leaves the preset behind.
Glow & paper grain: Glow strengthens the warm light behind the back sheet - the lightbox effect. Paper grain adds a subtle paper texture to every sheet.
Light & shadows: One light drives every shadow: its horizontal position (drag the sun or use the slider), the shadow strength and the softness. The shadows between the sheets are what makes the stack read as real depth.

sections.title: Layers & objects
sections.text:
A layer is an empty transparency, objects are the things on it - and objects keep their identity for as long as the picture exists.
The right panel lists the stack front to back: every layer with its objects nested underneath. Click a row to select it, use the arrows to change the depth order, and the two small arrows on an object move it to the layer behind or in front.
A layer has no shape of its own. A backdrop, a horizon, a frame edge - each of those is an OBJECT you place on a layer, which is why two ridges can share one layer and why a horizon can be picked up and dragged like everything else.
The stack: Layers front to back, each with its objects nested underneath. Reorder layers with the arrows, recolor them with the swatch, remove them with the x. Each layer also has its own shadow strength.
Objects: Anything placed on a sheet: animals, tree groups, plant patches, clouds, sun and moon, flocks, single flyers, corner branches and words. Click one in the picture to select it, drag to move it, hold Alt while dragging to turn it (or use the rotation slider), and set its size, kind and variation in the Selection card. Standing objects follow the horizon of their sheet and pivot on their feet when turned, so they never float and never sink; free objects go wherever you drag them.
Bands: Landscape objects with a profile edge: alpine ridge, rolling hills, dunes, scalloped water, a city skyline with setbacks and spires, or a plain flat ground. Horizon, height and ruggedness are dials on the object, and the seed rerolls its shape.
Trees & ground cover: Procedural plants that reroll with the seed: conifers with drooping tiers, broadleaf trees with a lobed crown, slender birches, palms with arcing fronds, shrubs, grass tufts, reeds, meadow flowers and boulders. Count, spread and height variation are yours - at no variation the trees line up like an orchard, at full variation they range like a wild stand.
Animals: Twenty-three animal silhouettes traced from public-domain originals, each one an object you place and drag. Ground dwellers (deer, moose, fox, hare, bear, wolf, cat, dog, owl, horse, squirrel, boar, ibex, robin, gull) stand on their sheet's horizon; whale and dolphin belong in the water; eagle, heron, gulls, songbirds, owl and butterfly fly in the sky, cut out of the backdrop.
Cloud sky: Clouds with real cumulus lobes, and two dials of their own: billow piles them up into a towering cumulus or keeps them a flat bank, fray breaks the outline into separate tufts. A sun, a full moon, a crescent or a flock can be paper on one layer or a hole punched in the next.
Text sheets: Your words as paper. Letters keep their real counters - the hole in an a, d or o is simply a hole, with nothing bridging it. Switch an object to "punch out of the paper" and the words become windows in the layer instead.
Frames: The frontmost layer can be a frame: circle, heart, arch, oval, hexagon or an initial letter, with an adjustable inset.
Corner branches: A branch grows in from a corner with twigs and leaves - the classic framing device of layered papercut art. Pick one or two corners, its reach and leaf size; it stays attached to its corner, so the sheet is one piece by design.

sections.title: Photo depth
sections.text:
A picture becomes paper layers along its real DEPTH - and the local subject cutout lifts a person onto the front layer.
Pick a source (the document, a layer, the media library or an upload) and the picture is sliced into up to twenty layers. The editor runs its own depth model on your device to do it, so what ends up in front really was in front. Where that model is not installed, the picture is sliced by brightness instead and the status line says so - nothing has to be installed for the studio to work.
Depth sheets & histogram: The layer count sets how many sheets the photo becomes, from two up to twenty. Slicing by depth needs no thresholds; when the picture is sliced by brightness instead, the band borders start at fair quantiles and each one is a draggable handle on the live histogram.
Smoothing & invert: Smoothing calms the brightness map before slicing, so the layer edges flow instead of crumbling. "Bright side front" flips the reading for pictures where the near things are the pale ones. Both apply to the brightness path.
Subject sheet: With one switch the picture's subject is cut out ON YOUR DEVICE (the same local model the free tools use - nothing is uploaded) and becomes the frontmost layer of the stack.

sections.title: The paper & the insert
sections.text:
What the paper looks like runs on three dials rather than a list of names.
Color comes either from the look's tonal ramp or straight FROM YOUR PHOTO, where each layer takes the average color of its own depth band. The paper surface is smooth or fibrous. And the layers are separated either by a deep, soft shadow - the lightbox - or by a narrow hard rim, which reads as a poster.
Color from: The look's palette, or the photo itself. With "the photo", every layer takes the average color of the band it adds, so the stack looks like the picture it came from instead of a tonal ramp.
Surface & separation: Smooth paper or a visible fibre; a deep soft shadow between the layers or a narrow hard rim. Together with the color source these three dials span the whole range from a white lightbox to a flat poster.
Detail: How closely the paper edges follow fine wiggles. Lower detail gives calmer, more confident curves; higher keeps more of the original shape.
Insert as layers: Insert places the picture as a group with ONE editable editor layer per sheet of paper, stamped so Edit Papercut Art reopens the studio with everything intact.

sections.title: City Diorama (overview & stage)
sections.text:
Any place on earth as a miniature: real streets, water and building footprints raised into a chunk of city - or wrapped around a sphere as a tiny planet.
Search a street with its town, drag the circle on the overview map until the corner you meant sits in the middle, and choose how much ground the piece takes. The map data comes from OpenStreetMap through your own site, so the browser never talks to the map services itself, and the attribution the licence asks for is drawn into the picture.
Drag the stage to orbit, hold Shift and drag to move the map underneath, scroll to zoom. More ground is fetched than the cut shows, so moving around inside the neighbourhood costs no waiting.
Places: Ten starter places with their coordinates built in, from Midtown and the Speicherstadt to Shibuya and Alfama. They work without a search, so a first diorama is one click.
Search: Free text through the editor's geo bridge: a street with its town, a house number, a square or a landmark. The proxy asks Nominatim and caches the answer on the server.
Overview map: A flat map of the whole fetched neighbourhood with the diorama drawn on it as a bright circle. Dragging the circle moves the diorama instantly - the data is already in memory - and only a move that reaches the edge of it fetches more.
Radius: How much ground the piece covers, from 200 m to 1600 m. It is also the character dial for the globe: the sphere is the area rolled up, so a wide area makes a planet and a narrow one makes a bristly asteroid.
Turn the city: Turns the city underneath a fixed shape, which is what decides which streets end up inside a heart or a square. The painted ground and the buildings turn together.

sections.title: The chunk, and the tiny planet
sections.text:
The shape the piece is cut with, what it stands on, and the globe that wraps the whole area around a sphere.
Shape: Circle, square, rounded square, hexagon, octagon, heart, a torn chunk with a seeded outline - and Tiny planet, which is not a cut at all. Every shape covers about the same amount of ground at the same radius.
Base: What the city stands on: a clean cut, a chunk torn from the ground with a faceted rocky flank, a tapered block, a plinth, or an island running to a point.
Depth: How deep the piece was cut out of the ground, from 60 m to 900 m. Only the slab shapes use it.
Tiny planet: The area wrapped onto a sphere: the centre of the map becomes the north pole and the streets run over the horizon and back. The ground is wrapped distance for distance so the city keeps its proportions, while the buildings stand rigid on the tangent plane at their own spot, like model houses glued to a globe. Choosing it widens a small area, because the sphere is the area rolled up.
Wrap around: How far around the sphere the area reaches, from a cap with plain ground behind it to the whole globe.
Atmosphere: A shell of light around the planet, catching the sun color at its rim.

sections.title: The city: massing, looks and light
sections.text:
Where the building heights come from, the fourteen looks, and the sun.
Building height: Lifts the low mass of the city until the streets read as canyons, while real landmarks keep close to their true proportion - a church tower stays a tower instead of becoming an antenna.
Measured and estimated heights: OpenStreetMap knows the height of some buildings and says nothing about the rest - often about half of them in a city centre, almost none in a village. What is measured is used as it stands. The rest is estimated by asking the measured neighbours first, because buildings stand in blocks and a block has one building culture, and by footprint size where the area is silent. The status line says how many were measured.
Towers with parts: Where a building outline carries the height of its tallest section and building:part pieces carry the real massing, the parts are used and the outline steps aside. That is what gives skyscrapers their setbacks instead of a block-sized slab at tower height.
Smallest building: The height nothing falls below, so a shed still reads as a building.
Trees: Where the map lists trees they stand where they really stand; otherwise a few are scattered over the green areas.
Variation: Rolls a new seed. Everything estimated - heights, tree places, the torn rim - is deterministic, so the same place and the same seed always give the same diorama.
Looks: Clay model, Cartoon with inked edges, Low poly, Porcelain, Brass & marble, Paper city, Blueprint, Neon, Timber model, First snow, Watercolor, Noir, Candy, and City at night with lit windows and street lamps. A look decides the ground, the walls, the edges and the light together.
Light: Sun direction and sun height place the shadows; Shadows sets how hard they are; Lit windows turns the windows on before dark.

sections.title: Markers, routes and what gets inserted
sections.text:
Marking the spots that matter, joining them, and what arrives in the document.
Markers: Click the ground in the view to drop a marker on your house, your venue or your shop, and give it a name. Up to twelve per scene, as a beam of light, a pin or a ring.
Labels: Marker names are drawn flat over the finished picture, upright and readable whatever the camera does, and stepped apart where two of them would overlap. The preview and the exported picture use the same drawing.
Route: Joins the markers, either one after another or all from the first, as a line that arcs above the roofs. Color, arc height and width are yours.
Title, subtitle and coordinates: Inserted as editable text layers, never baked into the picture, so the type stays yours to restyle.
Insert: Everything arrives as one group: the diorama as an image layer that keeps its settings, plus the caption layers. Reopen it any time through Edit City Diorama and the layer is updated in place.
Show document: Renders your current design behind the transparent diorama, so you can see how it will sit before you insert it.

sections.title: Particle Strokes overview
sections.text:
Paint with swarms of light.
You draw the stroke and a swarm of particles follows your hand, then keeps painting for a few seconds after you let go. That after-run is half the picture: a flick of the wrist carries on curling long after the wrist has stopped.
You paint on the canvas in the middle. The sheet color behind it is a backdrop only, so what you insert is a transparent layer. Every stroke is recorded and replayed rather than flattened, so reopening the layer lands on the same picture and Undo takes strokes back one at a time.
Insert strokes: Renders what you painted at export size and lands it as a re-editable layer. Reopen it and every stroke is still there to change.
Sheet: What you paint against: chequerboard, dark, or a color you pick. It is a backdrop for your eyes only and never lands in the layer.
Mirror: Repeats the stroke around the centre, up to twelvefold, so a scribble comes out as a mandala.
Stop on release: Ends the stroke exactly where you let go, for the times you want to place a mark rather than watch a swarm carry on.

sections.title: Particle Strokes movement
sections.text:
Twenty movements decide how the swarm behaves.
The movement is the single biggest decision in the extension. Flame circles your pointer into tongues, Trail runs after it, Ribbon and Strand lay parallel threads, Spring overshoots and swings back, Vortex and Orbit turn it into spirals and rings, Rain falls with wind, Jitter rattles into charcoal grain, and Stick flies briefly and then stays put.
Movement: Flame, Trail, Ribbon, Strand, Spring, Vortex, Fuzz, Sparks, Chain, Repel, Rain, Orbit, Jitter, Stick, Wave, Bounce, Zigzag, Drain, Float and Loop.
Amount, Size, Spacing: How many particles, how big their marks, and how far apart those marks sit along the path. Spacing is what turns a stroke from a solid line into single marks strung along it, so a leaf-shaped stamp really does scatter leaves.
Scatter, Unrest, Pull, Swirl: How far the swarm spreads from the path, how restless each particle is, how hard the path pulls them back, and how much they turn about it.
Marks per second: A live count of how many marks the current settings lay down. It is shown because the number decides whether a stroke reads as particles or as a painted line.
Glow: A real pass, not a blur over the top: bright parts are lifted out at a Threshold, blurred at two Spreads and added back with an Exposure.
Blend: How each mark meets the ones before it: Add, Screen, Lighten or Normal. The first three are what make light look like light.

sections.title: Particle Strokes stamp maker
sections.text:
Every particle leaves a stamp, and you can draw that stamp.
The stamp is a shape, so whatever you leave transparent stays empty. You build it in a square with six painting tools and seven kinds of element, or you press Surprise and get one of sixteen blueprints, from leaves and feathers to crystals and comets.
A stamp is kept as a recipe rather than as pixels, so it stays editable and comes out sharp at any export size.
Tools: Paint, Erase, Dots, Disc, Ring and Star.
Elements: Polygon, Bar, Leaf, Arc, Icon, Emoji and Image. Drag one to move it; each has its own settings such as Sides, Waist, Vein, Sweep and Line width.
Surprise: Rolls a whole stamp from one of sixteen blueprints: Stardust, Notched ring, Rays, Blossom, Halo star, Comet, Orbits, Cell, Shards, Arc pair, Snowflake, Bubble, Spark, Gear, Ripple and Nib.
Motion: What the stamp itself does while it travels: Still, Orbit, Spin, Swing, Drift, Flicker or Open up, with a Rate and an Offset.
Back to the dot: Drops the drawn stamp and goes back to the plain round particle.

sections.title: Particle Strokes dynamics
sections.text:
Give a stroke a shape instead of a constant fog.
Dynamics are switched on as a whole rather than always running. Chance varies the grain from one particle to the next, and speed makes slow strokes lay down fat grain and fast ones thin.
A curve panel, like a tone curve, lets you draw a shape for each of six things separately: size, amount, scatter, opacity, pull and swirl. A stroke can swell while its scatter narrows and its pull lets go.
Curve shapes: Fifteen ready shapes: Flat, Ease in, Ease out, Ease in and out, Vase, Spike, Swell, Pulse, Ramp up, Ramp down, Rise hold fall, Sine, Triangle, Zigzag and Steps.
Roll the curves: Fills a couple of the six curves with something worth looking at, for when you want a starting point rather than a blank grid.
Color from: Where a particle takes its color: fixed, over its life, one each and then fixed, from hand speed, or along the stroke. Hue turn shifts it as the stroke runs.

sections.title: Chaos Art overview
sections.text:
A society of independent painters makes one-of-a-kind abstract art in deep space - you choose the moment it is finished.
Press Start and a company of autonomous painters goes to work in a three-dimensional stage: some lay ink gestures, some grow coral, some build on hidden grids, some weave glowing threads. Nobody conducts them; the only thing they share is the artwork itself. There is no seed and no reproduce: before you start, you charge the piece with entropy by moving your pointer over a field, and the same settings will never produce the same picture twice.
A fresh studio starts self-directed: style, art movement, colors, medium and the temperament dials all stand on their choice, and the society draws its own configuration at every Start. Touching any control locks that one aspect in your hand; everything else stays theirs.
Charge the piece: Before the first stroke, the view shows an entropy field. Moving your pointer over it feeds position, timing and speed into the pool the artwork is born from - your movement becomes this piece, and it can never be painted again.
Start painting / Pause / Resume: Start puts the company on stage; painters enter staggered, each on its own cue. Pause freezes the world and opens the moment picker; Resume continues the same piece. Start over abandons it for a new one - with fresh draws for everything left on their choice.
Surprise: The first style card is no style at all: the society picks one itself, freshly at every Start. The status line reports what they chose.
Impulse: A manual jolt of energy through the space. The disruptor throws its own; this button is yours.
The pointer: While it paints, your pointer stays a disturbance in the space - stirring like wind, attracting or repelling, selectable in the Pointer card. Dragging borrows the camera from the cameraman, the wheel zooms, and a tap sends an impulse.

sections.title: The society
sections.text:
Eight characters and a changing company of painters, and none of them waits for another.
Every actor has its own inner clock and makes its decisions on its own beat. Painters work in gestures the way a hand paints: a stroke is planned, committed to - with an attack, a swing and a release, its width swelling and tapering - then the brush lifts, the painter travels without painting, and sets down again. Roughly one stroke in fourteen is huge: the backbone of a composition, laid in one decisive movement.
Nothing is fixed at the start. Finished strokes join the piece's living fashion, and other painters imitate the recent ones with mutation or improvise, so fashions emerge, drift and are displaced. A finished gesture also leaves its endpoint standing as a call that exactly one painter may answer - chains of strokes thread through the composition as visible conversations.
The timekeeper: Stretches and squeezes the world's own time - slow motion, racing passages, held breaths. During a freeze the camera keeps moving, which is where the bullet-time moments come from.
The cameraman: Moves the eye through the work in one of three moods - a near-still tableau, a slow drift, or a restless orbit with sudden dives - and changes its own mood now and then. The gaze wanders off center to find its own compositions.
The colorist: Slides the palette's heat and throws accent moments. When the colors are the society's own, she may change her mind entirely mid-piece: a new palette, an epoch in the picture. Painted stays painted.
The sculptor and the disruptor: The sculptor swells and thins every future stroke; the disruptor throws rare impulses - gusts, waves, small detonations - that every painter feels.
The transient one: Lets old matter crumble and fade so the stage never chokes: transience as a character rather than a technical limit.
The restless one: Retires painters and hires new ones mid-piece, re-tunes the society's temperament, and carries the upheavals: the longer a piece settles into itself, the more the pressure grows, until part of the cast, the palette, the clock, the light and the matter all break at once - and the piece may move house into a new region of space, leaving the old paint standing as an epoch.
The steckbrief: On pause the piece introduces itself: a title written by rules from its own chronicle, palette and fashion, and a one-line biography - style, school and its mid-life school change, upheavals, moves, marks. The title names the inserted layer and the process film.

sections.title: Styles, schools and media
sections.text:
Twelve styles, nine art movements and six media multiply into pieces that cannot repeat.
A style is a casting: which painters take the stage and how they are tempered. Ink Storm, Coral Garden, Neon Weave, Oil Nebula, Shatter, Echo Chamber, Ring Parade, Tile Works, Hive, Clockwork, Constellation - and the Ensemble, which draws a new mixed cast from all painter types at every Start.
An art movement is a school above the styles: it never talks to an actor, it educates the casting - who is favored, what mark a painter leaves, which colors and ground feel like home, where the dials rest, how the light treats the result. A medium decides what matter the same commands become: sculpted three-dimensional bodies, or flat textured strokes that follow the gesture, sit on paper and fade into bright air the way paint does.
Art movement: Impressionism, Pointillism, Cubism, Bauhaus, Surrealism, Op Art, Action Painting, Futurism and Minimalism, plus the free study. On their choice, a school is drawn fresh at every Start - and an upheaval may draw a new one mid-piece, so newly hired painters bring different manners than the ones already on stage.
Medium: Sculpted, Brush strokes, Watercolor, Pastel, Ink sketch and Splash. The painterly media are unlit on purpose, carry procedural stroke textures with a dried rim on the washes and tooth under the chalk, stand on their own paper tone and breathe with a still paper weave.
Palette: Curated palettes, your Brand Kits, custom colors - or their choice: the society generates palettes of its own from a harmony engine, colors nobody curated and nobody will see twice.
Temperament: Order to chaos, Energy, Density and Tempo. With the checkmark on, the society sets the dials itself at every Start and keeps re-tuning them as it paints; moving any slider takes that dial into your hand.
Ground and Look: The piece stands on a style ground, black void, paper, deep mist - or on its own darkest or lightest color. Bloom, depth blur, grain and vignette are dials, not fates.

sections.title: Moments and exports
sections.text:
The stop is the artistic act - and no moment is ever lost.
Because nothing here can be repeated, the moments keep themselves: a snapshot ring quietly holds the last minutes while it paints. Pause opens the moment picker - the snapshots plus the live end - and the chosen moment is what you keep.
Pick the moment: A strip of snapshots from the last minutes, newest at the end, with a live tile showing the current state. Click the moment you loved; resume painting any time - the stop is a pause plus a choice, not an ending.
Insert as picture / Update: Lands the chosen moment in your document's own proportions, covering the page like a print, as a re-editable layer named with the piece's own title. Editing reopens the studio with the settings; the painting itself will be new - chaos cannot repeat.
Process film: A WebM of the painting as it happened, from start to stop, recorded automatically while it paints. Download it or send it to the Media Library; the file carries the piece's title.
Embed (HTML): Copy snippet puts the living society on your own website: every page load charges its own entropy, so every visitor sees an original that has never existed before, in every dimension you left to their choice. A finished piece rests, then a new one begins - a gallery that repaints itself. The page keeps its scroll wheel until the visitor takes hold, and reduced motion is honored with a finished still.
No seed: There is no seed field anywhere, on purpose. A missed moment is gone and a kept one is yours alone - that is the point of the exercise.
